For a vertex \(x=[L]\), put \[ \begin{aligned} U_x&=1+\varpi_F^m\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O_D}(L),\\ e_x&=\frac{1_{U_x}}{\operatorname{vol}(U_x)},\\ U_\sigma&=\prod_{y\in\sigma^0}U_y,\qquad e_\sigma=\prod_{y\in\sigma^0}e_y. \end{aligned} \tag{6.115} \] Endomorphisms here are \(D\)-linear endomorphisms preserving \(L\). These definitions are independent of homothety and equivariant under \(G\). The vertex groups in a simplex mutually normalize, their product is a compact open subgroup, and \(e_\sigma\) is its probability average. In particular \(e_\sigma V=\bigcap_{y\in\sigma^0}V^{U_y}\). If \(z\) is adjacent to every vertex of \(\tau\) and \(z\in H(x,\tau)\), then \[ \begin{aligned} e_z e_\tau e_x&=e_\tau e_x,\\ e_x e_\tau e_z&=e_x e_\tau,\\ \tau\preceq\sigma\subset H(x,\tau) &\ \Longrightarrow\ e_xe_\sigma=e_xe_\tau. \end{aligned} \tag{6.116} \] The reverse-order version of the last identity holds as well.

Proof. A \(D\)-linear map preserves \(L\Pi^a\) exactly when it preserves \(L\), which proves homothety independence; geometric series prove that the displayed sets are groups. At adjacent vertices, normalize one lattice to \(\mathcal O_D^r\) and the other to exponents in \(\{0,1\}\). Since \(dm\ge1\), each congruence group fixes the other lattice. Each therefore normalizes the other's endomorphism order and congruence group. The product of mutually normalizing compact subgroups is a compact subgroup. The convolution of their probability measures is its invariant probability measure, in either order: invariance under each generating subgroup proves this assertion. The range is their common fixed space.

For the face assertion choose a common apartment and normalize \(x\) to zero. If \(a^y\) are the coordinates of the vertices of \(\tau\), and \(b\) those of \(z\), (6.113) implies \(b_i-b_j\ge\min(0,\min_{y\in\tau^0}(a_i^y-a_j^y))\). Gaussian elimination after conjugating the standard congruence group shows that \(U_z\) is generated by diagonal units \(1+\varpi_F^m\mathcal O_D\) and root transvections with entry valuation at least \(dm+b_i-b_j\). To see that there is no generation assumption here, eliminate a near-identity matrix in the standard order using its unit diagonal pivots. The remaining diagonal matrix still has diagonal entries congruent to one modulo \(\varpi_F^m\); conjugate the resulting finite factorization back.

Every root generator so obtained lies either in \(U_x\cap U_z\) or in \(U_y\cap U_z\) for some vertex \(y\) of \(\tau\). Diagonal generators lie in all these groups. Since \(U_z\) normalizes \(U_\tau\), so does \(U_x\cap U_z\). Reordering the finite generator word therefore writes each element of \(U_z\) as \(u_\tau u_x\), with \(u_\tau\in U_\tau\), \(u_x\in U_x\cap U_z\). It fixes \(e_\tau e_xv\): commute \(u_x\) past the \(U_\tau\)-average and use \(u_xe_x=e_x\). Averaging over \(U_z\) proves the first identity. Inversion of group measures reverses convolution and fixes every subgroup probability measure; since \(e_z\) commutes with \(e_\tau\), it proves the second. Apply that second identity successively to the vertices of \(\sigma\) to obtain the final assertion. All multiplication and elimination arguments are valid over noncommutative \(D\). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.49 — face intervals towards a vertex. For a fixed vertex \(x\) and any simplex \(\sigma\), there is a unique smallest nonempty face \(m_x(\sigma)\) such that \(\sigma\subset H(x,m_x(\sigma))\). For a finite convex subcomplex \(\Sigma\) containing \(x\), every nonempty fibre of \(m_x\) is an interval of faces \([\tau,\omega]\). Its alternating sum is zero unless \(\tau=\omega=x\), when it is one.

Proof. Handle \(\sigma=\{x\}\) first: its minimal nonempty face is itself. Otherwise choose an apartment for \(x,\sigma\). Choose a chamber \(\Delta\) containing \(\sigma\) whose local cone at an interior point of \(\sigma\) contains the direction towards \(x\). This is possible by taking the simplex traversed by a sufficiently short initial segment in that direction and extending it to a chamber. Write its affine simple roots as \(a_0,\ldots,a_{r-1}\), normalized by \(\sum a_j=1\). In type \(A\), they can be written, after ordering coordinates, as successive coordinate differences and \(1-a_1-\cdots-a_{r-1}\). They are integer-valued at vertices. The chamber choice gives \(a_j(x)\ge0\) whenever \(a_j\) vanishes on \(\sigma\). Set \[ I=\{j:a_j|_\sigma=0\text{ or }a_j(x)>0\}, \qquad \tau=\Delta\cap\bigcap_{j\in I}\{a_j=0\}. \tag{6.117} \] This is a nonempty face of \(\sigma\). Indeed \(I\) cannot contain every index. If \(\sigma\) has positive dimension, at least two of its simple coordinates are nonzero, and positivity of both integer values at \(x\) would contradict \(\sum a_j(x)=1\); the other values in \(I\) are nonnegative. If \(\sigma\) is a vertex, the same sum would force \(x=\sigma\), the case already handled.

If a face \(\eta\) of \(\sigma\) fails to contain \(\tau\), some \(j\notin I\) vanishes on \(\eta\). Then \(a_j(x)\le0\) while \(a_j\) is positive in the interior of \(\sigma\); its wall excludes \(\sigma\) from \(H(x,\eta)\). Conversely, consider any affine root \(\beta\) nonnegative on \(x\) and \(\tau\). A root has constant sign in the interior of a simplex. Thus it is nonnegative on \(\sigma\) unless it vanishes on \(\tau\) but not on \(\sigma\). Write \(\beta=\sum\lambda_j a_j\) with coefficients all nonnegative or all nonpositive. This elementary type-\(A\) root description follows by writing a coordinate difference as a consecutive sum of simple roots, adding full cycles for its integer constant, or taking the negative of such an expression. Vanishing on \(\tau\) forces \(\lambda_j=0\) for \(j\notin I\). Some nonzero coefficient has \(a_j|_\sigma\ne0\), hence \(a_j(x)>0\); every other \(a_j(x)\) in \(I\) is nonnegative. The inequality \(\beta(x)\ge0\) therefore rules out all coefficients being nonpositive. Hence \(\beta\ge0\) on \(\sigma\). Formula (6.113), equivalently the affine-root half-apartment description, proves \(\sigma\subset H(x,\tau)\). This proves the claimed minimality and uniqueness.

Next, the cofaces of any \(\tau\) contained in \(H(x,\tau)\) have a unique largest member \(\omega\). They all lie in one common apartment. If two did not span a simplex, an affine wall through \(\tau\) would place their interiors on opposite sides: in the coordinate-wall subdivision, compatible wall signs are exactly faces of one chamber. The enclosure lies on the side containing \(x\), or in the wall if \(x\) lies there, giving a contradiction. Their union consequently spans a simplex; there are finitely many cofaces at \(\tau\), so their total span is \(\omega\).

If \(m_x(\tau)=\tau\ne x\), this maximum strictly contains \(\tau\). Follow the segment from \(x\) to an interior point of \(\tau\). If its final short part is outside \(\tau\), its carrier is already a larger coface in \(H(x,\tau)\). If its final part is in \(\tau\), prolong it to a proper boundary face \(\eta\). The enclosure \(H(x,\eta)\) contains the segment and hence an interior point of \(\tau\); being a subcomplex, it contains all of \(\tau\), contrary to minimality. Convexity puts \(\omega\) in \(\Sigma\). Minimality is idempotent, and gives \[ \begin{aligned} \{\sigma\in\Sigma:m_x(\sigma)=\tau\}&=[\tau,\omega],\\ \sum_{\tau\preceq\sigma\preceq\omega}(-1)^{\dim\sigma} &=(-1)^{\dim\tau}(1-1)^{|\omega^0\setminus\tau^0|}. \end{aligned} \tag{6.118} \] The only singleton interval is \(\tau=\omega=x\); here its sum is one. This also proves the assertion in rank one directly. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.50 — the finite support projection. For every smooth \(V\) and finite convex \(\Sigma\), the finite operator \[ u_\Sigma=\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}(-1)^{\dim\sigma}e_\sigma \tag{6.119} \] is an idempotent with \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{im}u_\Sigma&=\sum_{x\in\Sigma^0}V^{U_x},\\ \ker u_\Sigma&=\bigcap_{x\in\Sigma^0}\ker e_x,\\ e_xu_\Sigma&=u_\Sigma e_x=e_x\quad(x\in\Sigma^0). \end{aligned} \tag{6.120} \] It has finite rank when \(V\) is admissible, and \(\pi(g)u_\Sigma\pi(g)^{-1}=u_{g\Sigma}\). If \(\Sigma_+,\Sigma_-\), their union \(\Sigma\), and their intersection \(\Sigma_0\) are finite convex subcomplexes, then, with the zero operator for an empty intersection, \[ \begin{aligned} u_{\Sigma_+}u_{\Sigma_-}&=u_{\Sigma_-}u_{\Sigma_+}=u_{\Sigma_0},\\ \operatorname{im}u_{\Sigma_+}\cap\operatorname{im}u_{\Sigma_-} &=\operatorname{im}u_{\Sigma_0}. \end{aligned} \tag{6.121} \]

Proof. Fix \(x\in\Sigma^0\) and group the terms of \(e_xu_\Sigma\) by \(\tau=m_x(\sigma)\). Lemma 6.48 gives \(e_xe_\sigma=e_xe_\tau\) throughout a fibre. Lemma 6.49 cancels every fibre except the vertex \(x\), whose contribution is \(e_x\). Reverse all convolution products to obtain \(u_\Sigma e_x=e_x\). Since each \(e_\sigma\) is a product of vertex idempotents, \(u_\Sigma^2=u_\Sigma\) follows term by term. Its image is contained in the indicated sum and it is the identity on that sum. Every vector in the indicated intersection of kernels is killed term by term, while \(u_\Sigma v=0\) implies \(e_xv=e_xu_\Sigma v=0\). This proves (6.120). Admissibility makes the finite sum of fixed spaces finite-dimensional; equivariance follows from (6.115).

For a nested pair, the image and kernel descriptions give \(u_0u_+=u_+u_0=u_0\), and likewise for the minus sign. Inclusion and exclusion of cells gives \(u_\Sigma=u_++u_--u_0\). Put \(P=u_+-u_0\), \(Q=u_--u_0\). These are idempotents and \(P+Q=u_\Sigma-u_0\) is idempotent. Hence \(PQ+QP=0\). Multiplication by \(P\) on both sides gives \(2PQP=0\); multiplication on just the left or right then gives \(PQ=QP=0\). Our coefficients are complex, so division by two is legitimate even when \(F\) has characteristic two. Expanding proves (6.121). \(\square\)

Proposition 6.51 — cofinal finite convex subcomplexes. Let \(L\) represent a base vertex and put \(K_l=1+\varpi_F^l\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O_D}(L)\), \(l\ge1\). The full subcomplex \(\Sigma_l\) on its fixed vertices is finite and convex, and these subcomplexes exhaust the building. In an apartment obtained by elementary divisors relative to \(L\), its fixed vertices satisfy exactly \[ \max_i a_i-\min_i a_i\le dl. \tag{6.122} \] There is also such an exhaustion invariant under the stabilizer of any fixed simplex. If \(V\) is irreducible smooth and \(V^{U_x}\ne0\) for one vertex at the chosen \(m\), then \(u_{\Sigma_l}v=v\) for all sufficiently large \(l\), for each \(v\in V\).

Proof. The group \(K_l\) is normal in the integral base stabilizer, so elementary divisors reduce the fixed-vertex question to diagonal lattices. Its root entries have valuation at least \(dl\); preservation of \(L(a)\) is equivalent to \(dl\ge a_i-a_j\) for every pair. Fixing the class is the same as preserving the actual lattice here, since \(|\operatorname{Nrd}(k)|=1\) for \(k\in K_l\): a nonzero homothety shift changes lattice covolume. This proves (6.122). Normalize \(\min a_i=0\). Only finitely many exponent tuples remain; each has finite orbit under the compact integral stabilizer, because its stabilizer is open. Thus there are finitely many vertices and, by local finiteness, finitely many simplices. Every element of \(K_l\) preserving the vertices of \(x,\tau\) fixes their enclosure by Lemma 6.47; hence the fixed subcomplex is convex. Every finite set of lattices is preserved by all sufficiently small \(K_l\), proving exhaustion.

For a simplex \(\eta\), use the order \(A_\eta=\bigcap_{y\in\eta^0}\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O_D}(L_y)\). Its full stabilizer permutes these orders, including when it permutes the vertices, so normalizes \(1+\varpi_F^l A_\eta\). These groups contain sufficiently small base congruence groups and have reduced norm of absolute value one. The same argument proves finiteness, convexity, exhaustion and stabilizer invariance. Finally all vertices are \(G\)-conjugate; the sum of all \(V^{U_y}\) is a nonzero invariant subspace and thus equals \(V\). Every vector is a finite sum from these fixed spaces. A sufficiently large \(\Sigma_l\) contains those vertices, and (6.120) fixes that vector. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.52 — finite elliptic fixed simplices. Every element with compact cyclic closure modulo \(Z\) stabilizes a simplex. On a compact subset \(B\) of the elliptic regular set there are only finitely many simplices stabilized by any element of \(B\). For an admissible smooth \(V\), the finite expression \[ L_{V,m}(g)=\sum_{g\sigma=\sigma}(-1)^{\dim\sigma} \operatorname{sgn}(g|\sigma^0) \operatorname{tr}(\pi(g)|V^{U_\sigma}) \tag{6.123} \] is locally constant on the elliptic regular set. The permutation sign is essential even if a stabilized simplex has no fixed vertex.

Proof: existence of a stabilized simplex. Lemma 6.39 supplies a common slope \(\nu\), an integer \(e\) with \(e\nu=a\in\mathbb Z\), and a lattice \(L\) preserved by \(u=\varpi_F^{-a}g^e\). Let \(\alpha_L\) be the minimum coordinate valuation in a lattice basis and define \[ \begin{aligned} \alpha(v)&=\min_{0\le j<e} \bigl(\alpha_L(g^jv)-jd\nu\bigr),\\ \Lambda_t&=\{v:\alpha(v)\ge t\}. \end{aligned} \tag{6.124} \] Both \(u\) and its inverse preserve every \(L\Pi^n\). Shifting the index in the minimum, and using \(\alpha_L(g^ev)=\alpha_L(v)+ed\nu\), gives \(\alpha(gv)=\alpha(v)+d\nu\). Also \(\alpha(vb)=\alpha(v)+v_D(b)\) and \(\alpha(v+w)\ge\min(\alpha(v),\alpha(w))\). Each \(\Lambda_t\) is a finite intersection of full lattices and is therefore a full lattice; \(\Lambda_{t+1}=\Lambda_t\Pi\). The finitely many jumps in a period give a periodic lattice chain, with at most \(r\) strict steps since its residue flags lie in an \(r\)-dimensional space. Translation of \(t\) by \(d\nu\) permutes its lattice classes. Their simplex is stabilized by \(g\).

Proof: uniform finiteness. A vertex stabilizer is compact modulo \(Z\): an element takes \(L\) to \(L\Pi^k\); there are only \(d\) possible shifts modulo central \(\varpi_F\), and each shift is a coset of the compact actual-lattice stabilizer. A simplex stabilizer \(C_\eta\) has a finite permutation action on its vertices, with kernel in a vertex stabilizer. It too is compact modulo \(Z\), and it is open. Choose representatives \(\eta\) for the finitely many simplex types. If \(x\in B\) stabilizes \(h\eta\), then \(h^{-1}xh\in C_\eta\). The absolute reduced norms of \(B\) stay in a compact annulus. The part of \(C_\eta\) in this annulus is an actual compact set: take compact representatives modulo \(Z\) and bound the central valuation using \(|\operatorname{Nrd}(z)|=|z|^{rd}\). Lemma 6.18, specifically its uniform elliptic assertion (6.39), now puts all such \(hZ\) in a compact subset of \(G/Z\). Its image in the discrete space \(G/C_\eta\) is finite. There are therefore only finitely many possible \(h\eta\), uniformly for \(x\in B\).

Proof: local constancy. Around an elliptic regular \(g\), choose a compact open neighbourhood \(B\) contained in that set; its openness was proved in the local charts of Theorem 6.7. Let \(S\) be the finite set of simplices just obtained. Choose an open subgroup \(H\) fixing all their vertices. For \(h\in H\) with \(gh\in B\), a simplex is stabilized by \(gh\) exactly when it is stabilized by \(g\), and its vertex permutation is the same. Shrink \(H\) further to fix a basis of each of the finitely many spaces \(V^{U_\sigma}\), \(\sigma\in S\). This is possible by smoothness and admissibility. The restrictions of \(\pi(gh)\) and \(\pi(g)\) on every stabilized fixed space then agree. All terms in (6.123) are constant on this neighbourhood. \(\square\)

Example 6.53 — an enclosure and a face that cannot be replaced by a vertex. In a rank-three apartment the enclosure of \((0,0,0)\) and \((3,1,0)\) has vertices \[ \begin{gathered} (0,0,0),\ (1,0,0),\ (2,0,0),\\ (1,1,0),\ (2,1,0),\ (3,1,0). \end{gathered} \tag{6.125} \] These are exactly the solutions of \(0\le b_1\le3\), \(0\le b_2\le1\), \(0\le b_1-b_2\le2\), with \(b_3=0\). The support projection is the sum of their six vertex averages minus the edge averages plus the triangle averages, with edges determined by spread at most one. The cancellation in Lemma 6.49 computes the projector without requiring distant vertex averages to commute.

For rank four put \(x=(0,0,0,0)\), \(y=(4,2,2,0)\), and \[ \begin{gathered} z_1=(4,2,1,0),\quad z_2=(4,3,2,0),\\ y\in H(x,[z_1,z_2]),\\ y\notin H(x,z_1)\cup H(x,z_2). \end{gathered} \tag{6.126} \] The two \(z\)'s are adjacent because their difference has spread one. Checking the six coordinate differences in (6.113) puts \(y\) in the face enclosure. But \(y_3-y_4=2\) exceeds the bound one from \(x,z_1\), while \(y_1-y_2=2\) exceeds the bound one from \(x,z_2\). Thus a face enclosure cannot in general be reduced to one of its vertex enclosures. Lemma 6.48 proves precisely the face identity needed in (6.119).

Theorem 6.50 describes the image and kernel of the support operator. The global cellular exactness is Theorem 6.56, and the finite convex assertion at \(dm\ge2\) is Theorem 6.63. The finite trace formula and Theorem 6.65 identify (6.123) with the actual character on the elliptic regular set; Theorems 6.69–6.70 supply stabilized finite traces and the character on the entire regular semisimple set. The freely available Meyer–Solleveld paper, §§2.3–2.5 and Proposition 4.1, treats support projections and character traces separately. The lattice enclosure, face consistency, support projection, exhaustion and elliptic finiteness used in this subsection have been proved above.

6.12. Global cellular resolutions and Euler–Poincaré tests

Keep the groups \(U_x,U_\sigma\) of (6.115), at one fixed depth \(m\ge1\), and denote the lattice building by \(\mathcal B\). Orient its simplices. For a smooth complex representation \(V\), put \[ \begin{aligned} C_q(\mathcal B,V)&=\bigoplus_{\dim\sigma=q} \mathbb C[\sigma]\otimes V^{U_\sigma},\\ \partial([\sigma]\otimes v)&= \sum_{\eta\prec\sigma}[\sigma:\eta][\eta]\otimes v. \end{aligned} \tag{6.127} \] The sum in the boundary is over codimension-one faces, with their incidence signs. Opposite orientations negate \([\sigma]\). Face inclusions of the fixed spaces make this well defined. Cancellation of the two orders of deleting vertices proves \(\partial^2=0\). The augmentation in degree zero sends \([x]\otimes v\) to \(v\). We prove global exactness and construct actual trace tests. We do not assume a regular-character theorem in doing so.

Lemma 6.54 — a scalar contraction with enclosure support. Fix a vertex \(o\) and let \(K_0\) be its compact actual-lattice stabilizer. The augmented scalar complex \(C_*(\mathcal B,\mathbb C)\to\mathbb C\) has a \(K_0\)-equivariant contraction \(h\) such that \(h_{-1}(1)=[o]\) and \[ \begin{gathered} \partial h+h\partial=1,\\ \operatorname{supp}h([\sigma])\subset H(o,\sigma). \end{gathered} \tag{6.128} \] Every individual image is a finite chain. No uniform bound on its size is asserted.

Proof: scalar exactness inside an apartment. A finite root-convex subcomplex \(P\) of an apartment has an exact augmented scalar complex. Here is a direct proof. If \(P\) is a simplex, prepend a fixed vertex to an oriented face not already containing it, with the sign given by that ordering, and send a face containing it to zero. The two boundary expansions give a contraction. Otherwise some affine root wall separates two points of \(P\) strictly. Indeed, if no wall did, the interior wall signs of all its cells would be compatible, placing them in one simplex; convexity and fullness would then make \(P\) a face. The two closed half-polytopes \(P_+,P_-\) and their intersection \(P_0\) are nonempty proper root-convex subcomplexes. Each has fewer cells. Degree by degree their augmented complexes have the exact sequence given by the maps \(c\mapsto(c,-c)\) and \((a,b)\mapsto a+b\).

For clarity, exactness passes across this sequence without a topological theorem. Lift a cycle in \(P\) to \(a+b\). The boundaries of \(a,b\) are opposite copies of a cycle in \(P_0\). Fill that cycle there, subtract its filling from \(a\) and add it to \(b\); the two resulting cycles fill in \(P_+,P_-\). The same argument in degree zero uses the augmentation on \(P_0\), which is onto. Their fillings add to a filling of the original cycle. Induction on the number of cells proves the assertion. These cuts take place only in the single apartment. By Lemma 6.47 they apply in particular to every finite enclosure \(H(o,\sigma)\).

Proof: equivariant construction. Suppose \(h\) has been defined in lower degrees, beginning with \(h_{-1}\). For an oriented \(q\)-simplex \(\sigma\), the finite chain \([\sigma]-h\partial[\sigma]\) is a cycle in \(H(o,\sigma)\): the induction identity proves that its boundary is zero, and every face enclosure is contained in that enclosure. Fill it there by the preceding paragraph. Average a filling over the compact stabilizer of the underlying simplex in \(K_0\), multiplying by its orientation character in this average. That stabilizer preserves the finite enclosure, so the average is a finite linear combination and its boundary is still the required cycle. The averaged filling has exactly the orientation equivariance needed to extend it to the \(K_0\)-orbit of \(\sigma\). Choose one representative per orbit and continue in degree. This constructs (6.128). It also constructs a map on constant chains with coefficients in any complex vector space by tensoring with the identity. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.55 — the invariant-chain contraction. Put \(K=U_o\). The contraction of Lemma 6.54, tensored with the identity of \(V\), preserves \[ C_*(\mathcal B,V)^K\longrightarrow V^K \tag{6.129} \] and contracts this augmented complex, naturally in every smooth \(V\).

Proof: the matrix factorization needed for averaging. For simplices \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\subset H(o,\sigma)\), let \(K_\tau\) be the subgroup of \(K\) fixing the vertices of \(\tau\). We claim \[ U_\tau\subset K_\tau U_\sigma. \tag{6.130} \] Choose a common apartment with \(o=\mathcal O_D^r\). Order its coordinates so that \(a_1^y\ge\cdots\ge a_r^y\) at every vertex \(y\) of \(\sigma\). Such an ordering exists because a simplex does not cross a coordinate wall through \(o\). For a simplex \(\eta\), define \[ c_{ij}(\eta)=\min_{y\in\eta^0}(a_i^y-a_j^y), \qquad q_{ij}(\eta)=dm+c_{ij}(\eta)\quad(i\ne j). \tag{6.131} \] The group \(U_\eta\) has a Gaussian factorization, in the order upper triangular, diagonal, lower triangular, whose root entries have thresholds \(q_{ij}(\eta)\) and whose diagonal entries belong to \(1+\varpi_F^m\mathcal O_D\). We verify this also for a face, rather than only a vertex. A root difference on a simplex has integer vertex values differing by at most one. Equivalently, its minimum is the floor of its value at an interior point. Thus \(c_{ij}+c_{jk}\ge c_{ik}-1\) and \(c_{ij}+c_{ji}\ge-1\). Since \(dm\ge1\), elimination preserves all the off-diagonal thresholds, and every diagonal correction has valuation at least \(dm\). Conjugating one vertex lattice to the standard lattice makes all off-diagonal thresholds nonnegative; their zero-threshold positions are strictly triangular after ordering the residue flag. Matrices in question are therefore invertible, with unit pivots congruent to one modulo \(\varpi_F^m\). Elimination gives the stated factors and their inverses. Each root threshold is attained at a vertex of \(\eta\), so each such root factor belongs to one of the vertex groups. Conversely every vertex group satisfies these thresholds. This proves that the factored group is exactly their product \(U_\eta\).

By (6.113), the coordinates of \(\tau\) have the same weak ordering. Its upper root factors have entry valuation at least \(dm\), so belong to \(K\). They preserve every lattice in \(\tau\), since \(dm+c_{ij}(\tau)\ge\max_{y\in\tau^0}(a_i^y-a_j^y)\). Thus the entire upper factor belongs to \(K_\tau\). For a lower root, (6.113) gives \(c_{ij}(\tau)\ge c_{ij}(\sigma)\), because the latter is nonpositive. Consequently the lower factor belongs to \(U_\sigma\), as does the diagonal factor. This proves (6.130), including over noncommutative \(D\).

Proof: coefficients after averaging. The group \(K_\tau\) normalizes \(U_\tau\). If \(v\in V^{U_\sigma}\), (6.130) gives \[ \begin{aligned} e_{K_\tau}\pi(u)v&=e_{K_\tau}v\quad(u\in U_\tau),\\ e_{K_\tau}v&=e_{K_\tau}e_\tau v\\ &=e_\tau e_{K_\tau}v\in V^{U_\tau}. \end{aligned} \tag{6.132} \] Here every \(e_H\) is the invariant probability average, so there is no index or volume factor missing in this identity.

Every invariant chain is a sum of vectors \(e_K([\sigma]\otimes v)\). Apply the scalar \(h\) to this expression. Its \(K\)-equivariance writes the result as the \(K\)-average of finitely many terms \([\tau]\otimes v\), with \(\tau\subset H(o,\sigma)\). At an image cell \(k\tau\), the coefficient of such a term is the appropriate orbit-mass scalar times \(\pi(k)e_{K_\tau}v\), with its orientation sign. Formula (6.132) puts this coefficient in \(V^{U_{k\tau}}\).

One may use the vertex-fixing stabilizer in this orbit computation. Indeed \(K\) preserves the type given by lattice covolume modulo \(r\); the vertices of a simplex have distinct types. Thus a member of \(K\) stabilizing the simplex fixes all its vertices and its orientation. All orbit averages are finite, since a compact group has finite orbit on a discrete cell set. This proves preservation of (6.129). Identity (6.128) now proves contraction there, and \(h_{-1}v=[o]\otimes v\) is allowed because \(V^K=V^{U_o}\). The construction commutes with equivariant maps of \(V\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.56 — exactness on the whole division-lattice building. Define \[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_m(V)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal B^0}V^{U_x},\\ 0\longrightarrow C_{r-1}(\mathcal B,V)\longrightarrow\cdots \longrightarrow C_0(\mathcal B,V)\longrightarrow\Phi_m(V) \longrightarrow0. \end{gathered} \tag{6.133} \] The functor \(\Phi_m\) on smooth representations is exact, and the displayed augmented complex is exact. In particular it resolves every \(V\) generated by \(V^{U_o}\). Every finitely generated smooth representation has this property for sufficiently large \(m\).

Proof: the exact functor. For an invariant subspace \(W\subset V\), \[ \Phi_m(W)=W\cap\Phi_m(V). \tag{6.134} \] Only the reverse inclusion needs proof. Express a vector in the right side as a finite sum from vertex fixed spaces. Proposition 6.51 supplies a finite convex \(\Sigma\) containing those vertices. Theorem 6.50 gives \(u_\Sigma v=v\). Since \(u_\Sigma\) is a finite expression in group averages, it preserves \(W\) and puts this vector in \(\sum_{x\in\Sigma^0}e_xW\). This proves (6.134). Compact averaging also makes \(V^{U_x}\to(V/W)^{U_x}\) onto: average any lift. Therefore \(\Phi_m\) is exact. The representations equal to their \(\Phi_m\) are closed under subobjects, quotients and extensions; the extension assertion follows immediately by lifting the quotient's generated vectors and applying (6.134) to the kernel.

Proof: invariant homology detects all homology. The complex (6.133) is a smooth \(G\)-complex. Each elementary tensor in a cell summand is fixed by \(U_x\) for any vertex of that cell: this group fixes the cell pointwise as well as its coefficient. All vertices are \(G\)-conjugate, so every chain module is generated by its \(K=U_o\)-fixed vectors. Hence its homology, a subquotient, also equals its \(\Phi_m\), by the preceding paragraph. Taking \(K\)-fixed vectors is exact by compact averaging, and commutes with homology: average a primitive of an invariant boundary to make it invariant. Lemma 6.55 shows that the invariant augmented complex is contractible. All augmented homology groups therefore have zero \(K\)-fixed space. A representation generated by such a space is zero. This proves exactness in every degree, including the kernel of augmentation. Finally finitely many smooth generators are fixed by one sufficiently small base congruence group \(U_o\); their \(G\)-span is then generated by \(V^{U_o}\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.56 concerns the full building. Its proof does not assert exactness for an arbitrary finite convex subcomplex: such a subcomplex need not be preserved by the vertex averages used to detect homology. The scalar assertion inside an apartment in Lemma 6.54 and the global coefficient assertion have different proofs. The finite convex assertion at \(dm\ge2\), used for the trace application, is Theorem 6.63.

Theorem 6.57 — projectivity with a fixed central character. Let \(V\) be smooth admissible with smooth central character \(\omega\), and choose \(m\) such that \(V=\Phi_m(V)\). For a simplex \(\sigma\), write \(C_\sigma=\{g:g\sigma=\sigma\}\), let \(\epsilon_\sigma\) be its vertex-permutation sign, and put \(\rho_\sigma=\epsilon_\sigma\otimes V^{U_\sigma}\). In the category of smooth representations with central character \(\omega\), (6.133) is a projective resolution with \[ C_q(\mathcal B,V)=\bigoplus_{[\sigma],\,\dim\sigma=q} \operatorname{c\!-!Ind}_{C_\sigma}^{G}\rho_\sigma. \tag{6.135} \] There are finitely many summands. For any smooth admissible \(W\) with that central character, all \(\operatorname{Ext}^q_{G,\omega}(V,W)\) are finite-dimensional and vanish for \(q\ge r\).

Proof. The simplex stabilizer is open and compact modulo \(Z\) by Proposition 6.52. Its action on a cell summand is exactly \(\rho_\sigma\); the orientation factor records the action on \([\sigma]\). Decomposing finitely supported chains into their finitely many \(G\)-orbits proves (6.135). The fixed spaces are finite-dimensional by admissibility.

Every finite-dimensional smooth \(C_\sigma\)-representation \(\rho\) with character \(\omega\) is projective in the fixed-central-character category. Indeed, lift a linear map from \(\rho\) through a surjection, then average the lift by \(c\mapsto\pi(c)A\rho(c^{-1})\) over \(C_\sigma/Z\). Central scalars cancel. Smoothness of finitely many images makes this a finite locally constant average on that compact quotient. Its image is an equivariant lift, since normalized Haar averaging is invariant. This proves exactness of \(\operatorname{Hom}_{C_\sigma}(\rho,-)\). The compact-induction adjunction is explicit here: prescribe the image of the function supported on \(C_\sigma\), then translate it and add over the finite support in \(G/C_\sigma\). It gives \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(\operatorname{c\!-!Ind}_{C_\sigma}^G\rho,W)=\operatorname{Hom}_{C_\sigma}(\rho,W)\), so proves projectivity of each summand.

These Hom spaces are finite-dimensional for admissible \(W\). Choose an open normal subgroup of \(C_\sigma\) fixing \(\rho\) pointwise; its common fixed space in \(W\) is finite-dimensional. Such a subgroup exists by intersecting the stabilizers of a basis and then their finitely many conjugates modulo \(Z\). Taking it compact and sufficiently small does not affect this conclusion. The Hom space embeds into the maps from \(\rho\) to that fixed space. Apply \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(-,W)\) to the finite projective resolution. Its cohomology computes the stated Ext groups and proves both assertions. Independence of the resolution follows directly by lifting comparison maps degree by degree through the surjections onto cycles; lifting their differences in the same way gives a chain homotopy. This is also the usual projective-resolution definition of Ext. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.58 — an actual Euler–Poincaré trace test. Use compatible Haar measures on \(G\), \(Z\), and \(G/Z\). The function \[ f_{V,m}(g)=\sum_{[\sigma]}(-1)^{\dim\sigma} \frac{1_{C_\sigma}(g)}{\operatorname{vol}(C_\sigma/Z)} \operatorname{tr}\rho_\sigma(g^{-1}) \tag{6.136} \] is smooth, compactly supported modulo \(Z\), and satisfies \(f_{V,m}(zg)=\omega(z)^{-1}f_{V,m}(g)\). For every smooth admissible \(W\) of central character \(\omega\), its finite-rank integrated action satisfies \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{tr}\pi_W(f_{V,m}) &=\sum_q(-1)^q\dim\operatorname{Ext}_{G,\omega}^q(V,W),\\ \pi_W(f)&=\int_{G/Z}f(g)\pi_W(g)\,d\bar g. \end{aligned} \tag{6.137} \] No unitarity of \(\omega\) or complex conjugation of a character is needed in this formula.

Proof. Smoothness and central covariance follow term by term. A finite-dimensional smooth \(\rho_\sigma\) has an open kernel; its character on \(C_\sigma\) is invariant on both sides by a sufficiently small compact open subgroup. Intersect those groups over the finitely many summands. Thus the integrated operator has image in one admissible fixed space and finite rank. For one summand, choose a compact open normal subgroup \(J\) of \(C_\sigma\) acting trivially on \(\rho_\sigma\), as in Theorem 6.57, and work in the finite-dimensional \(C_\sigma\)-invariant space \(W^J\). On \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(\rho_\sigma,W^J)\) the normalized operator \(A\mapsto\int_{C_\sigma/Z}\pi_W(c)A\rho_\sigma(c^{-1})\,d\bar c/\operatorname{vol}(C_\sigma/Z)\) is the projection onto its equivariant maps. Its trace is their dimension. The trace of each integrand is \(\operatorname{tr}\pi_W(c)\operatorname{tr}\rho_\sigma(c^{-1})\) on that finite space; hence the corresponding summand of (6.136) has trace \(\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{C_\sigma}(\rho_\sigma,W)\). The same summand equals its composition with \(e_J\), so this finite-space trace is its trace on \(W\). The alternating sum is the Euler characteristic of the finite Hom complex in Theorem 6.57. For any finite complex this is the Euler characteristic of its cohomology: in each degree split off boundaries and a complement of cycles; the differential identifies the latter with the next boundaries, whose two contributions cancel. This proves (6.137). \(\square\)

Proposition 6.59 — elliptic orbital integrals of the trace test. For elliptic regular \(\gamma\), normalize \(T=G_\gamma\) as in Section 6.3, with \(\operatorname{vol}(T/Z)=1\). Then the absolutely convergent orbital integral is \[ O_\gamma(f_{V,m})=L_{V,m}(\gamma^{-1}). \tag{6.138} \] For every regular \(\gamma\) with noncompact cyclic closure modulo \(Z\), this orbital integral is zero. These are assertions about the test function, not an identification of \(L_{V,m}\) with the character of \(V\).

Proof. All conjugates of \(\gamma\) in the support of (6.136) have its fixed absolute reduced norm. The compact-annulus argument of Lemma 6.18 turns that part of the support into an actual compact target. Proper regular orbital coordinates from the same lemma prove absolute convergence. For a fixed simplex representative \(\sigma\), the contributing double cosets \(ThC_\sigma\) correspond precisely to \(T\)-orbits of simplices \(\kappa=h\sigma\) stabilized by \(\gamma\). This is a finite set by Proposition 6.52. On such a double coset the character factor is constant, by conjugacy invariance in \(C_\sigma\), and quotient Haar integration gives its contribution \[ \frac{(-1)^{\dim\kappa}\epsilon_\kappa(\gamma) \operatorname{tr}(\pi_V(\gamma^{-1})|V^{U_\kappa})} {\operatorname{vol}((T\cap C_\kappa)/Z)}. \tag{6.139} \] Indeed the volume of this double coset in \(T\backslash G\) is \(\operatorname{vol}(C_\sigma/Z)/\operatorname{vol}((T\cap C_\kappa)/Z)\), which cancels the denominator in (6.136). The reciprocal remaining volume is exactly the size of the \(T\)-orbit of \(\kappa\), since \(T/Z\) has volume one. Its finite orbit has the same trace and sign at every simplex. Summing (6.139) over orbits and simplex types gives (6.123), at \(\gamma^{-1}\); inversion leaves its permutation sign unchanged. Finally an element of any \(C_\sigma\) has compact cyclic closure modulo \(Z\). A noncompact-cyclic \(\gamma\) consequently has no conjugate in the support, proving zero there. \(\square\)

Example 6.60 — an edge stabilized without a fixed vertex. For \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\) with \(\operatorname{char}F\ne2\), take \[ \gamma=\begin{pmatrix}0&\varpi_F\\1&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \gamma^2=\varpi_F I. \tag{6.140} \] Its Eisenstein polynomial is separable, so it is elliptic regular. It exchanges the vertices represented by \(\mathcal O_F^2\) and \(\varpi_F\mathcal O_F\oplus\mathcal O_F\). Its type shift is odd, so it fixes no vertex. This edge is the only stabilized edge: two distinct fixed midpoints in a tree would force the intervening path, including a vertex, to be fixed. The path assertion follows by uniqueness of the simple path, already proved for the lattice tree in Section 2.3. For the trivial representation, (6.123) consequently gives \((-1)^1(-1)\cdot1=1\), and (6.138) gives \(O_\gamma(f_{1,m})=1\). Omitting the orientation sign would give the wrong value.

Section 6.13 proves the finite cellular trace formula and identifies the finite alternating trace with the actual elliptic character at \(dm\ge2\). Formula (6.138) consequently agrees there with \(\Theta_V(\gamma^{-1})\). Theorems 6.69–6.70 prove the regular-character theorem on compact nonelliptic classes and the entire regular semisimple set. Theorem 6.271 proves elliptic character orthogonality. Completeness and the full representation transfer require further arguments. The invariant-chain averaging can be compared with Opdam–Solleveld, Section 2, Theorem 2.2; the enclosure contraction, exact generated-subrepresentation functor and trace-test arguments used here have been supplied explicitly.

6.13. Finite convex resolutions and elliptic characters

Choose the level in (6.115) so that \(dm\ge2\). This can always be done while retaining generation of a finitely generated smooth representation. We prove the finite convex statement needed to turn the cellular trace into an actual character on the elliptic regular set, using local lattice intersections.

Lemma 6.61 — a lattice-height ordering. Fix a base lattice \(L_o\). Each vertex \(x\) has a unique representative \(L_x\) such that \[ \begin{gathered} L_o\subset L_x,\qquad L_o\Pi^{-1}\not\subset L_x,\\ L_x=\bigoplus_i e_i\Pi^{-a_i}\mathcal O_D,\\ a_i\ge0,\qquad\min_i a_i=0. \end{gathered} \tag{6.141} \] The basis in this formula is an \(L_o\)-basis. Define \(i(x)\) to be the decreasing rearrangement of the \(a_i\), with one terminal zero omitted, and order these tuples lexicographically. These coordinates are the negatives of the apartment exponents in (6.112), with homothety normalized as displayed. Distinct adjacent vertices have distinct heights. On any simplex, increasing height orders its canonical lattices into an increasing periodic chain.

Let \(\eta=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) be ordered by increasing height and let \(\Sigma\) be a convex subcomplex containing \(o\) and \(\eta\). The finite set \[ M_\eta=\{z\in\Sigma^0:\{z\}\cup\eta\text{ is a simplex}, \ i(z)<i(x_1)\} \tag{6.142} \] is stable under intersection of its canonical lattices: if \(z,z'\in M_\eta\), then \(L_z\cap L_{z'}\) represents another member of \(M_\eta\). Its lattice is comparable with each of \(L_z,L_{z'}\), so its vertex is adjacent to each distinct one.

Proof. Elementary divisors relative to \(L_o\) prove (6.141), uniqueness and the independence of the sorted tuple from the chosen basis. To compare adjacent \(x,y\), use Lemma 6.47 to put \(o\) and the edge in one apartment. Before normalizing, their coordinate difference can be taken in \(\{0,1\}^r\). Normalizing its minimum to zero either leaves a coordinatewise increase, or subtracts one from every entry and leaves a coordinatewise decrease. A strict coordinatewise increase strictly increases the sorted tuple, and a decrease strictly decreases it. Thus increasing height is exactly increasing inclusion of the canonical lattices for adjacent vertices. The same comparison at every pair of vertices of a simplex gives the increasing periodic chain.

In particular, every vertex \(z\) adjacent to \(x\) with smaller height satisfies \(L_o+L_x\Pi\subset L_z\subsetneq L_x\). In the displayed coordinates, the first lattice has exponents \(\max(a_i-1,0)\). It strictly contains \(L_x\Pi\), since normalization says \(L_o\not\subset L_x\Pi\).

For \(z,z'\in M_\eta\), it follows that \[ L_{x_k}\Pi\subsetneq L_o+L_{x_k}\Pi \subset L_z\cap L_{z'}\subsetneq L_{x_1}. \tag{6.143} \] The intersection still contains \(L_o\) and does not contain \(L_o\Pi^{-1}\), so is canonical. It represents a vertex incident to every vertex of \(\eta\), and to \(z,z'\), by the chain inequalities. Its height is at most \(i(z)\): put its incident pair with \(z\) and the base vertex in an apartment and apply the inclusion comparison just proved.

Finally the intersection vertex belongs to \(H(z,z')\). Diagonalize the two actual lattices simultaneously. Their intersection has the coordinatewise maximum of their ordinary lattice exponents. For any two vectors \(a,b\), the difference between two coordinates of \(\max(a,b)\) lies between the corresponding differences for \(a\) and \(b\): the upper bound follows from \(a_i\le a_j+C\), \(b_i\le b_j+C\), and the lower bound follows the same way. Formula (6.113) proves the enclosure assertion. Convexity puts this vertex in \(\Sigma\); (6.143) and its height put it in \(M_\eta\). Local finiteness makes \(M_\eta\) finite. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.62 — exact local relations. At \(dm\ge2\), vertex groups associated to two neighbours of the same vertex mutually normalize, so their averages commute. For \(\eta,M_\eta\) as in Lemma 6.61, the following sequence is exact at its middle term, with the usual boundary signs: \[ \begin{gathered} \bigoplus_{\substack{z,z'\in M_\eta\\\{z,z'\}\text{ an edge}}} V^{U_{\{z,z'\}\cup\eta}}\longrightarrow\\ \bigoplus_{z\in M_\eta}V^{U_{\{z\}\cup\eta}} \longrightarrow V^{U_\eta}. \end{gathered} \tag{6.144} \] This holds for every smooth complex \(V\).

Proof: normalization. Represent two neighbours \(x,y\) of \(t\) by lattices between \(L_t\Pi\) and \(L_t\). Then \(L_y\Pi\subset L_x\subset L_y\Pi^{-1}\), and conversely. If \(A\) preserves \(L_x\), the inclusion \(L_y\subset L_x\Pi^{-1}\) shows that \(\varpi_F^m A L_y\subset L_x\Pi^{dm-1}\subset L_y\Pi^{dm-2}\subset L_y\). Every element of \(U_x\), and its inverse, consequently preserves \(L_y\). It normalizes \(U_y\). The symmetric argument gives mutual normalization and the probability-average argument of Lemma 6.48 gives commutation. All vertices of \(M_\eta\) are neighbours of \(x_1\), so their averages commute with one another and with \(e_\eta\).

Proof: the relation complex. Work on \(W=V^{U_\eta}\). Decompose this vector space by the finitely many commuting projections \(e_z\), \(z\in M_\eta\): for a subset \(S\subset M_\eta\), take the image of the product of \(e_z\) for \(z\in S\) and \(1-e_z\) for \(z\notin S\). The products are mutually orthogonal and sum to one. On that image the local middle term is one copy of the image for each \(z\in S\), and the left term has a copy at each edge with both ends in \(S\).

If this image is nonzero and \(z,z'\in S\), their intersection vertex \(w\) from Lemma 6.61 belongs to \(S\). Indeed \(w\in H(z,z')\) and is adjacent to \(z\); (6.116) gives \(e_z e_w e_{z'}=e_z e_{z'}\). Commutativity makes \(e_w\) the identity on the simultaneous image in question. A nonempty \(S\) is therefore closed under finite intersections. Its smallest lattice, the intersection of all its lattices, represents a member of \(S\) adjacent to every other member. The graph on \(S\) is connected. Its edge differences generate precisely the tuples whose sum is zero: subtract along the edges from that smallest vertex to the other vertices. This proves exactness on each simultaneous image. If \(S\) is empty the middle term is zero. Adding the finitely many images proves (6.144). Orienting each \((z,\eta)\) with \(z\) first identifies its last map with this sum; the two relevant faces of \((z,z',\eta)\) give the edge differences. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.63 — finite convex exactness. Let \(dm\ge2\) and let \(\Sigma\) be finite convex. Then \(C_*(\Sigma,V)\) has zero homology in positive degrees for every smooth \(V\). If \(V\) is admissible, its augmentation gives an exact finite-dimensional complex \[ 0\longrightarrow C_{r-1}(\Sigma,V)\longrightarrow\cdots \longrightarrow C_0(\Sigma,V)\longrightarrow u_\Sigma V \longrightarrow0. \tag{6.145} \]

Proof: eliminating a positive-degree cycle. Choose \(o\in\Sigma\) and the height of Lemma 6.61. In every simplex, all heights are distinct. For a \(q\)-simplex \(\sigma\), \(q\ge1\), let \(\sigma^-\) be the face obtained by omitting its least-height vertex. Order the height tuples of these faces lexicographically, listing each face's vertices in increasing height. For a finite \(q\)-cycle \(c\), take a largest such face tuple occurring in its support, and fix a face \(\eta\) with that tuple.

The only nonzero components of \(c\) contributing to its boundary at \(\eta\) have the form \(\{z\}\cup\eta\) with \(z\in M_\eta\). Adding a vertex of height larger than the least vertex of \(\eta\) would produce a strictly larger tuple for \(\sigma^-\), whose component is zero by choice. Since \(c\) is a cycle, the remaining components satisfy the last relation of (6.144). Fill this relation by its first term, using \((q+1)\)-simplices \(\{z,z'\}\cup\eta\). They belong to \(\Sigma\), which is full. Subtract their boundary from \(c\). This kills all components with \(\sigma^-=\eta\). Every other affected face contains both \(z,z'\), and hence has strictly smaller tuple for its minus face. Thus it changes no other face at the current maximal tuple and introduces no larger one.

Process the finitely many faces at that tuple and continue downwards. Since \(\Sigma\) is finite, this terminates. The resulting cycle is zero, and the accumulated fillings express the original cycle as a boundary. This proves positive-degree vanishing without a dimension assumption on the fixed spaces.

Proof: the augmented assertion. For admissible \(V\), every chain space is finite-dimensional. Theorem 6.50 and its explicit idempotent give \[ \dim u_\Sigma V=\operatorname{tr}u_\Sigma =\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}(-1)^{\dim\sigma}\dim V^{U_\sigma}. \tag{6.146} \] Positive-degree vanishing identifies the right side with \(\dim H_0(\Sigma,V)\). Augmentation maps this last space onto \(\sum_{x\in\Sigma^0}V^{U_x}=u_\Sigma V\); boundaries augment to zero. The two finite dimensions agree, so this map is an isomorphism. This proves (6.145). An empty \(\Sigma\) gives the zero complex. For \(r=1\), the nonempty building has one vertex and the assertion is immediate. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.64 — the finite cellular trace formula. Let \(V\) be smooth admissible and generated by \(V^{U_o}\) at a level with \(dm\ge2\). Let \(C\) be the full stabilizer of a simplex. For every \(f\in C_c^\infty(C)\), there is a finite convex \(C\)-invariant \(\Sigma_0\) such that every finite convex \(C\)-invariant \(\Sigma\supset\Sigma_0\) satisfies \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{tr}\pi_V(f)&=\int_C f(g)L_\Sigma(g)\,dg,\\ L_\Sigma(g)&= \sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma,\ g\sigma=\sigma} (-1)^{\dim\sigma}\epsilon_\sigma(g) \operatorname{tr}(\pi_V(g)|V^{U_\sigma}). \end{aligned} \tag{6.147} \] Here \(f\) is compactly supported in the actual group, so no central-character hypothesis or quotient integral is needed.

Proof. The operator \(\pi_V(f)\) has finite rank by admissibility. Express a basis of its image as finite sums from vertex fixed spaces. The \(C\)-invariant finite convex exhaustion in Proposition 6.51 supplies \(\Sigma_0\) containing these vertices. The operator \(u_\Sigma\) is the identity on the image, and \(C\)-invariance makes \(u_\Sigma V\) stable under \(C\). Thus the trace on \(V\) equals the trace on this finite-dimensional invariant space; the operator induced on the quotient has zero image.

Apply (6.145) to \(\Sigma\). It is a finite exact complex of \(C\)-representations. Additivity of trace across invariant subspaces gives the trace of \(f\) on its augmentation as the alternating trace on its chain spaces. To verify that additivity directly, choose a basis of an invariant subspace and extend it; the resulting block triangular matrix has trace the sum of its two diagonal-block traces. Apply this to boundaries and cycles in the exact complex; the boundary contributions cancel in adjacent degrees.

In a chain space, \(g\) sends the summand at \(\sigma\) to the one at \(g\sigma\). Its diagonal block is zero unless the simplex is stabilized. For a stabilized simplex it is \(\epsilon_\sigma(g)\pi_V(g)\) on its coefficient space. There are finitely many summands. Integrating these finite-dimensional traces against \(f\) proves (6.147). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.65 — an actual elliptic character. Every finitely generated smooth admissible \(V\) has a locally constant character density on the elliptic regular set. For any generating level with \(dm\ge2\), it is \[ \begin{aligned} \Theta_V(\gamma)&=L_{V,m}(\gamma),\\ L_{V,m}(\gamma)&=\sum_{\gamma\sigma=\sigma}(-1)^{\dim\sigma} \epsilon_\sigma(\gamma) \operatorname{tr}(\pi_V(\gamma)|V^{U_\sigma}). \end{aligned} \tag{6.148} \] The sum is finite. Its value is independent of that generating level and is conjugacy invariant. If \(V\) has central character \(\omega\), then \(\Theta_V(z\gamma)=\omega(z)\Theta_V(\gamma)\).

Proof. A sufficiently deep level generates \(V\), by Theorem 6.56. An elliptic regular \(\gamma\) stabilizes a simplex by Proposition 6.52; its full stabilizer \(C\) is open. Choose a compact open neighbourhood \(B\) of \(\gamma\) contained in \(C\) and in the elliptic regular set. Proposition 6.52 supplies a common finite set \(S\) containing every simplex stabilized by any \(g\in B\).

For a test function supported in \(B\), enlarge the finite \(C\)-invariant convex subcomplex used in Proposition 6.64 to contain \(S\). This is possible using the same exhaustive subcomplexes of Proposition 6.51. The finite inner sum in (6.147) is then precisely the full finite sum \(L_{V,m}(g)\), for every \(g\) in the support. Hence \[ \operatorname{tr}\pi_V(f)=\int_B f(g)L_{V,m}(g)\,dg \qquad(f\in C_c^\infty(B)). \tag{6.149} \] Proposition 6.52 already proves local constancy of this function. Thus (6.149) proves, rather than assumes, that it is the character density on \(B\). The neighbourhoods cover the elliptic regular set. Two locally constant densities defining the same distribution agree pointwise: integrate their constant difference over a sufficiently small compact open neighbourhood. This proves independence of level. Conjugation carries the finite fixed-simplex set and its coefficient spaces bijectively to the corresponding set for the conjugate, preserving all traces and signs. A central element fixes every simplex, and acts on its coefficient by \(\omega(z)\), proving the last assertion. \(\square\)

Together with Proposition 6.59, the normalized Euler–Poincaré test therefore satisfies \[ O_\gamma(f_{V,m})=\Theta_V(\gamma^{-1}) \qquad(\gamma\text{ elliptic regular}), \tag{6.150} \] when \(V\) also has the central character required in (6.136). The torus measure remains \(\operatorname{vol}(G_\gamma/Z)=1\). This identifies an orbital function with the actual elliptic character. It asserts no completeness of these characters in the elliptic comparison space.

Example 6.66 — a cyclic chamber in every split rank. Let \(D=F\), let \(\operatorname{char}F\) not divide \(r\), and define \(\gamma e_i=e_{i+1}\) for \(i<r\), \(\gamma e_r=\varpi_F e_1\). Then \[ \begin{gathered} \gamma^r=\varpi_F I,\qquad \det\gamma=(-1)^{r-1}\varpi_F,\\ L_j=\varpi_F\mathcal O_F^{\,j}\oplus \mathcal O_F^{\,r-j}\quad(0\le j<r). \end{gathered} \tag{6.151} \] The polynomial \(T^r-\varpi_F\) is irreducible: every root has valuation \(1/r\), so a monic factor of degree \(s\) would have constant term of valuation \(s/r\); for \(0<s<r\) this is not an integer. Its derivative \(rT^{r-1}\) is nonzero at every root, so it is separable. Thus \(\gamma\) is elliptic regular. It cycles the displayed standard chamber. Its action adds one to vertex type modulo \(r\). Any stabilized simplex must consequently have all \(r\) types, so is a chamber, and its vertex permutation is an \(r\)-cycle. Every term's orientation and dimension factors multiply to \((-1)^{r-1}(-1)^{r-1}=1\).

Apply (6.148) to the trivial representation. Its character is directly the constant function one, so the formula says that the number of stabilized chambers is one. Thus the standard chamber is the unique one. For a smooth determinant character, choose a generating level which fixes that character on every \(U_x\); the same chamber contributes \(\chi((-1)^{r-1}\varpi_F)\), as the direct one-dimensional character calculation requires. When the field characteristic divides \(r\), the displayed polynomial is inseparable. Theorem 6.148 supplies the finite character formula on the whole \(D\)-irreducible open set, and Solution 7.15 computes the quartic case.

The lattice-height criterion has a related formulation in Grosse-Klönne, Sections 1 and 3 of the free author preprint. The bound \(dm\ge2\) is used in the common-neighbour normalization in Lemma 6.62. Section 6.14 proves the ordinary regular-character assertion on compact nonelliptic classes and on the entire regular semisimple set. Theorem 6.271 proves discrete-series elliptic orthogonality. Completeness and the full representation transfer require further arguments.

6.14. Regular characters and stable cellular traces

The fixed simplices of a compact nonelliptic element need not form a finite set. They can nevertheless be controlled by finitely many orbits under its regular centralizer. This supplies the regular-set character theorem from the finite trace formula. Throughout, coefficients are complex, and \(G_{\mathrm{reg}}\) means the regular semisimple set.

Lemma 6.67 — products and the finite trace formula. The finite resolution and trace argument of Section 6.13 also apply to \(H=\prod_{j=1}^sG_j\), \(G_j=\mathrm{GL}_{r_j}(D)\), using product subcomplexes \(\Sigma=\prod_j\Sigma_j\), product cell groups and a level with \(dm\ge2\). If \(V\) is smooth admissible, the total cellular complex resolves \[ u_\Sigma V=\Bigl(\prod_j u_{\Sigma_j}\Bigr)V, \qquad V_\sigma=V^{\prod_jU_{\sigma_j}}, \quad \dim\sigma=\sum_j\dim\sigma_j. \tag{6.152} \] The action of \(H\) does not permute the factors, so the orientation sign is the product of their orientation signs. If \(V\) is generated by its product-vertex fixed space, Proposition 6.64 holds for tests in \(C=\prod_jC_j\), with each \(C_j\) a simplex stabilizer and with sufficiently large finite convex \(C_j\)-invariant factors \(\Sigma_j\).

Proof. For two factors, form the double complex whose \((p,q)\)-term is the sum of \(V^{U_{\sigma_1}\times U_{\sigma_2}}\) over the corresponding cells, with the second differential multiplied by \((-1)^p\). For a fixed cell in the second factor, \(V^{U_{\sigma_2}}\) is admissible for the first: its compact-open fixed spaces are fixed spaces for compact-open product groups in \(H\). Theorem 6.63 therefore makes the first augmented direction exact, with image \(u_{\Sigma_1}V^{U_{\sigma_2}}\). The latter equals \((u_{\Sigma_1}V)^{U_{\sigma_2}}\), since operators from different factors commute.

The space \(u_{\Sigma_1}V\), as a representation of the second factor, is admissible. It is a finite sum of spaces fixed by first-factor vertex groups, and taking any second-factor compact-open invariants puts it in a finite sum of admissible product fixed spaces. Apply Theorem 6.63 in the second direction. These two exact augmented directions prove exactness of the total complex. Explicitly, project the total complex to the second complex with coefficient \(u_{\Sigma_1}V\). In its kernel each first augmented row is exact. A cycle in that kernel can be filled starting with its largest second degree: first-direction exactness removes that component, introducing components only in smaller second degree. This terminates, so the kernel is acyclic. The projected complex is exact in positive degrees with the stated augmentation. This proves the two-factor assertion; induction proves (6.152).

Admissibility makes every final product-cell space finite-dimensional. The operators \(u_{\Sigma_j}\) commute, and their product is the identity on every product-vertex fixed vector once its vertices occur in the chosen factors. Generation and a finite basis of the image of a test operator therefore give the same finite-image containment as in Proposition 6.64. The exact total complex is invariant under \(C\). Taking its finite alternating trace proves the product trace formula. A finitely generated smooth \(H\)-representation is generated at a sufficiently deep product level, by intersecting the stabilizers of finitely many generators. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.68 — uniform toral control of fixed cells. Let \(\gamma\in G_{\mathrm{reg}}\), \(E=F[\gamma]\) and \(T=E^\times\). There is a compact toral neighbourhood \(B_T\) of \(\gamma\), all of whose elements generate \(E\) and are regular, and a finite set of simplices \(S\) such that \[ \{\sigma:y\sigma=\sigma\text{ for some }y\in B_T\} \subset T S. \tag{6.153} \] For any chosen level \(m\), there is a compact open subgroup \(U\subset T\) such that \(\gamma U\subset B_T\), and, for every \(t\in U\), \[ \mathcal B^{\gamma t}_{\mathrm{cells}} =\mathcal B^\gamma_{\mathrm{cells}}, \qquad \pi(t)|V^{U_\sigma}=1 \quad(\gamma\sigma=\sigma). \tag{6.154} \] The permutations of the vertices also agree. This assertion about coefficient spaces holds for every smooth \(V\). The same conclusions hold for a finite product \(H\), with \(E=\prod_jF[\gamma_j]\) and \(T=\prod_jF[\gamma_j]^\times\); no distinct-spectrum condition between different factors is required.

Proof: finite centralizer orbits. Lemma 6.18 proves uniform properness of \(T\backslash G\to G\) as the toral element varies in a sufficiently small compact \(B_T\) whose elements generate the fixed algebra \(E\). Recall why its uniform assertion applies: the field-factor idempotents in \(E\) stay fixed, normalizing the corresponding rows by centralizer scalars bounds them, and every limit intertwiner is invertible on each simple block. The condition that the powers of the toral element span \(E\) is open, so this argument supplies the required neighbourhood without changing the centralizer.

Choose representatives \(\eta\) of the finitely many simplex types. If \(y\in B_T\) stabilizes \(h\eta\), then \(h^{-1}yh\in C_\eta\). Restricting \(C_\eta\) to the compact annulus of absolute reduced norms occurring in \(B_T\) gives an actual compact set, since \(C_\eta/Z\) is compact. Uniform properness puts every such \(Th\) in a common compact subset of \(T\backslash G\). Its image in the discrete space \(T\backslash G/C_\eta\) is finite. Thus the possible cells have finitely many \(T\)-orbits, proving (6.153). For a product use the component reduced norms and the component properness assertions; their compact sets have compact product.

Proof: a common small torus subgroup. Choose \(U\) small enough that \(\gamma U\subset B_T\) and \(U\subset\bigcap_{\sigma\in S}U_\sigma\). Such a subgroup exists because this is a finite intersection of open identity neighbourhoods in \(T\). Each \(t\in U\) fixes these simplices pointwise and is the identity on their coefficient spaces. Since \(T\) is abelian and \(U_{a\sigma}=aU_\sigma a^{-1}\), the same statements hold on every cell in \(TS\). Every cell stabilized by \(\gamma t\), and every one stabilized by \(\gamma\), lies in \(TS\). Hence \(\gamma t\) stabilizes a cell exactly when \(\gamma\) does, with the same vertex permutation; and their coefficient actions coincide there. This proves (6.154). All steps apply to product cells and product groups too. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.69 — compact-mod-centre regular characters. Let \(V\) be a finitely generated smooth admissible representation of \(G\), or of a finite product \(H\) as in Lemma 6.67. At every regular \(\gamma\) with compact cyclic closure modulo the group's own centre, its trace distribution has a locally constant density on a neighbourhood of \(\gamma\). Choose a generating level with \(dm\ge2\), a simplex stabilizer \(C\) containing \(\gamma\), and put \[ L_\Sigma(g)=\sum_{g\sigma=\sigma,\ \sigma\in\Sigma} (-1)^{\dim\sigma}\epsilon_\sigma(g) \operatorname{tr}(\pi(g)|V_\sigma). \tag{6.155} \] For sufficiently large finite convex \(C\)-invariant \(\Sigma\), this finite sum at \(\gamma\) is independent of \(\Sigma\) and equals that density at \(\gamma\). In a product, take the cofinal product subcomplexes of Lemma 6.67. No sum over all fixed cells is required.

Proof: constancy before stabilization. Proposition 6.52 supplies a simplex stabilized by \(\gamma\), factor by factor in a product. Take its full stabilizer \(C\), which is open, and the small subgroup \(U\subset T\) from Lemma 6.68. Since \(\gamma\)'s stabilized simplex belongs to \(TS\), this \(U\) fixes it; hence \(\gamma U\subset C\). For every finite \(C\)-invariant \(\Sigma\), (6.154) gives \(L_\Sigma(\gamma t)=L_\Sigma(\gamma)\) for \(t\in U\). Also \(L_\Sigma\) is invariant under conjugation by \(C\): conjugation permutes the finite cell summands and identifies their coefficient spaces and orientation signs.

There is an open neighbourhood \(W\subset C\) of \(\gamma\) such that every \(x\in W\) has the form \[ x=k^{-1}\gamma t k,\qquad k\in K\subset C, \quad t\in U, \tag{6.156} \] where \(K\) is compact open. To prove this chart, write \(A=E\oplus\mathfrak s\), with \(\mathfrak s=(1-\operatorname{Ad}(\gamma^{-1}))A\). After separable splitting, these are the diagonal and off-diagonal matrix spaces, so \(1-\operatorname{Ad}(\gamma^{-1})\) is invertible on \(\mathfrak s\). These statements descend as linear equations over \(F\). The derivative of \((X,Y)\mapsto(1+X)^{-1}\gamma(1+Y)(1+X)\), with \(X\in\mathfrak s\), \(Y\in E\), becomes \(Y+X-\gamma^{-1}X\gamma\) after left translation. It is invertible. The complete-ball contraction proof in Theorem 6.42 gives an open inverse chart. Shrink its domain so that \(1+X\in K\subset C\) and \(1+Y\in U\). For a product do this componentwise. Consequently every \(L_\Sigma\), before any size condition on \(\Sigma\), is constant on this one \(W\), of value \(L_\Sigma(\gamma)\).

Proof: stabilization from one test. Shrink \(W\) to a compact open neighbourhood and let \(f_0=1_W/\operatorname{vol}(W)\). The finite trace formula supplies \(\Sigma_0\) such that, for every invariant finite \(\Sigma\supset\Sigma_0\), \[ L_\Sigma(\gamma)=\int f_0(g)L_\Sigma(g)\,dg =\operatorname{tr}\pi(f_0)=:c. \tag{6.157} \] This is eventual equality, with no exchange of an infinite sum and an integral. For any \(f\in C_c^\infty(W)\), choose a larger invariant finite subcomplex that also accommodates its finite-rank image as in Proposition 6.64 or Lemma 6.67. Its trace formula and (6.157) give \[ \operatorname{tr}\pi(f)=c\int_W f(g)\,dg. \tag{6.158} \] This proves the actual locally constant density and the stabilized value. Uniqueness follows by testing the constant difference of two such densities on a small compact open neighbourhood. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.70 — the character on the entire regular set. Every finitely generated smooth admissible \(V\) of \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), in either field characteristic, has a unique locally constant trace density \(\Theta_V\) on \(G_{\mathrm{reg}}\). If \(P_\gamma=M_\gamma N_\gamma\) is the slope parabolic of Lemma 6.39, then \[ \Theta_V(\gamma)=\Theta_{V_{N_\gamma}}(\gamma) =\delta_{P_\gamma}(\gamma)^{1/2} \Theta_{\pi_{P_\gamma}}(\gamma). \tag{6.159} \] The middle term uses the unnormalized Jacquet action; the last one uses normalized action. Precisely, the density assertion means \[ \operatorname{tr}\pi(f)=\int_{G_{\mathrm{reg}}} f(g)\Theta_V(g)\,dg \qquad(f\in C_c^\infty(G_{\mathrm{reg}})). \tag{6.160} \] It does not assert extension of this integral identity to tests meeting the singular set.

Proof. In each slope block, all eigenvalues have the same valuation. Lemma 6.39 shows that \(\gamma\) has compact cyclic closure modulo the centre of that block. It is regular in each block, since the full reduced polynomial is separable. The Levi is a finite product of division matrix groups. Its Jacquet module is admissible by Lemma 6.22 and finitely generated by Lemma 6.40. Theorem 6.69 therefore proves a locally constant density for its trace near \(\gamma\), with no irreducibility or fixed-central-character requirement. Theorem 6.42 applies and proves (6.159) and local regularity in \(G\). If there is just one slope, Theorem 6.69 already gives the assertion directly.

These open regular neighbourhoods cover \(G_{\mathrm{reg}}\). Their densities agree on overlaps by uniqueness against compact-open tests. Any compactly supported test in this regular set has a finite compact-open partition subordinate to this cover. Adding the local identities proves (6.160) and uniqueness on the whole regular set. The same reasoning gives the regular-set assertion for finite products when needed. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.71 — point traces and character operations. For regular \(\gamma\) and every sufficiently small compact open \(J\), \[ \Theta_V(\gamma)=\operatorname{tr}(\pi(\gamma)e_J) =\operatorname{tr}\bigl(e_J\pi(\gamma)e_J|V^J\bigr). \tag{6.161} \] Thus these normalized coset traces are eventually constant. The character is conjugacy invariant, additive on short exact sequences of finitely generated admissible representations, and has central covariance \(\Theta_V(zg)=\omega(z)\Theta_V(g)\) when \(V\) has central character \(\omega\). For irreducible admissible \(V\), its smooth contragredient satisfies \[ \Theta_{\widetilde V}(g)=\Theta_V(g^{-1}), \qquad \Theta_V(g^{-1})=\overline{\Theta_V(g)} \quad\text{if }V\text{ is unitary}. \tag{6.162} \] The Levi trace hypothesis in Theorem 6.4 is now proved for every finitely generated smooth admissible inducing module, so its normalized induction formula applies to all such modules.

Proof. Choose \(J\) so that \(\gamma J\) is contained in a constant-density neighbourhood. Apply (6.160) to its normalized indicator to obtain the first equality in (6.161). A finite-rank operator with finite-dimensional domain projection has the trace of its compression, proving the second. Conjugation carries such averages to the conjugated compact group and preserves their finite-rank traces. Central covariance follows from the scalar action on the same averages. Additivity follows by choosing a compact-open averaging group for the test and using exactness of its invariants; finite-dimensional traces on the resulting exact sequence add, and uniqueness of locally constant densities gives the pointwise identity.

For completeness, the natural pairing gives \(\widetilde V^J=(V^J)^*\): extend any functional on \(V^J\) by composing with \(e_J\). It is smooth and gives the required functional, while averaging proves nondegeneracy. The smooth contragredient of an irreducible admissible \(V\) is irreducible. A nonzero invariant subspace of it has invariant annihilator in \(V\), hence zero annihilator. Averaging on \(J\) shows that its \(J\)-fixed part separates the finite-dimensional \(V^J\), so equals \((V^J)^*\); taking the union over \(J\) proves irreducibility. It is admissible and finitely generated, so Theorem 6.70 applies. The two compressed operators at \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\) are transposes under this pairing, proving the first formula in (6.162). In the unitary case they are Hilbert adjoints, proving the second. The last assertion is Theorem 6.70 on the product Levi, inserted into the proved hypothesis of Theorem 6.4. \(\square\)

Example 6.72 — compact split characters near a singular element. For \(\gamma=\operatorname{diag}(a,b)\) with \(|a|=|b|\) and \(a\ne b\), Theorem 6.4 has two fixed lines and gives \[ \Theta_{I(\mu_1,\mu_2)}(\gamma) =\frac{\mu_1(a)\mu_2(b)+\mu_1(b)\mu_2(a)}{|1-a/b|}. \tag{6.163} \] Indeed \(\Delta_G(\gamma)^{1/2}=|a-b|/|ab|^{1/2}=|1-a/b|\), while the torus discriminant is one. For \(\tau=I(|\cdot|^{-1/2},|\cdot|^{1/2})\), both numerator terms are one. Its exact sequence with constants and Steinberg therefore gives \(\Theta_{\mathrm{St}}(\gamma)=2/|1-a/b|-1\). In particular, if \(b=1+\varpi_F^s u\), \(s\ge1\), \(u\) a unit, then \[ \Theta_{I(1,1)}(\operatorname{diag}(1,b))=2q_F^s, \qquad \Theta_{\mathrm{St}}(\operatorname{diag}(1,b))=2q_F^s-1. \tag{6.164} \] These are locally constant at every displayed regular element, although their values grow as the elements approach the nonregular identity. The regular-set theorem and the additional analytic assertions about behaviour across the singular set are distinct statements.

Meyer–Solleveld, Section 7 of the free author preprint, gives related local-constancy and Jacquet results with quantitative neighbourhoods. The finite centralizer-orbit argument above uses the uniform orbital coordinates of Lemma 6.18 and finite cellular exactness. Section 6.15 proves absolute unipotent integration and vanishing constant terms for every discrete series, together with positive nonelliptic orbital descent. Section 6.21 proves general elliptic orbital convergence. Elliptic orthogonality is Theorem 6.271. Completeness and the full representation transfer remain separate assertions.

6.15. Unipotent integration and cuspidal constant terms

Discrete-series coefficients need not be compactly supported modulo the centre. Their decay nevertheless makes every translated unipotent constant term absolutely convergent, and that constant term is zero. We prove this in every matrix rank and division degree, in either characteristic. We also give the positive orbital estimate that reduces nonelliptic convergence to elliptic convergence in smaller blocks.

Write \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), \(q_D=q_F^d\), \(K=\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_D)\), and \(|\Pi|_D=q_D^{-1}\). Let \(B\) be the upper triangular subgroup. Iwasawa decomposition, proved by the adapted-basis argument in Theorem 6.4, writes \(g=bk\). Put \[ e(g)=\delta_B(b)^{1/2},\qquad W_\alpha(g)=D_C(g)^{1/2}e^{-\alpha\sigma(g)} \quad(\alpha>0). \tag{6.165} \] The first function is well defined because the modulus is one on \(B\cap K\). The second uses the intrinsic Cartan functions of Lemma 6.33. All unipotent Haar measures below may be fixed arbitrarily; constants change with their normalization.

Lemma 6.73 — lattice heights for Iwasawa coordinates. Give \(\mathcal O_D^i\) volume one. Let \(R_i(g)\) be the volume of the image lattice obtained by projecting \(g\mathcal O_D^r\) to its last \(i\) coordinates, and let \(v(g)=\operatorname{vol}(g\mathcal O_D^r)\). Then \[ e(g)=\frac{v(g)^{(r-1)/2}}{\prod_{i=1}^{r-1}R_i(g)}, \qquad D_C(g)^{1/2}\le e(g). \tag{6.166} \] For a lower unitriangular \(n\), define \(h(n)=-\log_{q_D}e(n)^2\). This is a nonnegative integer. If \(r>1\), \[ h(n)=2\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}\log_{q_D}R_i(n),\qquad h(n)\le r(r-1)\sigma(n),\qquad \sigma(n)\le \frac r2h(n). \tag{6.167} \]

Proof. For upper triangular \(b\), the projected bottom lattice has volume the product of the absolute division norms of its last \(i\) diagonal entries. Right multiplication by \(K\) does not change any image lattice. Multiplying these products proves the first identity in (6.166).

The product of the largest \(i\) singular numbers of \(g\) bounds \(R_i(g)\). Here singular numbers mean the powers of \(q_D\) given by integral row and column diagonalization. The same diagonalization applies to a rectangular surjective matrix; its image-lattice volume is the product of its nonzero singular numbers. Its \(j\)-th singular number has the minimax proof of (6.80), with domain dimension \(r-j+1\). A coordinate projection has operator norm one, so this minimax description bounds each singular number of the projected map by the corresponding one of \(g\). Multiply these bounds. In the Cartan diagonal case the expression on the right of (6.166), with these largest-singular-number products in its denominator, is exactly \(D_C(g)^{1/2}\). This proves the inequality, without determinants of matrices over a noncommutative ring.

For lower unitriangular \(n\), each bottom projected lattice contains the lattice generated by its bottom-right square block. That triangular block has volume one, so \(R_i(n)\ge1\). For an entry \(n_{ab}\), \(b<a\), select the bottom \(r-a+1\) rows and columns \(b,a+1,\ldots,r\). The resulting square matrix has first row \((n_{ab},0,\ldots,0)\) and a unitriangular remaining diagonal. Its column lattice has volume \(|n_{ab}|_D\), and lies in that projected lattice. Consequently every entry of \(n\) has norm at most \(\max_iR_i(n)\). The finite expansion of \((1+(n-1))^{-1}\) bounds \(\|n^{-1}\|\) by \(\|n\|^{r-1}\). Thus \(\sigma(n)\le r\log_{q_D}\|n\|\le rh(n)/2\). Conversely \(R_i(n)\le\|n\|^i\) by the rectangular singular-number bound, and \(\log_{q_D}\|n\|\le\sigma(n)\), since both triangular matrices have a diagonal entry one. Summing proves (6.167). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.74 — a polynomial spherical bound. The normalized minimal principal series \(I_B^G(1)\) is unitary and admissible. Its spherical vector is \(e\), of norm one in the compact model. Its coefficient \[ \Xi(g)=\langle I_B^G(1)(g)e,e\rangle =\int_K e(kg)\,dk \le C D_C(g)^{1/2}(1+\sigma(g))^b \tag{6.168} \] is positive and \(K\)-bi-invariant, for some \(C,b\) depending only on the group.

Proof: the needed principal-series Jacquet calculation. For a standard \(P=MN\), the normalized Jacquet module of \(I_B^G(1)\) has a finite filtration whose quotients are copies of \(I_{B\cap M}^M(1)\). In particular the action of the field-scalar centre \(A_M\) of each block is unipotent, with a common finite nilpotence bound.

Here are the support and measure details. Successive pivots over \(D\) put a full flag relative to the fixed partial flag into a unique permutation position, up to permutations within the Levi blocks. At each pivot, the nonpivot entries give free division coordinates; the imposed earlier zero entries give its stratum. Rank conditions on initial row and column rectangles specify the closures: they are closed because the corresponding ranks of \(F\)-linear maps are specified by vanishing minors. Ordering these finitely many strata by their closures gives an open support filtration of the induced space. Restriction to a closed remaining stratum is onto: a compactly supported locally constant section extends on finitely many compact-open coordinate sets. Thus its successive quotients are the compactly supported sections on the individual strata.

Choose a permutation \(w\) increasing within each Levi block. Its stratum is \(B wP\). Its unipotent fibre is \(H_w\backslash N\), where \(H_w=N\cap w^{-1}Bw\); its Levi base is \((B\cap M)\backslash M\). Fibre integration computes the \(N\)-coinvariant quotient. To verify its kernel, exhaust \(N\) by compact subgroups. For a compactly supported locally constant function on \(H_w\backslash N\), choose one subgroup large enough to contain representatives of its support. Averaging over that subgroup is its integral times the normalized constant function on its compact orbit. Thus an integral-zero function is a finite sum of translation differences. For sections over the Levi base the same argument works on a finite compact-open partition, with one common subgroup. It also proves surjectivity, by choosing fibre functions of integral one on each part. Taking \(N\)-coinvariants is exact: its relation space is the increasing union of the compact-subgroup relation spaces, and averaging makes each compact-group coinvariant functor exact. Every relation or kernel witness involves finitely many vectors, hence occurs at one compact stage. Thus these fibre quotients give a filtration of the actual Jacquet module.

For completeness, let \(V_w=\operatorname{Lie}(N)/\operatorname{Lie}(H_w)\), and let \(\delta_{V_w}(z)\) be the absolute determinant of conjugation by \(z\in B\cap M\) on that quotient. The fibre-integrated function is \(\delta_P(m)^{-1/2}\int_{H_w\backslash N} f(w n m)\,dn\). Its transformation under \(z\) is \(\delta_{B\cap M}(z)^{1/2}\), because \[ \delta_B(wzw^{-1})\delta_{V_w}(z)^2 =\delta_P(z)\delta_{B\cap M}(z). \tag{6.169} \] Indeed each cross-block division entry either stays upper triangular after \(w\), contributing to \(H_w\), or becomes lower triangular, contributing to \(V_w\). Its modulus factor occurs with exponent \(+1\) or \(-1\) in the first term; multiplying by the square of the second factor makes both exponents \(+1\). Internal block factors give \(\delta_{B\cap M}\). This uses ordinary \(F\)-linear determinants on division-entry spaces and holds in both characteristics. The normalized Levi action is consequently exactly the stated induced action. On its block centre that action is trivial. A filtration of length \(l\) with trivial central actions on its quotients gives \((a-1)^l=0\) for every \(a\in A_M\), as asserted. Inserting inducing characters in the same fibre formula carries their permutation by \(w\) to the quotient. In rank two the two normalized minimal Jacquet quotients therefore have characters \(\mu_1\otimes\mu_2\) and \(\mu_2\otimes\mu_1\).

Proof: the coefficient bound. The normalized compact-model pairing is invariant. On a Gaussian flag chart, right action followed by triangular refactorization has coordinate Jacobian \(\delta_B(b)\): its tangent action on the lower entry coordinates is conjugation by \(b^{-1}\). The two normalized fibre factors contribute this same modulus, so change of variables preserves their integral. A finite compact-open chart partition proves invariance on all flags; the non-open pivot loci have measure zero, since a nonzero polynomial over a local field has a zero set of measure zero, by induction on its variables and Fubini. This proves unitarity directly. Admissibility was proved in Theorem 6.4.

Apply the exact every-face coefficient formula, Theorem 6.30 and Corollary 6.31, to the spherical pair. On each face its unbounded coordinates are the central positive elements of the corresponding Levi. The calculation above makes all their normalized Jacquet eigenvalues one, with only nilpotent polynomial factors. The bounded coordinates take finitely many values. Their modulus factors differ from the full Cartan modulus by bounded constants. The finite division-residue cover in Lemma 6.23 therefore bounds every face by \(C D_C(g)^{1/2}(1+\sigma(g))^b\). Taking the maximum of the finitely many degrees and constants gives (6.168). Positivity follows from the displayed integral of the positive function \(e\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.75 — absolute unipotent integration. Let \(P=MN\) be standard, and let \(\overline N\) be its opposite radical. There are constants \(C,b\) such that \[ \int_{\overline N,\ h(n)\le H} e(n)\,dn \le C(1+H)^b\quad(H\ge0). \tag{6.170} \] Consequently \(\int_{\overline N}e(n)e^{-\alpha\sigma(n)}dn<\infty\) for every \(\alpha>0\). In particular \(W_\alpha\) is integrable on every unipotent radical. Every smooth discrete-series coefficient is absolutely integrable on every translate \(g_1Ng_2\).

Proof. For \(a\in A_M\) the open flag cell gives \[ \Xi(a)=c_P\int_{\overline N}e(na)e(n)\,dn, \qquad c_P>0. \tag{6.171} \] We justify this formula before using it for convergence. Induction in stages is the explicit map \(f\mapsto F\), where \(F(g)(m)=\delta_P(m)^{-1/2}f(mg)\), from \(I_B^G(1)\) to \(I_P^G(I_{B\cap M}^M(1))\). Its covariance follows by multiplication, and its compact pairing agrees with the original pairing. In the open cell \(\overline N\) of \(P\backslash G\), that pairing is a constant times \(\int_{\overline N}\int_{K\cap M}e(kna)e(kn)\,dk\,dn\). The coordinate Jacobian is the same lower-block determinant calculation as in Lemma 6.74. A finite atlas on the compact partial flag space proves finiteness of this pairing; the omitted pivot loci have measure zero by the polynomial argument there.
