Since \(a\) commutes with \(K\cap M\), right \(K\)-invariance and the change \(n\mapsto knk^{-1}\) remove the inner average. Its Jacobian is one for compact \(k\). This proves (6.171), including its convergence, without an advance estimate on \(e\) over \(\overline N\).

Let the blocks of \(P\) have sizes \(r_1,\ldots,r_s\). Choose \(L=\lceil H/(2d)\rceil\) and \(a=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F^{L(s-1)}I_{r_1},\ldots,I_{r_s})\). Lemma 6.73 bounds every entry of an \(n\) with \(h(n)\le H\) by \(q_D^{H/2}\). Conjugation by \(a^{-1}\) contracts all its nonzero lower cross-block entries by at least \(q_D^{-dL}\); hence \(a^{-1}na\in K\). On this height ball, \(e(na)=e(a)=\delta_B(a)^{1/2}\). Positivity in (6.171), followed by (6.168), cancels that last factor and proves (6.170), since \(\sigma(a)\le C_0(H+1)\).

On the shell \(h(n)=j\), (6.167) gives \(\sigma(n)\ge j/(r(r-1))\). The integral with exponential weight is therefore bounded by a constant times \(\sum_{j\ge0}(1+j)^b\exp(-\alpha j/(r(r-1)))\), which converges. The case of a trivial radical is immediate. Inequality (6.166) proves the assertion for \(W_\alpha\). Permutation conjugation in \(K\) treats the upper radicals; the adapted-basis argument conjugates any parabolic to a standard one by an element of \(K\). Finally (6.81) bounds a discrete-series coefficient by a constant times some \(W_\alpha\), and (6.79) compares this weight under any fixed left and right translation. This proves the last assertion. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.76 — uniform decay after unipotent integration. Let \(D_{C,M}\) be the product of the Cartan weights of the Levi blocks. For every \(\alpha>0\), \[ \delta_P(m)^{-1/2}\int_{\overline N}W_\alpha(mn)\,dn \le C_\alpha D_{C,M}(m)^{1/2} e^{-\alpha\sigma(m)/2} \quad(m\in M). \tag{6.172} \] For the upper radical the factor on the left is \(\delta_P(m)^{1/2}\). The length on the right is the ambient length in \(G\), including relative central scales between the blocks.

Proof. Cartan decomposition in each block, \(K\)-bi-invariance of \(W_\alpha\), and conjugation invariance of Haar measure under \(K\cap M\) reduce to diagonal \(m\), sorted within its blocks. Triangularity of \(mn\) and its inverse shows \(\sigma(mn)\ge\sigma(m)\). Submultiplicativity gives \(\sigma(n)\le\sigma(m)+\sigma(mn)\le2\sigma(mn)\). Consequently \[ \begin{gathered} \sigma(mn)\ge\tfrac12\sigma(m)+\tfrac14\sigma(n),\\ D_C(mn)^{1/2}\le e(mn)=\delta_B(m)^{1/2}e(n). \end{gathered} \tag{6.173} \] Integrate these bounds and apply Theorem 6.75 with exponent \(\alpha/4\). For the sorted block diagonal, \(\delta_B(m)=\delta_P(m)D_{C,M}(m)\), giving (6.172). Applying the same proof with the opposite minimal subgroup and parabolic gives the upper-radical version. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.77 — vanishing discrete-series constant terms. If \(c(g)=\langle\pi(g)v,w\rangle\) is a smooth coefficient of any discrete series and \(P=MN\) is proper, then \[ \int_N c(g_1ng_2)\,dn=0 \quad(g_1,g_2\in G). \tag{6.174} \] These are absolute integrals. This assertion does not say that the proper Jacquet modules are zero.

Proof. Theorem 6.75 gives absolute convergence for every pair of smooth vectors. Define the Hermitian form \[ B_N(v,w)=\int_N\langle\pi(n)v,w\rangle\,dn. \tag{6.175} \] It is positive semidefinite. Indeed exhaust \(N\) by compact open subgroups \(N_j\). The integral on each is \(\operatorname{vol}(N_j)\langle P_{N_j}v,w\rangle\), whose value on \((v,v)\) is nonnegative. Absolute convergence gives the limit. Inversion gives Hermitian symmetry. Translation and unitarity make the form invariant under \(N\) in either variable, so it factors through \(V_N\).

Conjugation by \(m\in M\) changes Haar measure by \(\delta_P(m)\). Thus \(B_N(\pi(m)v,\pi(m)w)=\delta_P(m)B_N(v,w)\), and the induced form on the normalized Jacquet module is \(M\)-invariant. Let \(a_P\) be the product of the fundamental positive diagonals at the block boundaries of \(P\). On every finite Jacquet fixed space, its normalized powers tend to zero. To check this consequence precisely, use the canonical fixed-space identification of Lemma 6.22 at a sufficiently small principal level. The unnormalized operator there is \(T_{a_P}=\prod_{j\in J}T_{a_j}\). Since \(a_P\) is block central, \(\delta_P(a_P)=\prod_{j\in J}\delta_j\). Hence its normalized operator is \(\prod_{j\in J}\delta_j^{-1/2}T_{a_j}\). Theorem 6.25 makes each commuting factor have spectral radius less than one. Their powers, and therefore the product powers, tend to zero by the finite Jordan estimate in that theorem.

Any vector of \(V_N\) belongs to such a finite-dimensional fixed space, stable under the central \(a_P\), by admissibility. The form restricted to this finite space is continuous. Its invariance therefore makes its value on a vector equal to the limit of its value on the powers just shown to tend to zero. That value is zero. Polarization makes the whole form zero. Finally \(c(g_1ng_2)\) is the coefficient with input \(\pi(g_2)v\) and second vector \(\pi(g_1^{-1})w\). This proves (6.174). \(\square\)

Proposition 6.78 — positive orbital descent. Let \(\gamma\) be regular nonelliptic, and let \(M=\prod_{i=1}^sG_i\), \(s\ge2\), be its primary-factor Levi. Write \(\gamma=(\gamma_i)\) and \(T=\prod_iT_i\). Every \(\gamma_i\) is elliptic regular in \(G_i\). With the same positive weights on each block, \[ O_\gamma^G(W_\alpha) \le C_{\gamma,\alpha} \prod_{i=1}^s O_{\gamma_i}^{G_i}(W_{\alpha/(2s)}^{G_i}). \tag{6.176} \] Both sides are interpreted as nonnegative extended integrals. If the factors on the right are finite, every smooth discrete-series coefficient has an absolutely convergent orbital integral at \(\gamma\), and that orbital integral is zero. In particular this conclusion holds when every primary block has division rank one; it includes all split regular classes in \(\mathrm{GL}_r(F)\).

Proof. The quotient integration and polynomial unipotent change of variables in the proof of Theorem 6.20 apply to a nonnegative function by Tonelli, without an advance convergence assumption. Since \(W_\alpha\) is \(K\)-bi-invariant, they give \[ O_\gamma^G(W_\alpha)=J_N(\gamma)^{-1} \int_{T\backslash M}\int_N W_\alpha(m^{-1}\gamma m n)\,dn\,d\dot m. \tag{6.177} \] The upper-radical bound in (6.172) applies. Its parabolic modulus at \(m^{-1}\gamma m\) equals its fixed value at \(\gamma\), which enters the constant. The Levi Cartan weight is the product of the block weights. The ambient length is at least each block length and hence at least their sum divided by \(s\). The remaining integral is bounded by the product in (6.176), by product quotient integration and Tonelli.

Finiteness of those factors proves absolute convergence for a coefficient by (6.81). The now absolutely convergent version of (6.177) for that coefficient is (6.46); its innermost integrals vanish by Theorem 6.77. If every block has division rank one, \(G_i/F^\times\) is compact, as proved in Section 6.4, and therefore so is \(T_i\backslash G_i\). Its displayed weight is bounded, proving finiteness. Section 6.16 constructs the Schwartz algebra and its tempered trace action. Section 6.17 proves nilpotent orbital measures, unipotent orbital continuity and vanishing of nontrivial unipotent orbitals of discrete-series coefficients. Section 6.20 proves elliptic semisimple convergence and the coefficient–character identity in division rank two. Section 6.21 proves elliptic convergence in every division rank. Theorem 6.271 proves elliptic orthogonality. Completeness and the full representation transfer require further arguments. \(\square\)

Example 6.79 — the Steinberg unipotent integral. Normalize additive measure by \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O_F)=1\). Let \(v\) be the Steinberg unit vector of the edge between \(L_0=\mathcal O_F^2\) and \(L_1=\mathcal O_Fe_1+\varpi_F\mathcal O_Fe_2\), as in Proposition 2.12. For \(n(x)=\begin{pmatrix}1&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), \[ \langle\mathrm{St}(n(x))v,v\rangle= \begin{cases} 1,&|x|\le1,\\ -q_F^{-(2l-1)},&|x|=q_F^l,\quad l\ge1. \end{cases} \tag{6.178} \] Indeed \(n(x)\) fixes \(L_j=\mathcal O_Fe_1+\varpi_F^j\mathcal O_Fe_2\) exactly for \(j\ge l\), so the two edge paths first meet at \(L_l\) and have gallery distance \(2l-1\). The sign can also be checked directly: the average over either vertex stabilizer kills the edge vector, because the Steinberg vertex-fixed space is zero. Its \(q_F\) other edge cosets therefore have normalized average \(-v/q_F\). Alternating the two vertex moves follows the unique gallery without backtracking, so its coefficient is \((-1/q_F)^{2l-1}\). Root-group transitivity on these galleries, proved in Proposition 2.12, identifies this averaged coefficient with each individual one. For \(x\in\mathcal O_F\) the edge is fixed pointwise.

Consequently \[ \begin{gathered} \int_{\varpi_F^{-L}\mathcal O_F} \langle\mathrm{St}(n(x))v,v\rangle\,dx =1-(q_F-1)\sum_{l=1}^Lq_F^{-l}=q_F^{-L},\\ \int_F|\langle\mathrm{St}(n(x))v,v\rangle|\,dx=2, \qquad \int_F\langle\mathrm{St}(n(x))v,v\rangle\,dx=0. \end{gathered} \tag{6.179} \] The normalized Jacquet module of Steinberg is nonzero. Indeed the two-cell calculation in Lemma 6.74 applied to \(\tau=I(|\cdot|^{-1/2},|\cdot|^{1/2})\) gives successive characters \(\delta_B^{-1/2}\) and \(\delta_B^{1/2}\). The constant subrepresentation of \(\tau\) has normalized Jacquet character \(\delta_B^{-1/2}\). Exactness of Jacquet coinvariants in \(0\to1\to\tau\to\mathrm{St}\to0\) leaves the one-dimensional quotient of character \(\delta_B^{1/2}\). Thus a vanishing, absolutely convergent constant term is compatible with a nonzero Jacquet module; it is the integrated positive form (6.175) that vanishes.

Waldspurger, Lemma II.1.1 and §§II.3–II.4 of the freely accessible Plancherel article, gives related spherical and unipotent estimates. Bernstein–Zelevinsky, §5 and §6.4 of the freely accessible first induced-representations paper, gives the general support-filtration method. The lattice-volume bounds, principal-series filtration and its modulus factors, unipotent estimates, positive-form vanishing and orbital descent needed here have been proved above.

6.16. The Schwartz algebra and tempered trace operators

We now construct the function algebra on which discrete-series coefficients and tempered traces coexist. This supplies the analytic setting for the remaining orbital estimates. Throughout, \(\omega\) is a smooth unitary central character, \(Q=G/Z\) has the fixed quotient Haar measure, and functions in the algebra transform by \(\omega^{-1}\). All integrals of such functions are taken only when their full integrands descend to \(Q\).

Lemma 6.80 — spherical convolution and weighted integrability. For the positive spherical coefficient of Lemma 6.74 there are \(c,C>0\) and an integer \(b\ge0\) such that \[ \begin{gathered} cD_C(g)^{1/2}\le\Xi(g)\le C D_C(g)^{1/2}(1+\sigma(g))^b,\\ \Xi(g^{-1})=\Xi(g),\qquad \int_K\Xi(xky)\,dk=\Xi(x)\Xi(y). \end{gathered} \tag{6.180} \] Haar measure on \(K\) in this formula is probability measure. In particular \[ C_s:=\int_Q\Xi(x)^2(1+\sigma(x))^{-s}\,d\bar x<\infty \qquad(s>2b+r-1). \tag{6.181} \]

Proof. For a Cartan diagonal \(a\) with decreasing division valuations, choose a fixed principal subgroup \(H\subset K\) with its upper-diagonal-lower factorization. Since \(a^{-1}(H\cap\overline N_B)a\subset K\), every \(h\in H\) satisfies \(ha\in N_B(H\cap M_B)aK\). Thus \(e(ha)=\delta_B(a)^{1/2}=D_C(a)^{1/2}\). Integrating the positive compact-model formula for \(\Xi\) over \(H\) proves the lower bound uniformly in \(a\). The Cartan decomposition proves it on all of \(G\); the upper bound is Lemma 6.74.

The compact model has a one-dimensional \(K\)-fixed space, spanned by the unit vector \(e\). Hence its averaging projector sends \(\pi(y)e\) to \(\Xi(y)e\). Pairing after applying \(\pi(x)\) proves the product formula. Unitarity and positivity give \(\Xi(g^{-1})=\overline{\Xi(g)}=\Xi(g)\). Its central character is trivial, so all these weights descend to \(Q\).

Use the finite translated Cartan covering and exact volume bound (6.55)–(6.56). For each nonnegative tuple \(\ell\), its volume is bounded by a constant times \(D_C(t_\ell)^{-1}\), and \(\sigma\) differs from \(d\sum\ell_j\) by bounded constants. The finite division residues change \(D_C\) by bounded factors, by Lemma 6.33. The squared spherical bound cancels this volume weight. The integral is therefore bounded by a constant times \(\sum_{\ell\ge0}(1+\sum\ell_j)^{2b-s}\). The number of tuples of total \(n\) is at most \((1+n)^{r-2}\) times a fixed constant when \(r>1\), by choosing the first \(r-2\) coordinates. The resulting series converges for the stated \(s\). For \(r=1\), \(Q\) is compact and \(\sigma=0\), so convergence is immediate. \(\square\)

For a compact open \(J\subset K\), define \(\mathcal S_{\omega,J}\) to consist of the smooth \(J\)-bi-invariant functions with central rule \(\omega^{-1}\) for which all the norms \[ p_N(f)=\sup_{g\in G}|f(g)|\Xi(g)^{-1}(1+\sigma(g))^N \quad(N=0,1,2,\ldots) \tag{6.182} \] are finite. If \(\omega\) is nontrivial on \(J\cap Z\), this space is zero; sufficiently small \(J\) avoid that issue. Put \(\mathcal S_\omega=\bigcup_J\mathcal S_{\omega,J}\). Any compact open subgroup can be replaced by its intersection with \(K\), so these levels cover every smooth function with a compact-open left and right stabilizer satisfying the norms.

Theorem 6.81 — the Schwartz convolution algebra. Each \(\mathcal S_{\omega,J}\) is a complete Fréchet space for (6.182), and its compact-mod-centre tests are dense. The union \(\mathcal S_\omega\) is an associative convolution algebra with involution \(f^*(g)=\overline{f(g^{-1})}\). Every convolution integral is absolute. For every integer \(s>2b+r-1\), \[ p_N(f_1*f_2) \le C_s p_{N+s}(f_1)p_N(f_2). \tag{6.183} \] This gives joint continuity between any fixed pair of levels, with target their intersection level. If \(f_R=1_{\{\sigma\le R\}}f\), then \[ p_N(f-f_R)\le(1+R)^{-A}p_{N+A}(f) \quad(A,N\ge0). \tag{6.184} \] Every \(\mathcal S_{\omega,J}\) embeds continuously in the corresponding centrally covariant \(L^2(Q)\) space.

Proof: the integral estimate. Tonelli and the spherical product formula give the exact positive identity \[ \int_Q\Xi(x)\Xi(x^{-1}g)(1+\sigma(x))^{-s}\,d\bar x =C_s\Xi(g). \tag{6.185} \] Indeed replace \(x\) by \(kx\) and average in \(k\in K\). The first weight is unchanged; the average of \(\Xi(x^{-1}k^{-1}g)\) is \(\Xi(x)\Xi(g)\). The right side is finite by (6.181), so this argument also proves convergence of the original positive integral.

Submultiplicativity of the length gives \(1+\sigma(g)\le(1+\sigma(x))(1+\sigma(x^{-1}g))\). Bound \(f_1\) by its \(p_{N+s}\)-norm and \(f_2\) by its \(p_N\)-norm, multiply by \((1+\sigma(g))^N\), and apply (6.185). This proves (6.183) and absolute convergence. The convolution is left invariant under the first level and right invariant under the second, so is bi-invariant under their intersection. Its central transformation is \(\omega^{-1}\): changing a central factor in the integration variable cancels between the two factors, while a central factor in \(g\) remains in the second factor.

Applying the same estimate twice, with sufficiently many powers of decay, makes the absolute double integral for a triple convolution finite. Fubini therefore proves associativity. Inversion preserves the weights and quotient Haar measure, so \(p_N(f^*)=p_N(f)\); changing variables in the absolute convolution integral gives \((f_1*f_2)^*=f_2^**f_1^*\). The bilinear bound proves joint continuity on each pair of fixed levels.

Proof: completeness and approximation. A sequence Cauchy in all the norms has a pointwise limit and converges uniformly after multiplication by each fixed weight: this is completeness of the supremum norm, proved by taking pointwise limits in its Cauchy inequality. The limit keeps the central rule and the \(J\)-bi-invariance, hence is smooth. Applying the Cauchy inequality in every \(p_N\) proves that the limit lies in the space and that convergence holds there. The countable norms give a complete metrizable locally convex topology, for example through the metric \(\sum_N2^{-N}\min(1,p_N(f-g))\).

The length balls are compact and open modulo the centre by Lemma 6.33, and \(\sigma\) is \(K\)-bi-invariant. Thus \(f_R\) is a test at the same level. On its omitted support \((1+\sigma)^{-A}\le(1+R)^{-A}\), proving (6.184) and density. Finally \(\|f\|_2^2\le p_N(f)^2C_{2N}\) whenever \(2N>2b+r-1\). This proves the continuous Hilbert-space inclusion. \(\square\)

Here tempered means an irreducible admissible unitary representation whose smooth coefficients belong to every \(L^{2+\epsilon}(Q)\), \(\epsilon>0\). Corollary 6.26 proves its equivalent finite Jacquet eigenvalue criterion \(|\lambda|\le1\). This definition and criterion apply in both field characteristics.

Theorem 6.82 — tempered operators and traces on the Schwartz algebra. Let \(\pi\) be tempered with central character \(\omega\). There is an integer \(a_\pi\ge0\) such that every smooth coefficient satisfies \[ |\langle\pi(g)u,v\rangle| \le C_{u,v}\Xi(g)(1+\sigma(g))^{a_\pi}. \tag{6.186} \] For \(f\in\mathcal S_\omega\), the integrals \[ \langle\pi(f)u,v\rangle =\int_Q f(g)\langle\pi(g)u,v\rangle\,d\bar g \tag{6.187} \] converge absolutely for smooth \(u,v\) and define a finite-rank operator. They extend the compact-test action. The resulting action is a \(*\)-representation of the algebra, and at each fixed level its operator and trace are continuous. In particular, for suitable \(M\) and a constant depending on \(\pi,J\), \[ \begin{gathered} \pi(f_1*f_2)=\pi(f_1)\pi(f_2),\qquad \pi(f^*)=\pi(f)^*,\\ \|\pi(f)\|+|\operatorname{tr}\pi(f)| \le C_{\pi,J}p_M(f) \quad(f\in\mathcal S_{\omega,J}). \end{gathered} \tag{6.188} \] Its compact cutoffs obey, for any prescribed \(A\), \[ \|\pi(f)-\pi(f_R)\| +|\operatorname{tr}\pi(f)-\operatorname{tr}\pi(f_R)| \le C_{\pi,J}(1+R)^{-A}p_{M+A}(f). \tag{6.189} \]

Proof: coefficient growth. At a principal level, the commuting normalized positive operators \(\delta_j^{-1/2}T_{a_j}\) have eigenvalues of absolute value at most one by Corollary 6.26. Their finite Jordan expansions are bounded by polynomials in their nonnegative powers. The exact product identity (6.54) therefore bounds any fixed coefficient on the scalar chamber by its Cartan square root times a polynomial in the chamber coordinates. The finite translated covering of Lemma 6.23 treats all directions and division residues. This proves such a bound for one smooth pair. Algebraic irreducibility expresses every other smooth coefficient as a finite sum of its left and right translates, as proved in Proposition 6.19. Lemma 6.33 preserves the polynomial degree under each fixed translation. Thus one degree works for the representation, though its constants depend on the pair. The lower bound in (6.180) converts this bound to (6.186).

Proof: the actual operator. Combining (6.186) with \(p_M(f)\), for \(M>a_\pi+2b+r-1\), bounds the absolute integral in (6.187) by a constant times \(p_M(f)C_{M-a_\pi}\). If \(f\) is \(J\)-bi-invariant, averaging each smooth input over \(J\) does not change that integral. These averages are finite sums on smooth vectors, so this use of averaging preserves absolute convergence. The pairing therefore factors through the finite-dimensional \(V^J\) in each variable. Its matrix in an orthonormal basis defines \(\pi(f)=P_J\pi(f)P_J\), a bounded finite-rank operator, and proves the bound in (6.188). This definition is independent of the chosen level, since (6.187) specifies every smooth matrix entry. It agrees with the ordinary integrated action on compact tests. Density then proves uniqueness of the continuous extension at each level.

To justify multiplication, first use smooth \(u,v\). The absolute double integral with integrand \(f_1(x)f_2(y)\langle\pi(xy)u,v\rangle\) is finite. In fact the coefficient bound and \(1+\sigma(xy)\le(1+\sigma(x))(1+\sigma(y))\) reduce it, using sufficiently high seminorms, to the positive integral of \(\Xi(x)\Xi(y)\Xi(xy)(1+\sigma(x))^{-s}(1+\sigma(y))^{-s}\). Integration in \(y\) by (6.185), with inversion if needed, gives \(C_s\Xi(x)\); the remaining integral is \(C_s^2\). Fubini is consequently valid and gives the first identity in (6.188). Unitarity and inversion give the second. Finite-dimensional compression extends these identities to the Hilbert operators. Applying the operator bound to (6.184) gives (6.189). These statements concern trace operators; they do not presume a character integral for tests meeting the singular set. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.83 — discrete-series matrix units and individual Fourier blocks. For smooth vectors of a discrete series, the matrix-unit functions \(E^\pi_{u,v}\) of (6.85) belong to \(\mathcal S_\omega\). At a level fixing the vectors their compact cutoffs satisfy \[ p_N\bigl(E^\pi_{u,v}-1_{\{\sigma\le R\}}E^\pi_{u,v}\bigr) \le C_{N,u,v}e^{-\eta_\pi R/2}. \tag{6.190} \] The exact convolution identities of Theorem 6.36 thus hold within this Schwartz algebra. If \(f\in\mathcal S_{\omega,J}\) and \(u_1,\ldots,u_h\) is an orthonormal basis of \(V_\pi^J\), its orthogonal \(\pi\)-coefficient projection is \[ P_\pi f(g)=d_\pi\operatorname{tr} \bigl(\pi(g)^{-1}\pi(f)\bigr) =\sum_{i,j=1}^h \langle\pi(f)u_i,u_j\rangle E^\pi_{u_j,u_i}(g). \tag{6.191} \] It belongs to the same Schwartz level and depends continuously on \(f\). These projections are idempotent, and projections for inequivalent discrete series are orthogonal. No assertion about convergence of the sum of all these blocks in the Schwartz norms is made here.

Proof. Divide the exponential coefficient bound (6.81) by the lower spherical bound in (6.180). It bounds the weighted matrix-unit norm by a constant times \(e^{-\eta_\pi\sigma}(1+\sigma)^N\). On \(\sigma>R\), absorb the polynomial into half the exponential; this proves (6.190), including membership. The algebra products are the absolute products already computed in Theorem 6.36, now between elements of \(\mathcal S_\omega\).

The Schwartz function is in \(L^2\) by Theorem 6.81. Schur orthogonality gives \(\|E^\pi_{u_j,u_i}\|_2^2=d_\pi\) and \(\langle f,E^\pi_{u_j,u_i}\rangle_{L^2}=d_\pi\langle\pi(f)u_i,u_j\rangle\). Left and right \(J\)-averaging make every coefficient involving the orthogonal complement of \(V_\pi^J\) vanish. The orthogonal Hilbert-space projection is consequently the finite sum in (6.191). Expanding its finite trace gives the first formula. Each matrix entry is continuous by Theorem 6.82, and each displayed matrix unit lies at the same level, proving Schwartz continuity of this individual projection. Idempotence and cross orthogonality are those of the Hilbert coefficient spaces proved in Theorem 6.15. \(\square\)

Example 6.84 — the spherical borderline in rank two. In the split rank-two normalization \(\operatorname{vol}(KZ/Z)=1\), Example 6.32 gives \(\Xi(a_k)=(1+\beta k)q^{-k/2}\), where \(\beta=(q-1)/(q+1)\) and \(a_k=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F^k,1)\). The \(k\)-th vertex sphere has \((q+1)q^{k-1}\) elements for \(k\ge1\): the first step has \(q+1\) choices and every later nonbacktracking step has \(q\). Hence \[ \int_Q\Xi(g)^2(1+\sigma(g))^{-s}\,d\bar g =1+\frac{q+1}{q}\sum_{k\ge1} (1+\beta k)^2(1+k)^{-s}. \tag{6.192} \] The integral converges exactly when \(s>3\). In particular \(\Xi\) itself is not square-integrable, while its every \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) norm is finite: the remaining radial exponential is \(q^{-\epsilon k/2}\), which dominates its polynomial factor. This explains the role of the extra polynomial weights in (6.181).

The product estimate and Schwartz action can be compared with Waldspurger, Lemmas II.1.3–II.1.5, §III.6 and the opening of §III.7 in the free Plancherel article. Section 6.17 gives the orbital bound for every unipotent class. Section 6.20 gives the elliptic regular semisimple bound in division rank two, and Section 6.21 proves it in every division rank. The character integral across the singular set and elliptic completeness require further arguments.

6.17 Nilpotent measures and unipotent orbital integrals

Let \(A=M_r(D)=\operatorname{End}_D(V)\), where \(V\) is a right \(D\)-space of dimension \(r\), and let \(d^2=[D:F]\). A partition \(\lambda\) of \(r\) records the lengths of nilpotent Jordan chains over \(D\). Write \(c_i=\#\{j:\lambda_j\ge i\}\) for its column lengths, stopping at \(c_s>0\). Let \(P_\lambda\) stabilize the standard flag of dimensions \(c_1,c_1+c_2,\ldots,r\); its Lie algebra and strict upper block radical are \(\mathfrak p_\lambda\) and \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\). Put \(N_\lambda=1+\mathfrak n_\lambda\). The measures in this subsection are defined explicitly; they are not the measures on regular semisimple tori in the Weyl formula.

Lemma 6.85 — Jordan chains and the kernel flag. Nilpotent conjugacy classes in \(A\) are classified by the partitions of \(r\). For type \(\lambda\), \[ \begin{gathered} \dim_D\ker X^i=\sum_{j\le i}c_j,\qquad \dim_F A_X=d^2\sum_i c_i^2,\\ \dim_F\mathcal O_\lambda =d^2\left(r^2-\sum_i c_i^2\right) =2\dim_F(G/P_\lambda). \end{gathered} \tag{6.193} \] Here \(A_X=\{a:aX=Xa\}\), and \(\mathcal O_\lambda\) is the conjugacy orbit. For such an \(X\), the only flag of the indicated dimensions satisfying \(XF_i\subset F_{i-1}\) is \(F_i=\ker X^i\). The elements of type \(\lambda\) form an open subset of full additive measure in \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\).

Proof. Put \(V_i=\ker X^i\). The map induced by \(X\) from \(V_{i+1}/V_i\) to \(V_i/V_{i-1}\) is injective: an image zero means \(Xv\in V_{i-1}\), hence \(v\in V_i\). Thus the successive dimensions \(c_i\) decrease. Starting with a basis of the highest nonzero quotient, take its iterated images in the lower quotients. At each lower stage extend these independent images to a basis and choose lifts for the new vectors. The new lifts and their iterated images, together with the previously chosen chains, give bases in every successive quotient. Their union is a basis of \(V\). This constructs the Jordan chains over the division ring. Their lengths are determined by the \(c_i\), so the partition is unique; two resulting matrices with the same chains are conjugate over \(D\).

A commuting map from a chain of length \(a\) to one of length \(b\) is specified by the image of its top vector, which can be any vector killed by \(X^a\). It has \(D\)-dimension \(\min(a,b)\). Summing over ordered pairs of chains gives \(\sum_{a,b}\min(\lambda_a,\lambda_b)=\sum_i c_i^2\). The group centralizer is the open unit subset of this finite-dimensional \(F\)-algebra, so it is a smooth analytic group of that dimension. Gaussian elimination on a fixed choice of Jordan-chain pivots gives local analytic conjugating matrices: compute the kernel graphs on constant-rank charts, keep the chosen complementary top vectors, and take their successive images as in the chain construction above. To compute the quotient dimension, choose an \(F\)-linear complement \(E\) to \(A_X\) in \(A\). Multiplication \((Y,h)\mapsto(1+Y)h\), for \(Y\in E\) and \(h\in G_X\) near the identity, has derivative \((Y,H)\mapsto Y+H\), an isomorphism. The inverse-function argument of Theorem 6.2 gives local quotient coordinates of dimension \(\dim_F A-\dim_F A_X\). The flag has \(F\)-dimension \(d^2\sum_{i<j}c_ic_j\), proving (6.193).

Iterating \(XF_i\subset F_{i-1}\) gives \(F_i\subset\ker X^i\). Their dimensions agree, proving uniqueness. Every element of \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\) kills \(F_i\) under its \(i\)-th power, and hence has \(\operatorname{rank}_D X^i\le r-\sum_{j\le i}c_j\). A Jordan matrix adapted to its kernel flag attains all these bounds. Attaining them is an open condition. In a fixed \(F\)-basis of \(A\), failure of any one bound is contained in the zero set of an \(F\)-polynomial minor that is nonzero at this Jordan matrix. The zero set of a nonzero polynomial over \(F\) has additive measure zero: induction on the number of coordinates, followed by Fubini, reduces this to the finite root set of a nonzero one-variable polynomial. A finite union of these exceptional sets still has measure zero. The ranks determine the partition by the first formula, proving the last assertion. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.86 — an explicit nilpotent orbital measure. Give \(K=\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_D)\) probability measure and \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\) additive measure with \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\cap M_r(\mathcal O_D)\) of volume one. The formula \[ \mu_\lambda(\phi)= \int_K\int_{\mathfrak n_\lambda} \phi(kXk^{-1})\,dX\,dk \qquad(\phi\in C_c^\infty(A)) \tag{6.194} \] defines a locally finite invariant measure supported on the nilpotent cone and concentrated on \(\mathcal O_\lambda\). Its restriction to that orbit is a nonzero invariant orbital measure. The corresponding measure on the unipotent orbit \(1+\mathcal O_\lambda\) is \[ U_\lambda(f)=\int_K\int_{N_\lambda} f(knk^{-1})\,dn\,dk, \qquad f\in C_c^\infty(G), \tag{6.195} \] where \(N_\lambda\cap K\) has volume one. An orbital measure obtained from any other fixed Haar measure on the centralizer differs by a positive constant.

Proof. The pairing \((Y,X)\mapsto\operatorname{Trd}(YX)\) on \(A\) is nondegenerate by the matrix-unit splitting argument of Section 6.3. Its annihilator of \(\mathfrak p_\lambda\) is exactly \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\), as is seen by pairing opposite blocks and then diagonal blocks. Thus the cotangent bundle of the flag space is \[ \begin{gathered} T^*(G/P_\lambda)=G\mathbin{\times^{P_\lambda}}\mathfrak n_\lambda, \qquad [g,X]\longmapsto gXg^{-1},\\ Y_\lambda^\circ\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathcal O_\lambda, \qquad X\longmapsto\bigl((\ker X^i)_i,X\bigr) \text{ for the inverse.} \end{gathered} \tag{6.196} \] Here \(Y_\lambda^\circ\) means the part over matrices of type \(\lambda\). The equivalence in the associated bundle is \((g,X)\sim(gp,p^{-1}Xp)\). Lemma 6.85 proves the displayed bijection. On any fixed nonzero pivot minor, kernels of matrices of constant rank are graphs whose entries are obtained by elimination and inversion of that minor. These are analytic coordinates for the inverse. The forward map is polynomial in matrix charts. This proves the analytic isomorphism in (6.196), including in positive characteristic.

For clarity, the invariant density on a cotangent bundle needs no division by a factorial. In local flag coordinates \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\), with dual fibre coordinates \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_m\), take the product additive density \(dx\,d\xi\), using paired Haar measures. If the base coordinates change with derivative \(B\), the fibre derivative is \(B^{-\mathrm t}\); the full derivative is block triangular. Its absolute determinant is one. The densities consequently agree on overlapping charts. The cotangent lift of any analytic base automorphism preserves them by the same calculation. In particular this density is \(G\)-invariant in every field characteristic.

The Iwasawa decomposition makes \(K\) transitive on \(G/P_\lambda\). The compact stabilizer \(K\cap P_\lambda\) preserves additive measure on \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\): its determinant and its inverse both have absolute value at most one, so that determinant has absolute value one. Probability measure on the flag space and these transported fibre measures therefore give the product integral in (6.194). This density is a constant multiple of the cotangent density. Indeed both are translation invariant along each cotangent fibre, so their ratio depends only on the base; both are \(K\)-invariant, and \(K\) is transitive there. As a direct check on the cancellation, a refactorization by \(p\in P_\lambda\) has base determinant \(\delta_{P_\lambda}(p)^{-1}\) on \(\mathfrak g/\mathfrak p_\lambda\), and fibre determinant \(\delta_{P_\lambda}(p)\) on \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\). Their product is one. Hence (6.194) is \(G\)-invariant.

The exceptional fibre set has measure zero by Lemma 6.85 and Fubini, so (6.196) transports this measure onto the single orbit. It is nonzero on every sufficiently small open orbit chart. If \(\phi\) has compact support, compactness of \(K\) puts every \(X\) contributing to (6.194) in a bounded subset of \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\); its additive measure is finite. This proves local finiteness even near smaller nilpotent orbits in the closure. Invariant measures on a transitive orbit differ by a positive scalar: in a local section of the orbit map, disintegrate a Haar measure on \(G\) along a Haar measure on \(G_X\); left invariance fixes the resulting density up to that scalar. Existence of the invariant density also gives unimodularity of \(G_X\), since \(G\) is unimodular.

Finally \(X\mapsto1+X\) is equivariant and has the same centralizer. It identifies \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\) with \(N_\lambda\), preserving the indicated measures. To check the last statement without an exponential map, write all strict upper block entries in order of increasing block distance. Multiplication by a fixed \(1+Y\) is affine triangular in these coordinates with identity diagonal: an entry of \(YX\) or \(XY\) uses strictly shorter distances. Left and right translations have determinant one. Thus additive coordinate measure is Haar measure on \(N_\lambda\), and (6.195) follows. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.87 — polynomially weighted radical integration. There is an integer \(a_G\), depending only on \(G\) and the chosen length, such that for every standard parabolic \(P\), \[ B_P=\int_{N_P}\Xi(n)(1+\sigma(n))^{-a_G}\,dn<\infty. \tag{6.197} \] The same assertion holds for an opposite radical.

Proof. For the opposite radical, Theorem 6.75 gives \(e\)-mass at most \(C(1+H)^{b_P}\) on \(h\le H\). On \(h=j\), Lemma 6.73 gives \(\sigma(n)\ge j/(r(r-1))\) if \(r>1\). Consequently \(\int e(n)(1+\sigma(n))^{-t}dn\) is bounded by a constant times \(\sum_{j\ge0}(1+j)^{b_P-t}\), and is finite for \(t>b_P+1\). Lemmas 6.73 and 6.74 give \(\Xi(n)\le C D_C(n)^{1/2}(1+\sigma(n))^b\le C e(n)(1+\sigma(n))^b\). Choose \(a_G>b+b_P+1\). There are only finitely many standard block parabolics, so one integer works for all of them. Conjugation by the reversing permutation in \(K\) changes an upper radical into the opposite radical of the reversed block parabolic; \(\Xi\) and \(\sigma\) are \(K\)-bi-invariant. This proves the upper-radical assertion with its Haar normalization. A trivial radical has mass one and needs no estimate; this also treats \(r=1\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.88 — unipotent orbital continuity on the Schwartz algebra. For any smooth unitary central character and every partition \(\lambda\), formula (6.195) is absolutely convergent for each \(f\in\mathcal S_\omega\). It extends the compact-support orbital measure and satisfies \[ \begin{gathered} |U_\lambda(f)|\le B_{P_\lambda}p_{a_G}(f),\\ |U_\lambda(f-f_R)| \le B_{P_\lambda}(1+R)^{-A}p_{a_G+A}(f), \qquad f_R=1_{\{\sigma\le R\}}f,\quad A\ge0. \end{gathered} \tag{6.198} \] The constants here use precisely (6.195); changing an orbital measure multiplies its bounds by the same fixed positive scalar. The cutoff estimate holds for every nonnegative integer exponent. The estimates hold on every fixed Schwartz level.

Proof. By \(K\)-bi-invariance of the two weights, \(|f(knk^{-1})|\le p_{a_G}(f)\Xi(n)(1+\sigma(n))^{-a_G}\). Integrate and use (6.197). On the tail \(\sigma(n)>R\), use the higher seminorm and take out \((1+R)^{-A}\). This gives the second estimate directly and proves convergence of the compact cutoffs to the integral. For \(\lambda=(1^r)\), the radical is trivial and \(U_\lambda(f)=f(1)\), consistent with both assertions. Central-character functions need only be compactly supported modulo the centre for their cutoffs; the absolute formula defines their orbital integral without choosing a representative of a central coset. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.89 — discrete-series coefficients on unipotent orbits. Let \(c(g)=\langle\pi(g)v,w\rangle\) be any smooth coefficient of a discrete series of \(G\). Then \[ U_\lambda(c)= \begin{cases} \langle v,w\rangle,&\lambda=(1^r),\\ 0,&\lambda\ne(1^r). \end{cases} \tag{6.199} \] These are absolute orbital integrals with normalization (6.195).

Proof. Corollary 6.83 places \(c\) in the Schwartz space for its central character (use the inverse label in the definition of \(\mathcal S_\omega\) when necessary). Theorem 6.88 proves absolute convergence and permits Fubini. If the orbit is nontrivial, its column partition has at least two nonzero columns, so \(P_\lambda\) is proper. For each \(k\), the inner integral in (6.195) is zero by Theorem 6.77, applied to the conjugated smooth vectors. For the trivial orbit the assertion is evaluation at the identity. This uses the vanishing integrated constant term, not the assertion that the proper Jacquet module vanishes. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.90 — Fourier transforms of the nilpotent measures. Fix a nontrivial continuous additive character \(\psi\) of \(F\). Use self-dual Haar measure on \(A\) for the reduced-trace pairing and set \(\widehat\phi(X)=\int_A\phi(Y)\psi(\operatorname{Trd}(XY))dY\). Choose the measure \(dY\) on \(\mathfrak p_\lambda=\mathfrak n_\lambda^\perp\) dual to the already specified measure on \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\). Then, as distributions on \(A\), \[ \widehat\mu_\lambda(\phi):=\mu_\lambda(\widehat\phi) =\int_K\int_{\mathfrak p_\lambda} \phi(kYk^{-1})\,dY\,dk. \tag{6.200} \] For \(\lambda\ne(1^r)\), this distribution vanishes on the open elliptic regular set of \(A\), where elliptic means that the element preserves no proper nonzero right \(D\)-subspace.

Proof. Here is the needed subspace Fourier identity. Choose an \(F\)-linear complement to \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\), and dual coordinates in \(A\) under the trace pairing. For a compactly supported locally constant test, integrate first over an increasing sequence of compact additive lattices \(L\) in \(\mathfrak n_\lambda\). The character integral over \(L\) is \(\operatorname{vol}(L)\) when the dual coordinate is trivial on \(L\), and zero otherwise: translating by an element on which the character is nontrivial proves the zero assertion. For sufficiently large \(L\), the dual shrinking lattice is contained in the constancy lattice of the test in that coordinate. Its volume is \(\operatorname{vol}(L)^{-1}\) in the paired measures. The integral therefore equals the integral of the test on the zero dual coordinate. The other coordinates give exactly \[ \int_{\mathfrak n_\lambda}\widehat\phi(X)dX =\int_{\mathfrak n_\lambda^\perp}\phi(Y)dY. \tag{6.201} \] The Fourier transform of such a test is again compactly supported and locally constant: invariance under a compact open lattice forces its transform into the compact annihilator, while compact support forces a common constancy lattice for the transform. Thus these integrals are finite. Conjugation preserves the trace pairing and additive Haar measure on \(A\). Indeed the determinants of left and right multiplication by the same matrix cancel in their conjugation action. Apply (6.201) to \(\phi\circ\operatorname{Ad}(k)\) and integrate over compact \(K\). This proves (6.200).

Every element of \(k\mathfrak p_\lambda k^{-1}\) preserves the corresponding flag. The union of these subspaces is closed: if \(k_jY_jk_j^{-1}\) converges, compactness of \(K\) gives a convergent subsequence of the \(k_j\), and then of the bounded \(Y_j\); the limit remains in \(\mathfrak p_\lambda\). If \(P_\lambda\) is proper, an elliptic regular element belongs to none of these subspaces. A test supported in that elliptic open set consequently has zero integral in (6.200). No local character expansion or regularity theorem for this Fourier distribution was used or is inferred. \(\square\)

For the split group, Kivinen–Tsai, Definition 2.1 and equations (2.1)–(2.2) in their free author preprint, use the normalization (6.194)–(6.195). The kernel-flag and coordinate-density proof above supplies this formula for division matrix groups and in both field characteristics. It also proves the unipotent Schwartz estimates and coefficient vanishing directly. Section 6.18 proves the compact-support nilpotent and unipotent germ expansions and their scalar homogeneity. Sections 6.20–6.21 prove the every-rank regular Schwartz orbital bounds. Section 6.27 includes inseparable irreducible elements and one-chain primary orbits. Section 6.28 proves every linear or quadratic primary Schwartz bound when the division degree is odd. Section 6.29 proves all ordinary orbital Schwartz bounds in division rank two, and proper-flag bounds in rank three. Section 6.30 gives every-rank closed and nonclosed primary Schwartz bounds for ramified quadratic fields in even division degree when the residue characteristic is odd, and for purely inseparable quadratic fields in characteristic two. Other higher-rank repeated closed-primary bounds, general character integration and elliptic completeness require further arguments.

6.18 Compact-support orbital germs and scalar homogeneity

Continue with \(A=M_r(D)\), \(n=rd\), and the nilpotent measures of (6.194). Write \(\mathcal N\) for the nilpotent cone and \(A_{\mathrm{reg}}\) for the regular semisimple set. The reduced characteristic polynomial is \[ \operatorname{ch}_X(T)=T^n+a_1(X)T^{n-1}+\cdots+a_n(X), \qquad \chi(X)=(a_1(X),\ldots,a_n(X)). \tag{6.202} \] Its coefficients are continuous polynomial functions, \(\chi^{-1}(0)=\mathcal N\), and \(a_i(tX)=t^ia_i(X)\). These statements follow from the splitting-matrix definition and Cayley–Hamilton used in Section 6.1; they require no separability of a nilpotent element. For regular \(X\), use \(O_X(\phi)=\int_{G_X\backslash G}\phi(g^{-1}Xg)d\dot g\), with \(\operatorname{vol}(K)=1\) and Haar measure on the étale torus \(G_X=F[X]^\times\) giving its maximal compact subgroup volume one. In particular \(X\) and \(tX\), for \(t\ne0\), have exactly the same centralizer and Haar measure. These regular measures and the nilpotent measures remain different normalizations.

Lemma 6.91 — restriction to a closed fibre. Let \(q:X\to Y\) be a continuous map of locally compact totally disconnected Hausdorff spaces, and let a group \(H\) act continuously on \(X\), preserving its fibres. For a function \(v\), use \((hv)(x)=v(h^{-1}x)\), and let \(C_c^\infty(X)_H\) be the quotient by the span of \(hv-v\). Suppose \(v\in C_c^\infty(X)\) has zero class after restriction to \(X_y=q^{-1}(y)\). There is a compact open neighborhood \(W\) of \(y\) such that \[ 1_{q^{-1}(W)}v=\sum_{j=1}^m(h_jv_j-v_j), \qquad v_j\in C_c^\infty(q^{-1}(W)). \tag{6.203} \] For every closed subset \(Z\subset X\), restriction \(C_c^\infty(X)\to C_c^\infty(Z)\) is surjective, with kernel the extension by zero of \(C_c^\infty(X\setminus Z)\).

Proof. To prove the restriction assertion, partition the compact support of a test on \(Z\) into finitely many compact open subsets on which it is constant. Each such subset is the intersection with \(Z\) of a compact open subset of \(X\): choose small compact open neighborhoods of its points avoiding the remaining closed part of \(Z\), take a finite cover, and then make the cover disjoint by successive differences. Their characteristic functions extend the test. If an ambient locally constant test is zero on \(Z\), its compact support is disjoint from \(Z\), giving the kernel assertion.

The hypothesis about \(v\) means, by the definition of a linear span, that its restriction is a finite sum \(\sum_j(h_jw_j-w_j)\), with \(w_j\in C_c^\infty(X_y)\). Extend each \(w_j\) to a test \(\widetilde w_j\) on \(X\). The test \(v-\sum_j(h_j\widetilde w_j-\widetilde w_j)\) vanishes on \(X_y\). Its support \(S\) is compact, so \(q(S)\) is compact and does not contain \(y\). Choose compact open \(W\) disjoint from \(q(S)\). Multiplication by \(1_{q^{-1}(W)}\) commutes with every \(h_j\). The asserted identity follows with \(v_j=1_{q^{-1}(W)}\widetilde w_j\). Their supports are compact because \(q^{-1}(W)\) is closed. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.92 — all invariant distributions on the nilpotent cone. With the topology inherited from \(A\), \[ \bigl(C_c^\infty(\mathcal N)_G\bigr)^* =\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash r}\mathbb C\mu_\lambda. \tag{6.204} \] Thus the nilpotent orbital measures are a basis of the invariant linear functionals, and the coinvariant space has dimension equal to the number of partitions of \(r\). The same assertions hold for the unipotent cone \(1+\mathcal N\), with the measures \(U_\lambda\).

Proof. Theorem 6.86 gives locally finite extensions of all the orbit measures to \(\mathcal N\). This point matters: existence of a measure only on each open orbit would not suffice for the following subtraction argument.

The rank vector \((\operatorname{rank}_D X^i)_{1\le i\le r}\) determines the partition by Lemma 6.85. Rank can only drop in a limit, since rank lower bounds are open minor conditions. Among any remaining finite set of types, pick one whose rank vector is maximal in the coordinatewise order. Its orbit is open in the union of the remaining types: for each other type some rank is smaller, and requiring the selected ranks as lower bounds excludes it. Remove this orbit and repeat. At each stage the remainder is closed in the previous space.

An invariant linear functional on a single homogeneous orbit with an invariant measure is a scalar multiple of that measure. To justify this for all linear functionals, identify the orbit with \(G/H\) and use the averaging map \(p_!F(gH)=\int_HF(gh)dh\) from compact tests on \(G\) to tests on the orbit. Compactly supported local sections, obtained from the Gaussian quotient charts in Lemma 6.85, and a compact test on \(H\) of integral one show that this map is surjective. It commutes with left translation. Composing an invariant functional with it gives a left-invariant functional on compact tests on \(G\). Such a functional is a scalar Haar integral: its values on translates of a compact open subgroup are equal, finite-index subdivisions give their ratios for nested subgroups, and finite coset partitions cover every compact test. Quotient integration then gives the same scalar orbital integral on the surjective image of \(p_!\). The needed centralizer unimodularity and invariant orbit measure were proved in Theorem 6.86.

Restrict an invariant functional on the remaining cone to its selected open orbit, subtract that scalar multiple of \(\mu_\lambda\), and continue on the closed remainder. Lemma 6.91 identifies a functional zero on the open part with a functional on the closed remainder. Finitely many steps express it as a sum of the orbital measures. Applying this procedure to a zero sum proves their linear independence as well. Their common pairing with the coinvariant space separates its points, since every linear functional on that quotient is invariant. Thus that space injects into a finite-dimensional space with these coordinates. Independence makes the coordinate map surjective, so its dimension is precisely the number of partitions. Translation \(X\mapsto1+X\) proves the group assertion. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.93 — the compact-support germ expansion. There are conjugation-invariant locally constant functions \(g_\lambda\) on \(A_{\mathrm{reg}}\) such that, for each \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(A)\), a compact open neighborhood \(W_\phi\) of \(0\) in \(F^n\) satisfies \[ O_X(\phi)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash r} g_\lambda(X)\mu_\lambda(\phi) \quad\bigl(X\in A_{\mathrm{reg}},\ \chi(X)\in W_\phi\bigr). \tag{6.205} \] The functions' germs near the nilpotent fibre are uniquely determined. One neighborhood works for every test in any given finite-dimensional test space.

Proof. By Lemmas 6.91–6.92 choose tests \(\phi_\lambda\in C_c^\infty(A)\) with \(\mu_\kappa(\phi_\lambda)=\delta_{\kappa\lambda}\). Define \(g_\lambda(X)=O_X(\phi_\lambda)\).

These regular orbital integrals are finite and locally constant. To obtain this assertion from the proved group version rather than assume it for the Lie algebra, fix a compact test support and a small neighborhood of the chosen \(X\). Choose \(b\in F^\times\) small enough that \(1+bY\) is invertible for every matrix in that support and neighborhood. Then \(\phi(Y)=f(1+bY)\) for the compact group test \(f(g)=\phi((g-1)/b)\), extended by zero. The centralizers of \(X\) and \(1+bX\) agree. The properness and uniform fixed-torus assertion of Lemma 6.18, together with the local conjugacy charts of Theorem 6.2, prove the assertion. Explicitly, uniform properness puts all contributing quotient representatives in one compact set; smoothness of \(f\) makes its values unchanged on a sufficiently small torus neighborhood uniformly over that set. The conjugacy chart then gives a neighborhood in the whole regular set. This also proves conjugation invariance with the chosen torus normalization.

Subtract the finite test \(\sum_\lambda\mu_\lambda(\phi)\phi_\lambda\) from \(\phi\), and call the difference \(v\). Every nilpotent orbital integral of \(v\) is zero. Lemma 6.92 says precisely that its restriction to \(\mathcal N\) is zero in the coinvariant space. Apply Lemma 6.91 to \(q=\chi\), whose zero fibre is \(\mathcal N\). On \(\chi^{-1}(W_\phi)\), the test \(v\) is a finite sum of conjugation differences. Integration over a regular orbit in that set kills each difference, proving (6.205). All these integrations are of compact tests, so no Schwartz convergence assertion has entered.

If another family gives (6.205), insert the finitely many dual tests \(\phi_\lambda\). It agrees with \(g_\lambda\) on some common neighborhood of the zero fibre in the regular set. This is uniqueness of germs; it does not assert linear independence of their restrictions as functions. Finally intersect the finitely many neighborhoods belonging to a basis of a finite-dimensional test space and use linearity. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.94 — homogeneous representatives of the germs. Put \[ m_\lambda=\dim_F\mathfrak n_\lambda =\frac{d^2}{2}\left(r^2-\sum_i c_i^2\right). \tag{6.206} \] Each germ in Theorem 6.93 has a unique globally defined homogeneous representative \(\Gamma_\lambda\) on \(A_{\mathrm{reg}}\). It is conjugation invariant, locally constant, and satisfies \[ \begin{gathered} \mu_\lambda(\phi(t\,\cdot)) =|t|_F^{-m_\lambda}\mu_\lambda(\phi),\\ \Gamma_\lambda(tX)=|t|_F^{-m_\lambda}\Gamma_\lambda(X) \qquad(t\in F^\times). \end{gathered} \tag{6.207} \] Formula (6.205) holds with \(\Gamma_\lambda\) in place of \(g_\lambda\), after shrinking its neighborhood if necessary. The exponent uses the half dimension of the orbit; no square root of a scalar in \(F\) is required.

Proof. The first identity follows immediately by the change of variables \(Y=tX\) in the radical integral (6.194). Regular orbital measures instead satisfy \(O_{tX}(\phi)=O_X(\phi(t\,\cdot))\), since their centralizers and Haar measures are identical. Let \(\varpi=\varpi_F\) and \(q=q_F\). Apply (6.205) to each \(\phi_\lambda(\varpi\,\cdot)\). Their nilpotent integrals are \(q^{m_\lambda}\delta_{\kappa\lambda}\), giving \(g_\lambda(\varpi X)=q^{m_\lambda}g_\lambda(X)\) on one sufficiently small common neighborhood.

We also need a neighborhood uniform over all units. Each \(\phi_\lambda\) is supported in a lattice \(M\) and invariant under translation by a smaller lattice \(L\). For sufficiently large \(h\), every \(u\in1+\varpi^h\mathcal O_F\) has \((u-1)M\subset L\) and preserves \(M\). It therefore fixes \(\phi_\lambda\) under scalar substitution, including outside \(M\). The family \(\{\phi_\lambda(u\,\cdot):u\in\mathcal O_F^\times\}\) is consequently finite. Apply (6.205) to this finite family. The first identity of (6.207) makes its dual integrals unchanged, so \(g_\lambda(uX)=g_\lambda(X)\) for every unit on a single common neighborhood.

Inside that neighborhood choose \(U=\{X:|a_i(X)|_F\le\epsilon^i\text{ for every }i\}\) for a sufficiently small positive power \(\epsilon\) of \(|\varpi|_F\). It is invariant under units and stable under multiplication by \(\varpi\). The two identities just proved imply the required scalar rule whenever both endpoints lie in \(U\): intermediate powers of \(\varpi\) then stay in \(U\), and negative powers are obtained by reversing the same identities.

For arbitrary regular \(X\), take \(k\) large enough that \(\varpi^kX\in U\), and define \[ \Gamma_\lambda(X)=q^{-km_\lambda} g_\lambda(\varpi^kX). \tag{6.208} \] The relation for one power of \(\varpi\) makes this independent of all sufficiently large \(k\). The unit relation gives (6.207) for every scalar. A fixed \(k\) works on a neighborhood of any given regular \(X\), proving local constancy; conjugation invariance follows likewise. On \(U\) this equals \(g_\lambda\). Any homogeneous function with that germ agrees everywhere after scaling into \(U\), proving uniqueness and independence of the chosen dual tests. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.95 — group germs, finite packets and a scalar ray. For each compact group test \(f\), on a sufficiently small invariant neighborhood of the unipotent fibre, \[ O_g(f)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash r} \Gamma_\lambda(g-1)U_\lambda(f) \qquad(g\in G_{\mathrm{reg}}). \tag{6.209} \] For fixed regular \(X\) and fixed additive compact test \(\phi\), all sufficiently large integers \(k\) satisfy the exact equality \[ O_{\varpi^kX}(\phi)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash r} q^{km_\lambda}\Gamma_\lambda(X)\mu_\lambda(\phi). \tag{6.210} \] A common neighborhood, or a common sufficiently large \(k\), works for a finite-dimensional space of tests. In particular it works for tests with a common compact support bound and a common additive constancy lattice.

Proof. The function \(\phi(Y)=f(1+Y)\), extended by zero where \(1+Y\) is singular, is compactly supported and locally constant on \(A\). The support of \(f\) is a compact subset of the open set \(G\), so this extension is locally zero at the boundary. Equation (6.195) gives \(\mu_\lambda(\phi)=U_\lambda(f)\). The centralizers of \(g\) and \(g-1\) agree. Apply (6.205) to \(\phi\) and use Theorem 6.94. This proves (6.209) without an exponential map. Equation (6.210) follows by scaling into the neighborhood of (6.205) and then applying (6.207). The finite-packet assertion is the last part of Theorem 6.93. A common compact support bound meets only finitely many cosets of a fixed additive lattice, so the specified test space is finite dimensional. \(\square\)

Example 6.96 — quadratic orders and the rank-two germs. Let \(D=F\), \(r=2\), and keep precisely the measures above. There are two nilpotent types, \(0=(1,1)\) and \(\mathrm{nil}=(2)\), with \(m_0=0\), \(m_{\mathrm{nil}}=1\). For a split \(X\), let \(x,y\in F\) be its distinct eigenvalues. The three regular types have the following germs: \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} &\Gamma_0(X)&\Gamma_{\mathrm{nil}}(X)\\ \hline \text{split}&0&|x-y|_F^{-1}\\ E/F\text{ unramified quadratic} &-2/(q-1)&(q+1)|b|_F^{-1}/(q-1)\\ E/F\text{ ramified quadratic} &-1/(q-1)&q|b|_F^{-1}/(q-1) \end{array} \tag{6.211} \] In the field cases write \(X=a+b\theta\) in \(E\), where \(\mathcal O_E=\mathcal O_F+\mathcal O_F\theta\), taking \(\theta\) to be a residue-field generator in the unramified case and a uniformizer in the ramified case. Then \(b\ne0\). The formulas hold for separable quadratic fields, including wildly ramified fields and residue characteristic two.

Proof. Put \(\phi_R=1_{\varpi^{-R}M_2(\mathcal O_F)}\). From (6.194), \(\mu_0(\phi_R)=1\) and \(\mu_{\mathrm{nil}}(\phi_R)=q^R\). Consequently \(\phi_{\mathrm{nil}}=(\phi_1-\phi_0)/(q-1)\) and \(\phi_{0}^\vee=(q\phi_0-\phi_1)/(q-1)\) are dual tests for the two measures.

In the split case, Gaussian Iwasawa coordinates on \(T\backslash G\) give integration over \(n(z)k\), with \(dz\) of integral volume one and \(dk\) probability measure. The modulus cancels when the diagonal is placed before the upper radical, as in the quotient integration in (6.46). Conjugating \(\operatorname{diag}(x,y)\) by \(n(z)\) gives upper entry \((x-y)z\). Thus, whenever \(\varpi^Rx\) and \(\varpi^Ry\) are integral, \(O_X(\phi_R)=q^R|x-y|_F^{-1}\). The two dual tests give the first row near zero, and homogeneity gives it everywhere.

Here is a direct lattice count for the field cases. The stated integral bases exist without a tameness assumption. In the unramified case, independence of \(1,\overline\theta\) over the residue field prevents cancellation of their lowest valuations. In the ramified quadratic case the valuations of \(a\) and \(b\theta\) have different parity, so the same assertion holds with the ramified valuation. These observations show that integral elements have integral coordinates in the respective bases.

Every \(\mathcal O_F\)-lattice in \(E\), up to multiplication by \(E^\times\), is \(L_i=\mathcal O_F+\varpi^i\mathcal O_F\theta\), for a unique \(i\ge0\). Indeed scale its \(\mathcal O_E\)-saturation to \(\mathcal O_E\), then choose a unit in the lattice and scale it to \(1\). The quotient of the resulting lattice by \(\mathcal O_F\) is an ideal in the rank-one free module \(\mathcal O_E/\mathcal O_F\); subtracting an integral scalar from a lift of its generator gives the displayed form. Its ring of multipliers is \(\mathcal O_i=\mathcal O_F+\varpi^i\mathcal O_E=L_i\): a multiplier must lie there by evaluation on \(1\), and this module is itself a ring. Distinct \(i\) give distinct multiplier rings, proving uniqueness.

The double coset in \(E^\times\backslash G/K\) belonging to \(L_i\) has quotient measure \([\mathcal O_E^\times:\mathcal O_i^\times]\). This follows by quotient integration from \(\operatorname{vol}(K)=\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O_E^\times)=1\) and stabilizer \(\mathcal O_i^\times\). The index is one at \(i=0\). For \(i\ge1\), reduction modulo \(\varpi^i\mathcal O_E\) gives respectively \[ [\mathcal O_E^\times:\mathcal O_i^\times] =\frac{(q^2-1)q^{2i-2}}{(q-1)q^{i-1}} =(q+1)q^{i-1}, \qquad \frac{(q-1)q^{2i-1}}{(q-1)q^{i-1}}=q^i. \] These are just unit counts in the unramified and ramified quotient rings; the ramified residue field has size \(q\), even in the wild case.

Let \(l=v_F(b)\) and take \(R\) large enough that \(\varpi^Ra\) is integral and \(M=R+l\ge0\). The condition \(\varpi^RX L_i\subset L_i\) is exactly \(i\le M\), by the multiplier ring. Therefore \[ O_X(\phi_R)= \begin{cases} 1+(q+1)\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{M}q^{i-1} =\bigl((q+1)q^M-2\bigr)/(q-1),&E/F\text{ unramified},\\ 1+\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{M}q^i =\bigl(q^{M+1}-1\bigr)/(q-1),&E/F\text{ ramified}. \end{cases} \] For small \(X\), the dual tests above read off the last two rows of (6.211), since \(q^l=|b|_F^{-1}\). The global homogeneous extension proves the formulas for every regular \(X\) of those types. The two elliptic constant terms differ because the torus Haar measure gives its maximal compact subgroup volume one; it does not give \(E^\times/F^\times\) volume one in both cases. \(\square\)

Kottwitz, §§6.1–6.4 and Lemma 27.1 in the freely accessible Clay article, treats the compact-support localization method. The argument here proves the needed finite-commutator identity and nilpotent-measure input for \(\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), and derives its scalar factors and group passage directly. Neither the finite-packet neighborhood nor the fixed-ray formula is a uniform assertion for all Schwartz cutoffs. Section 6.20 gives exact rank-two formulas, and Section 6.21 proves the elliptic semisimple Schwartz bound in every division rank. Singular-set character integration, elliptic completeness and the full higher-degree representation transfer require further proofs.

6.19. Polynomial weights and parabolic orbital descent

Let \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), with the Cartan length and spherical function of Sections 6.9 and 6.15. For \(a\ge0\) write \[ V_a^G(g)=\Xi_G(g)(1+\sigma_G(g))^{-a}. \tag{6.212} \] For a standard Levi \(M=\prod_iG_i\), put \(\Xi_M(m)=\prod_i\Xi_{G_i}(m_i)\). We use the ambient length \(\sigma_G(m)\), which measures relative central scales between different blocks. All constants may depend on the fixed Haar measures.

Lemma 6.97 — a quantitative unipotent substitution. Let \(P=MN\) have \(s\) blocks, and let \(\gamma=(\gamma_i)\in M\) be regular with disjoint reduced-polynomial roots in different blocks. For \(m\in M\), set \(\mu=m^{-1}\gamma m\). The polynomial bijection \(\Phi_\mu\) of (6.45) has the following uniform estimate: \[ \sigma_G(n)\le C_\gamma+C_G\sigma_G(n^{-1}\mu n) \qquad(n\in N,\ m\in M). \tag{6.213} \] Here \(C_G\) depends only on the block sizes and \(D\); \(C_\gamma\) is independent of \(m,n\). In particular, for every \(q\ge0\), \[ (1+\sigma_G(n))^q \le C_{\gamma,q}(1+\sigma_G(n^{-1}\mu n))^q. \tag{6.214} \]

Proof. Give block matrices the maximum entry norm induced by \(|\cdot|_D\). For the corresponding operator norm on \(D^r\), Cartan diagonalization gives \(\|g\|\|g^{-1}\|=q_D^{\sigma_G(g)}\). Fix an \(\mathcal O_F\)-basis of \(\mathcal O_D\). The maximum of its coordinate absolute values, raised to the fixed power \(d\), is comparable to \(|\cdot|_D\). To see the lower comparison, the coordinate unit sphere is compact and contains no zero; the continuous division norm has a positive minimum there. Scaling by powers of \(\varpi_F\) proves the comparison everywhere. The upper comparison follows from the triangle inequality. The same comparisons apply to all the finitely many block coordinate spaces.

Write \(n=1+X\), \(u=\Phi_\mu(n)=1+U\), and order the coordinates by block height \(j-i\). In these coordinates \[ U_{ij}=L_{ij,\mu}(X_{ij})+Q_{ij,\mu}(X_{<j-i}), \qquad L_{ij,\mu}(Z)=Z-\mu_i^{-1}Z\mu_j. \tag{6.215} \] The second term is a polynomial in smaller heights: expand \((1+X)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{s-1}(-X)^k\). The degrees are bounded in terms of \(s\), and its coefficients are polynomials in entries of \(\mu\) and \(\mu^{-1}\). No exponential or logarithm of a matrix is used.

The maps \(L_{ij,\mu}\) are conjugate as \(F\)-linear maps to \(L_{ij,\gamma}\), by \(Z\mapsto m_iZm_j^{-1}\). Their determinants are thus fixed nonzero scalars. Nonvanishing follows by separable splitting: their eigenvalues are \(1-\alpha_j/\alpha_i\), with \(\alpha_i,\alpha_j\) from distinct blocks. In fixed \(F\)-coordinates, the adjugate formula bounds the entries of \(L_{ij,\mu}^{-1}\) by a fixed power of \(\max(1,\|\mu\|,\|\mu^{-1}\|)\), times a constant depending on these fixed determinants. Apply these inverses successively in (6.215). Induction on height gives integers \(B,L\), depending only on the block coordinate dimensions, such that \[ \max(1,\|X\|) \le C_\gamma \max(1,\|\mu\|,\|\mu^{-1}\|)^B \max(1,\|U\|)^L. \tag{6.216} \] This induction is a finite composition of polynomials and linear inverses, so the asserted bound follows by bounding each coefficient and each monomial. It is valid over any field characteristic.

The absolute reduced norm of \(\mu\) is fixed. If its Cartan integers are \(h_1\ge\cdots\ge h_r\), their sum is fixed, while their spread is \(\sigma_G(\mu)\). Therefore \(\log\max(1,\|\mu\|,\|\mu^{-1}\|)\le C_\gamma+C\sigma_G(\mu)\). For any unipotent \(1+U\), the same norm comparison bounds \(\log\max(1,\|U\|)\) by \(C\sigma_G(1+U)\); its inverse is a polynomial of degree at most \(s-1\). Applying these observations also to \(1+X\), (6.216) gives \[ \sigma_G(n)\le C_\gamma+C\bigl(\sigma_G(\mu)+\sigma_G(u)\bigr). \tag{6.217} \] Put \(y=\mu u=n^{-1}\mu n\). It is block upper triangular, with diagonal blocks \(\mu_i\). Both \(y\) and \(y^{-1}\) contain the respective diagonal blocks of \(\mu\) and \(\mu^{-1}\). Hence \(\|\mu\|\le\|y\|\), \(\|\mu^{-1}\|\le\|y^{-1}\|\), and \(\sigma_G(\mu)\le\sigma_G(y)\). Submultiplicativity gives \(\sigma_G(u)\le\sigma_G(\mu)+\sigma_G(y)\le2\sigma_G(y)\). This proves (6.213). Increasing the positive constant after taking the \(q\)-th power proves (6.214). \(\square\)

Proposition 6.98 — uniform Schwartz decay after radical integration. For every \(A\ge0\) there are an integer \(N\) and a constant \(C_A\) such that, for all \(m\in M\), \[ \begin{aligned} \delta_P(m)^{-1/2}\int_{\overline N}V_N^G(mn)\,dn &\le C_A\Xi_M(m)(1+\sigma_G(m))^{-A},\\ \delta_P(m)^{1/2}\int_N V_N^G(mn)\,dn &\le C_A\Xi_M(m)(1+\sigma_G(m))^{-A}. \end{aligned} \tag{6.218} \] Consequently the normalized constant term \[ f^P(m)=\delta_P(m)^{1/2} \int_N\int_K f(k^{-1}mnk)\,dk\,dn \tag{6.219} \] is absolutely convergent for \(f\in\mathcal S_\omega\), and \[ \sup_{m\in M} \frac{|f^P(m)|(1+\sigma_G(m))^A}{\Xi_M(m)} \le C_Ap_N(f). \tag{6.220} \] It is smooth and bi-invariant under a compact open subgroup of \(M\). The estimates define a continuous map at every fixed Schwartz level. They concern the ambient length modulo \(Z_G\), without imposing a character under the entire centre of \(M\).

Proof. Theorem 6.75 supplies, for every opposite standard radical, a polynomial height bound \(\int_{h(n)\le H}e(n)dn\le C(1+H)^{b_P}\). Choose an integer \(B>b_P+1\). By (6.167), \(\sigma_G(n)\ge h(n)/(r(r-1))\) when \(r>1\). Summing the height shells gives \[ \int_{\overline N}e(n)(1+\sigma_G(n))^{-B}dn<\infty. \tag{6.221} \] A trivial radical is given mass one and satisfies the same conclusion.

Reduce \(m\) by Cartan decomposition in each block, using \(K\cap M\) on both sides. These compact elements preserve radical Haar measure, and the functions on both sides of (6.218) are unchanged. Thus \(m\) may be taken diagonal and sorted within each block. The triangular norm argument in (6.173) gives \(\sigma_G(mn)\ge\sigma_G(m)\) and \(\sigma_G(mn)\ge\sigma_G(n)/2\). If \(b\) is the exponent in (6.168), that estimate and (6.166) give \[ \begin{aligned} \Xi_G(mn)&\le C\delta_B(m)^{1/2}e(n)(1+\sigma_G(mn))^b,\\ (1+\sigma_G(mn))^{-A-B} &\le 2^B(1+\sigma_G(m))^{-A}(1+\sigma_G(n))^{-B}. \end{aligned} \tag{6.222} \] Take an integer \(N\ge b+A+B\), integrate and use (6.221). Within-block sorting gives \(\delta_B(m)^{1/2}=\delta_P(m)^{1/2}D_{C,M}(m)^{1/2}\). The lower bound \(D_{C,M}^{1/2}\le\Xi_M\) follows by multiplying (6.168) for the Levi factors. This proves the first inequality in (6.218).

Reverse the order of the blocks by a permutation in \(K\). The upper radical becomes the opposite radical of that reversed parabolic. Its Levi spherical function is unchanged and its modulus is \(\delta_P(m)^{-1}\), proving the second inequality, with its stated normalization. The pointwise bound \(|f(k^{-1}mnk)|\le p_N(f)V_N^G(mn)\) then proves absolute convergence, Fubini and (6.220).

For smoothness, choose a principal congruence subgroup \(J_0\), normal in \(K\), contained in both stabilizers of \(f\). The compact conjugation average in (6.219) is bi-\(J_0\)-invariant. Left multiplication by \(J_0\cap M\) does not change its integral. For right multiplication, conjugate the radical variable by that compact Levi element, whose Haar Jacobian is one, and use right invariance of the average. Thus \(f^P\) is bi-\(J_0\cap M\)-invariant. Inequality (6.220) for differences proves continuity at a fixed level. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.99 — polynomially weighted orbital reduction. Let \(\gamma\) be regular, and choose its primary-factor Levi \(M=\prod_{i=1}^sG_i\), so that \(\gamma_i\) is elliptic regular in \(G_i\). Let \(w:G\to[0,\infty)\) be measurable, left \(M\)-invariant and right \(K\)-invariant, with \(w(n)\le C_w(1+\sigma_G(n))^q\) on \(N\), for some \(q\ge0\). For every \(a\ge0\) there are \(N\) and \(C_{\gamma,a,w}\) such that \[ \int_{T\backslash G}V_N^G(x^{-1}\gamma x)w(x)\,d\dot x \le C_{\gamma,a,w}\prod_{i=1}^s O_{\gamma_i}^{G_i}(V_a^{G_i}). \tag{6.223} \] The integrals are nonnegative extended integrals, so the assertion does not presume their finiteness. For \(s=1\), the weight is constant and the estimate is immediate with \(N\ge a\).

Proof. For \(s>1\), use the quotient coordinates of Theorem 6.20. At \(x=mnk\), the weight equals \(w(n)\) and \(\mu=m^{-1}\gamma m\). Lemma 6.97 bounds it by \(C_{\gamma,q,w}(1+\sigma_G(n^{-1}\mu n))^q\). The bijection \(u=\Phi_\mu(n)\) has the constant Haar Jacobian \(J_N(\gamma)>0\) of (6.45). By Tonelli and \(K\)-bi-invariance, the left side of (6.223) is therefore at most \[ C_{\gamma,q,w}J_N(\gamma)^{-1} \int_{T\backslash M}\int_N V_{N-q}^G(m^{-1}\gamma m\,u)\,du\,d\dot m. \tag{6.224} \] Choose \(N\) large enough that Proposition 6.98 applies to \(N-q\) with exponent \(sa\). The modulus at \(m^{-1}\gamma m\) equals its fixed value at \(\gamma\), and is absorbed into the constant. Thus (6.224) is bounded by \(C\int_{T\backslash M}\Xi_M(m^{-1}\gamma m)(1+\sigma_G(m^{-1}\gamma m))^{-sa}d\dot m\). For every block diagonal \(y=(y_i)\), \(\sigma_{G_i}(y_i)\le\sigma_G(y)\). Consequently \[ (1+\sigma_G(y))^{-sa} \le\prod_i(1+\sigma_{G_i}(y_i))^{-a}. \tag{6.225} \] Product quotient integration and Tonelli now give (6.223). This proves the reduction in either characteristic. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.100 — convergence when the primary blocks have division rank one. Under the hypotheses of Theorem 6.99, suppose that every \(G_i\) is \(D^\times\). Then the weighted orbital integral of every \(f\in\mathcal S_\omega\) is absolutely convergent and defines a continuous functional at each Schwartz level. For some integer \(N\), and every integer \(A\ge0\), \[ \begin{aligned} \left|\int_{T\backslash G}f(x^{-1}\gamma x)w(x)d\dot x\right| &\le C_{\gamma,w}p_N(f),\\ \int_{T\backslash G}|(f-f_R)(x^{-1}\gamma x)|w(x)d\dot x &\le C_{\gamma,w}(1+R)^{-A}p_{N+A}(f), \qquad f_R=1_{\{\sigma_G\le R\}}f. \end{aligned} \tag{6.226} \] This includes every split regular class in \(\mathrm{GL}_r(F)\). More generally, (6.223) gives the same conclusion at any regular class once the displayed elliptic factors are finite for some \(a\). Section 6.21 proves the required elliptic bound in every division rank and the resulting unconditional regular weighted convergence.

Proof. Section 6.4 proves compactness of \(D^\times/F^\times\). Hence each \(T_i\backslash D^\times\) is compact, and \(V_a^{D^\times}\) is bounded there. The right side of (6.223) is finite. Bound \(|f|\) by \(p_N(f)V_N^G\) to obtain the first assertion. On the tail \(\sigma_G(x^{-1}\gamma x)>R\), take the factor \((1+R)^{-A}\) out of the bound using \(p_{N+A}(f)\). This proves the second estimate without exchanging a conditionally convergent limit and an integral. The same argument proves the conditional extension when the elliptic factors are finite. \(\square\)

The polynomial weight hypothesis includes the convex-hull weights for this Levi. In the vector space \(\mathfrak a_M^G=\mathbb R^s/\mathbb R(1,\ldots,1)\), fix a Lebesgue measure and let \(v_M^G(x)\) be the volume of the convex hull of the finitely many Iwasawa vectors \(-H_Q(x)\), over parabolics \(Q\) with Levi \(M\). Use normalized block coordinates: if the Levi part in \(x=m_Qn_Qk_Q\) has blocks \(m_{Q,i}\) of division size \(r_i\), the \(i\)-th coordinate is \((r_id)^{-1}\log_{q_F}|\operatorname{Nrd}(m_{Q,i})|_F\). A central scalar therefore gives equal coordinates in every block. Left multiplication by \(m\in M\) adds the same vector \(H_M(m)\) to all of them; right multiplication by \(K\) leaves them fixed. Thus \(v_M^G\) has the required invariances. For a unipotent \(n\), its full lattice volume is one. Each projected image-lattice volume used in its Iwasawa decomposition is between fixed powers of \(\|n^{-1}\|^{-1}\) and \(\|n\|\), by the minimax calculation of Lemma 6.73, also after the finitely many block permutations. Its logarithm has absolute value at most \(C_G\sigma_G(n)\). Differences of consecutive projected logarithms give the block coordinates of \(H_Q(n)\), with the specified degree normalization and fixed conversion factors from division norms to reduced norms. Their convex hull is contained in a cube of side \(C_G(1+\sigma_G(n))\). In dimension \(s-1\) its volume is at most \(C'_G(1+\sigma_G(n))^{s-1}\). The zero-dimensional volume for \(M=G\) is one. This proves the polynomial weight hypothesis directly.

Arthur, The trace formula in invariant form, Section 8, Lemma 8.1, treats the corresponding convergence estimate over completions of \(\mathbb Q\). The estimates above use block matrix coordinates over \(D\) and do not require a restriction on the field characteristic.

6.20. Elliptic convergence in division rank two

Let \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\), \(d=\deg D\), \(q=q_D=q_F^d\), \(K=\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathcal O_D)\), and \(Z=F^\times\). Normalize \(\operatorname{vol}_G(K)=\operatorname{vol}_Z(\mathcal O_F^\times)=1\). Unless specified otherwise, the elliptic torus measure is the one from Section 6.6: \(\operatorname{vol}(T/Z)=1\). This convention matters when comparing an orbital integral with one normalized by \(\operatorname{vol}_T(\mathcal O_E^\times)=1\).

Lemma 6.101 — the lattice tree and its quotient measure. Vertices are right \(\mathcal O_D\)-lattices in \(D^2\), modulo \(\Lambda\sim\Lambda\Pi^j\). Two vertices are adjacent when representatives satisfy \(\Lambda\Pi\subsetneq\Lambda'\subsetneq\Lambda\). Give each edge length one. This graph \(\mathcal T\) is a \((q+1)\)-regular tree, and \[ \operatorname{dist}(x_0,gx_0)=\sigma(g),\qquad C:=\operatorname{Stab}_G(x_0)=\bigcup_{j\in\mathbb Z}(\Pi I)^jK, \qquad \operatorname{vol}(C/Z)=d. \tag{6.227} \] Here \(x_0=[\mathcal O_D^2]\), and \(\sigma\) is exactly the Cartan length used above.

Proof. Integral elimination over \(D\), as in Sections 6.1 and 6.9, puts a pair of lattice classes into the form \(\Lambda_0=v\mathcal O_D+w\mathcal O_D\), \(\Lambda=v\mathcal O_D+w\Pi^\ell\mathcal O_D\), with \(\ell\ge0\). The neighbours of any vertex are the lines of its two-dimensional residue space, hence number \(q+1\). If \(\ell>0\), there is exactly one neighbour of \([\Lambda]\) with relative spread \(\ell-1\): it is represented by \(v\Pi\mathcal O_D+w\Pi^\ell\mathcal O_D\). After right scaling by \(\Pi^{-1}\), this is the preceding lattice in the displayed chain. The other neighbours have representatives \((v+w\Pi^\ell b)\mathcal O_D+w\Pi^{\ell+1}\mathcal O_D\), with \(b\) ranging over residue representatives. Their relative spreads are \(\ell+1\), by an integral basis change of \(\Lambda_0\). Thus every nonbase vertex has one predecessor and all its other neighbours are farther away. The chains connect every vertex to \(x_0\); a cycle would give a farthest vertex with two predecessors. The graph is therefore a tree, and its distance is the relative spread. This proves the first equality in (6.227).

A stabilizing matrix satisfies \(g\mathcal O_D^2=\mathcal O_D^2\Pi^j\). Multiplying on the left by \((\Pi I)^{-j}\) puts it in \(K\), proving the description of \(C\). The element \(\Pi I\) normalizes \(K\), since conjugation by \(\Pi\) preserves \(\mathcal O_D\). A central scalar has division valuation in \(d\mathbb Z\), and \(\Pi^d/\varpi_F\) is a unit. Hence \(C/ZK\) has precisely \(d\) cosets. Quotient integration gives \(\operatorname{vol}(ZK/Z)=\operatorname{vol}(K)/\operatorname{vol}(Z\cap K)=1\); all \(d\) cosets have that volume. This proves (6.227). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.102 — the spherical function for \(\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\). Put \(\beta=(q-1)/(q+1)\). Then \[ \Xi(g)=(1+\beta\sigma(g))q^{-\sigma(g)/2}. \tag{6.228} \]

Proof. Write \(h=\Pi I\). The compact-model function \(e\) from (6.165) satisfies \(e(hg)=e(g)\), since \(h\in B\) and \(\delta_B(h)=1\). Conjugation by \(h\) preserves Haar probability on \(K\); therefore \(\Xi(hg)=\int_K e(khg)dk=\Xi(g)\). Cartan decomposition now makes \(\Xi(g)\) a function \(\phi_\ell\) of \(\ell=\sigma(g)\) alone.

For \(a=\operatorname{diag}(\Pi,1)\), the image lattice of the bottom row of \(ka\) is \(\mathcal O_D\) when \(k_{22}\) is a unit, and \(\Pi\mathcal O_D\) otherwise. These alternatives have probabilities \(q/(q+1)\) and \(1/(q+1)\), by uniform reduction of the primitive bottom row to a residue line. The full lattice volume is \(q^{-1}\). Formula (6.166) consequently gives \(\phi_1=(q q^{-1/2}+q^{1/2})/(q+1)=2\sqrt q/(q+1)\), while \(\phi_0=1\). The product formula (6.180), averaged over the neighbours of a vertex at distance \(\ell\ge1\), yields \[ q\phi_{\ell+1}+\phi_{\ell-1}=2\sqrt q\,\phi_\ell. \tag{6.229} \] There is one predecessor and \(q\) successors by Lemma 6.101. For \(u_\ell=q^{\ell/2}\phi_\ell\), this says \(u_{\ell+1}-u_\ell=u_\ell-u_{\ell-1}\). Its initial values are \(u_0=1\), \(u_1=1+\beta\), so \(u_\ell=1+\beta\ell\). This proves (6.228), with no restriction on the characteristic or on \(d\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.103 — exact elliptic radial orbital sums. Let \(\gamma\in G\) be elliptic regular, and let \(S_\gamma\) be its fixed set in the geometric tree. This set is either a finite subtree containing vertices or the midpoint of an inverted edge. In the first case put \(h_\gamma=\#(S_\gamma\cap\mathcal T^0)\) and \(b_\gamma=(q-1)h_\gamma+2\). For every vertex \(v\), \[ \operatorname{dist}(v,\gamma v) =2\operatorname{dist}(v,S_\gamma). \tag{6.230} \] For any nonnegative function \(F\) on the nonnegative integers, the orbital integral of the function \(g\mapsto F(\sigma(g))\) is the following extended integral: \[ O_\gamma(F\circ\sigma)= \begin{cases} d\displaystyle\left(h_\gamma F(0)+b_\gamma\sum_{j\ge1}q^{j-1}F(2j)\right), &S_\gamma\text{ contains a vertex},\\[2mm] 2d\displaystyle\sum_{j\ge0}q^jF(2j+1), &\gamma\text{ inverts an edge}. \end{cases} \tag{6.231} \] If instead \(T=E^\times\), \(E=F[\gamma]\), has maximal compact subgroup of volume one, divide the right side by the ramification index \(e(E/F)\).

Proof: the fixed set is finite. The quotient \(E^\times/F^\times\) is compact: valuations give only \(e(E/F)\) classes modulo central valuations, and each is represented by a compact unit set. Its image in \(G/Z\) is compact. A vertex stabilizer is open, so the orbit of \(x_0\) under the cyclic closure of \(\gamma\) is finite. Its finite convex hull is invariant. Repeatedly remove all end vertices of this finite tree. The remaining centre is a vertex or an edge, and its barycentre is fixed by \(\gamma\). Thus \(S_\gamma\) is nonempty. It is closed and convex: an isometry fixing the endpoints of a unique geodesic fixes that geodesic pointwise.

If the fixed set were unbounded, local finiteness would give a ray of fixed vertices. Indeed one can choose, successively, an outward edge containing infinitely many of those vertices; only finitely many choices occur at each step. Base the ray at a fixed vertex. A conjugate of \(K\) fixing that base acts transitively on vertices at each given distance, by integral diagonalization. The closed sets of its elements carrying a standard initial ray of length \(j\) to the given one are nonempty, nested and compact. Their intersection is nonempty. After one change of basis the ray thus has representatives \(\Lambda_j=v\mathcal O_D+w\Pi^j\mathcal O_D\), for every \(j\ge0\). Since \(\gamma\) fixes their classes, \(\gamma\Lambda_j=\Lambda_j\Pi^{a_j}\). Lattice volumes give \(2a_j=v_F(\operatorname{Nrd}\gamma)\), so the same integer \(a\) works for every \(j\). Intersecting these equalities shows \(\gamma(v\mathcal O_D)=v\mathcal O_D\Pi^a\). Thus the right \(D\)-line \(vD\) is invariant under \(\gamma\), contradicting the irreducible reduced polynomial, by the first part of Lemma 6.18. The fixed set is therefore bounded and finite as a subdivided tree. If it contains no original vertex, convexity makes it exactly one edge midpoint, and that edge is inverted.

Proof: displacement and counting. For a vertex outside \(S_\gamma\), let \(p\) be the closest point of this finite convex subtree. If \(p\) is a vertex, the first edge towards \(v\) cannot be preserved by \(\gamma\): otherwise that edge would be fixed pointwise, contradicting the choice of \(p\). The paths towards \(v\) and \(\gamma v\) therefore start in different components at \(p\). Their union is the geodesic from \(v\) to \(\gamma v\), proving (6.230). For an inverted edge, its two half-edges are exchanged, giving the same conclusion.
