If there are \(h=h_\gamma\) fixed vertices, the number of edges leaving their finite subtree is \((q+1)h-2(h-1)=(q-1)h+2=b_\gamma\). There are \(b_\gamma q^{j-1}\) vertices at distance \(j\ge1\) from it: choose the exit edge, then one of \(q\) forward edges at each further step. These branches never meet in a tree. For an inverted edge there are \(2q^j\) vertices at distance \(j+1/2\) from its midpoint.

Quotient integration, with \(\operatorname{vol}(T/Z)=1\), gives \(O_\gamma(F\circ\sigma)=\int_{G/Z}F(\sigma(x^{-1}\gamma x))d\bar x\). The integrand depends only on \(v=xx_0\), because its argument is \(\operatorname{dist}(v,\gamma v)\). Each vertex has measure \(\operatorname{vol}(C/Z)=d\) by (6.227). The shell counts prove (6.231), using Tonelli before any convergence claim. With maximal-compact torus normalization, \(\operatorname{vol}(T/Z)=e(E/F)\): there are that many valuation classes, each compact unit quotient having volume one. Dividing by this factor proves the final assertion. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.104 — elliptic Schwartz convergence and its sharp exponent. For \(V_a\) as in (6.212), \(O_\gamma(V_a)<\infty\) holds exactly when \(a>2\). Every Schwartz orbital integral is absolutely convergent. For \(f_R=1_{\{\sigma\le R\}}f\) and every nonnegative integer \(A\), \[ \begin{aligned} O_\gamma(|f|)&\le C_\gamma p_3(f),\\ O_\gamma(|f-f_R|)&\le C_\gamma(1+R)^{-A}p_{3+A}(f). \end{aligned} \tag{6.232} \] These constants are bounded as \(\gamma\) ranges over a compact subset of the elliptic regular set. At each fixed Schwartz level, the orbital functional is continuous. For the exponential Cartan majorant of (6.165), one also has the exact formulas \[ O_\gamma(W_\alpha)= \begin{cases} d\displaystyle\left(h_\gamma+ \frac{b_\gamma/q}{e^{2\alpha}-1}\right), &S_\gamma\text{ contains a vertex},\\[2mm] \displaystyle\frac{2d q^{-1/2}e^{-\alpha}}{1-e^{-2\alpha}}, &\gamma\text{ inverts an edge}, \end{cases} \qquad \alpha>0. \tag{6.233} \]

Proof. Insert (6.228) into (6.231). Outside a nonempty fixed-vertex subtree, the summands, apart from the positive constant \(db_\gamma/q\), are \((1+2\beta j)(1+2j)^{-a}\). For an inverted edge they are, apart from \(2dq^{-1/2}\), \((1+\beta(2j+1))(2j+2)^{-a}\). Both series have positive terms comparable to \((1+j)^{1-a}\). Grouping integers between consecutive powers of two proves convergence exactly for \(a>2\): the resulting block sums are comparable to \(2^{k(2-a)}\), including a nonzero lower bound at \(a=2\). Taking \(a=3\) gives the first estimate in (6.232). On the tail \(\sigma>R\), use \(p_{3+A}(f)\) and extract \((1+R)^{-A}\) to get the second. Substituting \(W_\alpha(g)=q^{-\sigma(g)/2}e^{-\alpha\sigma(g)}\) instead gives the two geometric series in (6.233).

For uniformity, let \(B\subset G\) be compact and elliptic regular. The set of matrices with \(\sigma\le1\) and absolute reduced norm in the compact annulus determined by \(B\) is compact: only finitely many Cartan pairs can occur. Lemma 6.18, (6.39), consequently places all central conjugator classes with \(\sigma(x^{-1}\gamma x)\le1\), \(\gamma\in B\), in one compact subset of \(G/Z\). Its image in the discrete vertex set is finite. This includes every fixed vertex and both endpoints of every inverted fixed edge for these \(\gamma\). The numbers \(h_\gamma\), hence \(b_\gamma\), are uniformly bounded. Formula (6.231) proves the required uniform bound for \(C_\gamma=O_\gamma(V_3)\). The seminorm estimate for differences proves continuity on each Schwartz level. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.105 — the actual elliptic character formula in division rank two. Let \(\pi\) be any irreducible admissible unitary discrete series of \(\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\), with formal degree \(d_\pi\) for the stated quotient Haar measure. For smooth vectors \(v,w\) and elliptic regular \(\gamma\), \[ O_\gamma\bigl(\langle\pi(\,\cdot\,)v,w\rangle\bigr) =\frac{\langle v,w\rangle}{d_\pi}\Theta_\pi(\gamma). \tag{6.234} \] The integral is absolute. Its value is locally constant in \(\gamma\), and \(\Theta_\pi\) is the actual regular character from Theorem 6.70. With maximal-compact torus normalization, the left side of (6.234) is divided by \(e(F[\gamma]/F)\).

Proof. Corollary 6.83 puts every smooth coefficient in the Schwartz space with its corresponding central rule. Corollary 6.104 proves absolute convergence. For a nonzero smooth \(u\), put \(c_u(g)=\langle\pi(g)u,u\rangle\). Its compact cutoffs have locally constant regular orbital integrals by Lemma 6.18. The second estimate in (6.232), uniformly on each compact elliptic regular neighbourhood, makes these orbital integrals converge uniformly to \(O_\gamma(c_u)\). Thus that function is continuous there.

Let \(f\) be a smooth inverse-central-character test supported compactly in the elliptic regular set modulo \(Z\). Choose compact representatives \(B\) of its quotient support. The uniform estimate gives \[ \int_{G/Z}|f(g)|\int_{G/Z}|c_u(x^{-1}gx)|\,d\bar x\,d\bar g \le \left(\sup_{g\in B}C_g\right)p_3(c_u)\|f\|_1<\infty. \tag{6.235} \] The inner integral is \(O_g(|c_u|)\), by quotient integration through the torus of volume one modulo \(Z\). Fubini is therefore applicable to the ordered finite-rank Schur identity (6.31). Invert its conjugation variable and obtain \(\operatorname{tr}\pi(f)=d_\pi\|u\|^{-2}\int f(g)O_g(c_u)d\bar g\). Theorem 6.70 supplies the same trace as the integral against \(\Theta_\pi\) on this open regular set. Its ordinary compact-test identity applies here by central averaging: use finitely many compact quotient charts over the support of \(f\), partition there into compact open pieces, and on each piece multiply a lift by a compact locally constant central function whose integral against \(\omega\) is one. The central average of the resulting compact test is \(f\); quotient integration and the central covariance of Corollary 6.71 identify both its operator and its character integral with those for \(f\). Both densities are continuous, so they agree pointwise. Indeed a nonzero value of their difference can be multiplied by a constant to have positive real part. Continuity preserves positive real part on a small compact open neighbourhood. A constant times its indicator is then an ordinary compact test with nonzero integral against the difference; central averaging gives an allowed quotient test with that same integral, a contradiction. It follows that \(O_\gamma(c_u)=\|u\|^2\Theta_\pi(\gamma)/d_\pi\), which also proves local constancy. For the sesquilinear orbital form in \(v,w\), subtract this scalar multiple of the inner product. Its diagonal is zero; expansion at \(v+w\) and \(v+iw\) makes both off-diagonal terms zero. This gives (6.234). The change of torus measure is the one in Theorem 6.103. No character integral over the singular set is required. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.106 — regular classes with primary division ranks at most two. In \(\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), suppose every primary-factor block of a regular \(\gamma\) has division rank one or two. The weighted orbital functional of Theorem 6.99 is then absolutely convergent and continuous at each Schwartz level, with a rapid cutoff bound of the form (6.226). In particular, every regular orbital integral of a smooth discrete-series coefficient of \(\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\) is absolute. For a nonelliptic class satisfying the primary-rank condition, \[ O_\gamma\bigl(\langle\pi(\,\cdot\,)v,w\rangle\bigr)=0. \tag{6.236} \] This last assertion concerns the unweighted orbital integral of a coefficient; it is not a pointwise vanishing assertion for its character.

Proof. Each division-rank-one factor has compact central quotient by Section 6.4. Each elliptic division-rank-two factor satisfies Corollary 6.104, in particular with exponent three. The right side of (6.223) is therefore finite with \(a=3\). This proves absolute convergence, and the higher-seminorm tail argument of Corollary 6.100 proves the stated cutoff bound. A nonelliptic \(\gamma\) has a proper primary Levi. The now absolutely convergent, unweighted descent formula (6.46) has zero inner constant terms by Theorem 6.77, proving (6.236). For \(r=2\), every nonelliptic primary block has rank one, while elliptic classes were treated above. These are all regular classes. \(\square\)

The lattice geometry and neighbour recurrences over a field are also treated in Casselman, Geometry of the tree, Sections 4 and 6, and Analysis on the tree, Sections 1–2. The arguments here use right division lattices and specify the full vertex stabilizer, torus measure and formal degree. Section 6.21 proves elliptic convergence in every division rank. Theorem 6.271 proves elliptic character orthogonality. Completeness and general local and global representation transfer require further arguments.

6.21. Angular averaging and convergence in every division rank

Let \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), \(K=\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_D)\), \(Z=F^\times\), and \(A=M_r(D)\). Retain the Cartan length \(\sigma\), the positive spherical function \(\Xi\), and the integer \(b\) in Lemma 6.80. All assertions in this subsection hold in either characteristic, with no restriction on the residue characteristic or on \(r\deg D\). An elliptic torus has quotient volume \(\operatorname{vol}(G_\gamma/Z)=1\), as in Section 6.3.

Write \(\mathcal X=B\backslash G=(B\cap K)\backslash K\) for the compact variety of full division flags, with its \(K\)-invariant probability measure \(\nu\). The compact model of \(I=I_B^G(1)\), proved unitary in Lemma 6.74, identifies its Hilbert space with \(L^2(\mathcal X,\nu)\), its spherical vector with the constant function \(1\), and its action with \[ (I(g)u)(\xi)=a(g,\xi)u(\xi g),\qquad a(g,\xi)>0. \tag{6.237} \] Here \(a\) is the positive square root of the measure-change factor. It is locally constant in \((g,\xi)\); on the Gaussian flag charts this is the absolute value of a nonvanishing analytic Jacobian to the power \(1/2\). The factorization and change of variables in the proof of Lemma 6.74 give (6.237), including its cocycle rule. In particular \(I(k)\) is ordinary right translation when \(k\in K\).

Lemma 6.107 — a bounded flag kernel for a compact conjugation average. For regular semisimple \(\gamma\), the operator \[ H_\gamma=\int_K I(k^{-1}\gamma k)\,dk \tag{6.238} \] has a nonnegative locally constant kernel \(h_\gamma(\xi,\eta)\) relative to \(\nu(\eta)\). It is of finite rank. For every compact subset \(C\subset G_{\mathrm{reg}}\), the kernels can be chosen jointly locally constant near \(C\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\), and there is \(M_C<\infty\) such that \[ 0\le h_\gamma(\xi,\eta)\le M_C, \qquad |H_\gamma u(\xi)|\le M_C\int_{\mathcal X}|u(\eta)|\,d\nu(\eta) \quad(\gamma\in C). \tag{6.239} \]

Proof: the differential is onto. The reduced-trace pairing \(\langle U,V\rangle=\operatorname{Trd}_A(UV)\) is nondegenerate. Indeed after a finite separable splitting extension it is the matrix trace pairing, which pairs the matrix units \(E_{ij}\) and \(E_{ji}\) in every characteristic; invertibility of its Gram matrix descends to \(F\). It is invariant under conjugation.

For a flag \(\eta\), let \(P_\eta\) be its right stabilizer and \(\mathfrak p_\eta\) its Lie algebra. Elementary block multiplication shows \(\mathfrak p_\eta^\perp=\mathfrak n_\eta\), the strict triangular radical for that flag. To see this without a split assumption on \(D\), pair each division entry with the opposite entry, using the nondegenerate reduced-trace pairing on \(D\). The annihilator of the permitted triangular entries is exactly the stated strict triangular space. Every member of \(\mathfrak n_\eta\) is nilpotent.

Consider \[ \Psi_\gamma:K\times\mathcal X\longrightarrow\mathcal X\times\mathcal X, \qquad(k,\xi)\longmapsto(\xi,\xi k^{-1}\gamma k). \tag{6.240} \] The Lie algebra of the open subgroup \(K\) is all of \(A\). At \(k=1\), put \(\eta=\xi\gamma\). The differential in the \(k\) variable, followed by the quotient to the tangent space at \(\eta\), is \[ A\longrightarrow A/\mathfrak p_\eta, \qquad X\longmapsto X-\gamma^{-1}X\gamma \pmod{\mathfrak p_\eta}. \tag{6.241} \] This follows by differentiating \((1-tX)\gamma(1+tX)\) and using right tangent coordinates; it is a calculation modulo \(t^2\), so requires neither an exponential map nor division by an integer. If \(Y\in\mathfrak n_\eta\) annihilates its image, invariance of the trace gives \(Y-\gamma Y\gamma^{-1}=0\). The centralizer of regular semisimple \(\gamma\) is the product of separable fields \(F[\gamma]\), by Section 6.1. It contains no nonzero nilpotent. Thus \(Y=0\), which proves that (6.241) is onto. At any other \(k\), the same calculation uses \(k^{-1}\gamma k\), with the same conclusion. The first component of (6.240) is \(\xi\) itself. Consequently \(\Psi_\gamma\) is a submersion everywhere.

Proof: push forward the measure in compact charts. Enlarge \(C\), if necessary, to a compact open subset of \(G_{\mathrm{reg}}\). The parameterized map \((\gamma,k,\xi)\mapsto(\gamma,\xi,\xi k^{-1}\gamma k)\) is a submersion by the same differential calculation and has compact domain over this parameter set. Push forward the positive measure \(a(k^{-1}\gamma k,\xi)\,dk\,d\nu(\xi)\), retaining \(\gamma\) as a parameter. It has a nonnegative locally constant density with respect to \(d\nu(\xi)d\nu(\eta)\), as the following chart argument verifies.

The flag measure and Haar measure have positive smooth densities in analytic coordinates: local Gaussian sections identify the quotient by \(B\cap K\) with a product of division-entry balls, and quotient integration of the smooth Haar density gives this assertion. At a point of the submersion, choose an invertible differential minor and append the unused source coordinates to the target coordinates. The inverse-function argument used in Theorem 6.7 makes these coordinates an analytic bijection on sufficiently small compact open balls. Shrink them so that the absolute Jacobian and the positive factor \(a\) are constant. Refine their images into product boxes in target and unused coordinates. A finite disjoint compact-open refinement covers the compact source. On each box, ordinary change of variables and integration in the unused coordinates give a constant times the indicator of the target box. Their finite sum is the asserted density, jointly locally constant in all parameters and bounded on the compact target. This construction uses only nonzero minors, so works also in positive characteristic.

The resulting integral operator is (6.238), by (6.237) and Fubini for bounded functions on compact spaces. Its kernel is bounded by a common \(M_C\), proving (6.239). A locally constant function on compact \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) is constant on the rectangles of a finite partition of \(\mathcal X\) into compact open sets: first cover by finitely many product neighbourhoods of constancy, then take a common refinement of their coordinate sets. The image of the operator is contained in the span of the indicators of this partition. This proves finite rank and extends the formula to \(L^2\), since this probability space has \(L^2\subset L^1\). \(\square\)

Corollary 6.108 — the angular spherical estimate. For compact \(C\subset G_{\mathrm{reg}}\), \[ \int_K\Xi(x^{-1}k^{-1}\gamma kx)\,dk \le M_C\Xi(x)^2 \qquad(\gamma\in C,\ x\in G). \tag{6.242} \]

Proof. Put \(u_x=I(x)1\). Formula (6.237) makes \(u_x\) positive, and \(\int_{\mathcal X}u_xd\nu=\langle I(x)1,1\rangle=\Xi(x)\). Unitarity, (6.238) and the kernel formula give \[ \begin{aligned} \int_K\Xi(x^{-1}k^{-1}\gamma kx)dk &=\langle H_\gamma u_x,u_x\rangle\\ &=\int_{\mathcal X^2}h_\gamma(\xi,\eta) u_x(\eta)u_x(\xi)d\nu(\eta)d\nu(\xi)\\ &\le M_C\left(\int_{\mathcal X}u_xd\nu\right)^2. \end{aligned} \tag{6.243} \] All functions here are nonnegative; the last inequality is precisely (6.239). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.109 — a quantitative elliptic conjugator bound. If \(C\) is a compact subset of the elliptic regular set, there is \(L_C\ge1\) such that \[ 1+\sigma(x)\le L_C\bigl(1+\sigma(x^{-1}\gamma x)\bigr) \qquad(\gamma\in C,\ x\in G). \tag{6.244} \]

Proof. The case \(r=1\) has \(\sigma=0\). Suppose \(r>1\), and write \(x=ka k'\), where \(a=\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^{\lambda_1},\ldots,\Pi^{\lambda_r})\), \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_r\). For each \(1\le j<r\), the top-right \(j\) by \(r-j\) block of \(k^{-1}\gamma k\) is nonzero. If it were zero, the last \(r-j\) coordinate lines would span a proper nonzero \(\gamma\)-invariant right division subspace. This contradicts the irreducibility argument in Lemma 6.18. The maximum norm of the entries in each of these blocks is therefore a positive continuous function on compact \(C\times K\). Its minimum is positive. Hence one integer \(c\ge0\) satisfies, for every such block and every \((\gamma,k)\), \[ \min_{i\le j<l}v_D((k^{-1}\gamma k)_{il})\le c. \tag{6.245} \] Let \(y=a^{-1}k^{-1}\gamma ka\), and let \(\nu_1\ge\cdots\ge\nu_r\) be its Cartan valuations. Their minimum \(\nu_r\) equals the minimum valuation of the matrix entries, by integral row and column elimination. An entry supplied by (6.245) has valuation at most \(c-(\lambda_j-\lambda_{j+1})\). Thus \[ \lambda_j-\lambda_{j+1}\le c-\nu_r \le c+\sigma(y)-m_\gamma/r, \qquad m_\gamma=v_F(\operatorname{Nrd}\gamma)=\sum_i\nu_i. \tag{6.246} \] The second inequality follows from \(m_\gamma/r\le\nu_r+(\nu_1-\nu_r)\). The integers \(m_\gamma\) are bounded on \(C\). Sum (6.246) over \(j\), use \(\sigma(x)=\lambda_1-\lambda_r\) and \(\sigma(y)=\sigma(x^{-1}\gamma x)\), and increase a constant to obtain (6.244). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.110 — elliptic Schwartz convergence and the discrete-series coefficient formula in every rank. Choose an integer \(s>2b+r-1\). For compact elliptic regular \(C\), there is \(A_C<\infty\) such that \[ \begin{aligned} O_\gamma(V_s)&\le A_C,\\ O_\gamma(|f|)&\le A_Cp_s(f),\\ O_\gamma(|f-f_R|)&\le A_C(1+R)^{-N}p_{s+N}(f), \qquad f_R=1_{\{\sigma\le R\}}f, \end{aligned} \quad\gamma\in C,\ N\ge0. \tag{6.247} \] The last assertion is for integer \(N\ge0\). These are absolute orbital integrals. Every \(f\in\mathcal S_\omega\) consequently has continuous elliptic orbital integrals, with uniform cutoff convergence on compact elliptic regular sets. For any discrete series \(\pi\), any smooth \(v,w\), and every elliptic regular \(\gamma\), \[ O_\gamma\bigl(\langle\pi(\,\cdot\,)v,w\rangle\bigr) =\frac{\langle v,w\rangle}{d_\pi}\Theta_\pi(\gamma). \tag{6.248} \] In particular this coefficient orbital integral is locally constant. With the alternative torus measure \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O_E^\times)=1\), where \(E=F[\gamma]\), and central measure \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O_F^\times)=1\), the right side of (6.248) is divided by \(e(E/F)\).

Proof: absolute convergence before interchange. Put \(Q=G/Z\). Since \(G_\gamma/Z\) has volume one, quotient integration identifies the extended nonnegative orbital integral with the corresponding integral on \(Q\). By Lemma 6.109, \[ \begin{aligned} O_\gamma(V_s) &\le L_C^s\int_Q\Xi(x^{-1}\gamma x)(1+\sigma(x))^{-s}d\bar x\\ &=L_C^s\int_Q(1+\sigma(x))^{-s} \int_K\Xi(x^{-1}k^{-1}\gamma kx)dk\,d\bar x\\ &\le L_C^sM_C\int_Q\Xi(x)^2(1+\sigma(x))^{-s}d\bar x<\infty. \end{aligned} \tag{6.249} \] The middle equality uses left invariance of quotient Haar measure and \(\sigma(kx)=\sigma(x)\); Tonelli justifies it for extended integrals before their finiteness is known. Corollary 6.108 gives the last inequality, and Lemma 6.80 gives its finiteness. Take \(A_C=L_C^sM_CC_s\), with \(C_s\) as in (6.181). Bounding \(|f|\) by \(p_s(f)V_s\) proves the second line of (6.247). On the indicated tail, bound it instead by \(p_{s+N}(f)V_s(1+R)^{-N}\), proving the third.

At a fixed smooth level, each \(f_R\) is compact modulo the centre, so its orbital integral is locally constant by Lemma 6.18. The uniform tail bound proves continuity of \(O_\gamma(f)\) on compact elliptic regular sets. This does not assert local constancy for every Schwartz function merely from continuity.

Proof: the actual character identity. The coefficient \(c_u(g)=\langle\pi(g)u,u\rangle\) of a nonzero smooth \(u\) is Schwartz by Corollary 6.83. For a compact-mod-centre inverse-central-character test \(f\) with elliptic regular support, choose compact representatives \(C\) of its support in \(G\). Formula (6.247) gives the genuine absolute bound \[ \int_Q|f(g)|\int_Q|c_u(x^{-1}gx)|d\bar x\,d\bar g \le A_Cp_s(c_u)\|f\|_1<\infty. \tag{6.250} \] Fubini is therefore valid in the ordered Schur identity (6.31). Inverting its conjugating variable gives \[ \operatorname{tr}\pi(f) =\frac{d_\pi}{\|u\|^2}\int_Qf(g)O_g(c_u)d\bar g. \tag{6.251} \] Theorem 6.70 gives this same trace by \(\Theta_\pi\), since these tests have regular support. To apply its ordinary compact-test formulation to quotient tests, take finitely many compact quotient charts, partition the support into compact open pieces, and multiply a lift on each piece by a compact central test with integral against \(\omega\) equal to one. Its central average is the desired quotient test. Quotient integration and central covariance give both the same operator and the same character integral, exactly as in the proof of Theorem 6.105.

The two densities in (6.251) are continuous. They agree pointwise: if their difference were nonzero, multiply by a constant so that its real part is positive at that point. It remains positive on a small compact open neighbourhood. Testing by the indicator of that neighbourhood, and then using the central lift just described, contradicts equality of the trace distributions. Thus \(O_\gamma(c_u)=\|u\|^2\Theta_\pi(\gamma)/d_\pi\). For the sesquilinear form in \(v,w\), subtract \(\langle v,w\rangle\Theta_\pi(\gamma)/d_\pi\). Its diagonal is zero; evaluating at \(v+w\) and \(v+iw\) makes both off-diagonal terms zero. This proves (6.248), including local constancy from that of \(\Theta_\pi\). No integration of a character across the singular set has been used.

Finally, under maximal-compact torus normalization, the valuation quotient \(E^\times/(F^\times\mathcal O_E^\times)\) has exactly \(e(E/F)\) elements. Each unit quotient has volume one by the specified unit measures. Hence \(\operatorname{vol}(E^\times/F^\times)=e(E/F)\); quotient orbital measure is divided by this number relative to our volume-one convention. This proves the last assertion. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.111 — polynomially weighted regular orbital integrals. For every regular semisimple \(\gamma\in G\), every weight \(w\) in Theorem 6.99, and every \(f\in\mathcal S_\omega\), the weighted orbital integral is absolute and continuous at each Schwartz level. For some integer \(t\) and constant \(A_{\gamma,w}\), \[ \begin{aligned} \int_{G_\gamma\backslash G}|f(x^{-1}\gamma x)|w(x)d\dot x &\le A_{\gamma,w}p_t(f),\\ \int_{G_\gamma\backslash G}|(f-f_R)(x^{-1}\gamma x)|w(x)d\dot x &\le A_{\gamma,w}(1+R)^{-N}p_{t+N}(f). \end{aligned} \tag{6.252} \] This includes the convex-hull weights defined in Section 6.19. Every regular orbital integral of a smooth discrete-series coefficient is absolute. At a nonelliptic regular class, its unweighted orbital integral is zero.

Proof. In each primary block \(G_i\), choose a common integer \(a\) greater than its threshold \(2b_i+r_i-1\). Theorem 6.110 makes every factor on the right of (6.223) finite; compact division-rank-one factors also satisfy this statement. Thus that nonnegative extended integral is finite for the \(t\) supplied by Theorem 6.99. Apply \(|f|\le p_t(f)V_t\), and take \((1+R)^{-N}\) out of the tail using \(p_{t+N}(f)\), to obtain (6.252). All changes of variables in the unweighted descent formula (6.46) are now justified by absolute convergence. For a nonelliptic class its primary Levi is proper; Theorem 6.77 makes the inner constant term of the discrete-series coefficient zero, so its orbital integral is zero. This is an assertion about a coefficient orbital integral, not a vanishing assertion for the nonelliptic character. \(\square\)

The arguments above establish the semisimple Schwartz convergence input and the elliptic coefficient identity. Theorem 6.271 proves elliptic character orthogonality. Completeness and the general local and global correspondences in Section 6 require further proofs.

6.22. Schwartz resolutions and compact discrete spectral tests

Fix a unitary central character \(\omega\). Write \(\mathcal H_\omega\) for the smooth compact-mod-centre convolution algebra with central rule \(f(zg)=\omega(z)^{-1}f(g)\), and \(\mathcal S_\omega\) for Section 6.16's Schwartz algebra. Put \(Q=G/Z\), \(\ell(g)=1+\sigma(g)\), and use quotient Haar measure throughout. This subsection proves a homological comparison and constructs compact tests separating discrete series from all other irreducible tempered representations. The elliptic integral pairing is a different assertion.

We specify the completions used in the comparison. A subset of \(\mathcal S_\omega\) is bounded if it lies at one principal smooth level and every seminorm \(p_N\) is bounded on it. An algebraic vector space has the fine bounded-set structure: a bounded set lies in a finite-dimensional subspace and is bounded there. Direct sums have bounded sets supported in a finite sum. Maps and bilinear maps are bounded when they preserve bounded sets, or products of bounded sets, respectively. Completed tensors represent bounded bilinear maps into complete spaces; balanced tensors additionally impose the module relations and complete the quotient. All module extensions used below admit a bounded linear section; the section need not be equivariant. Thus tensoring a linearly split extension is legitimate. We do not assert that algebraic tensoring with the Schwartz algebra preserves arbitrary exact sequences.

Lemma 6.112 — square norms and completed kernels. At a principal level \(J\) on which the central character is compatible, the norms \[ q_N(f)^2=\int_Q|f(g)|^2\ell(g)^{2N}\,d\bar g \tag{6.253} \] define the same complete space and bounded sets as the seminorms \(p_N\). With these bounded-set structures, the completed tensor \(\mathcal S_\omega\widehat\otimes\mathcal S_\omega\) is the Schwartz space of kernels \(F(a,b)\) with central rule \(\omega^{-1}\) in each variable. The product weight can be taken to be \(\ell(a)\ell(b)\).

Proof. For principal \(J\triangleleft K\), a \(K\)-double coset splits into at most \([K:J]^2\) \(J\)-double cosets. All pieces have the same volume, since \(K\) normalizes \(J\). The Cartan volume bounds (6.55)–(6.56), including the finitely many division residues modulo central scalars, consequently give \(\operatorname{vol}(JgJ/Z)\asymp_J D_C(g)^{-1}\), where this notation denotes the image of \(JgJ\) in \(Q\). The two bounds (6.180) imply \[ c_J\le\operatorname{vol}(JgJ/Z)\Xi(g)^2 \le C_J\ell(g)^{2b}. \tag{6.254} \] Only compatible central double cosets support a nonzero bi-\(J\) function; on such a coset its absolute value is constant. Cartan tuples show that the number of these cosets with \(\sigma\le R\) is bounded by a polynomial of degree \(r-1\). Thus (6.254), applied to the individual summands of (6.253) and then summed with a sufficiently large negative power of \(\ell\), gives \(p_N(f)\le C_Jq_N(f)\) and \(q_N(f)\le C'_Jp_{N+b+r}(f)\). Completeness follows from Theorem 6.81.

Choose a unit-modulus central section on each compatible double coset and normalize its indicator to have square norm one. In this basis the level space is the space of rapidly decreasing sequences, with weighted square norms \(\sum|c_x|^2\ell(x)^{2N}\). For kernels the basis is the product basis. Choose \(t\) with \(\sum_x\ell(x)^{-2t}<\infty\). Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[ \sum_{x,y}|c_{xy}|\ell(x)^N\ell(y)^N \le\left(\sum_{x,y}|c_{xy}|^2 \ell(x)^{2N+2t}\ell(y)^{2N+2t}\right)^{1/2} \sum_x\ell(x)^{-2t}. \tag{6.255} \] The series of coordinate tensors therefore converges in every completed projective seminorm. Conversely the kernel square norm of a product tensor is the product of the two square norms, by Fubini. This proves the tensor identification at each pair of levels and hence on their bounded direct limits. The argument also proves density of compactly supported kernels. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.113 — lattice truncation paths and a factorization at every cut. Let \(o=[L_0]\), \(L_0=\mathcal O_D^r\), and \(H=\operatorname{Stab}_G(o)\). Identify the vertex set with \(X=G/H\). For \(x\in X\), let \(L_x\subset L_0\) be its unique representative not contained in \(L_0\Pi\), and define \[ p_k(x)=[L_x+L_0\Pi^k],\qquad k=0,1,\ldots. \tag{6.256} \] These maps are \(H\)-equivariant, \(p_0(x)=o\), and \(p_k(x)=x\) for \(k\ge\sigma(x)\). Consecutive vertices have distance at most one. If \(d(x,y)\le R\), then \(d(p_k(x),p_k(y))\le2R\), where \(d(x,y)=\sigma(g_x^{-1}g_y)\).

Let \(J_m=1+\varpi_F^mM_r(\mathcal O_D)\), \(m\ge1\). If \(p_k(abH)=aH\) and \(v\in J_m\), there are \(u_1,u_2\in J_m\) such that \[ avb=u_1ab u_2,\qquad a^{-1}u_1a\in J_m,\qquad b u_2b^{-1}\in J_m. \tag{6.257} \] In particular insertion of \(v\) preserves the value of every bi-\(J_m\) test at \(ab\).

Proof. In an elementary-divisor basis, \(L_x\) has exponents \(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_r=0\). Its truncation has exponents \(\min(\lambda_i,k)\). This proves the endpoint and step assertions. If the relative Cartan spread is at most \(R\), the two canonical representatives satisfy \(L_x\Pi^R\subset L_y\subset L_x\Pi^{-R}\). Indeed, initially the inclusions have exponents \(a+R,a\); normalization inside \(L_0\), with a unit coordinate in each lattice, forces \(-R\le a\le0\). Taking sums with \(L_0\Pi^k\) gives both inclusions with exponent \(R\) for the truncations. Their relative spread is at most \(2R\).

The group \(H\) consists of \((\Pi I)^jK\), \(j\in\mathbb Z\): a matrix carrying \(L_0\) to \(L_0\Pi^j\) has precisely this form. These elements preserve the truncation construction after the same right homothety is applied to normalize a lattice. This proves equivariance. It also shows that every \(J_m\) is normal in \(H\), and that \(\sigma\) is bi-\(H\)-invariant.

Write \(ab=h_1\lambda h_2\), with \(h_1,h_2\in H\) and \(\lambda\) diagonal with decreasing nonnegative exponents and minimum zero. By (6.256), \(a=h_1\mu h_3\), \(b=h_3^{-1}\nu h_2\), where \(h_3\in H\), \(\mu\) has exponents \(\min(\lambda_i,k)\), and \(\nu=\mu^{-1}\lambda\) has exponents \(\max(\lambda_i-k,0)\). Both diagonals lie in the positive chamber. Gaussian elimination factors \(h_3vh_3^{-1}=v^+v^-\), with \(v^+\) upper triangular and \(v^-\) lower unitriangular, both in \(J_m\). Their entries stay in that principal group because all pivots are congruent to one. Positive chamber order gives \(\mu v^+\mu^{-1}\in J_m\) and \(\nu^{-1}v^-\nu\in J_m\). Take \[ u_1=h_1\mu v^+\mu^{-1}h_1^{-1},\qquad u_2=h_2^{-1}\nu^{-1}v^-\nu h_2. \tag{6.258} \] Normality in \(H\) and direct multiplication prove all three assertions of (6.257). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.114 — a bounded contraction of the Schwartz kernel complex. Let \(C_n(X)\) be the algebraic space on ordered \((n+1)\)-tuples of vertices, with consecutive repetitions set equal to zero. Its differential is the alternating sum of omissions, and its augmentation is the sum of coefficients. A set of tuples is controlled if their diameters are bounded. It meets finitely many \(G\)-orbits: move its first vertex to \(o\), after which all coordinates lie in a finite ball.

For each orbit representative \(\eta=(o,\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_n)\), put \(U_\eta=\bigcap_i\operatorname{Stab}_G(\eta_i)\). This group is open and compact modulo \(Z\). Complete the compact kernel space in the direct-sum decomposition \[ \mathcal P_n=\bigoplus_{[\eta]} \operatorname{Fix}_{U_\eta/Z} (\mathcal S_\omega\widehat\otimes\mathcal S_\omega), \qquad (a,b)\longmapsto(ag,g^{-1}b) \tag{6.259} \] for the action being averaged. Central factors cancel in this action. In these unscaled orbit coordinates, the augmentation \(\mathcal P_0\to\mathcal S_\omega\) is convolution divided by \(\operatorname{vol}(H/Z)\). Its kernel complex has a bounded contraction, and its augmentation has a bounded linear section.

Proof: the algebraic prism. A map \(f:X\to X\) acts on every coordinate of a tuple. For two maps \(f,g\), set \[ D(f,g)(x_0,\ldots,x_n)= \sum_{j=0}^n(-1)^j (f x_0,\ldots,f x_j,g x_j,\ldots,g x_n). \tag{6.260} \] Expansion of the omission differential cancels every deletion away from the change between \(f\) and \(g\) in pairs; its two endpoint terms are \(g_*\) and \(-f_*\). Thus \(\partial D+D\partial=g_*-f_*\). The operator \(D=\sum_{k\ge0}D(p_k,p_{k+1})\) is finite on each tuple, since the paths stop. It satisfies \(\partial D+D\partial=1-(p_0)_*\). The constant map \(p_0\) acts as zero on the reduced complex. The distance bounds in Lemma 6.113 show that \(D\) takes a controlled set into a controlled set.

Proof: the kernel estimates. A kernel in (6.259) can equivalently be written as \(\phi(g,\eta)\), with bounded tuple diameter, by assigning to an orbit representative the function \((a,b)\mapsto\phi(ab,a\eta)\). The boundary omits tuple coordinates and sums over the missing vertex; its augmentation is \(\alpha\phi(g)=\sum_x\phi(g,x)\). For \(n=0\), integration of the lifted kernel along \((a,a^{-1}g)\) repeats each vertex coset with volume \(\operatorname{vol}(H/Z)\). Thus \(\alpha\) is precisely the normalized convolution just specified. No change of Haar measure is made.

Fix a source representative \(\eta\) and a target representative \(\xi\), both starting at \(o\). For a prism term, let \(p_{j,k}\) denote its tuple map in (6.260). The corresponding block of \(1\otimes D\) is \[ \frac1{\operatorname{vol}(U_\eta/Z)} \sum_{k,j}(-1)^j \int_{\{g:\ p_{j,k}(ag\eta)=a\xi\}} F(ag,g^{-1}b)\,d\bar g. \tag{6.261} \] This follows by summing over \(G/U_\eta\); integration repeats each coset with the displayed stabilizer volume. Choose a principal \(J\subset U_\eta\), and let \(e_J\) be its central-character averaging idempotent. If \(f\) is right \(J\)-invariant, (6.261) applied to \(f\otimes e_J\) is \(A_{\xi\eta}f/\operatorname{vol}(U_\eta/Z)\), where \[ A_{\xi\eta}f(a,b)=c_{\xi\eta}(a,b)f(ab),\qquad c_{\xi\eta}(a,b)=\sum_{j,k}(-1)^j 1_{\{p_{j,k}(ab\eta)=a\xi\}}. \tag{6.262} \] The central phases in the two tensor factors cancel in this calculation.

Only \(k<\sigma(ab)+C_\eta\) can contribute to (6.262), because its nondegenerate target requires a path step at one of the source vertices. For each such \(k\), its first coordinate requires \(aH=p_k(abH)\). Hence, for fixed \(g=ab\), the possible \(a\)'s lie in at most \(C_\eta\ell(g)\) cosets of \(H/Z\), and \(|c_{\xi\eta}(a,b)|\le C_{n,\eta}\ell(g)\). On this support \(\sigma(a)\le\sigma(g)\), \(\sigma(b)\le2\sigma(g)\), by Lemma 6.113 and the length triangle inequality. Changing variables from \((a,b)\) to \((a,g)\) therefore gives the quantitative bound \[ q_N(A_{\xi\eta}f)^2 \le C_{N,n,\eta}\int_Q|f(g)|^2\ell(g)^{4N+3}d\bar g \le C'_{N,n,\eta}q_{2N+2}(f)^2. \tag{6.263} \] Here the kernel norm uses \(\ell(a)\ell(b)\); the finite constant includes \(\operatorname{vol}(H/Z)\).

These square estimates are accompanied by a uniform smooth level. Choose \(J_m\) contained in both tuple stabilizers and in the level of \(f\). The outside transformations \((a,b)\mapsto(ua,b)\) and \((a,b)\mapsto(a,bu)\), \(u\in J_m\), preserve each condition in (6.262), by equivariance and the stabilizer of \(\eta\). For insertion \(avb\), use (6.257). Its \(u_2\) fixes every \(\eta_i\), and \(a^{-1}u_1a\) fixes every \(\xi_i\). Since \(u_1\in H\), every \(p_k\) commutes with \(u_1\). Thus the entire prism condition is preserved, as well as \(f(ab)\). Applying the same argument with \(v^{-1}\) proves equivalence of the conditions in both directions. Consequently (6.262) is bi-\(J_m\) in each variable. This verifies uniform smoothness, not only a square-norm estimate.

The block (6.261) commutes with convolution in its second variable. For bi-\(J\) functions \(f,h\), its value on \(f\otimes h\) is consequently \(\operatorname{vol}(U_\eta/Z)^{-1}(A_{\xi\eta}f)*_2h\). Lemma 6.112 and the convolution estimates of Theorem 6.81 extend this bounded bilinear formula to completed kernels. A fixed input orbit has only finitely many output orbits, by the controlled-support assertion. Thus the full operator is bounded on the direct sum (6.259). All algebraic identities extend by density.

Finally the constant-map operator has the form \(\beta\alpha\), with \(\beta f(g,x)=f(g)1_{\{o\}}(x)\). Its lifted kernel is \(f(ab)1_H(a)\). This has a fixed smooth level by (6.257) at \(k=0\), and its square norms are bounded by those of \(f\), since \(\sigma(a)=0\) on \(H\) and \(\sigma(ab)=\sigma(b)\) there. Thus \(\beta\) is bounded and \(\alpha\beta=1\). The identity \(\partial D+D\partial=1-\beta\alpha\) proves the assertion. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.115 — comparison with the Schwartz category. Give smooth algebraic representations their fine bounded-set structure. If \(V,W\) are admissible tempered representations with central character \(\omega\), then \[ \operatorname{Ext}^q_{G,\omega}(V,W) \simeq\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\mathcal S_\omega}(V,W). \tag{6.264} \] The right side uses complete essential modules, bounded actions and linearly split extensions as specified above. Moreover, completing a projective \(\mathcal H_\omega\)-resolution of such a \(V\) by \(\mathcal S_\omega\widehat\otimes_{\mathcal H_\omega}-\) still gives a resolution of \(V\).

Proof: projectivity and the resolution. Both algebras have the nested local averaging units \(e_{J_m}\), with \(m\) sufficiently large for \(\omega\). On every bounded subset one unit acts as the identity. Their successive differences are orthogonal idempotents, so the regular module is the bounded direct sum of its principal idempotent modules. A module \(\mathcal S_\omega e\) is projective for our extensions: lift the image of \(e\) through a bounded linear section and apply \(e\) to the lift. The same proof with a parameter space shows that its completed tensor with any complete bounded space is relatively projective. Direct sums and bounded retracts retain projectivity. These observations apply to right modules and to bimodules as well.

Before completion, the ordered-tuple construction is a projective bimodule resolution of \(\mathcal H_\omega\). Indeed each orbit summand is induction from the diagonal compact-mod-centre group \(U_\eta\), with cancelling central characters. Averaging over \(U_\eta/Z\) makes it a retract of the free bimodule. Insertion of \(o\) contracts its underlying augmented vector-space complex. Completing on the left and right identifies its summands with (6.259): multiplication on each factor and compact stabilizer averaging give precisely those fixed kernels. Lemma 6.114 proves that the resulting augmented \(\mathcal S_\omega\)-bimodule complex is a linearly split resolution.

Here the contraction and section are already right-module-linear. In the coordinates \(\phi(g,\eta)\), the prism changes only \(\eta\), whereas right convolution changes only \(g\). Equivalently, (6.261) commutes with convolution in its second kernel variable, as used above. The same assertion holds for \(\beta\). It holds first for compact tests and extends to Schwartz convolution by boundedness and compact density. Tensoring these actual right-module homotopy identities with any essential left Schwartz module therefore preserves this resolution.

For clarity, the resulting Hom comparison can be read directly, without assuming flatness. In degree \(n\), tensoring the bimodule resolution with \(V\) gives the sum of the compact diagonal averages of \(\mathcal S_\omega\widehat\otimes V\). Its bounded Schwartz-module maps to \(W\) are \[ \prod_{[\eta]}\operatorname{Hom}_{U_\eta}(V,W). \tag{6.265} \] To verify the adjunction on one summand, a bounded equivariant map \(l:V\to W\) sends an averaged tensor \(f\otimes v\) to \(\pi_W(f)l(v)\). Its inverse evaluates a module map on the compact section \(s_v(g)=1_{U_\eta}(g)\pi_V(g^{-1})v/\operatorname{vol}(U_\eta/Z)\). This section is a finite tensor because a smooth vector has finite-dimensional orbit span under the compact quotient. Integration shows that the two constructions are inverse. Central phases cancel. The product in (6.265), rather than a direct sum, is required because Hom is taken from a direct sum.

The uncompleted ordered-tuple resolution of \(V\) is \(C_*(X)\otimes V\), with diagonal action. Compact averaging proves its projectivity, and insertion of \(o\) proves exactness. Its Hom complex is the same product (6.265), with the same omission differentials. On fine spaces every linear map and linear section is bounded. It computes ordinary algebraic Ext and proves (6.264).

The tensor assertion follows from the same bimodule argument. The uncompleted bimodule resolution, tensored with \(V\), is a projective Hecke resolution of \(V\); its Schwartz completion is the resolution just constructed. The natural multiplication \(\mathcal S_\omega\widehat\otimes_{\mathcal H_\omega}V\to V\) is an isomorphism: locally use the inverse \(v\mapsto e_J\otimes v\); balancing makes the inverses independent of the local unit, and compact density proves the identity on a general Schwartz tensor. Any two projective Hecke resolutions have comparison maps and homotopies obtained by lifting onto cycles. On fine spaces they are bounded, and their completed tensors retain those homotopies. Thus every projective resolution has the asserted completed homology. This proves the last assertion without an algebraic flatness claim. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.116 — discrete blocks are projective and injective. The smooth space of a discrete series is both projective and injective in the Schwartz category of Theorem 6.115. If \(V,W\) are irreducible tempered of central character \(\omega\), and one is discrete series, then \[ \operatorname{Ext}_{G,\omega}^q(V,W)=0\quad(q>0),\qquad \sum_q(-1)^q\dim\operatorname{Ext}_{G,\omega}^q(V,W) =1_{\{V\simeq W\}}. \tag{6.266} \]

Proof. For a fixed discrete series \(\pi\), Corollary 6.83's matrix units give a continuous Fourier-block projection of the Schwartz algebra. At level \(J\), its image is the finite matrix algebra on \(V_\pi^J\); its entries depend continuously on \(f\) by Theorem 6.82. Thus \(\mathcal S_\omega=I_\pi\oplus\ker\pi\) as bounded algebras. The products between the two summands are zero by the matrix-unit convolution formulas. Choose an orthonormal basis compatible with the nested finite fixed spaces of \(\pi\). Then \(I_\pi\) is the algebra of finitary matrices in this basis, with its fine bounded-set structure. It is not being identified with all finite-rank operators formed using arbitrary algebraic dual functionals.

An essential module for the finitary matrix algebra is determined by its first diagonal corner: the inverse construction is the algebraic column space tensored with that corner. The maps are multiplication by the matrix units. On bounded sets only finitely many units occur, so both constructions are bounded and preserve linearly split extensions. They give an equivalence with complex bounded vector spaces. Every extension in the latter category splits by its definition here. The column module, corresponding to \(\mathbb C\), is therefore projective and injective. Taking the product with the category for \(\ker\pi\) proves the first assertion. Now (6.264) gives positive-degree vanishing, and Schur's lemma gives degree zero. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.117 — compact pseudo-coefficients and quantized formal degrees. For a discrete series \(\pi\), let \(f_{\pi,m}\) be (6.136) at a generating level. For every irreducible tempered \(\tau\) of the same central character, \[ \operatorname{tr}\tau(f_{\pi,m})=1_{\{\tau\simeq\pi\}}, \qquad O_\gamma(f_{\pi,m})=\Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1}) \quad(\gamma\text{ elliptic regular}), \tag{6.267} \] and \[ d_\pi=f_{\pi,m}(1) =\sum_{[\sigma]}(-1)^{\dim\sigma} \frac{\dim V_\pi^{U_\sigma}}{\operatorname{vol}(C_\sigma/Z)}. \tag{6.268} \] There is \(\alpha_G>0\), independent of \(\pi\) and its generating level, such that \(d_\pi\in\alpha_G\mathbb Z_{>0}\). At a fixed compact open level \(J\) there are only finitely many such discrete series, and \[ \sum_\pi d_\pi\dim V_\pi^J\le\operatorname{vol}(JZ/Z)^{-1}, \qquad \#\{\pi:V_\pi^J\ne0\} \le(\alpha_G\operatorname{vol}(JZ/Z))^{-1}. \tag{6.269} \] If the central character is nontrivial on \(J\cap Z\), that set is empty.

Proof. Formula (6.137) and (6.266) give the trace assertion; (6.138) and Theorem 6.65 give the elliptic assertion.

We give the trace-at-identity argument for (6.268). The functional \(f\mapsto f(1)\) is a continuous trace on the Schwartz algebra: inversion in the absolute convolution integral gives \((f*h)(1)=(h*f)(1)\). Extend it to matrices by summing diagonal values. For a finite projective module represented by an idempotent \(p\), its value is independent of the representation: matrices \(A,B\) implementing an isomorphism satisfy \(AB=p\), \(BA=q\), and cyclicity gives the same trace. It is additive under direct sums. A finite split projective resolution consequently has the same alternating trace as its augmentation; this also follows by splitting cycles and cancelling them in consecutive degrees.

Complete the finite projective resolution of Theorem 6.57 by Theorem 6.115. Its augmentation \(V_\pi\) is Schwartz-projective by Proposition 6.116, so the completed finite resolution splits by bounded module maps. The matrix unit \(E^\pi_{u,u}\), for a smooth unit vector, represents this column module and has value \(d_\pi\) at one. For a compact-mod-centre stabilizer \(C\) and finite-dimensional unitary representation \(\rho\), its induced projective module has trace value \(\dim\rho/\operatorname{vol}(C/Z)\): decompose \(\rho\) into compact irreducibles, and use a diagonal compact matrix-unit idempotent for each copy. Schur averaging on \(C/Z\) gives its identity value \(\dim\rho/\operatorname{vol}(C/Z)\), with multiplicities added. Applying this to \(\rho_\sigma\) in (6.135) proves (6.268).

There are finitely many simplex orbits, independent of the level. All \(C_\sigma/Z\) are compact open subgroups of \(Q\), so their Haar volumes have rational ratios: intersect two of them and use the two finite subgroup indices. A common positive rational multiple of these finitely many inverse volumes therefore puts every integer sum in (6.268) in \(\alpha_G\mathbb Z\). Formal degrees are positive by Theorem 6.15, proving the strict lower bound. Finally apply the discrete Bessel inequality (6.86) to the central-character averaging test \(e_J\). Its square norm is \(\operatorname{vol}(JZ/Z)^{-1}\), and \(\pi(e_J)\) is the orthogonal projection of rank \(\dim V_\pi^J\). This proves the first inequality in (6.269), first for finite families and then by monotonicity. The lower bound \(d_\pi\ge\alpha_G\) proves finiteness and the second. \(\square\)

The general homological method is developed in Ralf Meyer, Homological algebra for Schwartz algebras of reductive p-adic groups, arXiv:math/0501548v2, Sections 4.2–6.1 and Theorems 39–41. The division-lattice truncations, factorization at a cut and square-kernel estimate (6.263) give the required contraction here. Compact pseudo-coefficients and the elliptic identities above do not by themselves identify the Euler–Poincaré pairing with an elliptic character integral or prove the full local and global representation transfers.

6.23. Finite commutators and matching compact Euler tests

Keep the division-matrix groups, quotient Haar measures and unitary central character conventions above. For an algebra \(A\), let \([A,A]\) mean the linear span of its commutators: its elements are finite sums \(ab-ba\). No closure is taken in the quotient \(A/[A,A]\), called the cocenter. This algebraic distinction will let us apply orbital functionals without a limiting commutator argument.

Lemma 6.118 — the projective trace in the algebraic cocenter. If \(P=A^np\) is represented by a finite idempotent matrix, define \[ \operatorname{Tr}_A[P]=\left[\sum_i p_{ii}\right] \in A/[A,A]. \tag{6.270} \] For the principal idempotent modules and their finite direct summands used in Section 6.22, this is independent of presentation and additive. The alternating projective trace of a finite split projective resolution is the trace of its augmentation. Consequently, for every discrete series \(\pi\), every generating level \(m\) and every smooth unit vector \(u\), there are finitely many \(a_j,b_j\in\mathcal S_\omega\) such that \[ f_{\pi,m}-E^\pi_{u,u}=\sum_{j=1}^h(a_j*b_j-b_j*a_j). \tag{6.271} \]

Proof. Maps between finite idempotent modules are represented by rectangular matrices over \(A\): the image of each of their finitely many idempotent columns determines its entries. Isomorphisms therefore give matrices \(X,Y\) with \(XY=p\), \(YX=q\), and \[ \sum_i(XY)_{ii}-\sum_j(YX)_{jj} =\sum_{i,j}[X_{ij},Y_{ji}]. \tag{6.272} \] This proves independence; block diagonal matrices prove additivity. In a split finite resolution the cycles are finite projective summands. Their occurrences in consecutive degrees cancel, leaving the augmentation. These are finite algebraic equalities.

We identify the class of a compact-induced summand explicitly. For an irreducible unitary \(\rho\) of a compact-mod-centre group \(C\), of dimension \(t\), let \(e_{ij}\) be its compact convolution matrix units, with factor \(t/\operatorname{vol}(C/Z)\). Schur averaging gives \(e_{ij}*e_{kl}=\delta_{jk}e_{il}\). A column module \(\mathcal S_\omega e_{11}\) is the completed compact induction of \(\rho\). Its character test is \(\operatorname{vol}(C/Z)^{-1}1_C(g)\operatorname{tr}\rho(g^{-1}) =t^{-1}\sum_i e_{ii}(g)\). Since \(e_{ii}-e_{11}=[e_{i1},e_{1i}]\), this test has class \([e_{11}]\). Decomposing a finite-dimensional \(\rho\) into compact irreducibles proves the assertion for every summand of (6.135), including its orientation character and multiplicities.

The completed finite resolution in Theorem 6.115 splits because its discrete-series augmentation is projective by Proposition 6.116. Its alternating projective trace is therefore the class of \(E^\pi_{u,u}\). The preceding compact calculation identifies its alternating character test with \(f_{\pi,m}\). Their classes agree in the algebraic cocenter. By its definition this says exactly (6.271), with finitely many commutators. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.119 — ordinary orbital functionals are Schwartz traces. Every regular semisimple orbital functional, and every unipotent orbital functional of Section 6.17, satisfies \[ O(f*h)=O(h*f) \qquad(f,h\in\mathcal S_\omega). \tag{6.273} \] This statement concerns ordinary, unweighted orbital integrals.

Proof. The nonnegative functions \(|f|,|h|\) belong to the trivial-central-character Schwartz algebra. Their convolution is Schwartz by Theorem 6.81. Its orbital integral is finite by Corollary 6.111, or by Theorem 6.88 in the unipotent case. Tonelli therefore gives the genuine absolute bound \[ \int_{\mathcal O}\int_Q|f(y)|\,|h(y^{-1}g)|d\bar y\,d\mu_{\mathcal O}(g) =O(|f|*|h|)<\infty. \tag{6.274} \] For fixed \(y\), conjugating the orbit variable by \(y\) identifies the integrals of \(h(y^{-1}g)\) and \(h(gy^{-1})\). The orbital measure is invariant. The two products with \(f(y)\) are independent of the representative of \(\bar y\), because their central phases cancel. Fubini is now justified, and inversion and translation of convolution variables give (6.273). The same positive argument applies to each invariant unipotent measure constructed in Theorem 6.86. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.120 — the complete regular orbital values of the compact discrete test. With the elliptic torus convention \(\operatorname{vol}(G_\gamma/Z)=1\), \[ O_\gamma(f_{\pi,m})= \begin{cases} \Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1}),&\gamma\text{ elliptic regular},\\ 0,&\gamma\text{ nonelliptic regular}. \end{cases} \tag{6.275} \] Every nonidentity unipotent orbital integral of \(f_{\pi,m}\) is zero, with the measures of Section 6.17. At central elements, \[ f_{\pi,m}(z)=d_\pi\omega(z)^{-1}. \tag{6.276} \] The nonelliptic assertion includes compact-cyclic classes.

Proof. Lemmas 6.118–6.119 identify each of these orbital values with its value on \(E^\pi_{u,u}=d_\pi\overline{\langle\pi(\,\cdot\,)u,u\rangle}\). Theorem 6.110 gives the elliptic value \(\overline{\Theta_\pi(\gamma)}\); unitarity and Corollary 6.71 identify it with \(\Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})\). Corollary 6.111 gives zero at every nonelliptic regular class. Corollary 6.89 gives zero on every nonidentity unipotent orbit. Finally (6.268) and the central rule give (6.276). Absolute convergence has already been proved for the functionals being used. No character integral across the singular set occurs here. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.121 — a contraction of fixed points from division norms. The geometric realization of the division-lattice building can be described by splittable ultrametric norms \(\alpha:D^r\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\), modulo multiplication by positive constants. They satisfy \(\alpha(va)=\alpha(v)|a|_D\) and \(\alpha(v+w)\le\max(\alpha(v),\alpha(w))\). Any two such norms have a common splitting basis. For \(0<t<1\), the formula \[ M_t(\alpha,\beta)(v)= \inf_{v=\sum_jv_j}\max_j \alpha(v_j)^{1-t}\beta(v_j)^t \tag{6.277} \] defines their interpolation norm. The sums are finite. Set \(M_0=\alpha\), \(M_1=\beta\). Its class depends only on their classes, is continuous, and is equivariant under \(G\). The fixed-point set \(\mathcal B^\gamma\), if nonempty, is contractible for every \(\gamma\in G\).

Proof: splitting and common bases. A split norm has finitely many value classes modulo multiplication by \(q_D\). Its restriction to a division subspace has the same property. The norm balls in one valuation period give a finite flag in \(L/L\Pi\), where \(L\) is its unit ball. Choosing a residue basis adapted to this flag and lifting it gives a splitting basis for the restricted norm: at the largest weighted coordinate, reduction in the corresponding flag quotient excludes cancellation, and division scaling reduces every vector to this case. Its unit ball is a full lattice in that subspace, since the original split coordinate bounds bound it above and below by full lattices.

In a \(\beta\)-splitting basis \(b_j\), the ultrametric inequality gives \(\alpha(w)/\beta(w)\le\max_j\alpha(b_j)/\beta(b_j)\). Equality is attained at a maximizing basis vector; choose it as \(v\). A coordinate attaining \(\alpha(v)\) in an \(\alpha\)-splitting basis gives a right-linear functional \(\varphi\) with \(\varphi(v)=1\) and \( |\varphi(w)|_D\le\alpha(w)/\alpha(v)\le\beta(w)/\beta(v)\). The projection \(w\mapsto v\varphi(w)\) is therefore contractive for both norms; so is its complementary projection, by the ultrametric inequality. Both norms split as the maximum on \(vD\oplus\ker\varphi\). Apply the same construction on the kernel, using its splitting bases just established. Induction gives a common splitting basis.

In that basis, writing \(v=\sum_i e_i a_i\), (6.277) is exactly \(\max_i |a_i|_D\alpha(e_i)^{1-t}\beta(e_i)^t\). The coordinate decomposition proves the upper inequality. For any decomposition in (6.277), each of its products bounds the corresponding coordinate term; the ultrametric inequality for the sum of those coordinates proves the lower inequality. Thus (6.277) is a split norm, independent of any basis choice.

If \(q_D^{-c}\alpha'\le\alpha\le q_D^c\alpha'\) and similarly for \(\beta,\beta'\) with constant \(c'\), then \[ q_D^{-((1-t)c+tc')}M_t(\alpha',\beta') \le M_t(\alpha,\beta) \le q_D^{(1-t)c+tc'}M_t(\alpha',\beta'). \tag{6.278} \] This follows directly from the infimum formula. Continuity in \(t\) follows from its finite splitting-basis formula. These inequalities prove joint continuity in the uniform logarithmic norm metric, and also after quotienting by positive scalars. That metric gives the building topology: on an apartment it is the coordinate supremum metric modulo constants; its bounded balls meet finitely many cells, by the lattice Cartan bounds and local finiteness in Section 6.11. The ball-filtration description identifies its real simplex coordinates with those of the building.

Changing every summand by a linear automorphism proves equivariance. Scaling the two input norms scales the result by the corresponding geometric mean, proving the assertion about classes. If both classes are fixed by \(\gamma\), equivariance makes every interpolated class fixed. Interpolating from one fixed class to every other class gives a continuous contraction of \(\mathcal B^\gamma\). \(\square\)

Define the compact Euler test, with trivial central character, by \[ \mathfrak e_G(g)=\sum_{[\sigma]}(-1)^{\dim\sigma} \frac{1_{C_\sigma}(g)\epsilon_\sigma(g^{-1})} {\operatorname{vol}(C_\sigma/Z)}. \tag{6.279} \] It is (6.136) for the trivial representation. It is independent of the depth, since every coefficient fixed space is one-dimensional.

Theorem 6.122 — all regular orbital integrals of the Euler test. In every division rank and either field characteristic, \[ O_\gamma(\mathfrak e_G)= \begin{cases}1,&\gamma\text{ elliptic regular},\\ 0,&\gamma\text{ nonelliptic regular}. \end{cases} \tag{6.280} \] The elliptic torus has quotient volume one. The zero assertion permits any compatible Haar measure on a nonelliptic centralizer.

Proof: the centralizer quotient. A class with noncompact cyclic closure has no conjugate in a simplex stabilizer, so contributes zero by Proposition 6.59. Suppose the cyclic closure is compact modulo \(Z\). It fixes a simplex and hence its barycentre, by Proposition 6.52. Its geometric fixed set is contractible by Lemma 6.121.

Write \(T=\prod_{i=1}^s E_i^\times\) for the regular centralizer. In its primary decomposition, let \(\Gamma\subset T/Z\) be generated by multiplication by \(\varpi_F\) on one of the first \(s-1\) blocks and by one on the other blocks. It is a discrete free abelian group of rank \(s-1\). Its quotient in \(T/Z\) is compact: the valuation directions modulo the common scalar direction are exhausted up to finite index, since the valuations of \(F^\times\) in \(E_i\) are \(e_i\mathbb Z\); the remaining unit quotient is compact. Put \(v_T=\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma\backslash(T/Z))\). For \(s=1\), take \(\Gamma=1\) and \(v_T=1\) by our torus convention.

No nontrivial element of \(\Gamma\) stabilizes a simplex: its unequal block valuations give a noncompact cyclic direction modulo \(Z\), whereas a simplex stabilizer is compact modulo \(Z\). Thus \(\Gamma\) acts freely on \(\mathcal B^\gamma\), including on its cells. Lemma 6.68 gives finitely many \(T\)-orbits of \(\gamma\)-stable simplices. For such a simplex \(\sigma\), put \(K_\sigma=(T\cap C_\sigma)/Z\). Its image is a compact open subgroup of the compact quotient \(\Gamma\backslash(T/Z)\), with the same Haar volume, because \(\Gamma\cap K_\sigma=1\). Consequently its \(T\)-orbit splits into exactly \[ v_T/\operatorname{vol}(K_\sigma) \tag{6.281} \] \(\Gamma\)-orbits. In particular the fixed-point set has a finite cell quotient.

Proof: the signs and the Euler number. The double-coset integration in (6.139) applies also here: compact support and regular properness prove absolute convergence, and there are finitely many centralizer orbits by Lemma 6.68. Thus \(O_\gamma(\mathfrak e_G)\) is the sum of \((-1)^{\dim\sigma}\epsilon_\sigma(\gamma)/\operatorname{vol}(K_\sigma)\) over the \(T\)-orbits of stable simplices. If the vertex permutation of one such \(n\)-simplex has \(c\) cycles, its fixed interior is an open simplex of dimension \(c-1\): barycentric coordinates are equal on each cycle. Its sign is \((-1)^{n+1-c}\), so \((-1)^n\epsilon_\sigma(\gamma)=(-1)^{c-1}\). The fixed intersections with the simplices form a locally finite cell complex; their faces are obtained by omitting complete permutation cycles. Formula (6.281) therefore identifies the orbital sum exactly as \[ O_\gamma(\mathfrak e_G) =v_T^{-1}\chi(\Gamma\backslash\mathcal B^\gamma). \tag{6.282} \]

For \(s=1\), the fixed set is finite and contractible, so its Euler number is one. For \(s>1\), its cellular chains are a finite free resolution of the trivial module over \(\mathbb C[\Gamma]\): the cells have free \(\Gamma\)-orbits, the quotient has finitely many cells, and the augmented complex is exact by contractibility. The standard resolution for \(\Gamma=\mathbb Z^{s-1}\) is the tensor product of the two-term Laurent-polynomial resolutions with differential \(t_i-1\). Each is exact by division of a Laurent polynomial by \(t_i-1\); tensoring over \(\mathbb C\) preserves this exactness, since the underlying vector-space sequences split. Its ranks are \(\binom{s-1}{j}\). Comparison maps between this resolution and the fixed-cell resolution are obtained by projective lifting onto cycles; their composites are homotopic to the identity by the same lifting. After taking \(\Gamma\)-coinvariants they still are homotopy equivalences. The first resolution then has zero differentials and dimensions \(\binom{s-1}{j}\). The finite fixed-cell quotient consequently has Euler number \(\sum_j(-1)^j\binom{s-1}{j}=(1-1)^{s-1}=0\). Substitution in (6.282) proves (6.280). In the one-factor case regularity is ellipticity, and in every other case it is nonellipticity, by Lemma 6.6. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.123 — explicit matching Euler tests in every degree. Let \(G_1=\mathrm{GL}_{r_1}(D_1)\) and \(G_2=\mathrm{GL}_{r_2}(D_2)\), with common reduced degree \(N=r_1d_1=r_2d_2\). Use the common central measure and matching volume-one elliptic torus measures. The pair \((\mathfrak e_{G_1},\mathfrak e_{G_2})\) has equal ordinary orbital integrals on every matching regular class. Each test has zero orbital integral on any regular class with no match on the other side. The same statements hold for \[ g\longmapsto\chi(\operatorname{Nrd}g)^{-1}\mathfrak e_{G_i}(g) \tag{6.283} \] for every smooth unitary character \(\chi:F^\times\to\mathbb C^\times\).

Proof. Ellipticity is irreducibility of the common reduced polynomial, so both values in (6.280) are simultaneously one or simultaneously zero. Every separable field of degree \(N\) embeds as a maximal field in both algebras by Theorem 6.2. Thus a class with no match is nonelliptic and has value zero. The reduced norms are the same constant coefficient of the matching polynomial, up to the common sign \((-1)^N\). This factor is constant on each orbit and proves the twisted assertion. The central rule in (6.283) is \(\chi(z^N)^{-1}\), the same on both sides. This constructs the displayed family of matching compact tests; it does not assert transfer for every test function or assign an irreducible representation. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.124 — elliptic measure is a probability measure. On the common degree-\(N\) elliptic class space, the measure in (6.16) has total mass one: \[ \sum_{[E:F]=N}\frac1{|\operatorname{Aut}_F(E)|} \int_{E^\times_{\mathrm{reg}}/F^\times}\Delta(t)\,d\bar t=1. \tag{6.284} \] Every bounded central-unitary class function consequently has finite elliptic norm, at most its supremum norm. More generally, if \(\mathcal D\) is a division algebra of degree \(N\), the functions \(b_\rho^G(\gamma)=(-1)^{r-1}\chi_\rho(\gamma_{\mathcal D})\), over its irreducible representations of fixed unitary central character, form a complete orthonormal basis of the elliptic class-function completion for \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\).

Proof. Use the local division algebra \(\mathcal D\) of invariant \(1/N\), whose existence and maximal fields were proved in Section 6.1. Its multiplicative group modulo the centre is compact. Normalize its quotient Haar volume to one. The nonregular subset is null: its reduced discriminant is a nonzero polynomial, since an unramified maximal field has separable generators; the polynomial zero-set argument of Corollary 6.8 applies also to the group and central quotient. Every regular element is elliptic. Its centralizer has quotient volume one, so the orbital integral of the constant function one is also one. Apply the nonnegative measurable version of the Weyl formula (6.14) to that constant function on the regular set. Its left side is one and its right side is exactly (6.284). The tori and discriminants for every other degree-\(N\) inner form are the same by Corollary 6.8, proving the assertion there as well. No finiteness of the set of field extensions is assumed. The norm bound follows by integration. Finally apply the complete division-group character basis of Theorem 6.10 and the isometry of Corollary 6.8, as in Corollary 6.12; the displayed sign has absolute value one. This remains a theorem about class functions, with no representation-existence inference for \(G\). \(\square\)

Corollary 6.125 — compact realization of a finite discrete spectral packet. Fix a compact open \(J\) and the unitary central character \(\omega\), and let \(\Pi_J\) be the discrete series with nonzero \(J\)-fixed vectors. This is a finite set by Corollary 6.117. For arbitrary complex numbers \(a_\pi\), \(\pi\in\Pi_J\), there is a compact-mod-centre smooth test \(f_a\), at one common sufficiently deep level, with the following values for every irreducible tempered \(\tau\) of central character \(\omega\): \[ \operatorname{tr}\tau(f_a)= \begin{cases}a_\tau,&\tau\in\Pi_J,\\0,&\tau\text{ irreducible tempered outside }\Pi_J, \end{cases} \quad O_\gamma(f_a)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_J}a_\pi\Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1}) \quad(\gamma\text{ elliptic regular}). \tag{6.285} \] Its ordinary nonelliptic regular and nonidentity unipotent orbital integrals vanish, and \(f_a(z)=\omega(z)^{-1}\sum_\pi a_\pi d_\pi\).

Proof. Choose a generating level for each member of the finite set and its compact test from Corollary 6.117. Their finitely many stabilizers contain a common deep principal subgroup. Take \(f_a=\sum_\pi a_\pi f_{\pi,m_\pi}\). The trace assertions follow from (6.267), and all orbital and central assertions follow from Theorem 6.120. Every sum here is finite. \(\square\)

The universal projective trace can also be compared with Meyer, Definitions 33–34 and Sections 7.2–7.4 of the free preprint cited above. The arguments in this subsection give ordinary orbital values and explicit matching tests. Identification of the actual elliptic character integral with the Euler–Poincaré pairing, spectral completeness by discrete-series characters, and the full higher-degree local and global representation correspondences require further arguments.

6.24. An explicit Iwahori sign discrete series and its degree

Put \(N=rd\), \(q=q_D\), \(K=\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_D)\), and \(Q=G/Z\). In this subsection \(K\) and the central subgroup \(\mathcal O_F^\times\) have volume one. Thus the image in \(Q\) of a subgroup of \(K\) containing \(\mathcal O_F^\times\) has its ordinary compact-group volume. We first use trivial central character. The construction uses a square-integrable convolution projection, not a character integration formula across singular elements.

Choose a division uniformizer \(\Pi\) with \(\Pi^d=\varpi_F\). Such a choice follows from the cyclic presentation in Lemma 6.1: if \(u^d=\varpi_F^a\), choose integers \(b,c\) with \(ab+dc=1\) and take \(\Pi=u^b\varpi_F^c\). For \(d=1\) take \(\Pi=\varpi_F\). Let \(I\subset K\) be the inverse image of the lower triangular subgroup of \(\mathrm{GL}_r(k_D)\). This is the stabilizer of the standard chain \(L_j=\Pi\mathcal O_D^{\,j}\oplus\mathcal O_D^{\,r-j}\), extended periodically. Write \(v_I=\operatorname{vol}(IZ/Z)\) and \([m]_z!=\prod_{j=1}^m(1+z+\cdots+z^{j-1})\). Counting complete residue flags, one line at a time, gives \[ v_I=[r]_q!^{-1}. \tag{6.286} \] Indeed the number of lines in \(k_D^m\) is \((q^m-1)/(q-1)\); choose a line and then a complete flag in its quotient. This induction proves the stated count, including \(r=1\).

Lemma 6.126 — division-chain double cosets and their convolution. For \(r\ge2\), let \(W_a\) be the affine permutation group of type \(\widetilde A_{r-1}\), with its \(r\) simple wall reflections and length \(\ell\). Let \(\tau\) send \(e_i\) to \(e_{i+1}\) for \(i<r\) and \(e_r\) to \(e_1\Pi\). Then \(\tau\) normalizes \(I\), \(\tau^r=\Pi I_r\), and \(\tau^N=\varpi_F I_r\). On \(Q\) the disjoint double cosets are \[ Q=\coprod_{0\le k<N,\,w\in W_a}\overline I\tau^k w\overline I, \qquad \operatorname{vol}(\overline I\tau^k w\overline I)=v_Iq^{\ell(w)}. \tag{6.287} \] Here and below \(\overline I=IZ/Z\); representatives of \(w\) are monomial matrices. Put \(T_x=v_I^{-1}1_{\overline I x\overline I}\). For every simple reflection \(s\), \[ T_s^2=(q-1)T_s+qT_1,\qquad T_xT_y=T_{xy}\quad\hbox{if }\ell(xy)=\ell(x)+\ell(y). \tag{6.288} \] Also \(T_\tau T_xT_\tau^{-1}=T_{\tau x\tau^{-1}}\). The functions \(T_x\) span the compact \(I\)-corner. If \(r=1\), omit \(W_a\); the corner is the group algebra of the \(d\) valuation cosets.

Proof: the simultaneous chain basis. A complete periodic lattice chain has successive quotients of dimension one over \(k_D\), and satisfies \(L_{i+r}=L_i\Pi\). The subgroup fixing every actual lattice in the standard chain is \(I\). Two chains have a common division basis. Here is a direct verification. For chains \(L_i,M_j\), filter the one-dimensional space \(L_i/L_{i+1}\) by the images of \(L_i\cap M_j\). The filtration is eventually the whole space in one direction and zero in the other. It has exactly one jump. Equivalently, the dimensions of \[ \frac{L_i\cap M_j} {(L_{i+1}\cap M_j)+(L_i\cap M_{j+1})} \tag{6.289} \] are zero except for one entry one in each row. Interchanging the chains gives one entry one in each column. These entries repeat under \((i,j)\mapsto(i+r,j+r)\). Lift their nonzero residue vectors for one period. They form a basis adapted to both chains: their successive nonzero leading residues are the basis of every indicated flag quotient. Successive division by \(\Pi\) proves that they generate every lattice. More explicitly, subtract the prescribed leading residues and repeat; completeness makes the remainder tend to zero, and a finite free lattice generated by the lifted basis is closed. Linear independence follows from its first nonzero flag residue. This proves the assertion without a simultaneous-apartment assumption.

The column-to-row assignment is a permutation of \(\mathbb Z\) satisfying \(w(i+r)=w(i)+r\). Its integer \(r^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^r(w(i)-i)\) records the total valuation shift. The permutations with shift zero form \(W_a\); shifting the chain index by one is \(\tau\). Thus every relative position is uniquely \(\tau^k w\) before reducing \(k\) modulo \(N\). Central multiplication by \(\varpi_F\) shifts the index by \(N\), proving precisely that reduction in (6.287). Simultaneous chain bases prove both exhaustiveness and disjointness.

Proof: volumes and products. Relative positions can be reduced by successive adjacent exchanges in the ordered periodic basis. Their length is the number of inversions, counted modulo simultaneous shift by \(r\). At a single wall the remaining choice is a line in a two-dimensional residue quotient. There are \(q+1\) such lines; after excluding the original line there are exactly \(q\) choices. Gaussian elimination in successive leading residues shows that a reduced sequence of exchanges has one independent residue parameter for each inversion. Its ordered parameters are unique: compare the first differing leading residue and continue in the smaller flag quotient. Therefore \(IxI/I\) has exactly \(q^{\ell(x)}\) members, and concatenation of length-additive exchanges gives the second formula in (6.288).

The index can also be read directly from entries, including arbitrarily large translations. Set \(a_{ij}=1\) for \(i<j\) and \(a_{ij}=0\) for \(i>j\). If \(xe_i=e_{\sigma(i)}\Pi^{m_i}\), the elementary entry \(c\) in position \((i,j)\) is conjugated to \(\Pi^{m_i}c\Pi^{-m_j}\) in position \((\sigma(i),\sigma(j))\). The intersection order therefore has off-diagonal thresholds \[ b_{\sigma(i),\sigma(j)} =\max\{a_{\sigma(i),\sigma(j)},a_{ij}+m_i-m_j\}, \qquad [I:I\cap xIx^{-1}]=q^{\sum_{i\ne j}(b_{ij}-a_{ij})}. \] For completeness, both threshold arrays satisfy \(b_{ij}+b_{jk}\ge b_{ik}\): each of the two original arrays does, and taking their maximum preserves that inequality. They contain the Iwahori thresholds. Unit-pivot elimination thus factors their unit groups into the ordered lower entries, diagonal units and upper entries; elimination preserves every threshold by that inequality. Diagonal pivots stay units because every upper-times-lower correction is in \(\Pi\mathcal O_D\). Unit multiplications and elementary additive shears preserve coordinate Haar measure, and the diagonal unit factor is unchanged. Each additional entry level contributes a factor \(q\), proving the index formula. Its sum counts exactly the periodic inversions, since the thresholds count the integer levels crossed by each ordered coordinate pair. In a length-additive product those inversion sets concatenate. The corresponding ordered residue parameters give the bijection of right cosets used above. The required elementary rearrangements use multiplication of division entries and \((1+ab)^{-1}\) with \(ab\in\Pi\mathcal O_D\); these exist in every residue characteristic.

For the quadratic formula, return through the same panel. A two-step path either returns to its original chamber, in \(q\) ways, or ends at any prescribed different chamber, in \(q-1\) ways. With the normalization \(T_1=v_I^{-1}1_{\overline I}\), these are exactly its two coefficients. The argument includes \(r=2\), where the two affine wall generators have no finite braid relation. Exchanges in disjoint coordinates commute; the two orders for three adjacent coordinates give the three-step braid by the same elimination. Alternatively these relations follow by moving a segment between alcove interiors across one codimension-two intersection at a time. Thus a reduced expression gives the same double coset and product regardless of the exchanges chosen. Conjugating the chain by \(\tau\) rotates its walls and preserves their residue parameters. This proves all assertions over the division residue field in either characteristic. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.127 — the exact affine growth sum. For \(0<t<1\), \[ P_a(t):=\sum_{w\in W_a}t^{\ell(w)} =\frac{1-t^r}{(1-t)^r}. \tag{6.290} \] For \(r=1\) the sum and the displayed quotient both equal one.

Proof. For \(r\ge2\), let \(S\) be the cyclic set of affine walls. Every proper \(J\subset S\) generates a finite product \(W_J\) of symmetric groups. Write \(L_J\) for its longest length and \(P_J(t)=\sum_{w\in W_J}t^{\ell(w)}\). Sorting each of its consecutive coordinate blocks gives the unique minimal representative of a right \(W_J\)-coset and adds lengths. An element has every member of \(J\) as a right descent exactly when its factor in \(W_J\) is longest.

No element has all the affine walls as descents. The affine simple functions are positive on the reference alcove and their sum is one; all of them cannot be negative on its inverse image. Every nonidentity element has a descent: remove the last exchange in a shortest gallery. Consequently inclusion and exclusion over its descent set gives \[ \frac1{P_a(t)} =\sum_{J\subsetneq S}(-1)^{|J|}\frac{t^{L_J}}{P_J(t)}. \tag{6.291} \] To justify summation first note polynomial growth. A periodic permutation is an integral translation of total shift zero followed by one of finitely many residue permutations. Its inversion count controls the differences of its translation coordinates up to a constant depending on \(r\); since their sum is zero, it controls every coordinate. There are \(O((1+L)^{r-1})\) elements of length at most \(L\). All series just used therefore converge absolutely for \(t<1\). The preceding sorting also proves the coset generating series required in (6.291).

We evaluate the finite sum rather than importing a growth formula. Put \(u=t^{-1}\). Inserting the largest letter of a permutation gives \(P_{S_m}(u)=[m]_u!\), and reversing a permutation gives \(t^{L_J}/P_J(t)=1/P_J(u)\). If the omitted walls divide the cycle into \(k\) nonempty blocks of sizes \(m_1,\ldots,m_k\), then \(|J|=r-k\) and \(P_J(u)=\prod_i[m_i]_u!\). Put \(E(z)=\sum_{m\ge0}z^m/[m]_u!\). Counting a marked omitted wall counts each cyclic division \(k\) times and each possible starting wall \(r\) times. The sum in (6.291) is thus \[ (-1)^{r+1}r[z^r]\log E(z) =\frac{(u-1)^r}{u^r-1}. \tag{6.292} \] For the equality on the right, the defining factorial gives \(E(uz)=(1+(u-1)z)E(z)\). Take formal logarithms and compare the coefficient of \(z^r\). This proves (6.292) using only finite coefficients of formal power series. Its reciprocal is (6.290). \(\square\)

Let \(|\eta|=1\) and \(\eta^N=1\). Define an \(I\)-bi-invariant function on \(Q\) by \[ \Phi_\eta(\tau^kw)=\eta^{-k}(-q)^{-\ell(w)}. \tag{6.293} \] The periodicity and the wall rotation make this unambiguous. The inverse phase in this formula is relevant for nonreal \(\eta\).

Theorem 6.128 — a minimal square-integrable projection. Put \[ C=Nv_I P_a(q^{-1}),\qquad p_\eta=C^{-1}\Phi_\eta. \tag{6.294} \] Then \(p_\eta\in\mathcal S_1\), \(p_\eta^*=p_\eta\), \(p_\eta*p_\eta=p_\eta\), and \(p_\eta*\mathcal S_1*p_\eta=\mathbb Cp_\eta\). The Hilbert closure of the left translates of \(p_\eta\) in \(L^2(Q)\) is an irreducible unitary representation \(\pi_\eta\). It is admissible and discrete series, has a one-dimensional \(I\)-fixed space, and satisfies \[ \pi_\eta(T_s)|_{\pi_\eta^I}=-1,\qquad \pi_\eta(T_\tau)|_{\pi_\eta^I}=\eta,\qquad d_{\pi_\eta}=\frac1C =\frac1N\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}(q^j-1). \tag{6.295} \] It is the unique irreducible unitary representation with this specified \(I\)-fixed eigenline. The \(N\) choices of \(\eta\) are inequivalent.

Proof: convergence and the convolution identity. Formula (6.287) gives \(\|\Phi_\eta\|_2^2=Nv_I P_a(q^{-1})=C\). It is also Schwartz. To see the stronger assertion, a monomial relative position is a translation followed by a finite permutation. Its affine length differs by at most the largest finite permutation length from \(\sum_{i<j}|\lambda_i-\lambda_j|\). The Cartan rearrangement changes this bound by only another constant depending on \(r,d\), since \(0\le k<N\). The same sum is the negative base-\(q\) logarithm of the positive Cartan modular character. The spherical lower bound of Lemma 6.73 and the Cartan height bounds therefore give \(|\Phi_\eta(g)|/\Xi(g)\le A(1+\sigma(g))^bq^{-\ell(w)/2}\) with fixed constants. Length controls height outside a bounded set. Multiplication by any power of \(1+\sigma\) remains bounded. The function is already bi-invariant at one compact open level, proving its Schwartz membership. In rank one the quotient is compact and the conclusion is immediate.

The inverse phase gives \(\Phi_\eta^*=\Phi_\eta\). The wall multiplication in Lemma 6.126 gives, on either side, \(T_s*\Phi_\eta=-\Phi_\eta\) and \(T_\tau*\Phi_\eta=\eta\Phi_\eta\). For example at \(w\), a length-increasing wall gives \(q\Phi_\eta(sw)=-\Phi_\eta(w)\); a decreasing wall gives \(\Phi_\eta(sw)+(q-1)\Phi_\eta(w)=-\Phi_\eta(w)\). These recurrences, and the value at the identity, determine the common eigenfunction uniquely on every double coset. Associativity and Schwartz convolution imply that \(\Phi_\eta*\Phi_\eta\) is another such eigenfunction. Its value at one is \(\|\Phi_\eta\|_2^2=C\), so it equals \(C\Phi_\eta\). This proves the idempotent identity.

For a compact \(I\)-corner test, multiplication with \(p_\eta\) is the scalar specified by these eigenrelations. General Schwartz corner tests are limits of compact corner tests by Theorem 6.81. Continuity of convolution and closedness of the one-dimensional space \(\mathbb Cp_\eta\) prove the asserted minimal corner.
