The finite-field Frobenius conventions agree with Conrad's free finite-field notes, Theorem 4.1. All duality, measure, stabilizer and exhaustive counting arguments used here are proved in this lesson.

6.36. Cubic fields with a noncommutative centralizer

Let \(E/F\) be any totally ramified cubic field embedded in a division algebra of degree \(d=3\delta\). Its centralizer \(\Delta=D_E\) has degree \(\delta\) over \(E\), and need not be commutative. The integral dual and primitive-row arguments give a complete cyclic-quotient orbit classification in every division rank. Power heights also recover the largest normalized quotient length. In degree three this recovery uses just the extreme Cartan coordinates, even when conjugation by an Eisenstein uniformizer is not of finite order.

Lemma 6.206 — power heights in every totally ramified degree. Under Theorems 6.191–6.192, let \([E:F]=e\mid d\), let \(\theta\) be a uniformizer of \(E\), and put \(\delta=d/e\), \(\tau=\operatorname{Ad}(\theta)\). Suppose \(L=gL_0\subset L_0\) is normalized. Let \(u\) be the greatest elementary length of \(L_0/L\), equivalently the least integer with \(L_0\mathfrak P^u\subset L\). Write \(X=g^{-1}(\theta I)g\), and define \[ \begin{gathered} d_j=-\nu_{\min}(g^{-1}\tau^j(g)) =j\delta-\nu_{\min}(X^j),\\ a=\nu_{\max}(X)-\delta,\qquad c=\delta-\nu_{\min}(X),\\ u=\max_{0\le j<e}d_j,\qquad \frac{u}{e-1}\le a,c\le u. \end{gathered} \tag{6.465} \] The conclusions include \(u=a=c=0\) when \(L=L_0\).

Proof. For any lattice \(M\), the least integer \(b\) with \(M\subset L\mathfrak P^{-b}\) is the negative minimum Cartan exponent of its relative basis matrix. Every relative matrix \(g^{-1}\tau^j(g)\) has reduced-determinant valuation zero, since conjugation preserves that valuation; its minimum exponent is therefore nonpositive. The saturation identity \(L_0=\sum_{j<e}\tau^jL\) gives \(L_0\subset L\mathfrak P^{-\max d_j}\), hence \(u\le\max d_j\). Conversely each \(\tau^jL\subset L_0\subset L\mathfrak P^{-u}\), so \(d_j\le u\). This proves the equality. The displayed expression in terms of \(X^j\) follows from \(X^j=g^{-1}\theta^jg=(g^{-1}\tau^j(g))\theta^j\): multiplication by \(\theta^j I\) shifts every Cartan exponent by \(j\delta\).

Both \(L\) and \(\tau L\) lie between \(L_0\mathfrak P^u\) and \(L_0\). The two relative inclusions give \(a,c\le u\). Products of \(j\) conjugates of \(g^{-1}\tau(g)\) have minimum entry valuation at least \(-jc\); thus \(d_j\le jc\), yielding \(u\le(e-1)c\). The stable sum is also \(\sum_{j<e}\tau^{-j}L\), by applying \(\tau^{-(e-1)}\) to it. The minimum exponent of \(g^{-1}\tau^{-1}(g)\) is \(-a\), because this matrix is the inverse of a \(\tau^{-1}\)-conjugate of \(g^{-1}\tau(g)\). The same product argument backwards yields \(u\le(e-1)a\). No finite-order hypothesis on \(\tau\) is used. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.207 — exact cubic extrema. For every totally ramified cubic \(E/F\), every \(d=3\delta\), and every normalized lattice in any division rank, \[ \max(a,c)=u. \tag{6.466} \] In division rank three this gives \[ \begin{gathered} \boldsymbol\nu(X)=(\delta+a,\delta+c-a,\delta-c),\\ \rho_G(X)=\sigma(X)=a+c=u+w,\\ \left\lceil\frac u2\right\rceil\le w=\min(a,c)\le u. \end{gathered} \tag{6.467} \] In particular \(3u/2\le\rho_G(X)\le2u\). The statements hold for every choice of uniformizer of \(E\), including wild and inseparable fields.

Proof. Lemma 6.206 gives \(u=\max(c,d_2)\) and \(a,c\le u\). If \(d_2\le c\), then \(c=u\) proves (6.466). Otherwise use the Eisenstein identity \(\theta^3=A_2\theta^2+A_1\theta+A_0\), where \(v_D(A_0)=3\delta\) and \(v_D(A_i)\ge3\delta\) for \(i=1,2\), allowing zero coefficients. It gives \[ X^{-1}=A_0^{-1}(X^2-A_2X-A_1I). \tag{6.468} \] The minimum entry valuations of the three terms in parentheses are respectively \(2\delta-d_2\), at least \(4\delta-c\), and at least \(3\delta\). When \(d_2>c\), the first is strictly smaller than both others, so cannot cancel. Consequently \(\nu_{\min}(X^{-1})=-\delta-d_2=-\delta-a\), proving \(a=d_2=u\).

In rank three the sum of the Cartan exponents is \(3\delta\), so its middle exponent is \(\delta+c-a\). Their ordering imposes \(c\le2a\) and \(a\le2c\); (6.467) follows from (6.466). Rank-three root height is its spread. This argument uses the Eisenstein inverse formula, rather than a presumed identity \(\tau^3=1\). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.208 — right coefficient lattices and their integral dual. For the cubic field, put \(Q=q_\Delta\), \(q=q_D=Q^3\), and choose a uniformizer \(\pi\in\Delta\), so \(v_D(\pi)=1\). Choose \(z\in\mathcal O_D\) whose residue lies outside \(\mathbb F_Q\). Then \[ D=\Delta\oplus z\Delta\oplus z^2\Delta,\qquad \mathcal O_D=\mathcal O_\Delta\oplus z\mathcal O_\Delta \oplus z^2\mathcal O_\Delta. \tag{6.469} \] These are right coefficient decompositions. Left multiplication by \(\mathcal O_D^\times\) is transitive on right \(\mathcal O_\Delta\)-sublattices of \(\mathcal O_D\) with cyclic cokernel of a specified positive length.

For every finite-length right \(\mathcal O_\Delta\)-module \(M\), its surjective generating \(r\)-tuples form one orbit under right \(\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_\Delta)\).

Proof: the right basis. The three residues \(1,\bar z,\bar z^2\) are independent over \(\mathbb F_Q\), since the residue extension has prime degree three. If a right coefficient sum has a common least coefficient valuation, multiply it on the right by the inverse power of \(\pi\); residue independence prevents cancellation. This proves independence. To expand an integral element, subtract a right coefficient combination matching its residue, divide the remainder on the right by \(\pi\), and repeat. Completeness gives three convergent coefficients in \(\mathcal O_\Delta\). Scaling proves (6.469).

Proof: the dual module. Put \(T=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_\Delta}(\mathcal O_D,\mathcal O_\Delta)\), with right \(\mathcal O_D\)-action \((\varphi\cdot b)(x)=\varphi(bx)\). Precomposition by left multiplication preserves right \(\Delta\)-linearity, by associativity. For any nonzero \(\varphi\), the map \(b\mapsto\varphi\cdot b\) on \(D\) is injective: a nonzero \(b\) is invertible. Its target \(\operatorname{Hom}_\Delta(D,\Delta)\) has \(F\)-dimension \(3[\Delta:F]=[D:F]\), hence this map is an isomorphism of right \(D\)-modules. Thus \(T\) is a full rank-one right \(\mathcal O_D\)-lattice. Under this identification it is principal, by choosing an element of least valuation.

Value multiplication by \(\pi\) on the left commutes with that right action. Its image \(\pi T\) has index \(Q^3=q_D\), because the integral dual of the right basis in (6.469) is free of rank three on the left over \(\mathcal O_\Delta\). It is therefore the unique maximal right \(\mathcal O_D\)-sublattice of \(T\). Primitive functionals, those whose values include a unit, are precisely \(T\setminus\pi T\), and form one right \(\mathcal O_D^\times\)-orbit. Every cyclic-cokernel lattice of length \(a\) is the inverse image of \(\mathfrak p_\Delta^a\) under a primitive integral functional: lift its surjection to \(\mathcal O_\Delta/\mathfrak p_\Delta^a\) in the basis (6.469). This proves the asserted transitivity, without a trace pairing or commutativity of \(\Delta\).

Proof: generating tuples. Choose a subset of a generating tuple which is a basis modulo \(M\mathfrak p_\Delta\). It generates \(M\), since iterating multiplication by \(\mathfrak p_\Delta\) kills a finite-length quotient. Subtract its right coefficient combinations from the redundant entries. Two resulting minimal generating tuples differ by a right coefficient matrix whose residue is invertible. A residue inverse lifts to an actual matrix inverse over \(\mathcal O_\Delta\) by the convergent geometric series, as in Theorem 6.192. Extending it by an identity block and undoing the elementary column operations proves the claim over this noncommutative local ring. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.209 — every cyclic-quotient orbit for a cubic field. Let \(E/F\) be any totally ramified cubic field embedded in \(D\), with \(d=3\delta\). Give \(H_0=\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_\Delta)\) volume one. Define \(P_{r,k}(Q)=\prod_{j=0}^{k-1}(1-Q^{j-r})\) for \(k\le r\). For \(r\ge3\), the normalized lattices with cyclic quotient of length \(n\ge1\) have exactly \(n+1\) orbits, represented by kernels modulo \(\mathfrak P^n\) of \[ v_{n,b}=(1,z,z^2\pi^b,0,\ldots,0),\qquad0\le b\le n. \tag{6.470} \] Their greatest stable sublattices have quotient lengths \((n,n,n-b,0^{r-3})\). Their exact masses are \[ W_{r,n,b}=\begin{cases} Q^{3(r-1)n}\dfrac{P_{r,3}(Q)}{1-Q^{-3}},&b=0,\\[4pt] Q^{3(r-1)n-(r-2)b}\dfrac{P_{r,3}(Q)}{1-Q^{-1}},&0<b<n,\\[4pt] Q^{(2r-1)n}\dfrac{P_{r,2}(Q)}{1-Q^{-1}},&b=n. \end{cases} \tag{6.471} \] For \(r=2\), there is exactly one such orbit at every \(n\), represented by \((1,z)\); its mass is \(Q^{3n}(1-Q^{-2})\) and its intersection lengths are \((n,n)\). Rank one has none. In every rank these orbits have the Cartan list (6.442) for a uniformizer of \(E\), and their masses sum to the complete count (6.441).

Proof: the invariant and completeness. For a primitive row \(v\), form the right \(\mathcal O_\Delta\)-lattice \(\Lambda_v=\sum_i v_i\mathcal O_\Delta+\mathfrak P^n\subset\mathcal O_D\). Changing lifts has no effect. A right \(H_0\) operation on the row preserves it, and a left \(\mathcal O_D\)-unit rescales it on the left. Normalization of the cyclic kernel is exactly that its residue row is not defined over \(\mathbb F_Q\), by Theorem 6.196. Its coordinate span therefore has dimension two or three over \(\mathbb F_Q\).

In dimension three \(\Lambda_v=\mathcal O_D\); write \(b=0\). In dimension two its quotient has elementary lengths \((b,0,0)\) for a unique \(1\le b\le n\). Lemma 6.208 makes all such \(\Lambda\) with fixed \(b\) equivalent by left units. For a fixed \(\Lambda\), the rows are exactly the generating \(r\)-tuples of \(M=\Lambda/\mathfrak P^n\), and the same lemma makes them one right \(H_0\)-orbit. Here \(M\) has lengths \((n,n,n-b)\). If \(b<n\), it needs three generators; if \(b=n\), it needs two. This proves the stated possibilities in ranks two and at least three, with representatives (6.470). The invariant \(b\) distinguishes them because left units are right \(\mathcal O_\Delta\)-linear and preserve \(\mathfrak P^n\).

Proof: intersections and actual masses. For the representative, a vector in \(\Delta^r\) belongs to its kernel just when the three right coefficients \(x_1,x_2,\pi^b x_3\) lie in \(\mathfrak p_\Delta^n\); the other coordinates are unrestricted. Extending this intersection to \(\mathcal O_D\) gives its greatest stable lattice, by Theorem 6.192. This proves the intersection lengths, with the same two-coordinate argument in rank two.

There is one possible \(\Lambda\) for \(b=0\). For \(b>0\), primitive right-module functionals and their free left target-unit action give \(N_b=Q^{2(b-1)}(Q^2+Q+1)=Q^{2b}(1-Q^{-3})/(1-Q^{-1})\) possibilities, exactly as in the primitive-row proof of Theorem 6.196, now over \(\mathcal O_\Delta\). The cardinality of \(M\) is \(Q^{3n-b}\). A random \(r\)-tuple generates a module of residue dimension \(k\) with fraction \(P_{r,k}(Q)\): this is the full-row-rank fraction for a \(k\)-by-\(r\) matrix over \(\mathbb F_Q\), obtained by choosing independent rows, and residue generation suffices by the finite-length argument above. Here \(k=3\) if \(b<n\), and \(k=2\) if \(b=n\).

Multiply this fraction by \(|M|^rN_b\), using \(N_0=1\), and divide by the free primitive-row target units, whose number is \(q^n(1-q^{-1})=Q^{3n}(1-Q^{-3})\). This gives (6.471). For \(r=2,b=n\), it gives \(Q^{3n}(1-Q^{-2})\). These are actual orbit cardinalities, hence exact reciprocal stabilizer volumes. Their sum is the total normalized primitive-row count because the classification is exhaustive, not because a finite numerical test matches it. The Cartan assertion is Theorem 6.196, with \(\pi\in\Delta\) commuting with \(\theta\). \(\square\)

Corollary 6.210 — dual families in every division rank. In rank \(r\ge3\), the normalized opposite-algebra duals of (6.470) have quotient lengths \[ (n,n-b,0^{r-2}),\qquad L_0/I:\ (n,n,n-b,0^{r-3}),\qquad \operatorname{mass}=W_{r,n,b}. \tag{6.472} \] They have the same conjugate Cartan lists as the cyclic kernels. Their complete subseries satisfies Theorem 6.197 for every generator of the cubic field, with \(t>b_G+1\) and polynomial tails. In rank two the unique normalized orbit at each length is carried to the unique orbit of the same length on the opposite side.

Proof. In the cyclic kernel basis, the first generator of its greatest stable sublattice is exactly the first basis vector. Killing it leaves independent relations \(\pi^n\) and \(\pi^{n-b}\) on the next two basis vectors; stable extra coordinates contribute zero quotient. Thus \(L/I\) has lengths \((n,n-b,0^{r-2})\). Transposing the elementary form of the inclusion \(I\subset L\) proves the first assertion after normalized duality. Theorem 6.200 preserves the intersection lengths, masses and conjugate Cartan lists and supplies the full dual-cyclic subseries bound for every generator. The rank-two calculation has one remaining relation \(\pi^n\), and uniqueness follows from Theorem 6.209. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.211 — every rank-three quotient type and the equal-length orbits. For every totally ramified cubic field in every \(d=3\delta\), the quotient-type count (6.461) holds with \(Q=q_\Delta\), \(q=Q^3\). For each \(u\ge1\), every normalized rank-three lattice with quotient lengths \((u,u,0)\) belongs to one orbit, the normalized dual of \((n,b)=(u,0)\). Its mass and conjugate Cartan list for any field uniformizer are \[ (q-Q)(q-Q^2)q^{2u-2} =q^{2u}(1-Q^{-1})(1-Q^{-2}),\qquad (\delta+u,\delta,\delta-u). \tag{6.473} \] The entire equal-length subseries has finite absolute contribution for every generator of \(E/F\) with \(t>b_G+1\), including all polynomial cutoff tails.

Proof. The proof of Lemma 6.204 uses only the residue Frobenius, the equality \(v_D|_\Delta=v_\Delta\), and right-DVR primitive-row and graph counts. All these hold here by Theorems 6.191–6.192. More explicitly, a positive two-length quotient has a residue line; it is normalized exactly when its three coordinates have rank three over \(\mathbb F_Q\), giving \((q-Q)(q-Q^2)\) such lines. For a fixed line, putting it on the third axis for counting gives the unique data \(M=\pi^vM'\subset D^2\) and a graph class in \(\mathfrak P\mathcal O_D^2/M\). There are \((q+1)q^{u-v-1}\) possibilities for \(M'\) when \(u>v\), one when \(u=v\), and \(q^{u+v-2}\) graph classes. This proves exactly (6.461), with no assumption on a binomial equation for \(\theta\) or commutativity of \(\Delta\).

Corollary 6.210 gives an orbit of quotient type \((u,u,0)\) and mass \(W_{3,u,0}\). That mass equals the total count just proved, since \(P_{3,3}(Q)/(1-Q^{-3})=(1-Q^{-1})(1-Q^{-2})\). It therefore contains every lattice of this type. Duality gives the Cartan list in (6.473). For a uniformizer, the mass cancels \(q^{-2u}\) in the spherical estimate, leaving one polynomial length sum. For any other generator the same conclusion with tails is already the complete dual-cyclic bound of Theorem 6.200. \(\square\)

Example 6.212 — a wild cubic whose conjugation is not periodic. Let \(F=\mathbb F_3((t))\), \(L=\mathbb F_{27}((t))\), and take \(z^3+2z+1=0\), \(\Pi^3=t\), \(\Pi a=a^3\Pi\) on the coefficient field. The polynomial has no root in \(\mathbb F_3\), so defines \(\mathbb F_{27}\). Put \(c=z^2\) and \(\theta=\Pi+c\Pi^2\). The elementary symmetric functions of \(z,z^3,z^9\) give \(\operatorname{Tr}(z)=0\), \(\operatorname{Tr}(c)=2\), and \(\operatorname{N}(c)=1\). Direct multiplication, keeping the skew order, gives \[ \theta^3=t+2t\theta+t^2,\qquad E=F(\theta),\quad[E:F]=3,\qquad \tau^3\ne1. \tag{6.474} \] Indeed write \(\theta=(1+c\Pi)\Pi\). Its cube is \((1+c\Pi)(1+c^3\Pi)(1+c^9\Pi)t\). The coefficients of \(\Pi,\Pi^2,\Pi^3\) in the product are respectively \(\operatorname{Tr}(c)\), \(c\operatorname{Tr}(c)\), \(\operatorname{N}(c)\). This proves the identity. The valuation of \(\theta\) is one in \(D\), so its \(F\)-valuation is \(1/3\) and it generates a totally ramified cubic field. Its polynomial \(T^3-2tT-t-t^2\) has derivative \(-2t=t\ne0\), so the extension is separable and wild. Since \(\theta^3=t(1+2\theta+t)\notin F\), its third conjugation power is not the identity on \(D\).

For the cyclic kernel \((1,z,z^2\theta)\) modulo \(\theta^2\), Theorem 6.209 gives \[ L_0/I:(2,2,1),\qquad \boldsymbol\nu(X)=(3,1,-1),\qquad W_{3,2,1}=3^{11}(1-3^{-2})(1-3^{-3})=151632. \tag{6.475} \] Its normalized dual has quotient lengths \((2,1,0)\), the same intersection, mass and Cartan list. The exact cubic height relation applies despite \(\tau^3\ne1\).

Figure 16. Lemma 6.206 and Theorem 6.207 give the exact power and cubic height relations. The lower boxes use the noncommutative centralizer in Theorem 6.209; Solution 7.24 computes each mass. Example 6.212 gives the wild cubic in the last two rows. The boxes denote module invariants, without assigning geometric distances to their positions.

For finite-field Frobenius, trace and norm, see Conrad's free finite-field notes, Theorems 4.1 and 4.6. The right-module duality, noncommutative tuple argument, exact counts, height identities and wild-field calculation needed here are proved above. Proposition 6.216 and Lemma 6.217 give the unequal-length estimates used in the full rank-three bound of Theorem 6.218.

6.37. Totally ramified orbital bounds in division rank three

Let \(G=\mathrm{GL}_3(D)\), and let \(E/F\) be totally ramified of degree \(e\ge3\), embedded in \(D\), with \(d=e\delta\). Put \(\Delta=D_E\), \(Q=q_\Delta\), \(q=q_D=Q^e\), and choose a uniformizer \(\pi\in\Delta\). It has \(D\)-valuation one and commutes with every element of \(E\). In this section \(s\in E^\times\) is any generator of \(E/F\). No separability hypothesis is imposed.

Normalization always means \(\Sigma L=L_0\), for the coefficient order of Theorem 6.192. The centralizer \(H=\mathrm{GL}_3(\Delta)\) is transitive on its stable lattices. Give \(K\) and \(H_0\) volume one. Exact incidence counts give the full ordinary orbital bound for this family, including generators whose conjugation acts trivially on residues.

Lemma 6.213 — quotient types and invariant subspaces. Every normalized lattice has elementary quotient lengths \((u,v,0)\), \(0\le v\le u\). Put \[ T=(q-Q)(q-Q^2),\quad A=T/q^2,\quad C_3=q^2+q-Q^2-Q. \qquad \begin{array}{c|c} \text{quotient type}&\text{actual lattice count}\\\hline (u,0,0),\ u\ge1&C_3q^{2u-2}\\ (u,v,0),\ 0<v<u&T(q+1)q^{2u-3}\\ (u,u,0),\ u\ge1&Tq^{2u-2}. \end{array} \tag{6.476} \] A strict positive two-length type has a residue line \(\ell\) whose coordinates have rank three over \(\mathbb F_Q\).

If a right \(D\)-subspace \(V\subset D^3\) is invariant under entrywise \(\tau_s=\operatorname{Ad}(s)\), then \(V\) is defined over \(\Delta\). The reduction of \(V\cap\mathcal O_D^3\) is an \(\mathbb F_Q\)-defined subspace of \(\mathbb F_q^3\).

Proof: the counts. A normalized lattice cannot lie in \(L_0\mathfrak P\), since that lattice is stable; hence its least quotient length is zero. The cyclic count is Theorem 6.196. For either positive two-length type, the residue is a line, and Theorem 6.192 says that normalization is exactly coordinate rank three over \(\mathbb F_Q\). Ordered independent triples in \(\mathbb F_q\), divided by projective scalars, give \(T\) such lines.

For a fixed line, put it on the third axis for counting. A lift has unique data \(M\subset\mathfrak P\mathcal O_D^2\) of quotient type \((u,v)\) and a graph class \((w,1)\), \(w\in\mathfrak P\mathcal O_D^2/M\). There are \(q^{u+v-2}\) graph classes. Writing \(M=\pi^vM'\), the rank-two lattice \(M'\) has cyclic quotient length \(u-v\), with \((q+1)q^{u-v-1}\) choices when \(u>v\), and one when \(u=v\). This proves (6.476) in every degree \(e\ge3\).

Proof: invariant subspaces. Choose coordinate positions for which the projection \(V\to D^m\), \(m=\dim_DV\), is an isomorphism of right spaces. The unique vectors in \(V\) projecting to the standard unit vectors are fixed by \(\tau_s\); their entries therefore lie in \(D_s=\Delta\). They give a right \(\Delta\)-basis of a space \(W\) with \(V=WD\). The lattice \(J=W\cap\mathcal O_\Delta^3\) is saturated: if \(xa\in J\) for \(x\in\mathcal O_\Delta^3\), \(a\ne0\), then \(x\in W\). Right-DVR elimination consequently extends a basis of \(J\) to a matrix in \(\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathcal O_\Delta)\). This matrix also belongs to \(K\), because the valuations agree. In its coordinates, \(V\cap\mathcal O_D^3=J\mathcal O_D\). Its reduction is thus the \(\mathbb F_q\)-span of a subspace over \(\mathbb F_Q\). This argument uses canonical coordinate vectors, not Galois descent or averaging by \(e\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.214 — extreme heights of a normalized frame. Write \(L=gL_0\), \(k_s=v_D(s)\), and \[ a=\nu_{\max}(g^{-1}sg)-k_s,\qquad c=k_s-\nu_{\min}(g^{-1}sg). \quad 0\le a,c\le u,\qquad \rho_G=\sigma=a+c. \tag{6.477} \] For a strict type \((u,v,0)\), there is a constant \(B_s\), independent of the lattice, such that \[ u-B_s\le\max(a,c)\le u. \tag{6.478} \] For a uniformizer \(\theta\) of \(E\), one can take \(B_\theta=0\). For equal-length types, both \(a,c\ge u-B_s\), and both equal \(u\) for a uniformizer.

Proof. Put \(g=kt\), \(t=\operatorname{diag}(\pi^u,\pi^v,1)\), \(k\in K\). Since \(s\pi=\pi s\), the relative matrix is \(g^{-1}\tau_s(g)=t^{-1}Bt\), \(B=k^{-1}\tau_s(k)\in K\). Its determinant valuation is zero. Both \(L\) and \(\tau_sL\) lie between \(L_0\mathfrak P^u\) and \(L_0\), giving \(0\le a,c\le u\); the middle Cartan coordinate of \(g^{-1}sg\) is \(k_s+c-a\), proving the last equality of (6.477).

The possible \(k\) for strict types form the compact open subset of \(K\) whose third residue column has \(\mathbb F_Q\)-rank three. On this set, \(B_{13}\) and \((B^{-1})_{13}\) cannot both be zero. Indeed, if both vanish, \((BB^{-1})_{13}=B_{12}(B^{-1})_{23}=0\). If \(B_{12}=0\), then \(B\) preserves the coordinate plane spanned by \(e_2,e_3\); otherwise \(B^{-1}\), and hence \(B\), preserves the line \(e_3D\). Thus \(\tau_s\) preserves either \(k(e_2D+e_3D)\) or \(ke_3D\). Lemma 6.213 makes its integral residue \(\mathbb F_Q\)-defined. It cannot contain the third residue column of rank three. This is a contradiction.

Compactness now bounds \(\min(v_D(B_{13}),v_D((B^{-1})_{13}))\) above by a fixed \(B_s\). The corresponding entries of \(t^{-1}Bt\) and its inverse have valuations \(v_D(B_{13})-u\) and \(v_D((B^{-1})_{13})-u\), proving (6.478).

For a uniformizer, the residue action \(\sigma\) has fixed field \(\mathbb F_Q\). The identical argument over the residue field excludes simultaneous vanishing of the two residue entries: a \(\sigma\)-invariant subspace has its unique coordinate-projection basis fixed over \(\mathbb F_Q\). Thus one entry is a unit, giving \(\max(a,c)=u\) in every degree. For \(v=u\), the projected column vectors \((B_{13},B_{23})\) and \(((B^{-1})_{13},(B^{-1})_{23})\) are separately nonzero, since otherwise the line \(ke_3D\) is invariant. Compactness bounds their minimum valuations separately; the residue argument makes them separately primitive for uniformizers. This proves the equal-length assertion. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.215 — top cyclic over-lattices. Fix a strict type \((u,v,0)\). Each normalized lattice \(L\) has exactly \(q^v\) over-lattices \(M\subset L_0\) with cyclic quotient \(L_0/M\) of length \(u\). All are normalized, and \(M\cap L_0\mathfrak P^v\subset L\). Let \(M_k\) be the unique cyclic over-lattice of \(M\) of quotient length \(k\). For \(1\le k\le u-v\), \[ c\le u-k \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \tau_sL\mathfrak P^{u-k}\subset L \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L\subset M\cap\tau_s^{-1}M_k. \tag{6.479} \] There is an integer \(C_s\ge0\) such that, in this range, \[ \#\{L\text{ of type }(u,v,0):c\le u-k\} \le K_s q^{2u-k}. \tag{6.480} \] The set is empty if \(k>v+C_s\). The same statements hold with \(a\) in place of \(c\).

Proof: the over-lattices. In \(L_0/L=R_u\oplus R_v\), a surjection to \(R_u\), normalized by its free left target-unit action, has row \((1,b)\), \(b\in\mathfrak P^{u-v}/\mathfrak P^u\). Thus there are \(q^v\) distinct kernels. Their preimages are the stated \(M\), and \(M/L\) is cyclic of length \(v\). They are normalized because \(L\subset M\subset L_0\).

Choose integral coordinates with \(M=\pi^u\mathcal O_De_1+\mathcal O_De_2+\mathcal O_De_3\). Since \(L\) contains \(L_0\mathfrak P^u\), its first summand is already in \(L\); hence \(L=\pi^u\mathcal O_De_1+L'\), with a rank-two cyclic kernel \(L'\) of length \(v\). This proves \(M\cap L_0\mathfrak P^v\subset L\). Because \(u-k\ge v\), the condition \(\tau_sL\mathfrak P^{u-k}\subset M\) is equivalent to its containment in \(L\). Reducing the annihilator row of \(M\) modulo \(\mathfrak P^k\) then proves (6.479).

Proof: uniform refinement bounds. Normalize an integral annihilator row of \(M\) to \((1,\alpha,\beta)\), after a coordinate permutation. At least one residue lies outside \(\mathbb F_Q\). On the compact set of such integral elements, \(x-\tau_s^{\pm1}x\) never vanishes, since the fixed algebra is \(\Delta\). Its valuation is therefore bounded above by an integer \(C_s\), as in Theorem 6.197. Subtract the row from its \(\tau_s^{-1}\)-conjugate. The difference has first coordinate zero and minimum valuation \(b\), \(0\le b\le C_s\).

If \(k>b\), divide this difference on the left by \(\pi^b\). It is an integral primitive row, independent in residue from the first row. Completing these two rows to an integral invertible matrix puts the pair \((M,J)\), \(J=M\cap\tau_s^{-1}M_k\), in the form \[ M=\operatorname{diag}(\pi^u,1,1)L_0,\qquad J=\operatorname{diag}(\pi^u,\pi^{k-b},1)L_0. \tag{6.481} \] The possible \(L\subset J\) of ambient type \((u,v,0)\) are exactly \(\pi^u\mathcal O_De_1\) plus rank-two cyclic kernels of length \(v\) refining the fixed kernel of length \(k-b\). Their number is \(q^{v-k+b}\) if \(k-b\le v\), and zero otherwise. This is the primitive-row lift count of Theorem 6.196. If \(k\le b\), then \(J=M\), and there are \((q+1)q^{v-1}\le2q^v\) possibilities. Dropping normalization only enlarges these refinement counts.

There are \(C_3q^{2u-2}\) normalized choices of \(M\). Count the pairs \((L,M)\) and divide by the exact multiplicity \(q^v\). The preceding bounds give (6.480), with fixed factor at most \(2q^{C_s}C_3/q^2\), and give emptiness when \(k>v+C_s\). Replacing \(\tau_s\) by its inverse gives the assertion for \(a\), since its relative minimum exponent is \(-a\). \(\square\)

Proposition 6.216 — the exact uniformizer height distribution. Let \(s=\theta\) be any uniformizer of \(E\), and put \(h=\min(v,u-v)\) for a strict type. Then \(a,c\ge\max(v,u-v)\), \(\max(a,c)=u\), and \[ \#\{L:c\le u-k\}=\#\{L:a\le u-k\}=Aq^{2u-k} \qquad(1\le k\le h). \tag{6.482} \] The actual number \(N_{u,v}(k)\) of lattices of root height \(2u-k\) is \[ N_{u,v}(k)=\begin{cases} A(1-q^{-1})q^{2u},&k=0,\\ 2A(1-q^{-1})q^{2u-k},&0<k<h,\\ 2Aq^{2u-h},&k=h. \end{cases} \tag{6.483} \] At greatest quotient length \(u\ge1\), including the cyclic and equal-length types, the entire root-weighted count is \[ \sum_{L:\,u(L)=u}q^{-\rho_G(g_L^{-1}\theta g_L)} =\frac{C_3}{q^2} +A\left[1+(u-1)(1+q^{-1}) +2(1-q^{-1})\left\lfloor\frac{u^2}{4}\right\rfloor\right]. \tag{6.484} \] Here \(u(L)\) denotes the greatest elementary quotient length.

Proof: the residue intersection. For a field automorphism \(\sigma\) with fixed field \(\mathbb F_Q\), a nonzero difference polynomial \(\sum_{j=0}^m\sigma^j(x)b_j\), \(b_m\ne0\), has kernel dimension at most \(m\) over \(\mathbb F_Q\). To prove this inductively, choose a nonzero root \(z\), substitute \(x=yz\), and set \(c_j=\sigma^j(z)b_j\). Since \(\sum c_j=0\), the expression becomes \(\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sigma^i(\sigma y-y)\sum_{j>i}c_j\). Its last coefficient is nonzero; the induction hypothesis bounds this latter kernel by \(m-1\), and \(\sigma-1\) has one-dimensional kernel. The zero-degree case is injective. This proves the bound and the independence of three consecutive Moore rows on three independent coordinates.

For uniformizers the row difference in Lemma 6.215 has depth zero. If the residue annihilator row \(w\) of \(M\) has coordinate rank two over \(\mathbb F_Q\), an \(\mathbb F_Q\)-basis change puts it at \((w_1,w_2,0)\). The intersection of its hyperplane with that of \(\sigma^{-1}w\) is the \(\mathbb F_Q\)-defined third axis. It cannot contain the normalized rank-three residue line of \(L\). Thus only residue rows of rank three contribute.

For such a row, \(w,\sigma^{-1}w,\sigma w\) are independent by the difference-polynomial bound. Their intersection line \(\ell=\ker w\cap\ker\sigma^{-1}w\) has coordinate rank three. Indeed, an \(\mathbb F_Q\)-row annihilating it would belong both to \(\operatorname{span}(w,\sigma^{-1}w)\) and to \(\operatorname{span}(\sigma w,w)\), hence to \(\mathbb F_qw\), contradicting the rank of \(w\). Consequently \(J\) in (6.481) is normalized, and every ambient refinement has that same normalized residue line.

There are exactly \(Tq^{2u-2}=Aq^{2u}\) choices of \(M\) with rank-three residue row: choose its residue row and its \(q^{2u-2}\) primitive lifts. Each has \(q^{v-k}\) refinements when \(k\le v\). Dividing the pair count by \(q^v\) proves (6.482), and the same proof applies backwards.

Proof: the defect range and summation. Choose a unit Cartan column \(w\in L\), right-normalized to have one coordinate one. Then \(L\subset w\mathcal O_D+L_0\mathfrak P^v\). If \(\tau_\theta L\mathfrak P^c\subset L\), comparison of that pivot coordinate gives \((\tau_\theta w_i-w_i)\pi^c\in\mathfrak P^v\) for every other coordinate. Some residue is outside \(\mathbb F_Q\), so its difference is a unit; hence \(c\ge v\). The backwards argument gives \(a\ge v\). If \(c<u-v\), set \(k=u-c\); it lies in the range of Lemma 6.215 but exceeds \(v\), where the refinement count is zero. Thus \(c\ge u-v\), and likewise \(a\ge u-v\).

Theorem 6.214 gives \(\max(a,c)=u\), so the two lower-extreme events are disjoint. Subtract consecutive cumulative counts in (6.482) to obtain (6.483), with its terminal term at \(k=h\). Their sum is the independent type count (6.476). After weighting by \(q^{-(2u-k)}\), the contribution of a strict type is \(A[2h(1-q^{-1})+1+q^{-1}]\). The identity \(\sum_{v=1}^{u-1}\min(v,u-v)=\lfloor u^2/4\rfloor\), obtained by pairing \(v\) with \(u-v\), and the cyclic and equal contributions \(C_3/q^2,A\), give (6.484). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.217 — defects for arbitrary generators. For a fixed generator \(s\), enlarge the constant \(C_s\) of Lemma 6.215 if necessary. For every strict type, \[ a,c\ge\max(v,u-v)-2C_s,\qquad 0\le k_L:=u-\min(a,c)\le h+2C_s, \qquad \#\{L:k_L\ge k\}\le K'_s q^{2u-k} \quad(0\le k\le h+2C_s). \tag{6.485} \]

Proof. The primitive-column argument just used now gives \(c\ge v-C_s\), since a nonfixed residue coordinate has difference valuation at most \(C_s\). It gives \(a\ge v-C_s\) backwards. Put \(c'=c+C_s\ge v\). If \(k=u-c'>0\), then \(k\le u-v\), and the weakened inclusion \(\tau_sL\mathfrak P^{c'}\subset L\) satisfies Lemma 6.215. Its nonemptiness forces \(k\le v+C_s\), proving \(c\ge u-v-2C_s\). If \(k\le0\), this bound is automatic. The same argument applies to \(a\).

For the tail, replace \(k\) by \(k_0=\max(0,k-2C_s)\le h\). If \(k_0>0\), apply (6.480) separately to \(a,c\) and pay at most a factor \(q^{2C_s}\). If \(k_0=0\), use the total type count (6.476) and the same fixed factor. This proves (6.485) for all allowable defects. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.218 — the full ordinary orbital bound. For every generator \(s\) of every totally ramified \(E/F\) embedded in \(D\), the ordinary orbital integral on \(\mathrm{GL}_3(D)\) is absolutely convergent and defines a continuous functional on the Harish–Chandra Schwartz space. For \(e\ge3\), any \(t>b_G+3\) gives \[ O_s\bigl(\Xi_G(1+\sigma)^{-t}\bigr) \le C_s\sum_{u\ge0}(1+u)^{b_G+2-t}<\infty. \tag{6.486} \] Increasing \(t\) gives every polynomial cutoff tail. These ordinary functionals are traces on the Schwartz algebra. The linear and quadratic cases are already Theorem 6.188.

Proof. For a strict type put \(k=k_L\) and \(\varepsilon=u-\max(a,c)\). Theorem 6.214 gives \(0\le\varepsilon\le B_s\), and \(\rho_G=\sigma=2u-k-\varepsilon\). By (6.485), the number of lattices at that exact defect is at most \(K'_s q^{2u-k}\). The factor \(q^{-\rho_G}\) in Lemma 6.80 cancels this count up to \(q^{B_s}\). Also \(u-B_s\le\sigma\le2u\), so \(1+\sigma\) and \(1+u\) are comparable, with fixed constants. There are at most \(u-1\) strict middle lengths and at most \(u/2+2C_s+1\) defects at fixed \(u\). This proves their contribution to (6.486).

The cyclic contribution is Theorem 6.197. For equal-length types Theorem 6.214 gives \(a,c\ge u-B_s\), while their count is \(Tq^{2u-2}\); the same cancellation gives a single convergent polynomial sum. The normalized stable lattice contributes one finite term. Thus every normalized lattice is included. For a uniformizer, (6.484) gives the exact quadratic root-weighted count underlying this estimate.

Lemma 6.152 is the actual nonnegative lattice decomposition of the ordinary orbital integral. Compact conjugation averaging leaves its majorant unchanged, so the estimate bounds arbitrary Schwartz tests by their majorant seminorm. A cutoff \(\sigma>R\) has \(u>R/2\), giving a tail \(C_{s,t}(1+R)^{b_G+3-t}\); choose \(t>b_G+3+A\) for any required exponent \(A\). Finally \(|f|*|h|\) is Schwartz by Theorem 6.81. Its now finite orbital integral supplies the positive double-integral bound (6.274), so Fubini and conjugacy invariance prove cyclicity exactly as in Lemma 6.119. No conditional rearrangement precedes this absolute bound. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.219 — primary partitions, germs and a singular Steinberg orbital. Let \(p\) be the polynomial of \(s\), and \(P=p^{3\delta}\). Every primary orbit in this fibre has a continuous absolute Schwartz orbital functional with polynomial tails. On the two nonclosed partitions \((2,1),(3)\), the orbitals of discrete-series coefficients, compact discrete tests and the Euler test are zero. Give central \(\mathcal O_F^\times\) volume one. The closed Euler value, Steinberg degree and unit Iwahori Steinberg coefficient orbital are \[ \eta_s=\frac{(Q-1)(Q^2-1)}{3d},\qquad d_{\mathrm{St}_G}=\frac{(q-1)(q^2-1)}{3d},\qquad O_s(c_{\mathrm{St}})=\frac{(Q-1)(Q^2-1)}{(q-1)(q^2-1)}. \tag{6.487} \] For nearby elliptic regular classes, with the centralizer measures of Section 6.26, \[ g_{P,(1^3)}(\gamma)=\frac1{e(F[\gamma]/F)\eta_s},\qquad \Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})=\frac{O_s(f_{\pi,m_0})}{\eta_s}. \tag{6.488} \] The closed germ is zero on nearby nonelliptic regular classes. The last value in (6.487) is an ordinary orbital at the repeated element, without an assertion of a character density there.

Proof. For the two nonclosed partitions, the intrinsic primary kernel flags have proper Levi blocks of division ranks one or two. Their closed-base bounds are Theorem 6.161 and the rank-one compact case. Formula (6.323), the positive radical estimate (6.218), and the product estimate (6.225) give absolute bounds and tails, as in the proof of Corollary 6.156. This uses the intrinsic module flag, including in inseparable fields, rather than a separable Jordan factorization. Positive convolution proves the trace identity before Theorem 6.77 kills the proper-flag coefficient integrals. The finite commutators (6.271) and Euler identity (6.309) give the compact-test zeros.

For the closed partition the full Schwartz bound is Theorem 6.218. Theorem 6.157 gives \(\eta_s\), with ramification \(e\), centralizer multiplicity three and \(e\delta=d\). Formula (6.295) gives the displayed Steinberg degree. Applying this continuous orbital trace to (6.309), with \(p_{\mathrm{St}}=d_{\mathrm{St}}c_{\mathrm{St}}\), proves their ratio, since the rank-three sign is positive. Finally cut the compact Euler and discrete tests to their reduced-norm annulus. All nonclosed coefficients vanish in (6.326); the Euler closed coefficient is nonzero, and its regular orbital is \(1/e(F[\gamma]/F)\) on elliptic classes and zero on nonelliptic ones. Division proves the germ formula, and (6.327) gives the actual elliptic character assertion. \(\square\)

Example 6.220 — an interior height distribution. For \(Q=2,u=4,v=2\), (6.483) gives the following exact cardinalities: \[ \begin{array}{c|r|r} \rho_G& e=3,\ q=8&e=4,\ q=16\\\hline 8&5505024&2642411520\\ 7&1376256&330301440\\ 6&196608&22020096\\\hline \text{total}&7077888&2994733056. \end{array} \tag{6.489} \] Their root-weighted sums are \(111/64\) and \(1617/512\). For \(Q=2,e=3,\delta=1\), the Euler value is \(1/3\), the Steinberg degree is \(49\), and its unit coefficient orbital is \(1/147\). For \(Q=2,e=4,\delta=1\), these are \(1/4,1275/4,1/1275\). The degree-four case includes the purely inseparable field \(\mathbb F_2((\Pi))/\mathbb F_2((\Pi^4))\). For the wild cubic of Example 6.212, (6.487) gives \(16/9,18928/9,1/1183\); for its quaternionic-centralizer comparison \(Q=4,e=3,\delta=2\), the values are \(5/2,28665/2,1/5733\).

Figure 17. Lemma 6.215 supplies the exact over-lattice multiplicity and refinement count. Proposition 6.216 gives the three cardinalities and normalized weights in the boxes; they are lattice counts, not numbers of centralizer orbits. Theorem 6.218 gives the complete ordinary orbital estimate for the stated totally ramified embedded-field family. The boxes do not represent building distances.

For finite-field Frobenius and fixed fields, see Conrad's free finite-field notes, Theorems 4.1 and 5.6. The invariant-subspace descent, difference-polynomial bound, incidence count, arbitrary-generator estimates and orbital consequences used here are proved in this lesson. Section 6.38 gives the estimates for fields with nontrivial residue extension. Higher division ranks require further estimates, and these ordinary orbital statements do not supply a general local or global representation transfer.

6.38. Coefficient orders and all ordinary orbitals in division rank three

Let \(E/F\) be any finite field extension embedded in \(D\), let \(s\in E^\times\) generate it, and put \(\Delta=D_E\). Write \[ e=[E:F]=a_Ef_E,\qquad d=e\delta,\qquad Q=q_\Delta,\qquad q=q_D=Q^{a_E}. \tag{6.490} \] Here \(a_E\) and \(f_E\) are the ramification index and residue degree. The field may be wild or inseparable. A coefficient order gives a normalization with finitely many least-length colors. It replaces the residue-line criterion of Section 6.37 when \(f_E>1\).

Lemma 6.221 — the integral coefficient order. The left \(\mathcal O_\Delta\)-module \(\mathcal O_D\) is free of rank \(e\). Choose a basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_e\), and let \[ \Sigma=\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O_\Delta} ({}_{\mathcal O_\Delta}\mathcal O_D) \tag{6.491} \] act entrywise on \(D^3\). It contains right multiplication by \(\mathcal O_D\) and \(\tau_s=\operatorname{Ad}(s)\). It commutes with \(H=\mathrm{GL}_3(\Delta)\). Its full stable right lattices are exactly \(\Lambda\mathcal O_D\), with \(\Lambda\) a full right \(\mathcal O_\Delta\)-lattice in \(\Delta^3\), so they form one \(H\)-orbit.

Put \(L_0=\mathcal O_D^3\), and normalize by \(\Sigma L=L_0\). If \(L_0/L\) has elementary lengths \((u,v,w)\), then \[ \begin{gathered} u\ge v\ge w,\qquad 0\le w<f_E,\\ v_D|_\Delta=f_Ev_\Delta,\qquad \Sigma(L_0\mathfrak P^{f_E})=L_0\mathfrak P^{f_E}. \end{gathered} \tag{6.492} \] For \(z\in L_0\), write \(z_i=\sum_j z_{ij}b_j\). Call \(z\) coefficient-primitive if the columns of \((\overline{z_{ij}})\) span \(\mathbb F_Q^3\). This is equivalent to \(\Sigma z=L_0\), and is a compact open condition on \(L_0\). If \(v\ge f_E\), the least-length Cartan column of a normalized \(L\) is coefficient-primitive.

Proof: the order and valuations. The dimension of \(D\) as a left \(\Delta\)-space is \(e\), by Theorem 6.165. The module \(\mathcal O_D\) is a finite torsion-free left \(\mathcal O_\Delta\)-module, so the left-handed version of the division-DVR elimination in Theorem 6.4 gives its free basis. Right multiplication is left \(\Delta\)-linear and preserves \(\mathcal O_D\). The map \(\tau_s\) is also left \(\Delta\)-linear, since \(s\) is central in \(\Delta\), and preserves the valuation. Both therefore lie in \(\Sigma\).

Matrix units on the coefficients show that a \(\Sigma\)-stable additive submodule has the form \(\bigoplus_j\Lambda b_j\), with the same right \(\mathcal O_\Delta\)-module \(\Lambda\) in every component. This is \(\Lambda\mathcal O_D\). A basis of \(\Lambda\) proves transitivity. Left matrices over \(\Delta\) commute with these coefficient operations.

Compare the ordinary \(F\)-linear determinant of left multiplication by \(x\in\Delta^\times\) on \(D\), first using its reduced norm and then its \(e\) left \(\Delta\)-summands. Since \(e\delta=d\), this gives \(v_F\operatorname{Nrd}_D(x)=v_FN_{E/F}\operatorname{Nrd}_\Delta(x)=f_Ev_\Delta(x)\). For integral \(y\in E^\times\), multiplication on the free \(\mathcal O_F\)-module \(\mathcal O_E\) has cokernel of cardinality \(q_E^{v_E(y)}=q_F^{f_Ev_E(y)}\). Its determinant therefore has \(F\)-valuation \(f_Ev_E(y)\), by integral DVR elimination. Central rescaling proves this field-norm valuation formula for every \(y\), also in inseparable extensions. Lemma 6.1 over \(F\) and \(E\) now gives \(q=Q^{a_E}\). If \(\pi\) is a uniformizer of \(\Delta\), then \(\pi L_0=L_0\mathfrak P^{f_E}\). Every coefficient operator commutes with left \(\pi\), proving its stability. Normalization consequently excludes \(w\ge f_E\).

Proof: coefficient primitivity. Matrix units identify \(\Sigma z\) with \(\bigoplus_j\Lambda_zb_j\), where \(\Lambda_z=\sum_j(z_{1j},z_{2j},z_{3j})^t\mathcal O_\Delta\). Residue spanning is equivalent to \(\Lambda_z=\mathcal O_\Delta^3\): lift three residue basis columns, and invert their integral matrix by the residue inverse and the convergent geometric series, as in Lemma 6.208. It is thus a condition on a finite coefficient quotient, proving compact openness.

For \(v\ge f_E\), the two deeper Cartan columns belong to \(L_0\mathfrak P^{f_E}\). The least-length column \(z\) therefore satisfies \(\Sigma z+L_0\mathfrak P^{f_E}=L_0\). In coefficients, the second summand has all entries in \(\mathfrak P_\Delta\), because \(\pi\mathcal O_D=\bigoplus_j\mathfrak P_\Delta b_j\). The same residue-basis argument makes \(z\) coefficient-primitive. \(\square\)

The following unrestricted counts will be used only as upper bounds for normalized lattices. Right-DVR elimination gives \[ \begin{gathered} \begin{array}{c|c} \text{length type}&\text{all lattices in }L_0\\\hline u>v>w&(q^2+q+1)(q+1)q^{2(u-w)-3}\\ u=v>w\text{ or }u>v=w&(q^2+q+1)q^{2(u-w)-2}\\ u=v=w&1. \end{array}\\ N_{u,v,w}\le C_q q^{2u}. \end{gathered} \tag{6.493} \] Indeed the first residue flag has \((q^2+q+1)(q+1)\) choices in the strict case and \(q^2+q+1\) in either repeated case. For each unequal pair of lengths \(\lambda_i>\lambda_j\), its remaining triangular parameter has \(q^{\lambda_i-\lambda_j-1}\) choices. Multiplication gives (6.493). This is the same elimination used for Theorem 6.4 and counts actual lattices, without a transitivity assertion for the centralizer.

Lemma 6.222 — normalized cyclic rows. There is \(C_s\ge0\) such that every normalized cyclic quotient \(M\subset L_0\) of length \(u\ge f_E\), with primitive annihilator row normalized to \((1,\alpha,\beta)\) after permutation, satisfies \[ b=\min\{v_D(\alpha-\tau_s\alpha), v_D(\beta-\tau_s\beta)\}\le C_s. \tag{6.494} \] The same bound can be chosen for \(\tau_s^{-1}\). The conjugate of \(s\) associated to this cyclic lattice has Cartan list \[ (k_s+M_s,\ k_s,\ k_s-M_s),\qquad k_s=v_D(s),\quad M_s=\max(0,u-b). \tag{6.495} \] Thus its two extreme deviations both equal \(u+O_s(1)\). There are at most \((q^2+q+1)q^{2u-2}\) normalized cyclic quotients.

Proof: transversality. Let \(M_{f_E}\) be the cyclic over-lattice of quotient length \(f_E\). Since \(M\subset M_{f_E}\subset L_0\), it is normalized too. The condition \(\Sigma M_{f_E}=L_0\) is a condition on \((\alpha,\beta)\) modulo \(\mathfrak P^{f_E}\), and hence defines a compact open subset of \(\mathcal O_D^2\).

This subset contains no pair \(\alpha,\beta\in\Delta\). For such a pair, the row map \(r=(1,\alpha,\beta)\) commutes with every entrywise coefficient operator: \(r(Tx)=T(rx)\). Since \(rM_{f_E}\subset\mathfrak P^{f_E}\), the stability in (6.492) would give \(r\Sigma M_{f_E}\subset\mathfrak P^{f_E}\), whereas \(rL_0=\mathcal O_D\). This contradicts normalization. The continuous pair of differences in (6.494) has no common zero on that compact set, since \(D_s=\Delta\). Their minimum valuation is bounded above. Apply the same argument backwards and enlarge \(C_s\).

Proof: the Cartan list. Choose any uniformizer \(\Pi\) of \(D\). A cyclic-kernel basis is \(g_M=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\Pi^u&-\alpha&-\beta\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). In \(g_M^{-1}sg_M\), the diagonal entries are \(\Pi^{-u}s\Pi^u,s,s\), all of valuation \(k_s\). Its only off-diagonal row is \(\Pi^{-u}(\alpha s-s\alpha,\beta s-s\beta)\), of minimum valuation \(k_s-u+b\). After removing the common valuation, integral diagonal units and a right rank-two basis change reduce it to a single off-diagonal entry of valuation \(b-u\). A two-by-two elimination gives exponents \((M_s,-M_s)\), with one further zero exponent. This proves (6.495); it does not require \(\Pi\) to commute with \(s\). The count is the cyclic case of (6.493). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.223 — compact coefficient frames. For normalized type \((u,v,w)\) with \(v\ge f_E\), write \(L=gL_0\), and let \(a,c\) be the extreme deviations in (6.477). There is \(B_s\ge0\), independent of \(u,v,w,L\), such that \[ \begin{gathered} 0\le a,c\le u,\qquad \rho_G=\sigma=a+c,\\ \max(a,c)\ge u-B_s,\qquad \min(a,c)\ge v-B_s. \end{gathered} \tag{6.496} \] In particular both deviations are at least \(u-B_s\) when \(u=v\).

Proof: the compact set. Choose \(\Pi\) as above and the commuting uniformizer \(\pi\in\Delta\). Write \[ \begin{gathered} g=k\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^u,\Pi^v,\Pi^w)=h t,\\ t=\operatorname{diag}(\pi^{n_1},\pi^{n_2},1),\qquad n_1=\lfloor u/f_E\rfloor,\quad n_2=\lfloor v/f_E\rfloor. \end{gathered} \tag{6.497} \] Here \(h=k\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^u\pi^{-n_1},\Pi^v\pi^{-n_2},\Pi^w)\). Each diagonal factor has valuation in \(\{0,\ldots,f_E-1\}\). Thus these frames lie in a fixed compact subset of \(G\), with inverses uniformly bounded. Their third columns are coefficient-primitive by Lemma 6.221. Requiring that condition gives a closed subset of this compact set, still compact.

Every \(\tau_s\)-invariant right \(D\)-subspace \(V\subset D^3\) is defined over \(\Delta\): the unique vectors projecting to standard unit vectors in an isomorphic coordinate projection are fixed by \(\tau_s\). This is the coordinate-basis proof of Lemma 6.213 and does not use equality of the valuations. A saturated integral basis over \(\mathcal O_\Delta\) extends to \(\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathcal O_\Delta)\subset K\), so \(V\cap L_0\) is \(\Sigma\)-stable. If \(V\) is proper, it cannot contain a coefficient-primitive vector.

Put \(B=h^{-1}\tau_s(h)\), \(C=B^{-1}\). If \(B_{13}=C_{13}=0\), then \(B_{12}C_{23}=0\). As in Theorem 6.214, this forces either an invariant coordinate plane containing \(e_3\), or an invariant coordinate line \(e_3D\). Transport by \(h\) contradicts the preceding paragraph. Compactness therefore bounds \(\min(v_D(B_{13}),v_D(C_{13}))\) above. The vectors \((B_{13},B_{23})\) and \((C_{13},C_{23})\) are separately nonzero as well; otherwise \(he_3D\) is invariant. Their minimum entry valuations are bounded above separately.

Since \(\pi s=s\pi\), the relative matrix and its inverse are \(t^{-1}Bt,t^{-1}Ct\). Their \((1,3)\) entries have valuation reduced by \(f_En_1\). In either projected third column, the reduction is at least \(f_En_2\). The compact bounds just obtained, with the remainders \(u-f_En_1,v-f_En_2<f_E\), prove both lower bounds in (6.496).

Finally \(L\) and \(\tau_sL\) lie between \(L_0\mathfrak P^u\) and \(L_0\mathfrak P^w\), giving \(a,c\le u-w\le u\). Their determinant valuations agree. The rank-three middle coordinate is \(k_s+c-a\), so \(\rho_G=\sigma=a+c\), as in (6.477). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.224 — incidence with a least-length color. Suppose \(u>v\ge w\) and \(u\ge f_E\). Each normalized \(L\) of type \((u,v,w)\) has exactly \(q^{v+w}\) normalized top cyclic over-lattices \(M\subset L_0\) of quotient length \(u\). For \(1\le k\le u-v\), \[ \begin{split} c\le u-k &\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \tau_sL\mathfrak P^{u-k}\subset L\\ &\ \Longleftrightarrow\ L\subset J=M\cap\tau_s^{-1}M_k, \end{split} \tag{6.498} \] where \(M_k\) is the cyclic over-lattice of quotient length \(k\). For fixed \((u,v,w)\), \[ \begin{gathered} \#\{L:c\le u-k\}\le K_s q^{2u-k},\\ \{L:c\le u-k\}=\varnothing\quad\text{if }k>v+C_s. \end{gathered} \tag{6.499} \] The same bounds hold for \(a\).

Proof: multiplicity and inclusion. A surjection \(R_u\oplus R_v\oplus R_w\to R_u\), normalized by its free left target-unit action, has first entry one and its other entries in \(\mathfrak P^{u-v}/\mathfrak P^u\) and \(\mathfrak P^{u-w}/\mathfrak P^u\). This gives exactly \(q^{v+w}\) kernels. Their preimages are the top \(M\), all normalized because they contain \(L\).

In integral coordinates for \(M=\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^u,1,1)L_0\), one has \(L=\Pi^u\mathcal O_De_1+L'\), with \(L'\subset\mathcal O_D^2\) of quotient type \((v,w)\). Indeed the first summand already belongs to \(L_0\mathfrak P^u\subset L\). Thus \(M\cap L_0\mathfrak P^v\subset L\). Since \(u-k\ge v\), containment of \(\tau_sL\mathfrak P^{u-k}\) in \(M\) is equivalent to its containment in \(L\). Reducing the annihilator row modulo \(\mathfrak P^k\) gives (6.498).

Proof: refinements. Normalize the row of \(M\) as in Lemma 6.222. The difference from its backwards conjugate has first coordinate zero and minimum valuation \(b\le C_s\). If \(k>b\), divide it on the left by \(\Pi^b\), and complete the first row and this independent primitive row to an integral basis. It gives \(J=\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^u,\Pi^{k-b},1)L_0\) in the same coordinates as \(M\). If \(k\le b\), then \(J=M\).

Put \(l=\max(0,k-b)\). The number of possible rank-two \(L'\) is \[ \begin{cases} 0,&l>v,\\ q^{v-l},&w<l\le v,\\ (q+1)q^{v-w-1},&l\le w<v,\\ 1,&l\le w=v. \end{cases} \qquad\le 2q^{v-k+b}\quad\text{when nonzero}. \tag{6.500} \] To see this, write \(L'=N\Pi^w\), where \(N\) is a rank-two cyclic kernel of length \(v-w\). If \(l\le w\), every such kernel qualifies. If \(l>w\), its primitive row must lift one fixed row of depth \(l-w\), giving \(q^{v-l}\) lifts when \(l\le v\). When \(v=w\), the only candidate is \(\mathcal O_D^2\Pi^w\). These arguments also prove zero when \(l>v\).

There are at most \((q^2+q+1)q^{2u-2}\) top \(M\). Dropping normalization from their refinements can only enlarge the count (6.500). Count pairs and divide by the exact multiplicity \(q^{v+w}\). Since \(w\ge0\) and \(b\le C_s\), this proves (6.499) and its asserted emptiness. Replacing \(\tau_s\) by its inverse proves the statement for \(a\). No exact normalized refinement count is required. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.225 — every embedded field in division rank three. For every finite \(E/F\) embedded in \(D\) and every generator \(s\in E^\times\), the ordinary orbital integral on \(\mathrm{GL}_3(D)\) is absolutely convergent and defines a continuous functional on the Schwartz space. With \(K,H_0\) of volume one, any \(t>b_G+3\) gives \[ O_s\bigl(\Xi_G(1+\sigma)^{-t}\bigr) \le C_{s,t}\sum_{u\ge0}(1+u)^{b_G+2-t}<\infty. \tag{6.501} \] It has every polynomial cutoff tail and is a trace on the Schwartz algebra. A fixed polynomial weight in the centralizer-quotient conjugator length \(\ell_H\) is also bounded by a Schwartz seminorm.

Proof: the interior types. Enlarge the constants of Lemmas 6.222–6.224 and Theorem 6.223 to one integer \(C_s\). For \(u>v\ge f_E\), the same defect argument as Lemma 6.217 gives \[ \begin{gathered} a,c\ge\max(v,u-v)-2C_s,\\ 0\le k_L=u-\min(a,c)\le\min(v,u-v)+2C_s,\\ \#\{L\text{ of type }(u,v,w):k_L\ge k\} \le K'_sq^{2u-k}. \end{gathered} \tag{6.502} \] For completeness, \(c+C_s\ge v\) by (6.496). If \(k=u-c-C_s>0\), it lies in the range \(k\le u-v\). The weakened inclusion of depth \(c+C_s\) invokes (6.499), whose nonemptiness implies \(k\le v+C_s\). Thus \(c\ge u-v-2C_s\); the backwards argument gives the same for \(a\). To bound the tail at \(k\), weaken it to \(k_0=\max(0,k-2C_s)\le\min(v,u-v)\), apply (6.499) to the union of the two extreme events, and pay the fixed factor \(q^{2C_s}\). At \(k_0=0\), use (6.493).

At exact defect \(k_L=k\), put \(\epsilon=u-\max(a,c)\). Then \(0\le\epsilon\le C_s\) and \(\rho_G=\sigma=2u-k-\epsilon\). The factor \(q^{-\rho_G}\) of Lemma 6.80 cancels (6.502) up to a fixed constant. There are at most \(f_E\) least colors, \(O(1+u)\) middle lengths and \(O(1+u)\) defects at fixed \(u\). Also \(1+\sigma\) is comparable to \(1+u\), by (6.496). This gives the series (6.501).

Proof: the boundary types. If \(u=v\ge f_E\), (6.496) gives both deviations at least \(u-C_s\). The count (6.493) is at most \(C_qq^{2u}\), so its weighted contribution is a single polynomial sum for each of the finitely many \(w\).

If \(v<f_E\) and \(u\ge f_E\), choose any top cyclic \(M\). The index length \(\operatorname{length}(M/L)=v+w<2f_E\) is bounded. Write \(g_L=g_Mh\). The Cartan spread of \(h\) is at most \(v+w\), since all its elementary divisors are nonnegative and their sum is that index. Subadditivity of spread gives \(\sigma(g_L^{-1}sg_L)\ge\sigma(g_M^{-1}sg_M)-2(v+w)\ge2u-C'_s\) by Lemma 6.222. In rank three \(\rho_G=\sigma\), so (6.493) again cancels the exponential, with only finitely many \(v,w\). The types with \(u<f_E\) form a finite set. This covers every normalized lattice.

The coefficient order commutes with \(H\), has transitive stable lattices and stable \(L_0\), so the proof of Lemma 6.152 applies to it verbatim. The nonnegative lattice sum is the actual ordinary orbital measure. Compact conjugation averaging and a Schwartz majorant prove continuity. Since \(\sigma\le2u\), restricting to \(\sigma>R\) restricts to \(u>R/2\); the series tail is bounded by \(C_{s,t}(1+R)^{b_G+3-t}\). Increase \(t\) for any specified polynomial decay. Lemma 6.144 bounds \(1+\ell_H(x)\) by \(C_s(1+\sigma(x^{-1}sx))\), so its polynomial weights are absorbed by a higher seminorm. Finally apply positive convolution and (6.274) before Fubini, exactly as in Theorem 6.218, to obtain the trace identity. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.226 — all ordinary orbitals in division ranks at most three. For \(r\le3\), every \(x\in\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\) has an absolutely convergent ordinary Schwartz orbital integral, continuous in the Schwartz topology, with every polynomial cutoff tail. It is a trace on the Schwartz algebra. In rank three every orbit outside the closed primary orbits has zero orbital on discrete-series coefficients, compact discrete tests and the Euler test.

Proof. Ranks one and two are Theorem 6.162 and the compact rank-one case. For a closed primary element in rank three, Theorem 6.165 gives \(3=hm\), with \(h=e/\gcd(d,e)\). If \(h=1\), then \(e\mid d\), the field embeds in \(D\), and the element is conjugate to scalar multiplication by its generator in \(M_3(D)\). Theorem 6.225 applies. If \(h=3\), then \(m=1\), so the element is \(D\)-irreducible and Theorem 6.147 applies. These are the only possibilities. All other elements, their positive flag bounds, traces and zeros are Corollary 6.163. That proof uses intrinsic primary modules and includes inseparable factors. Thus every element is covered, before any orbital trace or vanishing is invoked. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.227 — closed coefficients and the residue degree. For the embedded-field closed orbit above, let \(p\) be the polynomial of \(s\), \(P=p^{3\delta}\), and give central \(\mathcal O_F^\times\) volume one. Then \[ \begin{gathered} \eta_s=\frac{(Q-1)(Q^2-1)}{3a_E\delta} =\frac{f_E(Q-1)(Q^2-1)}{3d},\\ d_{\mathrm{St}_G}=\frac{(q-1)(q^2-1)}{3d},\qquad O_s(c_{\mathrm{St}})= \frac{f_E(Q-1)(Q^2-1)}{(q-1)(q^2-1)}. \end{gathered} \tag{6.503} \] All primary partitions in this fibre have absolute Schwartz traces. The two nonclosed partitions have zero discrete-test and Euler orbitals. Near its reduced polynomial the closed compact germ and elliptic character are \[ g_{P,(1^3)}(\gamma)=\frac1{e(F[\gamma]/F)\eta_s},\qquad \Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})=\frac{O_s(f_{\pi,m_0})}{\eta_s} \quad(\gamma\text{ elliptic regular}). \tag{6.504} \] The closed germ is zero on the nearby nonelliptic regular set.

Proof. Corollary 6.226 supplies all Schwartz traces and nonclosed zeros. Apply Theorem 6.157 with centralizer degree \(\delta\), multiplicity three and ramification \(a_E\). Formula (6.295) gives the degree, and the finite Euler cocenter identity (6.309) gives the unit-coefficient ratio; the rank-three sign is positive. The fixed reduced-norm-annulus cut of the compact Euler and discrete tests then reduces (6.326) to its closed coefficient. Its nonzero Euler coefficient gives (6.504), as in Theorem 6.166. These are ordinary singular orbitals and regular-set character values on their stated domains. \(\square\)

Example 6.228 — colors and an ambient refinement count. Let \(F=\mathbb F_2((t))\), let \(D\) have unramified maximal field \(E=\mathbb F_8((t))\), and write \(\Pi a=a^2\Pi\), \(\Pi^3=t\). Take \(s=\zeta\in\mathbb F_8\setminus\mathbb F_2\). Then \(\Delta=E\), \(a_E=1,f_E=3,Q=q=8\). The left coefficient basis is \(1,\Pi,\Pi^2\). Each of \(L_0,L_0\Pi,L_0\Pi^2\) is \(\Sigma\)-normalized: a nonzero coefficient component in each coordinate is carried to every other component by the matrix units. Thus all three least colors occur, even though a residue-line criterion over \(\mathbb F_Q=\mathbb F_q\) would give no rank-three line.

Let \(M\) have row \((1,\Pi,0)\) modulo \(\mathfrak P^6\). It is normalized. Since \(\Pi-\tau_s\Pi\) has valuation one, the incidence condition at \(k=2\) asks that a rank-two cyclic kernel of length three refine a fixed kernel of length one. There are \(9\cdot8^2=576\) ambient kernels and \(8^2=64\) such refinements. Write their primitive rows as \( (1,y)\), \(y=a_1\Pi+a_2\Pi^2\), \(a_i\in\mathbb F_8\). Their corresponding lattice is generated by \[ \Pi^6e_1,\qquad(-\Pi^4,\Pi^3,0)^t, \qquad(\Pi y,-y,1)^t. \tag{6.505} \] Only the last column contributes to its coefficient matrix modulo \(t\). Its three columns are \((0,0,1)^t,(0,-a_1,0)^t,(a_1^2,-a_2,0)^t\). They span precisely when \(a_1\ne0\). Hence exactly \(7\cdot8=56\) of the 64 refinements are normalized. The upper bound in Lemma 6.224 permits this strict inequality.

Formula (6.503) gives \((\eta_s,d_{\mathrm{St}},O_s(c_{\mathrm{St}}))=(147,49,3)\). For an unramified quartic in degree-four \(D\) over \(\mathbb F_2((t))\), the values are \((1275,1275/4,4)\).

There are also mixed inseparable examples. In degree-six \(D\) with residue field \(\mathbb F_{64}\), \(\Pi a=a^2\Pi\), \(\Pi^6=t\), put \(E=\mathbb F_8((\Pi^3))\). This is a field with \(a_E=2,f_E=3\): \(\Pi^3\) commutes with \(\mathbb F_8\) and its square is \(t\). If \(z\in\mathbb F_8\setminus\mathbb F_2\), then \(s=z+\Pi^3\) generates \(E/F\). Indeed \(s^2=z^2+t\), so \(z^2\), then \(z=(z^2)^4\), and finally \(\Pi^3=s-z\), lie in \(F[s]\). Here \(Q=8,q=64,\delta=1\), and the three values in (6.503) are \((147/2,28665/2,1/195)\). The proof of the ordinary orbital bound applies without choosing a separable Jordan decomposition.

Figure 18. Lemma 6.221 gives the finite colors and coefficient normalization. Example 6.228 proves the three refinement counts and distinguishes normalized kernels from ambient ones. Theorems 6.223–6.225 give the compact frame and ordinary-measure estimate, and Corollary 6.226 covers every orbit in division ranks at most three. The boxes carry module data, without metric lengths or angles.

The coefficient and incidence arguments, including their valuation and measure inputs, are proved here. Theorem 6.271 proves elliptic orthogonality. General higher-division-rank noncompact orbital estimates, individual elliptic character coefficients and the full local and global representation transfers remain separate conclusions.

6.39. Rank-four elliptic characters and quantitative trace excision

The rank-three orbital bound has a consequence in division rank four that does not require a bound for its repeated closed primary orbits. All proper Levi blocks have rank at most three. This gives the nonclosed-orbit zeros needed by the compact germ formula. We also distinguish two limiting operations: approximation of the elliptic character pairing by actual compact traces, and removal of the remaining trace on a shrinking discriminant neighborhood.

Lemma 6.229 — one higher rank for proper flags. Suppose every ordinary orbital in division ranks less than \(r\) is an absolute continuous Schwartz functional with polynomial tails. Then every orbit in \(\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\) outside the closed primary orbits has those properties and is a Schwartz trace. Its values on discrete-series coefficients, compact discrete tests and the Euler test are zero. In particular these assertions hold in division rank four, in both characteristics.

Proof. If there is more than one primary factor, its primary-factor flag has proper Levi blocks, each of right dimension less than \(r\). For a nonclosed primary type \(\lambda\), the intrinsic kernel flag (6.322) has blocks of dimensions \(hc_j\), where \(h\) is the simple right dimension and \(c_j\) are the partition's column lengths. Nonclosedness gives at least two columns, so every block has dimension less than \(r=hm\).

Use the flag measure (6.323), including for inseparable factors. The nonnegative radical estimate (6.218) and product estimate (6.225) bound its integral by the corresponding closed-block Schwartz integrals, with any required polynomial weights absorbed by increasing their seminorms. The assumed lower-rank bounds therefore prove absolute convergence and every polynomial tail before any vanishing is used. Positive convolution gives the finite double integral (6.274), and Fubini gives the trace identity. The translated proper constant terms of a discrete coefficient vanish by Theorem 6.77. Applying the trace to the finite commutators (6.271) gives the compact discrete-test zero, and (6.309) gives the Euler zero. This is the proper-flag argument of Corollary 6.163 with arbitrary proper block sizes. For \(r=4\), all its hypotheses are Corollary 6.226. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.230 — every primary compact germ in division rank four. Let \(G=\mathrm{GL}_4(D)\), and let \(P\) be a primary reduced polynomial with closed representative \(s\). Put \(E=F[s]\), \(e=[E:F]\), \(g=\gcd(d,e)\), \(\delta=d/g\), \(h=e/g\), and \(m=4/h\). Let \(a_E\) be the ramification index of \(E/F\), \(Q=q_\Delta\), and \(\epsilon_m=(-1)^{m-1}\). With the measures of Theorem 6.157, \[ \eta_s=O_s(\mathfrak e_G) =\epsilon_m\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(Q^j-1)}{a_E m\delta}\ne0. \tag{6.506} \] For regular \(\gamma\) sufficiently near \(P\), the closed compact germ is \[ g_{P,(1^m)}(\gamma)= \begin{cases} (e(F[\gamma]/F)\eta_s)^{-1},&\gamma\text{ elliptic},\\ 0,&\gamma\text{ nonelliptic}. \end{cases} \tag{6.507} \] For every discrete series \(\pi\), on the nearby elliptic regular set, \[ \Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})= O_s(f^\circ_{\pi,m_0,P})/\eta_s. \tag{6.508} \] The numerator is a compact-test orbital, using the fixed reduced-norm annulus. A common neighborhood works for a finite packet. These conclusions impose no separability condition on \(E/F\).

Proof. Theorem 6.165 gives \(hm=4\). Thus \(m\) is one of \(1,2,4\). Every nonclosed partition has a proper intrinsic flag, so Lemma 6.229 makes all its compact discrete-test and Euler coefficients zero. The sole remaining coefficient in (6.326) is the closed one. It is finite for compact tests by Theorem 6.139, and its Euler value is the nonzero number (6.506), by Theorem 6.157.

Cut the compact-mod-center Euler and discrete tests to the reduced-norm annulus containing \(P\). The cut is compact and agrees on the fibre and on a coefficient neighborhood. Their regular orbital values are Theorems 6.120 and 6.122. Division by \(\eta_s\) in (6.326), with the maximal-compact torus measure converted by \(e(F[\gamma]/F)\), gives (6.507) and (6.508), exactly as in Theorem 6.166. Intersect neighborhoods for finitely many tests. This proof uses no Schwartz orbital of a general rank-four closed representative and no character integral through its singular fibre. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.231 — finite real elliptic expansions. Let \(r\le4\), or let \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\) satisfy one of the other ranges of Theorem 6.167 or Corollary 6.189. Put \(N=rd\), fix a unitary central character \(\omega\), and let \(\mathcal D/F\) be a division algebra of degree \(N\). For every discrete series \(\pi\), \(F_\pi(b)=(-1)^{r-1}\Theta_\pi(\gamma_b)\) extends from regular semisimple elements to a locally constant conjugation-invariant function on all of \(\mathcal D^\times\), with central covariance \(\omega\). It has a finite expansion \[ \begin{gathered} F_\pi=\sum_\rho a_{\pi\rho}\chi_\rho,\qquad a_{\pi\rho}\in\mathbb R,\\ \sum_\rho a_{\pi\rho}\dim\rho =d_\pi/d_{\mathrm{St}_G}\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\qquad \|\Theta_\pi\|_{\mathrm{ell}}^2=\sum_\rho a_{\pi\rho}^2. \end{gathered} \tag{6.509} \] Here \(\rho\) runs over irreducibles of \(\mathcal D^\times\) with central character \(\omega\), and the elliptic measure is the probability measure \(\nu\) of Corollary 6.124. Individual integrality, positivity and norm one do not follow from (6.509).

Proof: extension and finiteness. The previously stated ranges are Theorem 6.167 and Corollary 6.189. In rank four repeat their extension argument with Theorem 6.230: for any \(b\in\mathcal D^\times\), its polynomial is \(p^{N/e}\) for the field \(F[b]\). Lemma 6.164 gives the corresponding closed primary representative in \(G\). Formula (6.508), applied to the contragredient, makes \(F_\pi\) constant on all nearby regular semisimple division elements. The nearcentral case is also Corollary 6.136. The regular set is dense because its discriminant polynomial is nonzero. The constants therefore agree on overlaps and extend uniquely. Conjugation invariance, central covariance and boundedness on compact representatives follow.

A finite cover of compact representatives supplies a normal principal congruence subgroup fixing the extension on both sides. After removing the central valuation character, its expansion is finite-group character theory on a finite quotient, as in Section 6.4. With \(\mu_{\mathcal D}\) the probability quotient Haar measure, its coefficients are \[ a_{\pi\rho}=\int_{\mathcal D^\times/Z} F_\pi(b)\overline{\chi_\rho(b)}\,d\mu_{\mathcal D}(b). \tag{6.510} \] The central value and positive integral degree ratio are Corollary 6.136. Orthogonality on the division group and the Weyl isometry give the two sums in (6.509).

Proof: reality. Unitarity and Corollary 6.71 give \(F_\pi(b^{-1})=\overline{F_\pi(b)}\) on the dense regular set, hence everywhere. Division characters satisfy the same identity. Conjugate (6.510) and replace \(b\) by \(b^{-1}\). Quotient Haar measure is invariant, and the product has trivial central covariance. The result is again (6.510), so \(\overline{a_{\pi\rho}}=a_{\pi\rho}\). This argument also proves reality in every earlier finite-expansion range. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.232 — a polynomial sublevel bound in either characteristic. Let \(P\ne0\) be a polynomial of positive degree at most \(D\) on \(F^l\), and let \(C\) be compact. For additive Haar measure there is \(B_{P,C}\) such that \[ \operatorname{vol}\{x\in C:|P(x)|_F\le q_F^{-n}\} \le B_{P,C}q_F^{-n/D}\qquad(n\ge0). \tag{6.511} \] No nonvanishing derivative is required.

Proof. Enclose \(C\) in a scalar multiple of \(\mathcal O_F^l\) and rescale. Let \(d_0\le D\) be the actual degree, and \(P_{d_0}\) its highest homogeneous part. A nonzero polynomial cannot vanish on the open set \(\mathcal O_F^l\), by the root-count induction of Lemma 6.85. Choose a primitive integral vector where \(P_{d_0}\ne0\), rescaling a nonzero such vector if necessary, and extend it to an integral basis. In these coordinates the coefficient of the last variable's \(d_0\)-th power is a fixed nonzero scalar \(c\), independent of the other coordinates.

For fixed other coordinates factor this one-variable polynomial in an algebraic closure, with multiplicities. The extended absolute value is unique. If its product has absolute value at most \(q_F^{-n}\), one of its \(d_0\) factors has absolute value at most \(r_n=(q_F^{-n}/|c|_F)^{1/d_0}\). The intersection of such a root ball with \(F\), if nonempty, is contained in an \(F\)-ball of the same radius: choose one point in the intersection and use the ultrametric inequality. Its Haar volume is at most \(q_Fr_n\). The union bound over the roots is uniform in the other coordinates. Fubini and the fixed coordinate-volume factors give \(Bq_F^{-n/d_0}\le Bq_F^{-n/D}\). This includes repeated purely inseparable roots. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.233 — quantitative elliptic discriminant excision. For \(N\ge2\) put \(D_N=N(N-1)\), and define on a degree-\(N\) inner form \[ \Delta(g)=\frac{|\operatorname{disc}(\chi_g)|_F} {|\operatorname{Nrd}(g)|_F^{N-1}},\qquad \zeta_n(g)=1_{\{\Delta(g)\ge q_F^{-n}\}}. \tag{6.512} \] This agrees with the Weyl discriminant on the regular set. It is invariant under the center, conjugation and inversion. Each \(\zeta_n\) is locally constant on the entire group and vanishes near the singular set. On the common elliptic class space, \[ \nu\{\Delta<q_F^{-n}\}\le B_Nq_F^{-n/D_N}. \tag{6.513} \] Also, with \(\ell=-\log_{q_F}\Delta\) on the elliptic regular set, for every \(A\ge0\), \[ \int_{\ell>n}(1+\ell)^A\,d\nu \le B_{N,A}(1+n)^Aq_F^{-n/D_N}. \tag{6.514} \] For \(N=1\), take \(\Delta=1\); the omitted set is empty.

Proof. After splitting, the quotient in (6.512) is \(\prod_{i<j}|(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2/(\alpha_i\alpha_j)|_F\). This proves the Weyl, central and inversion assertions. The reduced discriminant is a polynomial in matrix coordinates of degree at most \(D_N\), and is nonzero on a separable generator of an unramified maximal field. Continuity, its discrete nonzero absolute values, and its zero value at singular points make \(\zeta_n\) locally constant, also at those points.

Use the probability quotient of \(\mathcal D^\times\) in Corollary 6.124. Representatives of valuations \(0,\ldots,N-1\) form a compact union of \(N\) translates of \(\mathcal O_{\mathcal D}^\times\). On it the reduced norm is bounded away from zero. Multiplicative Haar measure is a constant times \(|\operatorname{Nrd}(x)|_F^{-N}\) times additive Haar measure; this follows from the determinant of left multiplication. Its density is therefore bounded on these representatives. The central-unit disintegration has a fixed finite factor. Apply (6.511) to their nonzero reduced-discriminant polynomial. The bounded norm denominator changes only the constant, proving (6.513). Matching classes have the same discriminant, and the Weyl probability measure agrees with this division-group measure.

On an elliptic class all roots have the same absolute value, so \(0<\Delta\le1\) and \(\ell\ge0\). Sum (6.513) over integral valuation shells. Writing their index as \(n+j\), use \((1+n+j)^A\le(1+n)^A(1+j)^A\); the remaining polynomial times geometric series converges. This proves (6.514). No finiteness of the family of field extensions is used. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.234 — actual compact traces approximate the elliptic Gram matrix. Fix a finite packet of discrete series of one \(G\) and one unitary central character, in a range of Theorem 6.231, with \(N\ge2\). Write \(f_\pi=f_{\pi,m_0}\), \(M_\pi=\sup|F_\pi|<\infty\), and set \[ f_{\pi,n}=\zeta_nf_\pi,\qquad H_{\sigma\pi}(n)=\int_{\mathcal E_N} \zeta_n\Theta_\sigma\overline{\Theta_\pi}\,d\nu. \tag{6.515} \] These are compact-mod-center smooth tests with regular support, and \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{tr}\sigma(f_{\pi,n})=H_{\sigma\pi}(n),\\ |H_{\sigma\pi}-H_{\sigma\pi}(n)| \le B_NM_\sigma M_\pi q_F^{-n/D_N},\qquad H_{\sigma\pi}=\int\Theta_\sigma\overline{\Theta_\pi}\,d\nu. \end{gathered} \tag{6.516} \] They may be chosen bi-invariant at a principal division-lattice depth \(m_n\le dn+C_f\). Thus every approximant is an actual finite fixed-space trace. The packet matrices \(H(n)\) are real symmetric positive semidefinite and increase to \(H\) in that order. For \(N=1\), the cutoff is identically one and the trace and Gram identities are exact, without an error exponent.

Proof: the trace identity. The cutoff is central and conjugation invariant. Thus \(O_\gamma(f_{\pi,n})=\zeta_n(\gamma)O_\gamma(f_\pi)\). Its nonelliptic regular orbitals vanish by Theorem 6.120. At elliptic regular elements they equal \(\zeta_n\overline{\Theta_\pi}\). The actual regular-support character theorem 6.70 and Weyl integration therefore give the first line of (6.516).

Here is the passage from compact-mod-center tests to that theorem. Give central units volume one and cut to \(0\le v_F(\operatorname{Nrd}g)<N\). The result is compact. Its central pushforward, with the central character, is the original test, because each central valuation class contributes one central-unit coset. Quotient integration gives the desired trace and character identities. This cut preserves regular support. All integrals at this step are on compact regular sets.

The second line of (6.516) is boundedness of the two elliptic extensions and (6.513). Positivity and monotonicity follow by applying the integral to \(|\sum c_\pi\Theta_\pi|^2\). Inversion of elliptic classes preserves \(\nu,\zeta_n\) and conjugates the product, so every entry is real. Symmetry follows as well.

Proof: a controlled finite level. On compact representatives of the support of \(f_\pi\), entries, inverse entries and reduced-norm valuations are bounded. In fixed \(\mathcal O_F\)-coordinates, left or right multiplication by \(K_m=1+M_r(\mathfrak P_D^m)\) changes every coordinate by an element of valuation at least \(\lfloor m/d\rfloor-C\). Expanding the finitely many monomials in the reduced-discriminant polynomial gives the same lower bound, with another fixed \(C\), for the change of that polynomial. Norm absolute values are unchanged under \(K_m\). Once \(m\ge d(n+C')\), the polynomial error has strictly larger valuation than the cutoff threshold throughout these representatives. The ultrametric inequality then preserves cutoff membership. Take \(K_m\) also inside a bi-invariance subgroup of \(f_\pi\). Central invariance extends this to its full support, proving the stated linear bound after increasing \(C_f\). A finite packet uses the maximum of these constants. Admissibility makes its fixed spaces finite-dimensional. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.235 — a fixed-space criterion for character integration. Let \(V\) be a finitely generated smooth admissible unitary representation, with regular density \(\Theta\) from Theorem 6.70. Let \(K_m\) be cofinal principal compact subgroups and \(P_m\) their averaging projections. Put \[ h_m(g)=\operatorname{tr}(\pi(g)P_m) =\sum_{i=1}^{\dim V^{K_m}}\langle\pi(g)e_i,e_i\rangle, \qquad |h_m(g)|\le\dim V^{K_m}. \tag{6.517} \] The following are equivalent:

  1. The regular density is locally integrable and represents the trace on every compact smooth test.
  2. \(h_m\to\Theta\) in \(L^1(C)\) for every compact \(C\), with arbitrary values assigned on the null singular set.
  3. For every compact \(C\), \[ \lim_{n\to\infty}\sup_m \int_{C\cap\{\Delta<q_F^{-n}\}}|h_m(g)|\,dg=0. \tag{6.518} \] This is a uniform condition in the fixed-space index \(m\).

Proof: finite traces and regular stabilization. Each \(P_m\) has finite rank; the trace is the finite sum in (6.517), independent of basis. Its terms are smooth coefficients, so \(h_m\) is locally constant. Unitarity gives the bound. If \(f\) is bi-\(K_m\)-invariant, its operator has image and coimage in \(V^{K_m}\). The finite sum therefore gives \[ \operatorname{tr}\pi(f)=\int_G f(g)h_m(g)\,dg. \tag{6.519} \] On a compact subset of the regular set, \(h_m=\Theta\) for every sufficiently large \(m\), uniformly on that subset. Indeed choose finitely many neighborhoods on which \(\Theta\) is constant and the regular trace identity holds, and take \(K_m\) small enough that every corresponding coset stays in one such neighborhood. The coset-test trace is (6.517). This is also Corollary 6.71. The singular set is null, by (6.511) on compact matrix charts.

Proof that 3 implies 2 and 1. Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(n\) for which the supremum in (6.518) is at most \(\varepsilon\). Fatou's lemma and the pointwise regular stabilization bound \(\int_{C\cap\{\Delta<q_F^{-n}\}}|\Theta|\) by \(\varepsilon\). Outside that tube the set is compact and regular, so eventual uniform equality holds and its integral is finite. Thus \(\Theta\in L^1(C)\). For all sufficiently large \(m\), the \(L^1(C)\) difference is at most \(2\varepsilon\), entirely inside the tube. This proves 2. Apply it to a compact support of \(f\) in (6.519), at levels fixing \(f\), to obtain 1.

Proof that 1 implies 2 and 3. The global trace identity applied to the coset test at \(gK_m\) gives \(h_m(g)=\operatorname{vol}(K_m)^{-1}\int_{K_m}\Theta(gk)\,dk\). These right averages converge in local \(L^1\). To verify this directly, enlarge \(C\) to the compact open set \(CK_1\). Compact-open simple functions are dense in \(L^1\) there: regularity of Haar measure approximates a finite-measure set from inside and outside, and finite compact-open partitions approximate those sets. Such a simple function is fixed by sufficiently small right \(K_m\). Averaging contracts the \(L^1\) error on \(C\), bounded by its error on \(CK_1\). This proves 2.

An \(L^1(C)\)-convergent sequence is uniformly absolutely continuous in integral: approximate the limit and all sufficiently late terms by one small error, and deal with the finitely many early integrable terms separately. The tube measures tend to zero by (6.511). This gives (6.518), proving 3 and all the equivalences. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.236 — an exact trace criterion for elliptic orthogonality. For the packet in Theorem 6.234, put \[ R_{\pi,n}=(1-\zeta_n)f_\pi,\qquad A=(a_{\pi\rho}),\qquad \mathfrak D=I-AA^t. \tag{6.520} \] Every entry of the actual trace matrix has the limit \[ \begin{gathered} \operatorname{tr}\sigma(R_{\pi,n}) =\delta_{\sigma\pi}-H_{\sigma\pi}(n),\\ \left|\operatorname{tr}\sigma(R_{\pi,n})-\mathfrak D_{\sigma\pi}\right| \le B_NM_\sigma M_\pi q_F^{-n/D_N}. \end{gathered} \tag{6.521} \] The packet's characters are elliptically orthonormal if and only if all these trace limits are zero. Condition (6.518) for each packet member is sufficient for that vanishing. Corollary 6.272 gives \(\mathfrak D=0\) for these actual packet matrices. In degree one the remainder is identically zero, as above.

Proof. The compact pseudo-coefficient trace (6.267) is \(\delta_{\sigma\pi}\). Subtract (6.516) to get the first line of (6.521). Parseval and the real expansions (6.509) give \(H=AA^t\); the error bound is the second line of (6.516). Thus zero trace limits are exactly \(H=I\). Under (6.518), Theorem 6.235 represents the trace by a locally integrable density.
