Estimate (6.593) identifies the limit with \(\mathcal I_f(h)\), proving (6.594). If \(N=1\), the cutoff is identically one and the quotient is compact, so the assertion follows directly. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.271 — the cuspidal trace identity and elliptic orthogonality. For every discrete series \(\pi\) and every \(f\in\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), \[ \operatorname{Tr}\pi(f)= \int_{\mathrm{ell}}\Theta_\pi(\gamma) O_\gamma^{\mathrm{unit}}(f)\,d\nu(\gamma). \tag{6.595} \] In particular, for all discrete series of central character \(\omega\), \[ \int_{\mathrm{ell}}\Theta_\pi(\gamma) \overline{\Theta_\sigma(\gamma)}\,d\nu(\gamma) =\delta_{\pi,\sigma},\qquad AA^{\mathsf t}=I. \tag{6.596} \] These statements hold in every division rank and both field characteristics.

Proof. Choose a compact very cuspidal representative \(g\) of \(f\), using Corollary 6.265. Choose such a representative \(F_\pi\) of its compact discrete test \(f_{\pi,m}\). Lemma 6.118, equation (6.271), and the compact cocenter identities give a finite Schwartz commutator expression for \(F_\pi-E^\pi_{u,u}\). Theorem 6.268 therefore gives \[ \mathcal I_g(F_\pi)=\mathcal I_g(E^\pi_{u,u}) =\operatorname{Tr}\pi(g). \] On the other hand (6.594) makes the left side \(\int_{\mathrm{ell}}O_\gamma(g)\overline{\Theta_\pi(\gamma^{-1})}\,d\nu\). Unitary inversion changes its second factor to \(\Theta_\pi(\gamma)\). Compact commutators are killed both by actual traces and by ordinary orbitals, so \(g\) can be replaced by \(f\). This proves (6.595).

Take \(f=f_{\sigma,m}\). Its actual trace is \(\delta_{\pi,\sigma}\) by (6.267), and its ordinary elliptic orbital is \(\Theta_\sigma(\gamma^{-1})\) by Theorem 6.120. This proves (6.596). The finite real character expansions of Theorem 6.256 identify the resulting Gram matrix with \(AA^{\mathsf t}\). \(\square\)

Corollary 6.272 — transfer traces and vanishing complementary traces. For every division irreducible \(\rho\), let \(t_\rho\) be the compact transfer of \(p_\rho=N^{-1}\overline{\chi_\rho}\). Then \[ \operatorname{Tr}\pi(t_\rho) =(-1)^{r-1}a_{\pi\rho}, \qquad B=A. \tag{6.597} \] More generally, put \(M_f=\sup_{\mathrm{ell}}|O_\gamma(f)|\) and \(M_\pi=\sup_{\mathrm{ell}}|\Theta_\pi(\gamma)|\). For \(N>1\) and \(f\in\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), \[ |\operatorname{Tr}\pi((1-\zeta_n)f)| \le B_N M_\pi M_f q_F^{-n/\mathfrak d}. \tag{6.598} \]

Proof. Substitute \(O_\gamma(t_\rho)=\overline{\chi_\rho(b_\gamma)}\) into (6.595), and use the coefficient formula (6.566), including its sign. This gives (6.597) for any of the compact cocenter representatives.

Multiplication by the conjugation-invariant cutoff preserves \(\mathcal V_\omega(G)\), since its value factors out of every ordinary orbital. Apply (6.595) to the complementary test. Its elliptic integral is over \(\Delta<q_F^{-n}\). The bounded profiles and (6.513) give (6.598). For \(N=1\) the complementary test is zero. \(\square\)

Example 6.273 — the two norm components for \(\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\). Let \(I\) be the edge parahoric, \(\operatorname{vol}(I)=1/(q_F+1)\), and \(\Omega=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\\varpi_F&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). On norm valuation zero the very cuspidal Euler representative is the inflated finite flag function \[ e_0=1-\tfrac12\chi_{\mathbb P^1(k_F)} \quad\text{on }K,\qquad 0\text{ elsewhere}. \tag{6.599} \] On valuation one it is \(e_1=(q_F+1)1_{\Omega I}/2\). Extend both centrally. The finite Gram identity (6.574), or the two permutation characters of \(S_2\), gives \(\|e_0\|_2^2=1/2\). At every positive Cartan height the lower-radical integration of Lemma 6.266 is already zero: the upper entry of \(g\) is in \(\varpi_F\mathcal O_F\), its diagonal entries are units, and the two finite radical averages separate. Thus \(K_{e_0,e_0}\) is \(1/2\) on \(K/Z\) and zero elsewhere.

Every element of \(\Omega I\) reverses the base edge. Its fixed set in the lattice tree is its midpoint: a second fixed midpoint would force a fixed vertex, impossible for odd type shift. Consequently a conjugate in \(\Omega I\) can occur only when the conjugator stabilizes that edge. Its stabilizer has quotient volume \(2/(q_F+1)\), and on it \[ K_{e_1,e_1}=\frac{q_F+1}{4},\qquad \mathcal I_{e_0}(e_0)=\mathcal I_{e_1}(e_1)=\frac12. \tag{6.600} \] Different norm components have zero cross-kernel. Therefore the full Euler representative has pairing one. These volume and sign calculations apply also in characteristic two.

The trace identity (6.595) is for the stated compact cuspidal orbital subspace and discrete-series traces. It proves elliptic orthogonality and the complementary-trace zeros without asserting arbitrary-test character integrability. Individual coefficient integrality, representation-transfer existence and bijectivity, general noncompact closed Schwartz estimates, and the global correspondences require additional arguments.

6.44 Global Whittaker coefficients and compact cuspidal functions

Let \(k\) be a global field, \(\mathbb A=\mathbb A_k\), and \(H=\mathrm{GL}_n\). A smooth function \(\phi\) on \(H(k)\backslash H(\mathbb A)\) is cuspidal here if its integral along \(R(k)\backslash R(\mathbb A)\) vanishes for the radical \(R\) of every proper \(k\)-parabolic. Smooth means smooth at the archimedean places and locally constant at the finite places. The arguments below apply to such functions without a spectral-finiteness assumption.

Lemma 6.274 — compact additive Fourier uniqueness. There is an additive character \(\psi\) of \(\mathbb A\), nontrivial at every place, for which \[ k^\perp=k,\qquad k\backslash\mathbb A\text{ is compact},\qquad \widehat{k\backslash\mathbb A}=\{x\mapsto\psi(ax):a\in k\}. \tag{6.601} \] On every finite power of this quotient, a continuous function with all Fourier coefficients zero is zero.

Proof for number fields: the rational field. On \(\mathbb R\) use \(e^{-2\pi ix}\), and on \(\mathbb Q_p\) use \(e^{2\pi i\{x\}_p}\), where the fractional part is the finite sum of its negative-power digits. Their product \(\psi_{\mathbb Q}\) is one on \(\mathbb Q\): subtracting the finitely many fractional parts of a rational number leaves an integer. Subtracting those parts from an adèle makes every finite component integral, and subtracting an integer puts its real component in \([0,1)\). Thus \([0,1]\times\prod_p\mathbb Z_p\) maps onto the quotient, proving compactness. The neighborhood \((-1/2,1/2)\times\prod_p\mathbb Z_p\) meets the diagonal only in zero, proving discreteness; a discrete subgroup of a Hausdorff topological group is closed, since two distinct subgroup points cannot lie in a sufficiently small translate of that neighborhood.

Every character of \(\mathbb Q_p\) is \(x\mapsto\psi_p(a_px)\). Indeed its open kernel contains \(p^h\mathbb Z_p\); its values on the cyclic groups \(p^{-m}\mathbb Z_p/p^h\mathbb Z_p\) give compatible residues of a unique \(a_p\in p^{-h}\mathbb Z_p\). These groups exhaust \(\mathbb Q_p/p^h\mathbb Z_p\), proving the assertion. On \(\mathbb R\), lifting the character to an angle near zero gives a continuous additive function, hence a linear one; subdivision extends this formula to all real arguments. Continuity on the restricted product forces a character to be trivial on \(\prod_{p\notin S}\mathbb Z_p\) for some finite \(S\): that subgroup can be put inside the inverse image of a circle arc containing no nontrivial subgroup. Consequently every adelic character is parametrized by a unique parameter adèle.

If a parameter annihilates \(\mathbb Q\), subtract a rational parameter to put it in \([0,1)\times\prod_p\mathbb Z_p\). Testing against one makes its real component zero. Testing against \(p^{-m}\) makes its \(p\)-component divisible by \(p^m\), for every \(m\), so all components are zero. This proves self-annihilation. Characters of the quotient, pulled back to the adèles, are therefore exactly the rational parameters.

For Fourier uniqueness, average a continuous quotient function over successively smaller finite-place compact open subgroups \(J\). Uniform continuity makes these averages converge uniformly. Finite-place additive approximation, obtained by the integer Chinese remainder theorem after clearing denominators, gives \(\mathbb A_f=\mathbb Q+J\). Hence an average descends to \(\mathbb R/(\mathbb Q\cap J)\), a circle, and its characters are among the rational parameters above. On a circle the Fejér kernels have mass one, are nonnegative and concentrate at zero. These properties follow from \(m^{-1}|1+e^{it}+\cdots+e^{i(m-1)t}|^2\): its constant coefficient is one, and outside any fixed neighborhood of zero it is bounded by a constant times \(m^{-1}\). Convolution therefore converges uniformly to a continuous function. Zero Fourier coefficients make these convolutions zero. Apply this to each finite-place average and then take its uniform limit. Products give Fourier uniqueness on every finite power of the rational quotient.

Proof for function fields: the rational field. First put \(K=\mathbb F_q(t)\), \(s=t^{-1}\), and fix a nontrivial additive character \(\psi_q\) of \(\mathbb F_q\). At each place use the character \(x\mapsto\psi_q(\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa(v)/\mathbb F_q}\operatorname{res}_v(x\,dt))\). It is nontrivial: in a local parameter, multiplication by the nonzero differential \(dt\) only shifts a Laurent coefficient and multiplies it by a unit. The finite-field trace pairing is nondegenerate. Indeed finite fields are separable, so their trace form is nondegenerate, as follows by writing the distinct conjugates in a Vandermonde matrix.

Partial fractions show that the sum of these traced residues of a rational differential is zero: a simple finite pole contributes the negative of its contribution to the coefficient at infinity, and higher-pole terms contribute zero. Thus the product character \(\psi_K\) is trivial on \(K\). Removing the finitely many finite principal parts of an adèle by a rational function, and then removing its polynomial part at infinity, gives \[ \mathbb A_K=K+C_K,\qquad C_K=\prod_{v\ne\infty}\mathcal O_v\times s\mathbb F_q[[s]], \qquad K\cap C_K=0. \tag{6.602} \] The principal parts can be prescribed by the polynomial Chinese remainder theorem. A rational function integral at every finite place is a polynomial; membership in \(s\mathbb F_q[[s]]\) then makes it zero. This proves the intersection assertion. In particular the additive quotient is compact and has a compact open additive group of representatives.

Suppose an adèle annihilates \(K\). Subtract an element of \(K\) to put it in \(C_K\). Pairing with \(\alpha t^m\), for \(\alpha\in\mathbb F_q\) and \(m\ge0\), makes every coefficient at infinity zero: since \(dt=-s^{-2}ds\), the residue selects its coefficient of \(s^{m+1}\). Varying \(\alpha\) uses the nondegenerate finite-field pairing. At a finite prime \(P\), now pair with rational functions having poles only at \(P\). Their local principal parts exhaust \(K_P/\mathcal O_P\), by the same Chinese remainder theorem. All other residues vanish. The Laurent-coefficient pairing therefore makes that component zero too. This proves \(K^\perp=K\).

For completeness, every continuous character of a local Laurent-series field is a Laurent-coefficient character of this form. Its open kernel bounds one end of the coefficient list; its values on the successive coefficient groups determine the other coefficients uniquely, using finite-field trace duality. This also identifies the topologies: annihilators of fractional ideals are fractional ideals. On a restricted product, continuity makes the character trivial on the integral groups outside finitely many places. Hence the local descriptions identify every character of \(\mathbb A_K\) with a unique parameter adèle. A character of \(C_K\) extends by one on \(K\) in (6.602), so its parameter lies in \(K^\perp=K\). This proves (6.601). Finite-group Fourier inversion applies to every finite quotient of \(C_K\). Averaging a continuous function over successively smaller open subgroups converges uniformly, proving Fourier uniqueness.

Proof for finite extensions in either characteristic. Every one-variable function field \(k\) over a finite field admits a separating element. Here is the algebraic point. For any transcendental \(t\) with \([k:\mathbb F_q(t)]=e\), Frobenius and the degree formula give \([k:k^p]=p\). Choose \(f\notin k^p\); then \(k=k^p(f)\), and \(k/\mathbb F_q(f)\) is finite separable. To check the last implication, a finite extension \(L/M\) is separable precisely when \(L=ML^p\). In the separable direction the minimal polynomial of a primitive element remains separable over \(M(\alpha^p)\), whereas \(\alpha\) is purely inseparable over that field, forcing equality. Conversely, iterate \(L=ML^p\). A sufficiently large common \(p\)-power of finitely many generators has separable minimal polynomial over \(M\), obtained by removing all its powers of \(X^p\). Thus the iterated equality puts all of \(L\) in its separable subextension. This proves the criterion and the separating-element assertion.

Take \(K=\mathbb Q\) for a number field and \(K=\mathbb F_q(f)\) for a function field. Choose trace-dual \(K\)-bases \(b_i,c_i\) of \(k\), and set \[ \psi_k(x)=\psi_K(\operatorname{Tr}_{k/K}x),\qquad \mathbb A_k\simeq\mathbb A_K^{[k:K]},\qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{k/K}(b_i c_j)=\delta_{ij}. \tag{6.603} \] The middle map is the additive basis map. To check its restricted-product topology, omit the finitely many places at which a basis vector or a trace-dual vector is nonintegral. There are only finitely many: each vector satisfies a monic polynomial whose coefficients have only finitely many denominators. At every remaining place an integral element has integral coordinates \(\operatorname{Tr}(x c_i)\), and integral coordinates give an integral element. At the exceptional places the finite-dimensional local basis maps are topological isomorphisms. Factoring a separable defining polynomial over a completion identifies the local tensor algebra with the product of the completions above that place, so this basis map is the asserted adelic map. It carries the diagonal \(k\) to \(K^{[k:K]}\). Trace duality gives compactness, discreteness, self-annihilation and the full character-group assertion from the corresponding rational case. Every local trace of a finite separable extension is a nonzero linear functional, hence surjective, proving local nontriviality of \(\psi_k\). The quotient is a finite product of rational additive quotients, so the Fourier uniqueness proved above transfers as well. \(\square\)

Normalize all rational unipotent quotients below to have volume one. Their compactness and the required disintegrations can be seen directly: order upper-triangular entries by their columns, choose a compact additive fundamental set for \(k\backslash\mathbb A\), and successively remove the rational part of each entry by left multiplication by a rational elementary matrix. Later entries change polynomially, but already treated entries do not change. This gives compact representatives. Multiplication and conjugation on the successive root coordinates are triangular with diagonal one; rational linear changes have adelic determinant of absolute value one by the product formula. Thus iterated integration over these additive quotients is invariant and has the stated normalization.

Lemma 6.275 — the successive nonzero Fourier coefficients. For \(1\le i\le n\), put \[ U^{(i)}=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}I_i&X\\0&u\end{pmatrix}:u\in U_{n-i}\right\}, \qquad \psi_i(u)=\psi\left(\sum_{j=i}^{n-1}u_{j,j+1}\right), \tag{6.604} \] where \(U_a\) denotes the upper unitriangular group of size \(a\), and \(U^{(n)}=1\). Let \(V_i\), for \(2\le i\le n\), consist of the entries in column \(i\) above the diagonal. Thus \(V_i\simeq\mathbb G_a^{i-1}\) and \(U^{(i-1)}=V_iU^{(i)}\), with \(U^{(i)}\) normal. Define \[ F_i(g)=\int_{[U^{(i)}]}\phi(ug)\overline{\psi_i(u)}\,du, \qquad C_{i,a}(g)=\int_{[V_i]}F_i(v(x)g)\overline{\psi(a x)}\,dx, \tag{6.605} \] where \([R]=R(k)\backslash R(\mathbb A)\) and \(a\in k^{i-1}\) is a row. Then \[ C_{i,0}=0,\qquad C_{i,e_{i-1}}=F_{i-1}. \tag{6.606} \] If \(F_i\ne0\), then \(F_{i-1}\ne0\).

Proof. The compact quotient integrals are absolute, including uniformly for \(g\) in a compact set. Conjugation by \(V_i\) preserves \(\psi_i\), since its additional root entries lie strictly above the simple root in column \(i+1\). Hence \(F_i(v(x)g)\) descends to \([V_i]\), and the disintegration above gives the second identity in (6.606).

For the constant coefficient, decompose \(U^{(i-1)}\) as the radical of the parabolic \((i-1,n-i+1)\), followed by the upper unitriangular group in its last block. The character in \(C_{i,0}\) is trivial on that radical. Integrate over it first. Cuspidality makes the integral zero, proving the first identity.

The rational group \(\mathrm{GL}_{i-1}(k)\) in the first block normalizes \(U^{(i)}\) and preserves \(\psi_i\). Consequently \(F_i(hg)=F_i(g)\) for such \(h\). Direct change of the column variable gives \[ C_{i,e_{i-1}}(h g)=C_{i,e_{i-1}h}(g). \tag{6.607} \] Every nonzero row is \(e_{i-1}h\): extend it to an invertible matrix by a basis completion. If \(F_i(g)\ne0\), its continuous function on \([V_i]\) is nonzero at zero. Fourier uniqueness and \(C_{i,0}=0\) give a nonzero coefficient with a nonzero row. Formula (6.607) and (6.606) make \(F_{i-1}\) nonzero. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.276 — global Whittaker injectivity in every degree. The map on smooth cuspidal functions \[ \phi\longmapsto W_\phi(g)= \int_{U_n(k)\backslash U_n(\mathbb A)} \phi(ug)\overline{\psi\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}u_{j,j+1}\right)}\,du \tag{6.608} \] is injective. It intertwines right translation and has left \((U_n(\mathbb A),\psi)\)-covariance. In particular every nonzero cuspidal automorphic representation of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb A)\) is globally generic.

Proof. For a nonzero \(\phi\), start with \(F_n=\phi\). Lemma 6.275 gives \(F_{n-1}\ne0\), then \(F_{n-2}\ne0\), and finally \(F_1=W_\phi\ne0\). This is a finite induction on compact quotient integrals; no rearrangement of an infinite Whittaker expansion is needed. Right equivariance is immediate. Left covariance follows by right translation of the variable in the unipotent quotient and the character identity. For \(n=1\) the map is the identity. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.277 — local genericity. Suppose an irreducible cuspidal representation is written in its algebraic restricted tensor-product realization \(\Pi=\bigotimes_v'\Pi_v\). Every finite local factor is generic for \(\psi_v\).

Proof. Theorem 6.276 makes \(\Lambda(\phi)=W_\phi(1)\) nonzero after a right translation. Pure tensors span, so choose one on which it is nonzero. Holding all factors but \(v\) fixed gives \[ \lambda_v(\xi)=\Lambda(\xi\otimes\xi^v),\qquad \lambda_v(\Pi_v(u)\xi)=\psi_v(u)\lambda_v(\xi),\qquad \lambda_v\ne0. \tag{6.609} \] This is the required Whittaker functional. No uniqueness or product formula for these functionals is used. The algebraic tensor realization is the one in Lesson 12: its finite tensor-algebra and one-dimensional-tail proof applies to a given admissible restricted product with these local groups. The assertion here concerns factors in that realization and does not supply a new spectral-existence theorem. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.278 — nonzero compact cuspidal Poincaré functions. Let \(\eta\) be a unitary character of \(k^\times\backslash\mathbb A^\times\). Prescribe finitely many local smooth compact-mod-centre functions \(f_v\), with central covariance \(\eta_v\), all satisfying \(f_v(1)\ne0\). Include all archimedean and all ramified-character places. Suppose one prescribed finite place \(v_*\) has the stronger vanishing property \[ \int_{R(k_{v_*})}f_{v_*}(a u b)\,du=0 \quad\text{for every proper parabolic radical }R \text{ and all }a,b\in H(k_{v_*}). \tag{6.610} \] After choosing the usual central-covariant maximal-compact indicators at the other places and shrinking one further finite component, the function \[ P_f(g)=\sum_{\gamma\in Z(k)\backslash H(k)}f(\gamma g) \tag{6.611} \] is smooth, nonzero, cuspidal, of central character \(\eta\), and compactly supported on \(H(k)Z(\mathbb A)\backslash H(\mathbb A)\). It is therefore square-integrable on that quotient.

Proof: local finiteness. Central covariance and \(\eta|_{k^\times}=1\) make (6.611) well defined. Conjugation on \(M_n\) embeds rational matrices modulo scalars into rational matrices of size \(n^2\). If two conjugation actions agree, their quotient commutes with every matrix unit, hence is scalar. Consequently for every compact \(C\subset H(\mathbb A)/Z(\mathbb A)\), \[ \#\{\gamma\bmod Z(k):\gamma\in C\}<\infty. \tag{6.612} \] Indeed its conjugation matrices lie in a compact adelic matrix set. Each rational entry has finitely many possibilities, since \(k\) is discrete and closed in \(\mathbb A\); compactness of its additive quotient was proved in Lemma 6.274, and the basis or number-field construction there also proves discreteness. Injectivity of conjugation gives (6.612). Apply it to the support of \(f\) times the inverse of any compact set of \(g\)'s. This proves uniform local finiteness of the sum and of its differentiated sums, hence smoothness.

Proof: nonvanishing. Start with a maximal-compact component at an extra finite place \(w\), outside the prescribed set. At \(g=1\), (6.612) leaves finitely many rational candidates. A noncentral rational matrix is noncentral at \(w\): its off-diagonal entries and differences of diagonal entries cannot become zero in a field completion unless they were already zero. In the Hausdorff local quotient \(H(k_w)/Z(k_w)\), shrink a principal subgroup \(J_w\) to exclude all these finitely many noncentral classes. Choose it inside the kernel of \(\eta_w\) on its central intersection. The central extension of \(1_{J_w}\) is well defined and has value one at the identity. Shrinking cannot introduce another rational candidate. Only the rational scalar class remains, so \[ P_f(1)=f(1)=\prod_v f_v(1)\ne0. \tag{6.613} \]

Proof: cuspidality and support. For a proper rational radical \(R\), integrate over its compact quotient. Uniform local finiteness justifies absolute unfolding. Right multiplication of \(R(k)\) on \(Z(k)\backslash H(k)\) is free, since a unipotent scalar is one. Thus \[ \int_{[R]}P_f(ug)\,du= \sum_{\gamma\in Z(k)\backslash H(k)/R(k)} \int_{R(\mathbb A)}f(\gamma u g)\,du=0. \tag{6.614} \] Each unfolded integral is absolute. Compact support modulo scalars, with the determinant fixed on \(\gamma Rg\), bounds the scalar absolute values and then all unipotent coordinates. This gives actual compact support for that integral; the same argument works uniformly on compact sets. Its local factor at \(v_*\) is zero by (6.610), proving the displayed zero. Compact representatives for \([R]\) also show directly that the absolute sum of these integrals is finite, before unfolding. Finally the support of \(P_f\) in the automorphic quotient is contained in the compact image of the support of \(f\) modulo the centre. A smooth function on this compact support is bounded, and quotient Haar measure is finite on compact sets. This proves square integrability. \(\square\)

Property (6.610) holds for a compact-mod-centre matrix coefficient of a smooth representation whose proper Jacquet modules vanish. To see the zero, choose a compact open subgroup of \(R\) fixing the coefficient vector. The radical is an increasing union of compact subgroups: in standard upper root coordinates use valuation lower bounds \(-M(j-i)\) on entry \((i,j)\). Multiplication and inversion preserve these bounds because root heights add. Zero coinvariants therefore say that a sufficiently large compact \(R\)-average of the vector is zero: write it as a finite sum of differences and enlarge the compact averaging group to contain their elements. Enlarge again to contain the compact support of its coefficient on \(R\). Its full coefficient integral is then zero. Left and right translations merely change the two vectors. This explains the stronger hypothesis in (6.610); unaveraged integrals on \(lR\) alone do not assert it for arbitrary \(aRb\).

Example 6.279 — a trace zero is not an operator zero. In the standard representation of \(S_3\) on the basis \(e_1-e_2,e_2-e_3\), the group-algebra element \(a=(12)-(23)\) acts as \[ \begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix} -\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}-2&1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}\ne0, \qquad\operatorname{Tr}(a)=0. \tag{6.615} \] Its traces on the trivial and sign representations are zero too. Thus vanishing traces on unwanted irreducibles do not make convolution by a test vanish on those representations. Theorem 6.278 constructs a nonzero smooth cuspidal function. Extracting an irreducible automorphic constituent with prescribed discrete-series components additionally requires a spectral-existence argument and a trace isolation or an actual local projection. Global genericity in Theorem 6.276 supplies one input to that problem; it does not by itself prove local generic pseudo-coefficient isolation or exact discrete-series globalization.

6.45 Regular mirabolic models and discrete-series genericity

In this subsection \(F\) is nonarchimedean, of either characteristic. Fix an additive character \(\psi\) trivial on \(\mathcal O\) and nontrivial on \(\varpi^{-1}\mathcal O\), with self-dual measure \(dx\), so \(\operatorname{vol}(\mathcal O)=1\). Write \(q=|\mathcal O/\varpi\mathcal O|\). Put \(P_1=1\), and for \(n=m+1\) put \[ P_n=\left\{(h,x)=\begin{pmatrix}h&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}: h\in H_m=\mathrm{GL}_m(F),\ x\in F^m\right\},\qquad (h,x)(h',x')=(hh',x+hx'). \tag{6.616} \] Thus \(P_n\) fixes the last standard row. For the coordinate calculations use \[ dh=|\det h|^{-m}\prod_{i,j}dh_{ij},\qquad dp_n=|\det h|^{-1}dh\,dx,\qquad \Delta_{P_n}(h,x)=|\det h|^{-1}. \tag{6.617} \] Our modular convention is \(\int f(pp_0)\,dp=\Delta(p_0)^{-1}\int f(p)\,dp\). Direct left and right changes of variables in (6.616) prove (6.617). These densities need not give a maximal compact subgroup volume one. Multiplying a Haar measure by \(c>0\) gives an isometric regular model by multiplication of functions by \(c^{1/2}\); thus the coefficient embeddings of Theorem 6.35 apply with the corresponding formal degree.

Lemma 6.280 — row coordinates and their Haar density. Let \(Y_m=F^m\setminus\{0\}\), with row coordinates, and \(e=e_m\). Choose the first coordinate \(j\) at which \(|\xi_j|=\|\xi\|_\infty\). Let \(t_\xi\) have first \(m-1\) rows the standard rows other than \(e_j\), in increasing order, and last row \(\xi\). Then \[ e t_\xi=\xi,\qquad |\det t_\xi|=\|\xi\|_\infty, \qquad t_e=I_m, \qquad d\nu_m(\xi)=\frac{d\xi}{\|\xi\|_\infty}. \tag{6.618} \] The section is continuous on a finite clopen partition of \(Y_m\). For fixed \(\xi\ne0\), every \(h\in H_m\) has unique coordinates \[ \eta=\xi h,\qquad s=t_\xi h t_\eta^{-1}\in P_m, \qquad h=t_\xi^{-1}s t_\eta, \qquad dh=dp_m(s)\,d\nu_m(\eta). \tag{6.619} \] For \(m=1\), interpret \(dp_1\) as unit mass on the trivial group.

Proof. The pivot inequalities define clopen sets away from zero, and the determinant is \((-1)^{m-j}\xi_j\). At \(e\) the pivot is \(m\). Multiplying the middle expression in (6.619) by \(e\) proves that it lies in \(P_m\), and proves uniqueness.

It remains to compute the measure. First take \(\xi=e\), so \(h=s t_\eta\). Write \(s=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Its top \(m-1\) rows are obtained by right multiplication of the rows of \((A,b)\) by \(t_\eta\); the last row is \(\eta\). The additive Jacobian is \(|\det t_\eta|^{m-1}\). This remains true as \(\eta\) varies on a pivot chart, since the last-row variables make the full Jacobian block triangular. Moreover \(|\det h|=|\det A|\,|\det t_\eta|\). Hence \[ |\det h|^{-m}\,d h_{\mathrm{entries}} =\frac{dA\,db}{|\det A|^m} \frac{d\eta}{|\det t_\eta|}. \tag{6.620} \] The first factor is exactly \(dp_m\). For general fixed \(\xi\), left translation by \(t_\xi\) preserves \(dh\). This proves (6.619), including its normalization. \(\square\)

For a strongly continuous unitary representation \(\tau\) of \(P_m\), define a representation on \(L^2(Y_m,d\xi;\mathscr K_\tau)\) by \[ \begin{split} b(\xi,h)&=t_\xi h t_{\xi h}^{-1}\in P_m,\\ \bigl(\Sigma_n(\tau)(h,x)\Phi\bigr)(\xi) &=|\det h|^{1/2}\psi(\xi x)\tau(b(\xi,h))\Phi(\xi h). \end{split} \tag{6.621} \] The cocycle identity \(b(\xi,hh')=b(\xi,h)b(\xi h,h')\) proves the group law. The change \(\xi\mapsto\xi h\) has Jacobian \(|\det h|\), proving unitarity. Compact-open averages converge strongly to the identity in a strongly continuous unitary representation, so smooth fibre values are dense. Strong continuity follows first for compactly supported locally constant sections with such values. On their compact support the section and cocycle are continuous, and sufficiently small group elements fix the finitely many values and their partition. These sections are dense; unitary boundedness passes continuity to the completion.

Theorem 6.281 — the regular mirabolic decomposition. Let \(\lambda_{P_n}\) be left translation on \(L^2(P_n,dp_n)\). Then \[ \lambda_{P_n}\simeq 1_{L^2(Y_m,d\nu_m)}\otimes\Sigma_n(\lambda_{P_m}). \tag{6.622} \] Define \(\sigma_1=1\), \(\mathscr K_1=\mathbb C\), and recursively \[ \sigma_n=\Sigma_n(\sigma_{n-1}),\qquad \mathscr K_n=L^2(Y_{n-1},d\xi;\mathscr K_{n-1}). \tag{6.623} \] There is a separable Hilbert space \(\mathscr M_n\) such that \(\lambda_{P_n}\simeq1_{\mathscr M_n}\otimes\sigma_n\). No irreducibility assertion is needed for this decomposition.

Proof. Fourier transform the column variable using the positive kernel, and compensate for the density in (6.617): \[ \widehat f(h,\xi)=|\det h|^{-1/2} \int_{F^m}f(h,x)\psi(\xi x)\,dx. \tag{6.624} \] Additive Plancherel makes this a unitary map to \(L^2(H_m\times F^m,dh\,d\xi)\). That Plancherel identity follows by Fourier inversion on the compact additive quotients supporting locally constant tests, then density in \(L^2\). Left translation becomes \[ \widehat{\lambda(h_0,x_0)f}(h,\xi) =|\det h_0|^{1/2}\psi(\xi x_0) \widehat f(h_0^{-1}h,\xi h_0). \tag{6.625} \] The fibre \(\xi=0\) has additive measure zero: arbitrarily many distinct translates of a singleton lie in the compact group \(\mathcal O^m\), so a singleton cannot have positive measure. On its complement use (6.619), so the variables are \((\eta,\xi,s)\), with measure \(d\nu_m(\eta)d\xi\,dp_m(s)\). Formula (6.625) leaves \(\eta\) fixed and replaces \[ (\xi,s)\longmapsto (\xi h_0,b(\xi,h_0)^{-1}s). \tag{6.626} \] This is precisely (6.621) with the left regular fibre action. The change of variables is a measurable bijection on the displayed charts and preserves the computed measure. First applying it to compactly supported tests and then completing proves the unitary identity (6.622).

If the fibre representation is \(1_{\mathscr M}\otimes\tau\), (6.621) leaves the \(\mathscr M\)-coordinate fixed. Starting from \(P_1=1\), induction in (6.622) therefore gives (6.623), with \(\mathscr M_n=L^2(Y_{n-1},d\nu_{n-1})\otimes\mathscr M_{n-1}\). All the spaces are separable, since their local coordinate spaces are second countable. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.282 — smooth evaluation and a separating Whittaker functional. Write \(\psi_{U_n}(u)=\psi(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}u_{i,i+1})\). There is a linear functional \(\ell_n\) on the smooth vectors of \(\sigma_n\) satisfying \[ \ell_n(\sigma_n(u)v)=\psi_{U_n}(u)\ell_n(v). \tag{6.627} \] Its \(P_n\)-translates separate those smooth vectors. For \(J_n(a)=P_n\cap(1+\varpi^a M_n(\mathcal O))\), \(a\ge1\), it obeys \[ |\ell_n(v)|\le q^{a n(n-1)/4}\|v\| \qquad(v\in\mathscr K_n^{J_n(a)}). \tag{6.628} \]

Proof: evaluation is defined. In (6.623), first let \(\Phi\) be fixed by the embedded compact group \(L=1+\varpi^a M_m(\mathcal O)\subset H_m\). Its row orbit at \(e\) is \[ B=e+\varpi^a\mathcal O^m, \qquad\operatorname{vol}(B)=q^{-am},\qquad J=L\cap P_m=J_m(a). \tag{6.629} \] On \(B\) the pivot is \(m\) and \(t_\xi\in L\). Pull the section back to \(L\) by \(A(h)=\sigma_m(b(e,h))\Phi(eh)\). Probability Haar measure on \(L\) pushes forward to the normalized additive measure on \(B\): both are invariant under the transitive \(L\)-action, which has determinant of absolute value one. The pullback is therefore a well-defined \(L^2\) function. It has left \(J\)-covariance, and \(L\)-invariance of \(\Phi\) makes it right invariant on \(L\). Averaging right translations on this compact group makes \(A\) equal almost everywhere to one vector \(v\), with \(v\in\mathscr K_m^J\). The constant section \(v\) has precisely this pullback, because \(b(e,h)\in J\) for \(h\in L\). The pullback is an isometry after normalizing the measure of \(B\), hence injective. Consequently \(\Phi(\xi)=v\) almost everywhere on \(B\). Define \[ \operatorname{ev}_e\Phi=v\in\mathscr K_m^{J_m(a)},\qquad \|\operatorname{ev}_e\Phi\|\le q^{am/2}\|\Phi\|. \tag{6.630} \] Shrinking \(L\) leaves the same vector on an open intersection of positive measure, so the definition is independent of the chosen level. Every smooth vector is fixed by a sufficiently small such embedded \(L\). Translating this construction gives preferred point values at every nonzero row. They are locally constant sections and agree on overlaps, since almost-everywhere equality of locally constant sections implies equality everywhere. Thus (6.621) holds at these point values, rather than only on unspecified \(L^2\) representatives.

Proof: character, separation and bound. Set \(\ell_1=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C}\) and recursively \(\ell_n=\ell_m\operatorname{ev}_e\). For \(u=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}u_m&x\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in U_n\), one has \(e u_m=e\), \(b(e,u_m)=u_m\), and \(|\det u_m|=1\). Hence \[ \operatorname{ev}_e(\sigma_n(u)\Phi) =\psi(x_m)\sigma_m(u_m)\operatorname{ev}_e\Phi. \tag{6.631} \] Induction gives (6.627). If \(\Phi\ne0\), a preferred value \(\Phi(\xi)\) is nonzero somewhere. Applying \(\sigma_n(t_\xi,0)\) brings this to a nonzero smooth value at \(e\), multiplied by \(|\det t_\xi|^{1/2}\). By induction, a \(P_m\)-translate of that value has nonzero \(\ell_m\). The same \(P_m\) embedded in \(H_m\) fixes \(e\); its action on the value has only the additional nonzero factor \(|\det p|^{1/2}\). This proves separation by translates.

For a \(J_n(a)\)-fixed vector the evaluation in (6.630) is \(J_m(a)\)-fixed. Multiply its bound by the inductive bound. Since \(am/2+a m(m-1)/4=a n(n-1)/4\), this proves (6.628). In particular the functional is continuous on each fixed-level Hilbert subspace. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.283 — restriction of the central regular representation. Let \(G_n=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\), \(Z_n=F^\times I_n\), and let \(\omega\) be unitary. The restriction to \(P_n\) of left translation on \(L^2(Z_n\backslash G_n,\omega^{-1})\) is a Hilbert multiplicity of \(\lambda_{P_n}\), hence of \(\sigma_n\).

Proof. Use the first maximal pivot of a projective row, normalize that coordinate to one, and call the resulting representative \(y\). Before the pivot its coordinates are in \(\varpi\mathcal O\); after it they are in \(\mathcal O\). These finite clopen projective charts have additive coordinate measures \(dy\), and their total measure is \[ \nu(\mathbb P^{n-1}(F))= 1+q^{-1}+\cdots+q^{-(n-1)}. \tag{6.632} \] Use the same row section \(t_y\), now with \(|\det t_y|=1\). Every \(g\) has a unique decomposition on these charts \[ g=z p t_y,\qquad z\in F^\times,\ p\in P_n. \tag{6.633} \] The last row of \(g\) determines \(z\) and \(y\), and then determines \(p\). Write \(p=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). The last row \(zy\) has additive Jacobian \(|z|^{n-1}\); the top \(n-1\) rows have Jacobian \(|z|^{n(n-1)}\). Since \(|\det g|=|z|^n|\det A|\), the matrix Haar density is exactly \[ dg=\frac{dz}{|z|}\, \frac{dA\,db}{|\det A|^n}\,dy =d^\times z\,dp_n\,dy. \tag{6.634} \] Here \(d^\times z=dz/|z|\). Thus the quotient norm is \[ \|f\|^2=\int_{\mathbb P^{n-1}(F)}\int_{P_n} |f(p t_y)|^2\,dp_n\,dy. \tag{6.635} \] Central covariance has absolute value one. For \(p_0\in P_n\), left translation replaces \(p\) by \(p_0^{-1}p\) and leaves \(z,y\) unchanged. This proves the multiplicity assertion by an explicit isometry. No invariant measure on the projective space under all of \(G_n\) is asserted; only the displayed coordinate measure is used. Theorem 6.281 proves the last assertion. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.284 — discrete-series genericity in every split degree. Every unitary discrete series \(\pi\) of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\) has a nonzero \(\psi_{U_n}\)-Whittaker functional on its smooth vectors. This holds in both field characteristics.

Proof. Fix a unit Hilbert vector \(v_0\). Schur orthogonality in Theorem 6.35 gives the closed isometric coefficient embedding \[ u\longmapsto d_\pi^{1/2}\langle u,\pi(g)v_0\rangle \quad\text{into }L^2(Z_n\backslash G_n,\omega^{-1}), \tag{6.636} \] intertwining \(\pi\) with left translation. Use the formal degree for the measures in (6.634), as permitted by (6.617). By Theorems 6.281 and 6.283 its restriction embeds into \(\mathscr M\otimes\mathscr K_n\), with \(P_n\) acting trivially on the multiplicity space \(\mathscr M\). Partial inner product against some vector of \(\mathscr M\) gives a nonzero bounded \(P_n\)-intertwiner \(T:\mathscr H_\pi\to\mathscr K_n\): otherwise all its coefficients on the dense elementary tensors would be zero.

Smooth \(G_n\)-vectors are dense. Boundedness and equivariance make \(T\) carry them to smooth \(P_n\)-vectors, and some such image is nonzero. The separating assertion of Theorem 6.282 then shows that \(\ell_nT\) is nonzero after translating that vector by an element of \(P_n\). Its \(U_n\)-equivariance is (6.627). The fixed-level bound there makes this a well-defined continuous functional on every fixed compact-open \(G_n\)-level. This is the required Whittaker functional.

If \(\psi_c(x)=\psi(cx)\), conjugation by \(\operatorname{diag}(c^{n-1},c^{n-2},\ldots,1)\) replaces \(\psi_{U_n}\) by \((\psi_c)_{U_n}\). Precomposing the functional with that diagonal action gives the assertion for every nontrivial additive character. For \(n=1\), \(U_1=1\) and the assertion is immediate. \(\square\)

Example 6.285 — sharp smooth evaluation and projective masses. For \(a\ge1\), set \(v_1=1\) and recursively \[ v_n(\xi)=1_{e+\varpi^a\mathcal O^{n-1}}(\xi)v_{n-1}. \quad \ell_n(v_n)=1,\qquad \|v_n\|^2=q^{-a n(n-1)/2}. \tag{6.637} \] These vectors are \(J_n(a)\)-fixed. Indeed the principal linear subgroup preserves the indicated row ball and its cocycle lies in \(J_{n-1}(a)\); its determinant has absolute value one. The column subgroup contributes \(\psi(\xi x)=1\), since \(\xi\) is integral and \(x\in\varpi^a\mathcal O^{n-1}\). The norm is the product of the row-ball volumes. Thus (6.628) is sharp. Evaluation is unbounded on the full Hilbert norm as \(a\to\infty\), although it is bounded at every fixed smooth level.

With the matrix Haar density, the compact part of \(P_n\) has volume \(\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-q^{-j})\). Formula (6.634) gives \[ (1-q^{-1})\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(1-q^{-j}) (1+q^{-1}+\cdots+q^{-(n-1)}) =\prod_{j=1}^{n}(1-q^{-j}), \tag{6.638} \] the matrix Haar volume of \(\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal O)\). The centre contributes the first factor. This checks both the projective density and the central normalization.

The conclusion of Theorem 6.284 is existence of a Whittaker functional. Its proof supplies neither its dimension nor uniqueness of a generic irreducible at a given cuspidal support. The generic pseudo-coefficient identity is Theorem 6.374. Integral representation transfer and exact global spectral extraction require further arguments.

6.46 Transpose symmetry and Whittaker uniqueness

Keep \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\), with \(F\) nonarchimedean of either characteristic, and write \(U\) for its upper unitriangular subgroup. Fix a nontrivial additive character and put \(\theta(u)=\psi(\sum_i u_{i,i+1})\). All representation spaces and test functions have complex scalars. Let \(w_0\) reverse the standard basis, and set \[ \tau(g)=w_0g^{\mathsf t}w_0,\qquad \sigma(g)=\tau(g^{-1}),\qquad f^\tau=f\circ\tau. \tag{6.639} \] The map \(\tau\) is an anti-involution, \(\sigma\) is an involutive automorphism, and \(\theta(\tau u)=\theta(u)\), \(\theta(\sigma u)=\theta(u)^{-1}\). Both maps preserve Haar measure: they take Haar measure to Haar measure since \(G\) is unimodular, and their square is the identity, so the positive proportionality factor is one.

Lemma 6.286 — transpose in the algebraic cocenter. Every \(g\in G\) is conjugate to \(g^{\mathsf t}\), including matrices with inseparable primary factors. For \(f\in C_c^\infty(G)\), \[ O_g(f\circ{\mathsf t})=O_g(f),\qquad f^\tau-f\in[\mathcal H(G),\mathcal H(G)], \qquad\operatorname{Tr}\pi(f^\tau)=\operatorname{Tr}\pi(f) \tag{6.640} \] for every admissible \(\pi\). The commutator span is algebraic.

Proof. On a cyclic summand \(A=F[T]/(p)\), of dimension \(a\), let \(L\) take the coefficient of \(T^{a-1}\) in the remainder, and use \(B(x,y)=L(xy)\). This symmetric form is nondegenerate: if \(x\) has degree \(j\) and nonzero leading coefficient \(c\), then \(B(x,T^{a-1-j})=c\). Multiplication by \(T\) is self-adjoint. The cyclic decomposition of the \(F[T]\)-module, as in Lemma 6.137, gives a nonsingular Gram matrix \(S\) with \(g^{\mathsf t}S=Sg\). No separability or division by two is used.

Transposition therefore acts on each individual conjugacy orbit. Its pushforward takes an invariant positive orbital measure to an invariant positive orbital measure: it intertwines conjugation by \(h\) with conjugation by \(h^{-\mathsf t}\). Such a measure is unique up to a positive constant by the orbit integration in Theorem 6.141. The square of the map is the identity, so that constant is one. This proves the first equality. All compact ordinary orbitals converge by Theorem 6.139. The compact case of Lemma 6.239 turns the difference into a finite commutator sum. Inner conjugation by \(w_0\) gives the assertion for \(\tau\). Actual finite-rank admissible traces kill these commutators. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.287 — trace separation and the contragredient. Distinct irreducible admissible smooth representations have distinct traces on \(\mathcal H(G)\). For every such representation, \[ \pi^\vee\simeq\pi\circ\sigma. \tag{6.641} \]

Proof: the finite corner. Choose a compact open \(J\) fixing nonzero vectors in the two representations, and put \(A=e_J\mathcal H(G)e_J\). Each fixed space is a nonzero finite-dimensional simple \(A\)-module: applying \(e_J\) to the cyclic span of any nonzero fixed vector gives the entire fixed space.

For clarity, these fixed modules determine the representations. Given a simple \(A\)-module \(M\), the module \(\mathcal H(G)e_J\otimes_A M\) is generated by its \(e_J\)-part \(M\). Divide by the sum of all its submodules annihilated by \(e_J\). The quotient is simple: a submodule with zero \(e_J\)-part is zero, while one with nonzero \(e_J\)-part contains \(M\) and generates the quotient. This is the unique simple quotient with fixed space \(M\).

The image of a unital algebra on a finite-dimensional simple complex module \(M\) is \(\operatorname{End}(M)\). Here is a useful proof. Its commuting endomorphisms are scalar, by the eigenspace argument. For independent \(v_1,\ldots,v_r\), induct on \(r\) to prescribe their images simultaneously. The image in \(M^r\) projects onto \(M^{r-1}\). Its kernel in the last factor is either zero or all of \(M\). In the zero case the image is the graph of a module map \(M^{r-1}\to M\), whose components are scalars. Applying the identity operator contradicts independence of the \(v_i\). Thus the kernel is all of \(M\), completing the induction and the claim.

A full matrix algebra has only one simple module up to isomorphism: for a nonzero vector in the image of a diagonal matrix unit, the other matrix units produce the standard coordinate basis, whose span is an invariant simple submodule and hence the whole module. Thus the annihilators of two inequivalent fixed modules are distinct maximal two-sided ideals \(I,J\). Their sum is the whole algebra. Write \(i+j=1\), with \(i\in I\), \(j\in J\). Then \(j\) acts by identity on the first module and by zero on the second. Its traces differ, proving separation.

Proof: duals and symmetry. The smooth dual is irreducible and admissible. Indeed its fixed spaces are the duals of the finite fixed spaces. A nonzero invariant subspace of the smooth dual has zero annihilator in the original irreducible module; its restrictions onto each finite fixed-space dual are consequently surjective. Compact averaging puts those entire dual fixed spaces in the subspace, proving irreducibility. The same fixed-space calculation gives the smooth bidual identification.

Let \(f^\iota(g)=f(g^{-1})\). Transposing the finite operator on a common fixed space gives \(\operatorname{Tr}\pi^\vee(f)=\operatorname{Tr}\pi(f^\iota)\). Also \(f\circ\sigma=(f^\iota)^\tau\). Lemma 6.286 and Haar invariance give the same trace for \(\pi\circ\sigma\). The separation just proved establishes (6.641). \(\square\)

We next prove the symmetry needed for Whittaker functionals directly on tests. Let \(H=U\times U\) act by \((u,v)g=ugv^{-1}\), and let its action on functions be \(T_{u,v}f(g)=f(u^{-1}gv)\). Put \[ \chi(u,v)=\theta(u)\theta(v)^{-1},\qquad Q(X)=C_c^\infty(X)\big/ \langle T_hf-\chi(h)f:h\in H\rangle \tag{6.642} \] for an invariant locally closed subset \(X\subset G\).

Lemma 6.288 — exact twisted coinvariants and localization. The functor of \((H,\chi)\)-coinvariants is exact. Suppose an invariant continuous map \(p:X\to B\) has locally compact Hausdorff totally disconnected domain and base. If a compactly supported test is zero in the twisted coinvariants of every fibre, it is zero in \(Q(X)\).

Proof. The group \(H\) is an increasing union of compact open subgroups, using the root-height valuation bounds in Section 6.44. On a compact subgroup \(K\), averaging \[ E_{K,\chi}=\frac1{\operatorname{vol}K} \int_K\chi(h)^{-1}T_h\,dh \tag{6.643} \] is a finite smooth projection and annihilates the twisted differences from \(K\). If a vector of a submodule becomes zero in the larger module's coinvariants, one sufficiently large \(K\) annihilates it. Subtracting its average expresses it as twisted differences within that submodule. This proves injectivity; surjectivity and right exactness follow from the quotient definition.

For localization, express the restriction to a fixed fibre as finitely many twisted differences and lift their test functions to \(X\). Compact locally constant functions on a closed subset extend to compact locally constant functions: cover their compact support by finitely many compact open neighborhoods and refine to a disjoint partition. The remaining test is zero on the fibre. Its support is compact and disjoint from that fibre, so its image under \(p\) is a compact closed set omitting the base point. On a neighborhood of that point the lifted identity is therefore exact. A finite such cover of \(p(\operatorname{supp}f)\), refined to a disjoint compact open partition, gives a global finite sum of twisted differences. Multiplication by these invariant base cutoffs commutes with the differences. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.289 — the relevant Bruhat profiles. Let \(T\) be the diagonal torus and \(w\in S_n\), represented by its permutation matrix. Set \(U_w=U\cap wU^-w^{-1}\). The Bruhat cell has unique coordinates \[ C_w=U_w w T U,\qquad g=a w t b. \tag{6.644} \] Its twisted quotient is zero unless \(w=w_0w_M\), where \(M\) is a standard block Levi and \(w_M\) reverses each of its blocks. In that case \[ Q(C_w)\simeq C_c^\infty(Z_M),\qquad J_w f(t)=\int_{U_w}\int_U f(a w t b)\theta(a)\theta(b)\,db\,da \quad(t\in Z_M), \tag{6.645} \] where \(Z_M\) consists of the invertible block-scalar diagonal matrices.

Proof: coordinates and stabilizers. Gaussian elimination, using upper row and column operations, chooses the pivot permutation and gives (6.644). Within a cell the coordinates and their inverses are continuous. The factorization of \(U\) used here can also be checked by increasing root height: each entry in a product is the sum of the entries at that height and a polynomial in entries of smaller height. Assigning roots to \(U_w\) or \(U\cap wUw^{-1}\) gives a unique factorization, with triangular additive Jacobian one. This proves the asserted coordinate uniqueness and fixes the product Haar measures.

At \(wt\), its stabilizer in \(H\) is parametrized by \(v\in U\cap w^{-1}Uw\), with \(u=wtv t^{-1}w^{-1}\). It has trivial \(\chi\)-character precisely when \[ \theta(wtv t^{-1}w^{-1})=\theta(v) \qquad(v\in U\cap w^{-1}Uw). \tag{6.646} \] If \(w(i)<w(i+1)\), insert \(v=1+xE_{i,i+1}\). Its right side is \(\psi(x)\). Its left side can equal it for all \(x\) only if \[ w(i+1)=w(i)+1,\qquad t_i=t_{i+1}. \tag{6.647} \] Decompose the permutation into its maximal increasing runs. The first condition makes each run a consecutive interval of values. The intervals are disjoint; at every boundary there is a descent. Thus those intervals occur in strictly decreasing order. These are exactly the permutations \(w_0w_M\).

For such a permutation, a positive root remains positive under \(w\) exactly when its two indices lie in the same block. Within that block its height is unchanged. Hence the stabilizer in (6.646) is \(U_M\), and (6.646) holds exactly when all adjacent \(t_i\)'s in each block are equal. Higher root groups contribute no further character condition. This proves that the compatible parameter set is exactly \(Z_M\); it is empty for every other permutation. Nontriviality of \(\psi\) suffices here, since multiplication by any nonzero field scalar is surjective on \(F\).

Proof: the quotient. On a fixed fibre, the product measure \(da\,db\) is invariant under \(H\): the left \(U\)-action is the quotient action in the root factorization just described, and the remaining action on \(b\) is a unipotent translation. The stabilizer is unipotent, so its modular character is one. If (6.646) holds, the function \(\kappa(a w t b)=\theta(a)\theta(b)\) is well defined and satisfies \(\kappa(hx)=\chi(h)\kappa(x)\).

Here is an elementary coinvariant calculation on this fibre. The compact support of any test lifts to a compact subset of \(H\) by (6.644), hence lies in \(K\cdot wt\) for some compact subgroup \(K\subset H\). If the stabilizer character is nontrivial, enlarge \(K\) to contain an element of that stabilizer with nontrivial character. The average (6.643) is then zero on \(K\cdot wt\), hence zero everywhere. If the character is trivial, multiplying by \(\kappa\) converts the twisted average to ordinary compact averaging. Its image is one-dimensional on the transitive compact orbit, and its scalar is the weighted orbital integral. Thus the fibre quotient is one-dimensional with quotient map \(J_w\) in the compatible case, and zero otherwise.

Lemma 6.288 proves that the kernel of (6.645) is exactly the finite twisted-difference span. The map takes values in compact locally constant profiles: the preimage of a compact subset of the cell in its coordinates is compact, and integration of the locally constant test has a common compact root support. It is onto. Extend any compact locally constant function on the closed subset \(Z_M\subset T\) to \(T\), and multiply it in (6.644) by compact root functions whose \(\theta\)-weighted integrals are one. This constructs its preimage and completes the proof. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.290 — transpose symmetry of the twisted quotient. Transposition acts as the identity on \(Q(G)\), with \(\tau\) as in (6.639). Equivalently, every linear functional \(D\) satisfying \[ D(L_uR_v f)=\theta(u)\theta(v)^{-1}D(f) \quad(u,v\in U) \quad\text{satisfies}\quad D(f^\tau)=D(f). \tag{6.648} \] Here \(L_u f(g)=f(u^{-1}g)\) and \(R_vf(g)=f(gv)\).

Proof: the finite filtration. The southwest rectangle ranks \(r_{ij}(g)=\operatorname{rank}(g_{n-i+1,\ldots,n;1,\ldots,j})\) characterize the Gaussian pivot cell. They have finitely many possible tuples, and every condition \(r_{ij}\ge a\) is open, by a nonzero minor. Among the tuples still present, the maximal tuples in the coordinatewise order therefore give open cells. Remove them and repeat. This constructs a finite filtration by closed invariant subsets with Bruhat cells as the successive disjoint open pieces. Since \(r_{ij}(\tau g)=r_{ji}(g)\), it can be chosen \(\tau\)-stable by removing all maximal tuples at each step.

The exact sequence of tests for an open subset and its closed complement follows from compact locally constant extension. Lemma 6.288 makes its twisted coinvariants exact. Also \(\tau\) preserves these coinvariants: it sends \((u,v)\) to \((\tau(v)^{-1},\tau(u)^{-1})\), which preserves \(\chi\).

Proof: the action on a cell quotient. The incompatible cells have zero quotient. On a compatible cell \(w=w_0w_M\), every \(t\in Z_M\) commutes with \(w_M\), so \[ \tau(wt)=w_0t w_M=w_0w_Mt=wt. \tag{6.649} \] Thus \(\tau\) preserves every compatible fibre and its character function \(\kappa\). Its pushforward orbital measure is another positive invariant measure on that same transitive fibre. Uniqueness makes it a positive multiple; applying \(\tau\) twice makes the multiple one. Consequently \(J_w(f^\tau)=J_w(f)\). The action on every successive quotient is the identity.

This does imply the identity on the whole quotient, using the involution. The operator \(N=\tau-1\) lowers the finite filtration, hence is nilpotent. The operator \(\tau+1=2+N\) is invertible by a finite geometric sum. Since \((\tau-1)(\tau+1)=0\), one has \(N=0\). The scalar two here is in \(\mathbb C\), even when \(F\) has characteristic two. This proves (6.648). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.291 — Whittaker multiplicity one. For every irreducible admissible smooth representation \(V\) of \(G\), \[ \dim\operatorname{Hom}_U(V,\theta)\le1. \tag{6.650} \] Thus this dimension is one when \(V\) is generic; in particular it is one for every discrete series in Theorem 6.284.

Proof: smoothing distribution vectors. Suppose \(\ell\ne0\) lies in this Hom space. Lemma 6.287 identifies \(V^\vee\) with \(V\circ\sigma\), so it supplies a nonzero \(\ell'\in\operatorname{Hom}_U(V^\vee,\theta^{-1})\). Regard \(\ell'\) as a vector in the algebraic dual of \(V^\vee\). For \(f\in\mathcal H(G)\), define \[ \langle\pi(f)\ell',v^\vee\rangle =\ell'\bigl(\pi^\vee(f^\iota)v^\vee\bigr), \qquad D_{\ell,\ell'}(f)=\ell\bigl(\pi(f)\ell'\bigr). \tag{6.651} \] This is an actual smooth vector. If \(f\) is left \(J\)-invariant, the pairing depends only on \(e_Jv^\vee\); the finite-dimensional fixed-space bidual places it in \(V^J\). Similarly \(\ell\pi(f)\) belongs to the smooth dual, since \(f\) is right invariant by some compact open subgroup.

On distribution vectors \(\pi(v)\ell'=\theta(v)\ell'\) for \(v\in U\). Thus \[ D_{\ell,\ell'}(L_uR_vf) =\theta(u)\theta(v)^{-1}D_{\ell,\ell'}(f). \tag{6.652} \] Theorem 6.290 makes this functional \(\tau\)-invariant. As \(\tau\) preserves Haar measure and reverses multiplication, \[ D_{\ell,\ell'}(f_1*f_2) =D_{\ell,\ell'}(f_2^\tau*f_1^\tau). \tag{6.653} \]

Proof: kernels and Schur's lemma. The maps \(f\mapsto\pi(f)\ell'\) and \(f\mapsto\ell\pi(f)\) are nonzero and onto \(V\) and \(V^\vee\), respectively. Their images are invariant under left and right translations, respectively, so irreducibility proves surjectivity. Nonzero follows by applying a small-subgroup identity to a vector on which the corresponding functional is nonzero. Write \[ R_{\ell'}=\{f:\pi(f)\ell'=0\},\qquad L_\ell=\{f:\ell\pi(f)=0\}. \tag{6.654} \] These are the right and left kernels of the bilinear form \((f_1,f_2)\mapsto D_{\ell,\ell'}(f_1*f_2)\), because the two maps are onto and the smooth dual separates vectors. Equation (6.653) gives \[ L_\ell=(R_{\ell'})^\tau. \tag{6.655} \] Fix \(\ell'\). All nonzero \(\ell\)'s therefore give the same kernel for the surjective map \(\mathcal H(G)\to V^\vee\), \(f\mapsto\ell\pi(f)\). It intertwines right translation \(R_h\) with \(\pi^\vee(h)\). Two such quotient identifications differ by a \(G\)-endomorphism of the irreducible admissible \(V^\vee\), hence by a scalar. To verify this form of Schur's lemma, restrict an endomorphism to a nonzero finite-dimensional fixed space, choose a complex eigenvector, and use irreducibility on its eigenspace kernel. Consequently \[ \ell_1\pi(f)=c\,\ell_2\pi(f)\quad\text{for all }f \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\ell_1=c\ell_2. \tag{6.656} \] The implication follows by choosing \(f=e_J\) for any vector fixed by \(J\). This proves (6.650). Diagonal conjugation identifies all nondegenerate simple-root characters, so the same statement holds for each of them. \(\square\)

Whittaker uniqueness and the genericity theorem do not alone classify generic irreducibles or isolate a discrete series among them by a compact trace test. The generic factorization and trace identity are Theorems 6.373–6.374. Individual transfer-coefficient integrality and the full local and global representation correspondences require additional arguments.

6.47 Whittaker coinvariants of induction and actual induced traces

Let \(G_n=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\), with \(F\) nonarchimedean of either characteristic. Retain the upper unitriangular group \(U_n\) and the character \(\theta_n(u)=\psi(\sum_i u_{i,i+1})\). For a smooth module \(V\), write \[ V_{H,\eta}=V/\langle\rho(h)v-\eta(h)v\rangle, \qquad i_P^G(W)=\{F:G\to W:F(pg)=\delta_P(p)^{1/2}\rho(p)F(g)\}. \tag{6.657} \] The induced sections are smooth, the action is right translation, and \(\rho\) is inflated from the Levi quotient of \(P\). The flag space \(P\backslash G\) is compact. No support condition beyond smooth induction is therefore needed. The algebraic dual of \(V_{U_n,\theta_n}\) is exactly \(\operatorname{Hom}_{U_n}(V,\theta_n)\), directly from the quotient definition.

Lemma 6.292 — twisted coinvariants of compactly induced unipotent sections. Let \(U=U_n\), let \(H\subset U\) be closed, and let \(W\) be a smooth \(H\)-module. Give \(U\) and \(H\) Haar measures and \(H\backslash U\) the corresponding invariant quotient measure. For \(\eta=\theta_n\), the map \[ \Phi(F)=\int_{H\backslash U}\eta(u)^{-1}[F(u)]\,d\bar u :\bigl(\operatorname{c-Ind}_H^U W\bigr)_{U,\eta} \ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } W_{H,\eta|_H} \tag{6.658} \] is an isomorphism. The sections in this compact induction satisfy \(F(hu)=\rho(h)F(u)\). All relations and quotients here are algebraic.

Proof: compact averaging and the integral. Choose an increasing exhaustion of \(U\) by compact open subgroups, using the root-height bounds of Section 6.44. Their intersections with \(H\) give such an exhaustion of \(H\). Both groups are unimodular: the modular character of any element is one on a compact subgroup containing that element.

The quotient measure can be constructed directly. On the compact open image of \(K\), assign to a scalar test \(\varphi\) the integral \(\operatorname{vol}(H\cap K)^{-1}\int_K\varphi(Hk)\,dk\). For \(K\subset L\), the inverse image of that set in \(L\) is the union of \([H\cap L:H\cap K]\) left translates of \(K\); the two formulas agree. Each is a scaled compact Haar pushforward, so they define a Radon measure on the exhaustion. Right invariance is checked inside a larger \(L\) containing the translating element. This also proves the asserted quotient normalization.

The images of the exhausting compact open subgroups cover \(H\backslash U\). Hence the support of any compactly induced section is contained in \(H K\) for one such \(K\). Twisted compact averaging is exact, by the proof of Lemma 6.288, which applies to any such increasing compact exhaustion. Put \(F_K=E_{K,\eta}F\) and \(v=F_K(1)\). Then \[ F_K(hk)=\rho(h)\eta(k)v, \qquad \rho(h)v=\eta(h)v\ (h\in H\cap K), \qquad \Phi(F)=\frac{\operatorname{vol}K}{\operatorname{vol}(H\cap K)}[v]. \tag{6.659} \] Indeed \(F_K\) has support in \(HK\), and \(R_kF_K=\eta(k)F_K\). The integrand in (6.658) is well defined on left cosets, since \([\rho(h)w]=\eta(h)[w]\). Its compact support and local constancy make the integral a finite vector-space sum. Right translation by \(a\) multiplies the integral by \(\eta(a)\), after substituting \(u'=ua\). Averaging therefore preserves it, and quotient integration on \((H\cap K)\backslash K\) gives (6.659).

Proof: kernel and surjectivity. If \(\Phi(F)=0\), then \(v=0\) in \(W_{H,\eta}\). One sufficiently large compact subgroup of \(H\) annihilates \(v\) by twisted averaging. Choose a compact open \(L\subset U\) containing it and \(K\). Since \(HK\cap L=(H\cap L)K\), direct quotient integration gives \[ (E_{L,\eta}F_K)(1)= \frac{\operatorname{vol}K\operatorname{vol}(H\cap L)} {\operatorname{vol}L\operatorname{vol}(H\cap K)} E^{\rho}_{H\cap L,\eta}v=0. \tag{6.660} \] The averaged section has support in \(HL\) and is determined there by its value at one, so it is zero. Each averaging difference is a finite sum of twisted translation differences. This proves the asserted kernel, without a closure.

Conversely, for any \(w\in W\), choose \(K\) small enough that \(H\cap K\) fixes \(w\) and \(\eta\) is trivial there. Define \(F(hk)=\rho(h)\eta(k)w\) on \(HK\) and zero elsewhere. This is well defined. Its support in \(H\backslash U\) is compact open, and it is smooth because it is right invariant under \(K\cap\ker\eta\). Formula (6.659) gives a nonzero positive scalar times \([w]\); rescaling proves surjectivity. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.293 — parabolic orbit sections and their stabilizers. Let \(P=MN\) be the standard parabolic with block sizes \(n_1,\ldots,n_s\). Write \(I_j\) for its consecutive index blocks and \(b(a)=j\) when \(a\in I_j\). The \(U_n\)-orbits in \(P\backslash G_n\) have representatives \(Pw\), where \(w^{-1}\) preserves the order within each \(I_j\). Their section modules are \[ \operatorname{c-Ind}_{H_w}^{U_n} W_w, \qquad H_w=U_n\cap w^{-1}Pw, \qquad \rho_w(h)=\rho(whw^{-1}). \tag{6.661} \] For every orbit except the open one, its \((U_n,\theta_n)\)-coinvariants vanish, for every smooth \(M\)-module \(W\).

Proof: flags and sections. Gaussian elimination on a flag chooses exactly one shuffle of the blocks: within each block its values appear in increasing order. These are the specified left \(W_M\)-coset representatives. The stabilizer of \(Pw\) is visibly \(H_w\). In root coordinates, it consists of the entries \(E_{ij}\), \(i<j\), for which \(b(w(i))\le b(w(j))\). The complementary roots have strictly decreasing block labels. Each set of roots is closed under addition when that addition is a root. Multiplication in increasing root height gives a unique factorization with one coordinate for every root: an entry at a given height is its assigned variable plus a polynomial in smaller-height variables. Thus it has triangular Jacobian one. In particular these coordinates give continuous polynomial sections of \(H_w\backslash U_n\).

At \(Pw\), the action on the fibre is \(\rho_w\); the parabolic modulus is one on these unipotent elements. A section on this orbit is consequently exactly the compactly induced section in (6.661). For the finite filtration assertion, use the southwest ranks of the bottom rows at the block-tail dimensions and of the first \(j\) columns. These are invariant under left \(P\) and right \(U_n\), and Gaussian elimination shows that they characterize the shuffle. Nonvanishing minors make every lower rank bound open. Removing all coordinatewise maximal rank tuples successively therefore gives a finite closed filtration with these orbits as its open layers.

Restriction to a closed layer and extension by zero from an open layer give an exact sequence of compactly supported sections. Here are the required extension details. The transverse Gaussian charts trivialize the associated section space with fibre \(W\). A smooth section is locally a fixed vector in such a chart; changes of chart apply a continuous \(P\)-valued function to finitely many fixed vectors, which is locally constant by smoothness of \(W\). On a closed subset, cover the compact support by finitely many compact open chart neighborhoods and refine to a disjoint compact open partition. Extend each fixed vector on its piece and take zero elsewhere. This proves restriction is onto. A section vanishing on the closed subset has compact support in the open complement, proving the other exactness assertion. Twisted coinvariants preserve these exact sequences by compact averaging.

Proof: the character obstruction. The word \(b(w(1)),\ldots,b(w(n))\) determines the shuffle. Unless it is weakly decreasing, it has an adjacent ascent, say \(b(w(i))<b(w(i+1))\). The corresponding simple-root subgroup lies in \(H_w\) and is taken into the radical \(N\), where \(\rho\) acts trivially. Choose \(x\) with \(\psi(x)\ne1\). Then \[ h=1+xE_{i,i+1}\in H_w,\qquad \rho_w(h)=1,\qquad\theta_n(h)=\psi(x)\ne1. \tag{6.662} \] Its twisted relation annihilates every vector of \(W_w\). Lemma 6.292 therefore annihilates the orbit section quotient. There is exactly one weakly decreasing block word: put the last block first, then the next-to-last, preserving the order inside each. Its permutation and stabilizer are \[ w_*=w_Mw_0,\qquad H_*=w_*^{-1}U_Mw_* ,\qquad U_M=U_n\cap M. \tag{6.663} \] This is the open cell. Explicitly, the minors in the last \(d\) rows and first \(d\) columns are nonzero for every proper block-tail size \(d\). These finitely many open conditions give exactly that shuffle. Under \(h\mapsto w_*hw_*^{-1}\), the character on \(H_*\) is the product of the standard simple-root characters on the blocks: their positions in the block word are consecutive. This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.294 — Whittaker coinvariants commute with parabolic induction. For every smooth \(M\)-module \(W\), there is a natural isomorphism \[ \bigl(i_P^{G_n}W\bigr)_{U_n,\theta_n} \simeq W_{U_M,\theta_M}. \qquad \bigl(i_P^{G_n}(V_1\otimes\cdots\otimes V_s)\bigr)_{U_n,\theta_n} \simeq\bigotimes_{j=1}^s(V_j)_{U_{n_j},\theta_{n_j}}. \tag{6.664} \] Here \(\theta_M\) is the product of the block characters, and the Haar measures fix the scalar of the first isomorphism.

Proof. The sections supported compactly in the open orbit form a \(U_n\)-submodule of the induced module. Its inclusion is an isomorphism on twisted coinvariants: filter the closed complement by Lemma 6.293 and apply exactness, since each of its quotients has zero coinvariants. Lemma 6.292 and (6.663) identify the open-orbit quotient with \(W_{U_M,\theta_M}\). On an open-orbit section, the map is the actual finite integral \[ F\longmapsto \int_{H_*\backslash U_n} \theta_n(u)^{-1}[F(w_*u)]\,d\bar u. \tag{6.665} \] The bracket is in the indicated Levi quotient. Left \(H_*\)-covariance makes the integrand well defined. This integral is asserted only for sections with compact support in the open orbit. For a general induced section the isomorphism is defined by the finite-quotient argument; (6.665) need not converge for that section.

Finally, for a tensor product over a product of groups, the span of the twisted relations is the sum of the relation spaces in the individual factors. One inclusion follows by allowing only one nonidentity group element. For the other, expand the difference of a product action and its product scalar by telescoping, changing one factor at a time. Quotienting the tensor product by this sum gives the tensor product of its quotients, proving the second assertion. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.295 — the generic factor in a finite composition series. Suppose the \(V_j\) are irreducible admissible generic representations. Then the Whittaker quotient in (6.664) is one-dimensional. If their induced module has a finite composition series, exactly one occurrence of an irreducible factor is generic, and it occurs with multiplicity one. More generally, for any such finite series with factors \(\pi_a\), \[ \sum_a\dim(\pi_a)_{U_n,\theta_n} =\prod_j\dim(V_j)_{U_{n_j},\theta_{n_j}}. \tag{6.666} \]

Proof. Each factor quotient is one-dimensional by Theorem 6.291 and its nonzero Whittaker functional. Exactness of coinvariants gives additivity of dimensions along a given finite series, and (6.664) computes their sum. The induced module is admissible by the finite fixed-space argument in Theorem 6.296 below, so its irreducible subquotients are admissible: compact averaging makes taking fixed spaces exact, and their dimensions are bounded by those of the original module. Theorem 6.291 therefore bounds each summand by one. The sum is one, giving exactly the stated occurrence and multiplicity. This assertion assumes a finite composition series; it is not a proof of its existence for every induction. \(\square\)

For the next two statements return to \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\) in any division rank and either field characteristic. Fix the scalar centre \(Z=F^\times\) and a smooth central character \(\omega\), as in Section 6.41. The Levi modules have this character on \(Z\), without a prescribed character on their whole centre.

Theorem 6.296 — Frobenius adjunction and the actual induced trace. For a smooth \(G\)-module \(V\) and a smooth \(M\)-module \(W\), normalized induction satisfies \[ \operatorname{Hom}_G(V,i_P^GW) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_M(r_PV,W). \tag{6.667} \] If \(W\) is admissible, then \(i_P^GW\) is admissible, and for every \(f\in\mathcal H_\omega(G)\), with the normalization (6.547), \[ \operatorname{Tr}(i_P^GW)(f) =\operatorname{Tr}W(R_Pf). \tag{6.668} \] These are traces of actual finite-rank operators.

Proof: adjunction. If \(A:V\to i_P^GW\), set \(q(v)=A(v)(1)\). Evaluation gives \(q(\pi(mn)v)=\delta_P(m)^{1/2}\rho(m)q(v)\). Thus it factors through the \(N\)-coinvariants and is \(M\)-equivariant for \(r_PV=\delta_P^{-1/2}V_N\). Conversely, for such a \(q\), put \[ A_q(v)(g)=q(\pi(g)v). \tag{6.669} \] It has the required left parabolic covariance, is right fixed by any compact open subgroup fixing \(v\), and intertwines the right \(G\)-action. Its support modulo \(P\) is automatically compact. Evaluation and this construction are inverse, proving (6.667).

Proof: finite fixed spaces. Take a sufficiently deep principal subgroup \(J\) as in Lemma 6.251, put \(J_M=J\cap M\), and use the \(t\) flag pieces in Lemma 6.251. A map \(\mathcal H_\omega(G)e_J\to i_P^GW\) is determined by the image of \(e_J\), which is an arbitrary \(J\)-fixed vector. Conversely that vector defines the map by convolution. Apply (6.667) and (6.549) to obtain \[ \bigl(i_P^GW\bigr)^J \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_M\bigl(r_P(\mathcal H_\omega(G)e_J),W\bigr) \simeq\bigoplus_{i=1}^t W^{J_M}. \tag{6.670} \] This is finite-dimensional by admissibility. Every compact open subgroup contains a sufficiently deep principal subgroup, so all its fixed spaces are finite-dimensional too. Without a fixed central character the same argument uses the ordinary principal Hecke module: Lemma 6.251 gives the same coordinates before its central pushforward.

Proof: the operator and its diagonal trace. Choose \(J\) sufficiently small that \(f=e_J*f*e_J\). Right convolution by \(f\) on the principal module induces, by precomposition on its Hom space, exactly the operator \((i_P^GW)(f)\) on (6.670): a map with vector \(v\) sends \(a\) to \(\pi(a)v\), and its precomposition with right convolution sends it to the map with vector \(\pi(f)v\). In the finite Levi coordinates its diagonal entries are precisely those computed in (6.554), namely \[ b_i(m)=\frac{\delta_P(m)^{1/2}}t \int_N f(k_i^{-1}mnk_i)\,dn, \qquad \operatorname{Tr}(i_P^GW)(f)=\sum_{i=1}^t\operatorname{Tr}W(b_i). \tag{6.671} \] Precomposition transposes the finite matrix of blocks; its diagonal and their traces are unchanged. Each \(b_i\) is bi-\(J_M\)-invariant, so its trace on \(W^{J_M}\) is its actual finite-rank trace on \(W\). Theorem 6.252 proves the finite algebraic cocenter identity \([R_Pf]=\sum_i[b_i]\). Admissible traces annihilate each of its finite commutators. This gives (6.668) for the entire operator, without character integration or an interchange of infinite spectral sums. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.297 — compact discrete tests annihilate proper induced traces. Let \(P\ne G\), and let \(f_{V,m}\) be the compact Euler–Poincaré test of Theorem 6.254. For every admissible smooth \(M\)-module \(W\) with the specified scalar central character, \[ \operatorname{Tr}(i_P^GW)(f_{V,m})=0. \tag{6.672} \] In particular this holds for every compact discrete pseudo-coefficient \(f_{\pi,m}\), with no temperedness hypothesis on \(W\).

Proof. Theorem 6.254 says that \(R_Pf_{V,m}\) is a finite commutator sum in \(\mathcal H_\omega(M)\). Its actual admissible trace on \(W\) is zero. Apply (6.668). If a generic irreducible of split \(G_n\) is itself a proper parabolic induction, this proves its zero pseudo-coefficient trace. No assertion that every other generic irreducible has that form is needed for this conclusion. \(\square\)

Example 6.298 — one generic factor and a nonzero trace. For split \(G_2\), put \(\nu=|\cdot|_F\). The normalized induction of \(\nu^{-1/2}\otimes\nu^{1/2}\) is the unnormalized induction of the trivial Borel character. It is the space of locally constant functions on \(B\backslash G_2\simeq\mathbb P^1(F)\), with the constants as its trivial submodule. Its quotient is the usual Steinberg representation from Section 2.3. Thus \[ 0\longrightarrow\mathbf1\longrightarrow I=i_B^{G_2}(\nu^{-1/2}\otimes\nu^{1/2}) \longrightarrow\mathrm{St}\longrightarrow0. \tag{6.673} \] The trivial module has zero Whittaker quotient: \((1-\theta_2(u))v\) is a defining relation and some \(\theta_2(u)\ne1\). Formula (6.664) gives \(\dim I_{U_2,\theta_2}=1\), so exactness gives \(\dim\mathrm{St}_{U_2,\theta_2}=1\). The Steinberg is a unitary discrete series, by the tree construction in Section 2.3 or the rank-two case of Section 6.24. For its compact discrete test, Corollary 6.117 and (6.672) give \[ \operatorname{Tr}I(f_{\mathrm{St},m})=0,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\mathrm{St}(f_{\mathrm{St},m})=1,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\mathbf1(f_{\mathrm{St},m})=-1. \tag{6.674} \] Trace additivity is an actual finite-dimensional calculation: compact averaging makes the \(J\)-fixed version of (6.673) exact, and a bi-\(J\)-invariant test has its entire trace there. Thus vanishing on the whole reducible induction and uniqueness of its generic factor do not imply vanishing on that factor. To isolate a discrete series among all generic irreducibles, one must also control the irreducibility or composition of the relevant inductions. The full local representation correspondence and the global spectral extraction require further arguments.

6.48 Mirabolic detection and finite length of cuspidal induction

Let \(F\) be nonarchimedean of either characteristic. Write \(P_n\) for the mirabolic subgroup with last row \((0,\ldots,0,1)\), and \(N_n\simeq F^{n-1}\) for its last-column subgroup. Thus \(P_n=G_{n-1}\ltimes N_n\), with \(G_j=\mathrm{GL}_j(F)\). Put \(P_1=U_1=\{1\}\). For every smooth complex module, use the unnormalized twisted coinvariants of (6.657). Define \[ \Omega_n=\left\{\theta_a(u)=\psi\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}a_i u_{i,i+1}\right): a_i\in\{0,1\}\right\}, \qquad D_n(V)=\sum_{\theta\in\Omega_n}\dim V_{U_n,\theta}. \tag{6.675} \] Here \(\Omega_1=\{1\}\). No admissibility, irreducibility or finite generation is assumed in the first three results.

Lemma 6.299 — compact additive projectors detect nonzero modules. Let \(V\) be a smooth \(F^m\)-module. If \(V_{F^m,\psi_\xi}=0\) for every row \(\xi\in F^m\), where \(\psi_\xi(x)=\psi(\xi x)\), then \(V=0\).

Proof: finite projector identities. Let the conductor of \(\psi\) be \(\varpi^c\mathcal O\): the character is trivial on this ideal and not on \(\varpi^{c-1}\mathcal O\). For a homothetic lattice and its annihilator, \[ L=\varpi^b\mathcal O^m,\qquad L^\perp=\{\xi:\psi(\xi x)=1\ (x\in L)\} =\varpi^{c-b}\mathcal O^m. \tag{6.676} \] To check the reverse inclusion, if a coordinate has valuation less than \(c-b\), choose the corresponding coordinate of \(x\in L\) so that its product is any specified element on which \(\psi\) is nontrivial in \(\varpi^{c-1}\mathcal O\). This is possible by multiplying by a unit and a nonnegative power of \(\varpi\).

For the dual ball \(B=\xi+L^\perp\), define \[ E_B=E_{L,\xi}=\frac1{\operatorname{vol}L} \int_L\psi(-\xi x)\pi(x)\,dx. \tag{6.677} \] This is a finite smooth average. Changing \(\xi\) within \(B\) leaves it unchanged, and (6.676) determines \(L\) from \(B\). If \(L\subset M\), abelian translation and compact-character orthogonality give \[ E_{M,\eta}E_{L,\xi}= \begin{cases}E_{M,\eta}&\eta-\xi\in L^\perp,\\0&\eta-\xi\notin L^\perp. \end{cases} \qquad E_BE_C=E_{B\cap C},\quad E_\varnothing=0. \tag{6.678} \] Indeed \(E_{M,\eta}\) transforms by \(\psi_\eta\) under every element of \(L\); averaging it with \(\psi_\xi^{-1}\) gives the first identity. The integral of a nontrivial compact-group character is zero: translate it by an element on which its value is not one. Any two homothetic dual balls are nested or disjoint, proving the second identity.

For \(L_0\subset M\), one also has the finite partition identity \[ E_{L_0,0}=\sum_{\zeta\in L_0^\perp/M^\perp}E_{M,\zeta}. \tag{6.679} \] The pairing of \(M/L_0\) with \(L_0^\perp/M^\perp\) is nondegenerate by the coordinate argument for (6.676), and both finite groups have the same order. Summing its characters is therefore \([M:L_0]\) on \(L_0\) and zero elsewhere. Inserting this finite sum into (6.677), and using \(\operatorname{vol}M=[M:L_0]\operatorname{vol}L_0\), proves (6.679). This uses only finite character sums, not a spectral decomposition of \(V\).

Proof: detection. Compact averaging gives \[ v=0\text{ in }V_{F^m,\psi_\xi} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E_{M,\xi}v=0\text{ for some homothetic averaging lattice }M. \tag{6.680} \] For the forward implication, put the finitely many translation elements in a witness relation into one sufficiently large lattice; its twisted average kills every relation. For the reverse implication, the difference from a finite smooth average is itself a finite sum of twisted relations, as in Lemma 6.288.

Fix \(v\) and a lattice \(L_0\) fixing it, so \(E_{L_0,0}v=v\). For each \(\xi\in B_0=L_0^\perp\), the hypothesis and (6.680) give \(M_\xi\supset L_0\) with \(E_{M_\xi,\xi}v=0\). The balls \(B_\xi=\xi+M_\xi^\perp\subset B_0\) cover the compact set \(B_0\). Choose a finite cover and a homothetic \(M\) containing all its averaging lattices. The cosets of \(M^\perp\) partition \(B_0\); each lies in one covering ball. By (6.678) each of its projectors kills \(v\). Equation (6.679) then gives \(v=0\). Since \(v\) was arbitrary, \(V=0\). All reciprocal integers and Haar factors are complex scalars, including when \(F\) has characteristic two. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.300 — a finite family detects every mirabolic module. Every nonzero smooth \(P_n\)-module has a nonzero \((U_n,\theta)\)-quotient for some \(\theta\in\Omega_n\).

Proof. For \(n\ge2\), set \(e=(0,\ldots,0,1)\) and form \[ A(V)=V_{N_n,1},\qquad B(V)=V_{N_n,\psi_e},\qquad \pi(h):V_{N_n,\psi_\xi}\xrightarrow{\sim} V_{N_n,\psi_{\xi h^{-1}}}. \tag{6.681} \] The first module is smooth for \(G_{n-1}\), the second for the stabilizer of \(e\), which is exactly \(P_{n-1}\). The last assertion follows by conjugating the last column \(x\mapsto hx\). The group \(G_{n-1}\) is transitive on nonzero rows. Thus if both \(A(V)\) and \(B(V)\) were zero, every last-column character quotient would be zero, and Lemma 6.299 would give \(V=0\).

The assertion for \(n=1\) is immediate. Inductively, if \(A(V)\ne0\), apply the assertion to its restriction to \(P_{n-1}\); if \(B(V)\ne0\), apply it to that module.
