The semidirect product \(U_n=U_{n-1}\ltimes N_n\) and invariance of \(\psi_e\) under \(U_{n-1}\) give \[ V_{U_n,\theta_{(a',0)}}\simeq A(V)_{U_{n-1},\theta_{a'}},\qquad V_{U_n,\theta_{(a',1)}}\simeq B(V)_{U_{n-1},\theta_{a'}}. \tag{6.682} \] These identities follow directly by taking the normal last-column relations first and then the upper-left unipotent relations. Appending zero or one to the detected character proves the lemma. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.301 — a finite mirabolic length criterion. If \(D_n(V)<\infty\), then \[ \operatorname{length}_{P_n}V\le D_n(V). \qquad \operatorname{length}_{G_n}V\le\operatorname{length}_{P_n}V \quad\text{when }V\text{ is a }G_n\text{-module}. \tag{6.683} \]

Proof. Every \((U_n,\theta)\)-coinvariant functor is exact. The proof is compact averaging as in Lemma 6.288: its argument uses only a smooth character and the compact exhaustion, so it applies to every character in \(\Omega_n\). Subquotients have finite \(D_n\), and this integer is additive along their exact sequences. By Lemma 6.300 it is positive on every nonzero smooth \(P_n\)-module. Hence any finite strict chain from zero to \(V\) satisfies \[ D_n(V)=\sum_{j=1}^l D_n(V_j/V_{j-1})\ge l, \qquad0=V_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq V_l=V. \tag{6.684} \] The possible integer lengths of these chains are bounded. Choose one of maximal length; every successive quotient is simple, since otherwise inserting a proper submodule would lengthen the chain. This is a finite composition series with the stated bound. Every \(G_n\)-submodule chain is a \(P_n\)-submodule chain; the same argument gives the second assertion. The zero module has length zero. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.302 — cuspidal genericity and irreducible mirabolic restriction. Let \(\rho\) be an irreducible admissible cuspidal representation of \(G_k\), where cuspidal means that every proper Jacquet module is zero. Its nondegenerate Whittaker quotient is one-dimensional, every degenerate quotient belonging to \(\Omega_k\) is zero, and its restriction to \(P_k\) is irreducible.

Proof. If a coefficient of \(\theta_a\) is zero, let \(Q\) have Levi blocks equal to the maximal intervals joined by coefficients one. Its radical \(N_Q\) is nontrivial and \(\theta_a\) is trivial there. Taking normal radical relations first gives \[ \rho_{U_k,\theta_a} \simeq(\rho_{N_Q})_{U_k\cap M_Q,\theta_a|_{U_k\cap M_Q}} =0\qquad(\theta_a\text{ degenerate}). \tag{6.685} \] By Lemma 6.300 the nonzero \(P_k\)-module \(\rho\) has some nonzero quotient in \(\Omega_k\), so the fully nondegenerate one is nonzero. Theorem 6.291 makes it one-dimensional, using the dual identification after (6.657). Thus \[ D_k(\rho)=1,\qquad \dim\rho_{U_k,\theta_{(1,\ldots,1)}}=1,\qquad \operatorname{length}_{P_k}\rho=1. \tag{6.686} \] Theorem 6.301 gives the last equality. In degree one it follows at once from Whittaker uniqueness with \(U_1=1\). No unitary hypothesis is required. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.303 — exact cuspidal-induction profiles and finite length. Let \(I=i_P^{G_n}(\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_s)\), where the \(\rho_j\) are irreducible admissible cuspidal representations of degrees \(n_j\). Regard the labels \(1,\ldots,s\) as distinct occurrences, even if some representations are isomorphic. For \(\theta_a\in\Omega_n\), let \((m_1,\ldots,m_t)\) be the consecutive interval lengths obtained by cutting \(1,\ldots,n\) at exactly the positions where \(a_i=0\). Then \[ \dim I_{U_n,\theta_a} =\#\left\{(S_1,\ldots,S_t): \coprod_{h=1}^t S_h=\{1,\ldots,s\},\ S_h\ne\varnothing,\ \sum_{j\in S_h}n_j=m_h\right\}. \tag{6.687} \] The sets in this count are ordered. In particular the formula depends only on the inducing degrees and labelled occurrences.

Proof: the finite orbit filtration for an arbitrary character. Lemma 6.293 gives a finite filtration by shuffle orbits, independently of the unipotent character. Only multiplicativity and local constancy of the character were used in (6.658)–(6.660); substituting \(\theta_a\) there computes the twisted quotient of its orbit section module as \[ (W_w)_{H_w,\theta_a|_{H_w}},\qquad W=\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_s, \qquad wH_ww^{-1}\supset U_M. \tag{6.688} \] The inclusion holds because \(w^{-1}\) preserves the order of the values in each Levi block. Restricting the defining relations to \(w^{-1}U_Mw\) makes this a quotient of \(W_{U_M,\eta_w}\), with \(\eta_w(h)=\theta_a(w^{-1}hw)\).

For adjacent values \(b,b+1\) inside an original Levi block, put \(i=w^{-1}(b)\), \(j=w^{-1}(b+1)\). Then \(i<j\), and its simple-root coefficient in \(\eta_w\) is \[ \begin{cases}a_i&j=i+1,\\0&j>i+1. \end{cases} \tag{6.689} \] Higher Levi roots have nonadjacent preimage positions, since an intermediate value of the same block lies between them. They contribute zero. Corollary 6.302 therefore kills the orbit unless every original block occupies a consecutive interval of positions and every internal coefficient there is one. The surviving shuffle is consequently a concatenation of entire original blocks in some order \(\beta\in S_s\).

Let \(d_h=n_{\beta_1}+\cdots+n_{\beta_h}\). At a boundary between these blocks, a simple-root subgroup lies in the stabilizer radical precisely when \(\beta_h<\beta_{h+1}\). The fibre action there is trivial, so its coefficient must be zero. At a descent that root is absent from the stabilizer. Thus the complete compatibility conditions are \[ \begin{aligned} a_i&=1 &&\text{inside each original block},\\ a_{d_h}&=0 &&\text{if }\beta_h<\beta_{h+1},\\ a_{d_h}&\in\{0,1\} &&\text{if }\beta_h>\beta_{h+1}. \end{aligned} \tag{6.690} \] These conditions are sufficient as well. The stabilizer factors into the conjugated \(U_M\) and a subgroup mapped into \(N\), by its root-pattern triangular coordinates. On the latter subgroup \(\theta_a=1\): its only possible simple roots are the ascent boundaries just set to zero, and all its higher roots have zero character. The inducing module is also trivial there. Its full twisted quotient is therefore exactly \(W_{U_M,\eta_w}\), not merely a quotient of it. Every block character is nondegenerate, so this space has dimension one by Corollary 6.302 and the tensor-relation calculation of Theorem 6.294.

For a compatible \(\beta\), cut at the zero boundary coefficients. Within each resulting group the labels strictly decrease. Conversely, order each \(S_h\) in decreasing order and concatenate the lists. This produces a unique compatible \(\beta\) with exactly these cuts. The group degrees must be \(m_h\). This is the bijection in (6.687). Exactness of twisted coinvariants along the finite orbit filtration adds these one-dimensional contributions, proving the formula.

Proof: length and the generic factor. Summing (6.687) over \(\Omega_n\) counts every ordered partition of the \(s\) labels once. Equivalently, a permutation \(\beta\) has forced cuts at its ascents and optional cuts at its descents. If \({s\brace t}\) denotes the number of unordered partitions into \(t\) nonempty sets, then \[ D_n(I)=F_s:=\sum_{\beta\in S_s}2^{\operatorname{des}(\beta)} =\sum_{t=1}^s t!{s\brace t}. \tag{6.691} \] The second equality also follows by forgetting and then ordering the groups of an ordered partition; each has exactly \(t!\) orders. Every step is a finite count. Theorem 6.301 gives \[ \operatorname{length}_{G_n}I \le\operatorname{length}_{P_n}I\le F_s<\infty, \qquad \dim I_{U_n,\theta_{(1,\ldots,1)}}=1. \tag{6.692} \] The induced module is admissible by Theorem 6.296, so its irreducible factors are admissible. Exactness and Theorem 6.291 now show that precisely one occurrence in a composition series is generic, with multiplicity one. There is no additional finite-series hypothesis for this cuspidal induction. Its values for one through five inducing blocks are \[ F_1=1,\quad F_2=3,\quad F_3=13, \quad F_4=75,\quad F_5=541. \tag{6.693} \] For example, the unordered partition counts for \(s=4\) are \(1,7,6,1\), and for \(s=5\) they are \(1,15,25,10,1\). For two groups count nonempty subsets modulo complement; for three groups in degree five the size patterns are \((3,1,1)\) and \((2,2,1)\), with \(10\) and \(15\) choices. The remaining displayed counts follow by choosing the sole pair or the sole merged group. Multiplying by group-order factorials gives (6.693). \(\square\)

Example 6.304 — three blocks of degrees two, one and two. Give the three labelled cuspidal factors degrees \((2,1,2)\). The complete list of nonzero profiles is \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr} (m_1,\ldots,m_t)&(5)&(1,4)&(4,1)&(2,3)&(3,2)&(2,1,2)&(2,2,1)&(1,2,2)\\ \dim I_{U_5,\theta_a}&1&1&1&2&2&2&2&2. \end{array} \qquad D_5(I)=13. \tag{6.694} \] For two groups, choose the first nonempty proper subset of the labels. Its degree is one in one case, two in two cases, three in two cases and four in one case. For three groups, all are singletons; each ordering of the degree multiset \((2,1,2)\) has two labelled realizations. The one-group profile is unique. All other compositions of five have dimension zero. Hence the induction has finite mirabolic and general-linear lengths at most thirteen and precisely one generic occurrence. This is a bound, not a claim that either length equals thirteen.

Example 6.305 — the integer bound need not be the length. For this example only, use the finite group \(P_3(\mathbb F_2)\) and its projection onto \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb F_2)\). The latter permutes its three nonzero column vectors as the full symmetric group: the action is injective and both groups have order six. Inflate its two-dimensional module \[ W=\{(z_1,z_2,z_3)\in\mathbb C^3:z_1+z_2+z_3=0\},\qquad \dim W_{U_3,\theta_{(a_1,a_2)}}= \begin{cases}1&a_2=0,\\0&a_2=1. \end{cases} \tag{6.695} \] It is irreducible. A nonzero vector in the sum-zero space has two unequal coordinates; subtract its transposition to obtain a nonzero multiple of a coordinate difference. Permutations of that difference span \(W\). The last-column subgroup acts trivially, so its nontrivial character kills the quotient when \(a_2=1\). When \(a_2=0\), the remaining order-two upper-left root subgroup acts by a transposition, with one-dimensional positive and negative eigenspaces. They give (6.695) for either value of \(a_1\). Therefore \[ \operatorname{length}_{P_3(\mathbb F_2)}W=1, \qquad D_3(W)=2. \tag{6.696} \] This finite calculation explains why the length criterion is an inequality. The local-field statements above use the complete compact-average and finite-filtration proofs. Finite length and a unique generic occurrence still do not determine which irreducibles occur in different inductions or when a generic representation is itself an irreducible proper induction. Example 6.298 shows why that composition information remains necessary for generic trace isolation and the subsequent globalization argument.

6.49 Cuspidal embeddings and finite length under induction

All groups in this section are split general linear groups over a nonarchimedean field of either characteristic, or finite products of them. Induction and Jacquet modules are normalized as in Section 6.47. For tensor factorization we use the general algebraic tensor-product theorem, Lesson 12, Theorem 4.1. Its proof applies to arbitrary Hecke algebras with local units and finite-dimensional fixed spaces.

Lemma 6.306 — exactness, transitivity and products. For every short exact sequence of smooth Levi modules, normalized induction gives a short exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow i_P^G W_1\longrightarrow i_P^G W_2 \longrightarrow i_P^G W_3\longrightarrow0. \tag{6.697} \] If \(P=MN_P\subset G\), \(Q=LN_Q\subset M\), and \(R=LN_R\subset G\) is the refined standard parabolic, then Jacquet functors and induction are transitive. They also commute with finite external products.

Proof: exactness. Choose a sufficiently deep principal subgroup \(J\). The natural coordinates (6.670) identify the \(J\)-fixed induced space with a finite direct sum of copies of \(W^{J_M}\). These coordinates hold for every smooth \(W\); admissibility was used only to make their dimensions finite. Compact averaging makes taking \(J_M\)-invariants exact. Hence every \(J\)-fixed section with values in \(W_3\) lifts to one with values in \(W_2\). Every smooth section is fixed at some such principal level. Kernels and injections are pointwise, proving (6.697). Use the ordinary Hecke coordinates before the central pushforward in (6.670); thus this assertion imposes no scalar central character on the sequence.

Proof: the normalizations and transitivity. The group \(N_P\) is normal in \(N_R\), with quotient \(N_Q\). Its root coordinates split the determinant of conjugation into two products. On \(L\) this gives \[ \delta_R(l)=\delta_P(l)\delta_Q(l),\qquad \delta_{(n_1,\ldots,n_s)}(m) =\prod_{i<j}|\det m_i|^{n_j}|\det m_j|^{-n_i}. \tag{6.698} \] For the second equality, conjugation on a rectangular \(n_i\)-by-\(n_j\) upper block is \(x\mapsto m_ixm_j^{-1}\); its additive determinant is exactly the indicated factor. Refinement partitions these rectangular root spaces into the old cross-block spaces and the new within-block spaces, proving the first equality as well.

Taking normal \(N_P\)-relations first and then \(N_Q\)-relations gives the same quotient as taking all \(N_R\)-relations. The character \(\delta_P\) is trivial on \(N_Q\). Including (6.698) therefore proves \[ r_Q^M(r_P^G V)\simeq r_R^G V. \tag{6.699} \] For induction the maps are explicit: \[ \begin{aligned} i_P^G(i_Q^M W)&\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }i_R^G W,& f(g)&=F(g)(1),\\ F(g)(m)&=\delta_P(m)^{-1/2}f(mg). \end{aligned} \tag{6.700} \] The first map has the required \(R\)-covariance by (6.698). For its inverse, the same identity and triviality on \(N_P\) give \[ F(g)(qm)=\delta_Q(q)^{1/2}\rho(q)F(g)(m),\qquad F(pg)=\delta_P(p)^{1/2}\bigl(i_Q^M W\bigr)(p)F(g). \tag{6.701} \] In the second formula \(N_P\) acts trivially in the inner module. Conjugating an element of \(N_P\) past \(m\) keeps it in \(N_P\), which verifies that assertion directly in (6.700). If a compact open \(J\) fixes \(f\) on the right, it fixes the outer variable of \(F\). For fixed \(g\), the inner variable is fixed by \(M\cap gJg^{-1}\), on which \(\delta_P=1\); this proves its smoothness. Both flag spaces are compact, so no extra support condition occurs. The two substitutions in (6.700) give inverse maps, and both commute with right \(G\)-translation.

Proof: products. Product sections induce \[ \bigotimes_i i_{Q_i}^{G_i}W_i \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } i_{\prod_iQ_i}^{\prod_iG_i}\left(\bigotimes_iW_i\right),\qquad \bigotimes_iF_i\longmapsto\left((g_i)_i\mapsto\bigotimes_iF_i(g_i)\right). \tag{6.702} \] At a product of principal levels, the finite flag coordinates on each side are the same finite direct sum of \(\bigotimes_i W_i^{J_{M_i}}\). The compact averaging projector on a tensor product for a product group is the tensor product of the projectors: on each finite sum of pure tensors both integrals are finite sums and factor. The displayed map is the identity in these coordinates. Every smooth vector lies at one product level, proving injectivity and surjectivity. Jacquet modules commute with these products too: in the tensor product, quotienting the relations in each radical factor gives the tensor product of the quotients, by the telescoping relation argument of Theorem 6.294. The moduli factor as products, completing the proof. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.307 — every irreducible admissible module has a cuspidal embedding. For every irreducible admissible \(G_n\)-module \(V\), there exist a standard parabolic \(P\) and irreducible admissible cuspidal \(\rho_i\) on its Levi factors such that \[ V\ \hookrightarrow\ i_P^{G_n}(\rho_1\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_s). \tag{6.703} \] The assertion allows \(P=G_n\).

Proof: a cuspidal quotient of a Jacquet module. Among the finitely many standard parabolics with \(r_PV\ne0\), choose one whose Levi has as many blocks as possible. The set is nonempty since \(r_GV=V\). Irreducibility makes \(V\) cyclic: the span of the translates of any nonzero vector is a nonzero invariant subspace. Lemma 6.40 makes \(S=r_PV\) finitely generated, and Lemma 6.22 makes it admissible; the normalizing character preserves both properties.

The nonzero module \(S\) has an irreducible quotient. Indeed the union of a chain of proper submodules is proper: if it contained the finitely many generators, one member of the chain would contain all of them and would be \(S\). Zorn's lemma gives a maximal proper submodule. Let \(S\twoheadrightarrow\rho\) be its quotient. Compact averaging makes \(\rho^J\) a quotient of \(S^J\) for every compact open \(J\), so \(\rho\) is admissible. For every proper standard parabolic \(Q\subset M\), the refinement \(R\) has more blocks. Consequently \[ S=r_PV\twoheadrightarrow\rho,\qquad r_QS=r_RV=0,\qquad r_Q\rho=0. \tag{6.704} \] The last equality uses exactness of unipotent coinvariants, proved by compact averaging in Lemma 6.251; normalization is a character twist. Thus \(\rho\) is cuspidal on \(M\). No character on the whole centre of \(M\) has been imposed on \(S\).

Proof: the Levi factors and the embedding. The Hecke algebra of a finite product is its algebraic tensor product. A compact smooth function has a finite compact-open rectangle partition: cover its compact support by finitely many such rectangles on which it is constant and refine the coordinate partitions. This expresses it as a finite sum of product functions and proves the assertion. Product compact-open averaging identities are its local units. Their ranges on \(\rho\) are finite-dimensional by admissibility. The full hypotheses of Lesson 12, Theorem 4.1, therefore apply, and iteration gives irreducible admissible factors \(\rho_i\).

Each factor is cuspidal. If a proper radical in one factor had a nonzero Jacquet module, the product relation identity would give \[ \rho\simeq\bigotimes_i\rho_i,\qquad r_{Q_i\times\prod_{j\ne i}G_{n_j}}^M\rho \simeq(r_{Q_i}\rho_i)\otimes\bigotimes_{j\ne i}\rho_j\ne0, \tag{6.705} \] contrary to (6.704). A tensor product of finitely many nonzero complex vector spaces is nonzero, as is seen by extending nonzero vectors to bases. Finally Frobenius adjunction gives \[ 0\ne\operatorname{Hom}_M(r_PV,\rho) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{G_n}(V,i_P^{G_n}\rho). \tag{6.706} \] The map corresponding to the quotient is nonzero, and its kernel is zero by irreducibility of \(V\). This proves (6.703). It proves existence of a cuspidal embedding, without asserting uniqueness of its inducing data. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.308 — finite-length closure and generic occurrences. If \(W\) is an irreducible admissible module of a standard Levi \(M\subset G_n\), then \(i_P^{G_n}W\) has finite length for both \(G_n\) and \(P_n\). Every irreducible admissible \(G_n\)-module also has finite-length mirabolic restriction.

Proof: actual embeddings. Factor \(W=\bigotimes_i\tau_i\) by Lesson 12, Theorem 4.1, and apply Theorem 6.307 in each factor. Tensoring the resulting injections is injective over \(\mathbb C\): choose vector-space complements or extend bases. Formula (6.702) embeds \(W\) into a cuspidal induction \(i_Q^M\rho\). Exactness and transitivity now give actual injections \[ i_P^{G_n}W\ \hookrightarrow\ i_P^{G_n}(i_Q^M\rho) \simeq i_R^{G_n}\rho. \tag{6.707} \] If the chosen \(\rho\) has \(t\) cuspidal factors, the target has mirabolic length at most \(F_t\), by Theorem 6.303. Restricting the injection to \(P_n\) preserves injectivity, and submodules of a finite-length module have finite length, by intersecting a composition series and discarding repeated terms. Thus \[ \operatorname{length}_{G_n}(i_P^{G_n}W) \le\operatorname{length}_{P_n}(i_P^{G_n}W)\le F_t\le F_n, \qquad\operatorname{length}_{P_n}V\le F_n \quad(V\text{ irreducible admissible}). \tag{6.708} \] For the last assertion use (6.703) directly. Every cuspidal degree is positive, so \(t\le n\). The inequality \(F_t\le F_n\) follows by injecting ordered partitions of \(t\) labels into those of \(t+1\) labels: add the new label to the first group. Repetition proves monotonicity. These are bounds, not assertions about the exact lengths or the intrinsic number of cuspidal factors.

More generally let \(W\) be a finite-length admissible Levi module, with irreducible factors \(W_a\). The factors are admissible by compact averaging. Exact induction and a composition series give a filtration with quotients \(i_P^G W_a\). Refine each finite quotient series by taking inverse images. If \(t_a\) is a number of cuspidal factors in a chosen embedding for \(W_a\), this proves \[ \operatorname{length}_{G_n}(i_P^G W) \le\operatorname{length}_{P_n}(i_P^G W) \le\sum_a F_{t_a}<\infty. \tag{6.709} \]

Proof: the generic conclusions. For irreducible admissible factors \(\tau_i\), Theorem 6.294 and the finite series just proved give \[ \sum_{\pi\text{ in a composition series of }i_P^G(\bigotimes_i\tau_i)} \dim\pi_{U_n,\theta_n} =\prod_i\dim(\tau_i)_{U_{n_i},\theta_{n_i}}. \tag{6.710} \] The sum counts occurrences. Each term and each input dimension is zero or one by Theorem 6.291. If every \(\tau_i\) is generic, there is exactly one generic occurrence, with multiplicity one; if some input quotient is zero, none is generic. This removes the separate finite-series assumption of Corollary 6.295 for these inputs.

If \(V\) itself is generic, choose its embedding (6.703). Exactness of Whittaker coinvariants and Theorem 6.303 show \[ V\hookrightarrow I_{\mathrm{cusp}},\qquad V_{U_n,\theta_n}\xrightarrow{\sim} (I_{\mathrm{cusp}})_{U_n,\theta_n}\simeq\mathbb C. \tag{6.711} \] The submodule \(V\) therefore accounts for the unique generic occurrence in that chosen induction. This assertion concerns the embedding chosen for \(V\); it does not assert that the generic factor of every induction is a submodule or compare differently ordered inducing data. \(\square\)

Example 6.309 — refinement and the possible degree-three embeddings. Let \(G=G_3\), let \(P\) have blocks \((2,1)\), and refine its first block by the upper Borel of \(G_2\). Thus \(Q=B_2\times G_1\subset M\) and \(R=B_3\). For \(m=\operatorname{diag}(A,c)\) and \(l=\operatorname{diag}(a,b,c)\), \[ \delta_P(m)=|\det A|\,|c|^{-2},\qquad \delta_Q(l)=|a/b|,\qquad \delta_P(l)\delta_Q(l)=|a|^2|c|^{-2}=\delta_{B_3}(l). \tag{6.712} \] The cancellation of \(|b|\) is the root determinant identity: the inner root has weight \(a/b\), and the two outer roots have weights \(a/c\) and \(b/c\). For any three smooth characters, the nested and full normalized principal series are identified by \[ f(g)=F(g)(1),\qquad F(g)(A,c)=|\det A|^{-1/2}|c|\, f(\operatorname{diag}(A,c)g). \tag{6.713} \] Both are admissible and of finite length. Their common mirabolic length is bounded by \(F_3=13\), and they have a unique generic occurrence.

For an arbitrary irreducible admissible \(G_3\)-module, (6.703) permits exactly the following degree patterns, according to which maximal-block nonzero Jacquet module is chosen: \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{cuspidal inducing degrees}&\text{number of factors}& \text{mirabolic length bound for the embedded module}\\ (3)&1&1\\(2,1)&2&3\\(1,2)&2&3\\(1,1,1)&3&13. \end{array} \tag{6.714} \] The two ordered patterns \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\) are both retained here; the existence proof has not identified their induced modules. If the original module is generic, it is the unique generic occurrence in its chosen cuspidal embedding. The exact generic factorization and segment-product criterion are Theorem 6.373 and Corollary 6.375; the generic trace identity is Theorem 6.374. General nongeneric composition questions and the local and global representation correspondences require further arguments.

6.50 Compact cuspidal coefficients and actual Hecke projections

Let \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), where \(D/F\) is a central division algebra of degree \(d\), and put \(N=rd\), \(Z=F^\times\). The field \(F\) is nonarchimedean of either characteristic. Representations and Hecke algebras have complex scalars. Cuspidal means that every proper Jacquet module is zero. No Whittaker multiplicity assertion for an inner form is used here.

Lemma 6.310 — compact coefficients before unitarization. If \(V\) is a smooth cuspidal \(G\)-module, then for every \(v\in V\) and smooth-dual functional \(\ell\in V^\vee\), the image of the support of \(g\mapsto\ell(\pi(g)v)\) in \(G/Z\) is compact. Neither admissibility nor a scalar central character is required for this assertion.

Proof. Use \(K=\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_D)\), its normal principal groups \(K_m\), and the Cartan cover of Lemma 6.23. With a division uniformizer \(\Pi\), it is \[ G=\bigcup_{b\in B,\,\ell_0\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r-1}} ZK b t_{\ell_0}K,\qquad B=\{\operatorname{diag}(\Pi^{\epsilon_i}):0\le\epsilon_i<d\}, \qquad t_{\ell_0}=\prod_{j=1}^{r-1} \operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F I_j,I_{r-j})^{(\ell_0)_j}. \tag{6.715} \] Unit factors are absorbed in \(K\), as proved there. The diagonal field scalars \(t_{\ell_0}\) commute with every \(b\). In particular the finite set \(B\) must be retained when \(d>1\).

The compact \(K\)-orbits of a smooth vector and a smooth-dual functional are finite. Therefore the sets \[ \mathcal V=\{\pi(k)v:k\in K\},\qquad \mathcal L=\{\ell\circ\pi(kb):k\in K,\ b\in B\} \tag{6.716} \] are finite. Choose \(m\) so that \(K_m\) fixes every member of both sets. Every functional \(\phi\circ\pi(z)\), \(\phi\in\mathcal L\), \(z\in Z\), is still \(K_m\)-fixed, because \(z\) commutes with \(K_m\). This observation handles central actions that are not scalar.

For the maximal \((j,r-j)\)-parabolic let \(N_j\) be its rectangular radical, put \(K_j^+=K_m\cap N_j\), and write \(a_j=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F I_j,I_{r-j})\). Since \(V_{N_j}=0\), the finite-relation averaging criterion (6.552) gives an integer \(b_j\ge1\) with \[ E_{a_j^{-b_j}K_j^+a_j^{b_j}}v_2=0 \qquad(v_2\in\mathcal V). \tag{6.717} \] One bound works for the finite set of vectors, and increasing it preserves vanishing. These compact groups exhaust \(N_j\): every off-diagonal division entry is expanded by \(\varpi_F^{-b_j}\).

Write \(t_{\ell_0}=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F^{q_i})\), with \(q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_r=0\). If \((\ell_0)_j=q_j-q_{j+1}\ge b_j\), all cross-block differences are at least \(b_j\). On a cross entry the two relevant division ideals have exponents \[ m-d(q_i-q_h)\le m-db_j\quad(i\le j<h),\qquad a_j^{-b_j}K_j^+a_j^{b_j}\subset t_{\ell_0}^{-1}K_j^+t_{\ell_0}. \tag{6.718} \] Here \(v_D(\varpi_F)=d\); all scalings used are central, so noncommutativity causes no change. For \(\phi\in\mathcal L\), its central translate is fixed by the first averaging group below. Thus \[ \begin{aligned} \phi\bigl(\pi(z)\pi(t_{\ell_0})v_2\bigr) &=\phi\bigl(\pi(z)E_{K_j^+}\pi(t_{\ell_0})v_2\bigr)\\ &=\phi\bigl(\pi(z)\pi(t_{\ell_0}) E_{t_{\ell_0}^{-1}K_j^+t_{\ell_0}}v_2\bigr)=0. \end{aligned} \tag{6.719} \] The last average factors through the smaller annihilating average in (6.717): for nested compact subgroups, their probability projectors satisfy \(E_LE_H=E_L\) when \(H\subset L\). Therefore the support is contained in \[ \bigcup_{b\in B,\ 0\le(\ell_0)_j<b_j}ZKbt_{\ell_0}K. \tag{6.720} \] The support is bi-invariant by one compact open subgroup fixing both original entries. Its central saturation is a union of subgroup cosets, as is its complement, so its image in \(G/Z\) is closed. By (6.720) that image is contained in a finite union of compact sets, hence is compact. For \(r=1\) there are no gaps and the Cartan cover already makes \(G/Z\) compact. This proves the lemma in every rank. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.311 — a unitary twist with the original smooth module. Every irreducible admissible cuspidal \(\rho\) of \(G\) has a positive unramified twist that is the smooth module of an irreducible admissible unitary discrete series.

Proof. An endomorphism of an irreducible admissible module is scalar. It preserves a nonzero finite-dimensional compact-open fixed space, has a complex eigenvector there, and the kernel of the corresponding scalar difference is a nonzero invariant subspace. Apply this to each central element. The resulting central character \(\omega\) is smooth, since a compact-open stabilizer of a nonzero vector makes it trivial on the intersection with \(Z\). Its absolute value is trivial on \(\mathcal O_F^\times\), because this compact group has no nontrivial character into the positive real numbers. Hence, for one real \(a\), \[ |\omega(z)|=|z|_F^a,\qquad \chi(g)=|\operatorname{Nrd}(g)|_F^{-a/N},\qquad \pi=\chi\rho,\qquad |\omega_\pi(z)|=1. \tag{6.721} \] Indeed \(\operatorname{Nrd}(zI_r)=z^N\). The twist is trivial on the radicals, so \(\pi\) is still cuspidal, admissible and irreducible, with the same coefficient support property.

The smooth dual is nonzero: choose a nonzero functional on a finite fixed space and compose it with its compact averaging projector. For one such \(\ell\), Lemma 6.310 makes the following integral finite: \[ \|v\|_\ell^2=\int_{G/Z}|\ell(\pi(g)v)|^2\,d\bar g, \qquad C_{\pi(h)v}(g)=C_v(gh),\quad C_v(g)=\ell(\pi(g)v). \tag{6.722} \] Its absolute integrand descends to the quotient because the central character is unitary. The coefficient map has an invariant kernel and is nonzero, so irreducibility makes it injective. It defines a positive definite inner product by polarization. Right translation and unimodularity of \(G/Z\) make it invariant. Smooth vectors give strong continuity on the dense algebraic module; unitarity extends that continuity to its Hilbert completion \(H\).

Compact averaging is a bounded orthogonal projection on \(H\). Its image on the dense original space is the finite-dimensional \(V^J\), already closed, so \[ H^J=V^J,\qquad H^{\mathrm{smooth}}=V. \tag{6.723} \] Every nonzero closed invariant Hilbert subspace has a nonzero smooth vector: sufficiently small compact averages converge to the identity, by strong continuity. Algebraic irreducibility therefore makes \(H\) irreducible. For smooth \(w\), the functional \(v\mapsto\langle v,w\rangle_H\) is in the smooth dual. Lemma 6.310 makes its coefficients compact modulo \(Z\), hence square-integrable. Thus this is a unitary discrete series with exactly the original smooth module; Theorem 6.15 supplies its formal degree. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.312 — compact idempotents and fixed-central-character projectivity. Let \(\rho\) be irreducible admissible cuspidal with central character \(\omega\). There is a compact-mod-centre smooth idempotent \(e_\rho\in\mathcal H_\omega(G)\) such that the actual left ideal \(\mathcal H_\omega(G)e_\rho\) is isomorphic to \(\rho\). In the category of smooth modules with this scalar central character, \(\rho\) is projective.

Proof: the unitary case. First suppose \(\rho\) is unitary, as in Theorem 6.311. Fix a smooth unit vector \(w\) and the formal degree for the chosen quotient Haar measure. With the convention linear in the first inner-product entry, put \[ e(g)=E^\rho_{w,w}(g)=d_\rho\langle w,\rho(g)w\rangle, \qquad e(zg)=\omega(z)^{-1}e(g),\qquad e*e=e=e^*. \tag{6.724} \] Lemma 6.310 makes this an element of the compact Hecke algebra itself. It is bi-invariant by a sufficiently small compact open subgroup fixing \(w\). The identities are exactly the absolutely convergent matrix-unit formulas (6.90). Direct convolution also gives \[ f*e=E^\rho_{\rho(f)w,w},\qquad L_hE^\rho_{u,w}=E^\rho_{\rho(h)u,w}. \tag{6.725} \] In the first formula, move \(\rho(y^{-1})\) from the second entry of the inner product to the first. All integrals have compact quotient support. The Hecke translates of \(w\) span the smooth module: its group translates span by irreducibility, and each translate is realized by a translated compact-subgroup probability test. Schur orthogonality and (6.725) therefore give \[ A e\simeq V_\rho,\quad A=\mathcal H_\omega(G),\qquad \|E^\rho_{u,w}\|_2^2=d_\rho\|u\|^2,\qquad \rho(e)u=\langle u,w\rangle w. \tag{6.726} \] The first identification uses left translation. The coefficient norm proves injectivity and the preceding span proves surjectivity.

Proof: projectivity and twisting. For every smooth module \(X\) with the prescribed scalar centre, evaluation at \(e\) gives \[ \operatorname{Hom}_G(Ae,X)\simeq eX, \qquad x=ex\longmapsto\bigl(ae\mapsto ax\bigr). \tag{6.727} \] The inverse formula is well defined: if \(ae=0\), then \(ax=aex=0\). It is Hecke-linear. Hecke-linear maps of smooth modules are group-linear: for a vector fixed by a compact open \(J\), a translated subgroup probability test realizes its translate by any \(g\), and Hecke-linearity preserves that relation. Conversely group-linearity preserves the finite averages defining Hecke actions. Thus (6.727) is the claimed group-module identification. The functor \(X\mapsto eX\) is exact: lift an element of a quotient and apply \(e\). This proves projectivity.

For a smooth character \(\zeta\) of \(G\), write \(\omega'=\zeta|_Z\omega\). The algebra and module twist are \[ \mathcal H_{\omega'}(G)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal H_\omega(G), \quad f\longmapsto\zeta f,\qquad e_{\zeta\rho}=\zeta^{-1}e_\rho. \tag{6.728} \] Multiplicativity of \(\zeta\) proves compatibility with convolution, and its central rule gives the displayed domain and target. Also \((\zeta\rho)(f)=\rho(\zeta f)\). This is an exact equivalence of the fixed-central-character categories and preserves quotient-compact support. Apply it to the twist in Theorem 6.311 to return to the original \(\rho\). Idempotence and projectivity persist; self-adjointness is asserted for the unitary construction. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.313 — actual isolation among all irreducibles. For any irreducible smooth \(\tau\) with the same scalar central character, \[ \tau(e_\rho)=0\quad(\tau\not\simeq\rho),\qquad \operatorname{rank}\rho(e_\rho)=1,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\tau(e_\rho)=\delta_{\tau,\rho}. \tag{6.729} \]

Proof. The range \(e_\rho V_\tau\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(Ae_\rho,V_\tau)\) by (6.727). Since \(Ae_\rho\simeq\rho\), a nonzero map between the irreducibles is an isomorphism. For \(\tau=\rho\), admissible Schur's lemma makes this Hom space one-dimensional. Thus the idempotent operator is zero or rank one as stated. It is finite rank, so its trace is its rank. Admissibility of \(\tau\) is not needed: a nonzero range would already force \(\tau\simeq\rho\). More generally, for a finite-length smooth module \(X\) with this scalar centre, exactness of \(e_\rho X\) along a composition series shows that its dimension, hence the finite-rank trace of \(X(e_\rho)\), is the number of occurrences of \(\rho\). Thus that trace is a nonnegative integer. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.314 — no cuspidal subquotient of proper induction. Let \(P\ne G\). A cuspidal irreducible admissible \(\rho\) is not a subquotient of \(i_P^GW\) if \(W\) is smooth with a scalar character on \(Z\). The same conclusion holds for every finite-length admissible Levi module \(W\), even with nonscalar central action.

Proof: scalar central action. Since \(\delta_P(z)=1\) for central \(z\), the induction has the same scalar central character as \(W\), and so does any subquotient. If a submodule \(S\) mapped onto \(\rho\), projectivity in that category would split the map. This would give an injection of \(\rho\) into the induction, contradicting normalized Frobenius adjunction, Theorem 6.296: \[ S\twoheadrightarrow\rho\ \Longrightarrow\ \rho\hookrightarrow i_P^GW,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_G(\rho,i_P^GW) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_M(r_P\rho,W)=0. \tag{6.730} \]

Proof: a finite Levi series. Induction is exact for these inner forms as well. The ordinary finite fixed-space coordinates (6.670), proved for every \(\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), reduce surjectivity to exact compact-subgroup invariants, just as in Lemma 6.306. Thus \[ 0\to W'\to W\to W''\to0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0\to i_P^GW'\to i_P^GW\to i_P^GW''\to0 \tag{6.731} \] without a scalar-centre hypothesis. Apply this to a finite composition series of \(W\). Each irreducible factor \(W_j/W_{j-1}\) is admissible and has scalar action of \(Z\), by the compact-averaging quotient argument and the Schur proof in Theorem 6.311. Set \(I_j=i_P^GW_j\).

If \(S\subset I=i_P^GW\) had a surjection \(q:S\to\rho\), intersect with this finite filtration. The subspaces \(q(S\cap I_j)\) are invariant in the irreducible \(\rho\), so each is zero or all of \(\rho\). At the first nonzero index one obtains \[ (S\cap I_j)/(S\cap I_{j-1})\ \hookrightarrow\ I_j/I_{j-1}, \qquad (S\cap I_j)/(S\cap I_{j-1})\ \twoheadrightarrow\rho. \tag{6.732} \] This makes \(\rho\) a subquotient of the scalar-central induced piece, contrary to the first part. Only the finite series of \(W\) was used; no finite-length assertion about arbitrary inner-form induced pieces is needed. \(\square\)

Example 6.315 — a local division algebra in characteristic two. Let \(k=\mathbb F_4\) and \(\sigma(a)=a^2\). Define the skew Laurent series algebra \[ D=k((\Pi;\sigma)),\qquad \Pi a=\sigma(a)\Pi, \qquad \Pi^2=\varpi,\qquad F=\mathbb F_2((\varpi)). \tag{6.733} \] Multiplication of two monomials is \((a\Pi^i)(b\Pi^j)=a\sigma^i(b)\Pi^{i+j}\); the automorphism identity proves associativity. The lowest nonzero exponent is additive under multiplication, since its coefficient is nonzero. Factoring out the leading monomial and inverting the remaining \(1+h\), with positive valuation, by its convergent geometric series proves that every nonzero element is invertible. Commuting with \(k\) forces the exponents in a central series to be even, and commuting with \(\Pi\) forces their coefficients to lie in \(\mathbb F_2\). Thus the centre is \(F\). Writing even and odd terms separately gives \(D=k((\varpi))\oplus k((\varpi))\Pi\), of dimension four over \(F\). This is a degree-two central division algebra.

Over \(L=k((\varpi))\), the matrices \(a\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(a,\sigma(a))\) and \(\Pi\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}0&\varpi\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) respect the relations. After scalar extension they generate all matrix units: an element with \(a\ne\sigma(a)\) separates the diagonal entries, and the displayed \(\Pi\)-matrix supplies both off-diagonal units. They therefore split \(D\), and their determinant gives \[ \operatorname{Nrd}(a+b\Pi)=a\sigma(a)+\varpi b\sigma(b),\qquad v_F(\operatorname{Nrd}x)=v_D(x)\quad(x=a+b\Pi\ne0). \tag{6.734} \] The two terms have valuations \(2v_L(a)\) and \(1+2v_L(b)\), so they cannot cancel when both are nonzero; these are exactly the even and odd leading valuations of \(x\). The one-term cases are immediate.

Its residue field is \(k\). Put \(U^1=1+\Pi\mathcal O_D\). Reduction of units and valuation modulo two give \[ D^\times/(F^\times U^1)\simeq k^\times\rtimes\langle\bar\Pi\rangle \simeq C_3\rtimes C_2\simeq S_3, \qquad \operatorname{vol}(D^\times/F^\times)=2, \qquad\text{mass of each quotient element}=\tfrac13. \tag{6.735} \] The action of \(\Pi\) is squaring, hence inversion on \(C_3\), and its square is scalar. The volume normalization gives the unit quotient \(\mathcal O_D^\times/\mathcal O_F^\times\) mass one; there are two valuation classes and three residue-unit classes. This proves every measure factor in (6.735).

Choose a generator \(\alpha\in k^\times\) and identify its class with \((123)\), and the class of \(\Pi\) with \((12)\). These choices satisfy the inversion relation. Inflate the irreducible sum-zero permutation module of \(S_3\), as in Example 6.305, and use its standard Hermitian norm. It is a two-dimensional irreducible admissible representation \(\rho\) of \(D^\times\), with trivial central character. There are no proper parabolics in division rank one, so it is cuspidal. For \[ W=\{(z_1,z_2,z_3):z_1+z_2+z_3=0\},\qquad w=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1,0),\qquad d_\rho=\frac{\dim W}{\operatorname{vol}(D^\times/F^\times)}=1, \tag{6.736} \] the compact coefficient idempotent is \(e(g)=\langle w,\rho(g)w\rangle\). The degree formula is the compact Schur calculation (6.21), also the rank-one case of Theorem 6.15. On the displayed finite quotient its exact values are \[ \begin{array}{c|rrrrrr} g&1&(12)&(13)&(23)&(123)&(132)\\ e(g)&1&-1&\tfrac12&\tfrac12&-\tfrac12&-\tfrac12. \end{array} \tag{6.737} \] These follow by permuting the coordinates of \(w\). In the basis \(e_1-e_3,e_2-e_3\) of \(W\), the resulting operator is \[ \rho(e)=\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad e*e=e,\qquad \|e\|_2^2=\frac13\sum_{g\in S_3}|e(g)|^2=1, \qquad\operatorname{Tr}\rho(e)=1. \tag{6.738} \] The convolution uses mass \(1/3\) on each quotient element. The trivial and sign modules give zero operators; Corollary 6.313 gives zero on every other irreducible admissible \(D^\times\)-module with this central character, including those not factoring through this finite quotient. All coefficients and projections are over \(\mathbb C\); the fractions do not take place in \(F\).

More generally, for a rank-one \(D^\times\) representation of dimension \(m\) and unitary central character, with quotient volume \(V_D\), \[ d_\rho=\frac m{V_D},\qquad e(1)=\frac m{V_D}, \qquad\operatorname{rank}\rho(e)=1. \tag{6.739} \] Such an irreducible admissible representation is finite-dimensional: compactness of \(D^\times/Z\) gives finitely many \(Zg_iJ\) covering \(D^\times\), for a subgroup fixing a cyclic vector; its translates span finitely many vectors up to central scalars. Thus the rank-one operator assertion does not identify the representation's dimension with one.

Example 6.316 — why the scalar centre matters. For \(G=F^\times\), a character \(\eta\) is projective in the category where the whole group acts by that scalar character. In the unrestricted smooth category the representation \[ E(z)=\eta(z)\begin{pmatrix}1&v_F(z)\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad 0\longrightarrow\eta\longrightarrow E \longrightarrow\eta\longrightarrow0 \tag{6.740} \] is a nonsplit extension, as in Solution 7.36. Its uniformizer operator satisfies \[ \operatorname{rank}\bigl(E(\varpi_F)-\eta(\varpi_F)I\bigr)=1, \qquad \ker\bigl(E(\varpi_F)-\eta(\varpi_F)I\bigr)=\mathbb Ce_1. \tag{6.741} \] The sole eigenline is the given submodule, so no invariant complementary line splits the quotient. If \(\eta\) were projective in that larger category, this surjection would split. Theorem 6.312 therefore uses exactly its stated fixed-scalar-centre category. The idempotents of Theorem 6.312 isolate cuspidal representations. No projector for a noncuspidal discrete series, or integral realization of a transfer expansion, is asserted here.

6.51 Geometric Jacquet quotients and cuspidal inducing data

Let \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\), with \(D/F\) central division of degree \(d\), over a nonarchimedean local field of either characteristic. Fix standard parabolics \(P=MN\) and \(Q=LU\). The functor to be computed is \(r_P^G i_Q^G\): induction has left \(Q\)-covariance and right group action. All section spaces and coinvariants below are algebraic smooth complex modules. Compact support on a homogeneous space means compact support in that quotient, with the specified fibre covariance.

Lemma 6.317 — two division flags and their section filtration. The \(P\)-orbits on \(Q\backslash G\) are indexed by nonnegative integer matrices \(C=(c_{ab})\) whose row sums are the division block dimensions of \(L\) and whose column sums are those of \(M\). Each orbit is locally closed and has a representative \(Qw\) for a permutation matrix \(w\). The induced module restricted to \(P\) has a finite filtration by support whose orbit quotients are compactly induced from \(H=P\cap w^{-1}Qw\).

Proof: flags and representatives. Let \(E_b\) be the cumulative standard \(P\)-flag in the right \(D\)-space \(D^r\). A point \(Qg\) gives the flag \(F_a=g^{-1}E^Q_a\); right \(P\)-translation acts on this flag by inverse linear maps preserving \(E\). Put \(t_{ab}=\dim_D(F_a\cap E_b)\), with zero boundary indices. Then \[ c_{ab}=t_{ab}-t_{a-1,b}-t_{a,b-1}+t_{a-1,b-1},\qquad \sum_b c_{ab}=\dim_D(F_a/F_{a-1}),\quad \sum_a c_{ab}=\dim_D(E_b/E_{b-1}). \tag{6.742} \] These numbers are nonnegative. Choose a complement \(V_{ab}\) to \((F_{a-1}\cap E_b)+(F_a\cap E_{b-1})\) in \(F_a\cap E_b\). The two summands intersect in \(F_{a-1}\cap E_{b-1}\). Induction on \(a+b\) gives \(F_a\cap E_b=\bigoplus_{i\le a,j\le b}V_{ij}\), and \(\dim_D V_{ab}=c_{ab}\). Choosing bases of these complements gives a simultaneous adapted basis of both flags. Thus the matrix determines the orbit. Conversely a direct sum of coordinate spaces of the stated dimensions constructs that orbit.

Choose the representative by ordering the summands within each \(P\)-block by their \(Q\)-labels, and within each \(Q\)-block by their \(P\)-labels. Match the ordered bases. This gives a permutation \(w\); its index subsets have both labels. Write \(p_i=b\) for the target \(P\)-block and \(q_i=a\) for the \(Q\)-block containing \(w(i)\). Define \[ \begin{gathered} H=P\cap w^{-1}Qw,\quad H_N=H\cap N,\quad R=M\cap w^{-1}Qw,\quad S=L\cap wPw^{-1},\\ T=M\cap w^{-1}Lw\simeq\prod_{a,b:c_{ab}>0}\mathrm{GL}_{c_{ab}}(D). \end{gathered} \tag{6.743} \] The matrix entries allowed in \(H\) satisfy both \(p_i\le p_j\) and \(q_i\le q_j\). Its diagonal \(P\)-blocks are invertible upper block-triangular matrices in the \(q\)-order, so their block-diagonal projection lies in \(R\). Factoring out that projection proves \[ H=R\ltimes H_N,\qquad H_N\longrightarrow N_S\text{ is onto under the }L\text{-projection of }whw^{-1}, \qquad\ker=H_N\cap w^{-1}Uw. \tag{6.744} \] Indeed \(H_N\) has entries \(p_i<p_j,\ q_i\le q_j\). Its entries with equal \(q\)-label form exactly the radical of \(S\); set all other off-diagonal entries to zero to lift that radical. The unequal-label entries are the kernel. In particular \(R\) is parabolic in \(M\) with Levi \(T\), and \(S\) is parabolic in \(L\) with Levi \(wTw^{-1}\). These facts use invertible division blocks, so no commutativity of \(D\) is assumed.

Proof: topology and sections. The conditions \(t_{ab}\ge k\) are closed. In a flag chart, an intersection is the kernel of a matrix over \(D\); after choosing an \(F\)-basis of \(D\), its rank is a constant multiple of its division rank, and the ordinary \(F\)-matrix minors prove the closedness. Gaussian elimination over \(D\), at fixed nonzero pivots, uses addition, multiplication and inversion, all continuous. It gives charts for each rank stratum and continuous local sections of \(H\backslash P\to Q\backslash QwP\). The adapted-basis classification therefore identifies this orbit, with its topology, with \(H\backslash P\), not just with a set of flags.

Order the finitely many feasible intersection tuples by a linear extension of their componentwise order, smallest first. A lower ideal is open: it is a finite union of sets on which every \(t_{ab}\) is bounded above, which are open by the preceding closed-rank criterion. Thus the successive unions \(X_j\) of the first \(j\) orbits are open, and the new orbit \(O_j=X_j\setminus X_{j-1}\) is closed in \(X_j\). The flag space is compact by division Iwasawa, Lemma 6.40. Its associated bundle with fibre \(W\) has locally constant vector sections in Gaussian charts: the transition maps act locally constantly on each fixed vector, by smoothness of \(W\).

Restriction to a closed subset of a chart is onto for compactly supported locally constant sections. To see this, cover the compact support by finitely many compact open chart neighborhoods on whose closed-subset intersections the section is a fixed vector. Refine their union to a disjoint compact open partition and extend those vectors there, taking zero elsewhere. This preserves compact support and gives the required section. A section restricting to zero has support compactly contained in the open complement. Consequently \[ \begin{gathered} 0\longrightarrow C_c(X_{j-1},W)\longrightarrow C_c(X_j,W) \longrightarrow C_c(O_j,W)\longrightarrow0,\\ C_c(O_j,W)\simeq\operatorname{c-Ind}_{H}^{P}\eta_w, \qquad \eta_w(h)=\delta_Q(whw^{-1})^{1/2}\tau(whw^{-1}). \end{gathered} \tag{6.745} \] Here \(\tau\) is inflated from \(L\) to \(Q\). Evaluation on \(wp\) gives the last covariance. Conversely that covariance defines the orbit section. Compact support and smoothness agree in the quotient charts; a finite cover of a compact support supplies a common open right stabilizer. This proves the filtration and its module identifications. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.318 — an untwisted algebraic fibre integral. Let \(N\) be a division upper-block unipotent group, let \(H_0\subset N\) be closed, and let \(W\) be a smooth \(H_0\)-module. Choose Haar measures and the induced quotient measure. Then \[ Y=\operatorname{c-Ind}_{H_0}^{N}W,\qquad q:Y\longrightarrow W_{H_0},\quad q(y)=\int_{H_0\backslash N}[y(n)]\,d\bar n, \qquad Y_N\simeq W_{H_0}. \tag{6.746} \] The kernel is the algebraic span of right \(N\)-translation differences.

Proof. A strictly contracting central diagonal for the block radical gives an increasing exhaustion by compact open groups \(K_j=a^{-j}K_0a^j\). Rectangular entry valuations show that these groups contain every compact subset of \(N\). Their intersections exhaust \(H_0\). Both groups are unimodular, since each element belongs to a compact subgroup and the modular character is trivial there. The quotient measure is constructed on the compact open images of \(K_j\) by dividing their Haar measures by \(\operatorname{vol}(H_0\cap K_j)\). Nested-index cancellation makes these measures agree, and right invariance follows in a larger compact group. This is also the quotient construction in Lemma 6.292, now with trivial character and division entries.

The integrand is well defined in \(W_{H_0}\), is locally constant and has compact support, so its integral is a finite vector-space sum. It is unchanged by right translation. Given \(y\), take \(K\) in the exhaustion with support contained in \(H_0K\), average \(y\) on the right over \(K\), and put \(v=(E_Ky)(1)\). Then \[ (E_Ky)(hk)=h v,\quad v\in W^{H_0\cap K},\qquad q(y)=\frac{\operatorname{vol}K}{\operatorname{vol}(H_0\cap K)}[v]. \tag{6.747} \] If this is zero, the finite-relation averaging criterion makes \(E_{H_0\cap L}v=0\) for a sufficiently large compact open \(L\supset K\). The criterion follows directly by writing \(v\) as a finite sum of \(hw-w\) and choosing one compact subgroup containing those finitely many \(h\)'s; averaging kills each difference. Quotient integration gives \[ (E_LE_Ky)(1)= \frac{\operatorname{vol}K\operatorname{vol}(H_0\cap L)} {\operatorname{vol}L\operatorname{vol}(H_0\cap K)}E_{H_0\cap L}v=0. \tag{6.748} \] The averaged section is supported in \(H_0L\) and determined by this value, hence is zero. Averaging differences are finite sums of translation differences because compact orbits of smooth vectors are finite. This proves the kernel assertion. Conversely, lift any vector of \(W_{H_0}\) to \(w\in W\), choose a sufficiently small compact open \(K\subset N\) with \(H_0\cap K\) fixing \(w\), and define \(y(hk)=hw\) on \(H_0K\), zero elsewhere. It is well defined and smooth, and (6.747), after a nonzero scalar rescaling, gives the desired quotient vector. Thus \(q\) is onto and proves (6.746). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.319 — uniformity over the compact Levi flag. Suppose \(P=M\ltimes N\), \(H=R\ltimes H_0\), where \(R\) is parabolic in \(M\) and normalizes \(H_0\). Assume \(H_0\) is a unipotent division-block pattern subgroup, as in (6.744): its allowed root entries are closed under root addition. Let \(\eta\) be any smooth \(H\)-module. Put \(Y=\operatorname{c-Ind}_{H_0}^N\eta\). Then the \(N\)-quotient of \(\operatorname{c-Ind}_H^P\eta\), with its ordinary \(M\)-action, is \[ \bigl(\operatorname{c-Ind}_H^P\eta\bigr)_N \simeq\operatorname{c-Ind}_{R}^{M} \bigl(\kappa\otimes\eta_{H_0}\bigr),\qquad \kappa(r)=\frac{\delta_N(r)}{\delta_{H_0}(r)},\quad \delta_A(r)=|\det_F(\operatorname{Ad}(r)|_{\operatorname{Lie}A})|_F. \tag{6.749} \] The fibre integral defining this map is onto, and its kernel is exactly the algebraic \(N\)-relation space.

Proof: sections in stages. Write \(\mathcal F_f(m)(n)=f(nm)\). Substitution gives \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{c-Ind}_{H}^{P}\eta&\simeq\operatorname{c-Ind}_{R}^{M}Y,& (r\cdot y)(n)&=\eta(r)y(r^{-1}nr),\\ \mathcal F_{\pi(n_0)f}(m)&=R_{mn_0m^{-1}}\mathcal F_f(m),& \mathcal F_{\pi(m_0)f}(m)&=\mathcal F_f(mm_0). \end{aligned} \tag{6.750} \] For completeness, the first map and its inverse \(f(nm)=\mathcal F(m)(n)\) preserve the actual smooth section spaces. Compact support restricts on each fibre to compact \(H_0\)-quotient support. A section on \(M\) has a finite compact open cover of its support modulo \(R\), and hence finitely many values \(y_i\in Y\) on compact sets \(C_i\subset M\) of representatives, after choosing a common open right stabilizer. The corresponding \(f\) has support in the image of a finite union of compact products of their fibre supports and \(C_i\)'s. Continuity of conjugation and compactness of the \(C_i\)'s give one open subgroup of \(N\) whose conjugates by every \(m\in C_i\) fix \(y_i\). Together with the open right stabilizer in \(M\), it gives an open stabilizer in \(P\). The reverse smoothness follows by restriction. The displayed \(R\)-action on \(Y\) is smooth explicitly as follows. Choose a compact open \(K\subset N\) fixing \(y\) on the right, and finitely many cosets \(H_0n_iK\) covering its support, with values \(w_i=y(n_i)\). A sufficiently small open subgroup of \(R\) normalizes \(K\), fixes all \(w_i\) under \(\eta\), and satisfies \(r^{-1}n_ir\in n_iK\) for every \(i\). Existence of the normalizing neighborhood follows from continuity on the compact set \(K\), then the same condition for inverses; the remaining conditions are finitely many open conditions. Such elements preserve each support coset and its complement, and the formula in (6.750) makes them fix \(y\) there by \(H_0\)-covariance. Thus the stabilizer is open.

Ordinary compact induction from \(R\) to \(M\) is exact even for smooth \(R\)-modules on which its radical is not trivial. Indeed \(R\backslash M\) is compact. At any compact open right level \(J\), there are finitely many double cosets \(Rm_iJ\), and the section values form \(\bigoplus_iY^{R\cap m_iJm_i^{-1}}\). These are invariants under compact groups, so surjections lift by compact averaging. The union over right levels gives exactness of the full section functor. This proof does not assume admissibility or an equivariant section of a quotient map.

Apply that exact functor to the quotient \(q:Y\to\eta_{H_0}\) of Lemma 6.318. Change of variables on \(H_0\backslash N\) gives \[ q(r\cdot y)=\kappa(r)\eta(r)q(y),\qquad f\longmapsto\left(m\longmapsto\int_{H_0\backslash N}[f(nm)]\,d\bar n\right). \tag{6.751} \] Here conjugation scales quotient Haar measure by the ratio in (6.749). This follows directly in ordered unipotent block coordinates: the coordinate multiplication is triangular with diagonal one, conjugation has the indicated linear block determinants, and quotient integration divides the two factors. It holds for the unipotent radical of \(R\) too; its determinants are one.

Proof: the uniform kernel. The induced map is onto by the exactness just proved. If it kills \(f\), the finitely many values \(y_i\) on the compact representative sets \(C_i\) lie in \(\ker q\). By Lemma 6.318, choose compact open \(K_i\subset N\) with \(E_{K_i}y_i=0\). The union of the compact sets \[ \bigcup_i\{m^{-1}km:m\in C_i,\ k\in K_i\} \tag{6.752} \] is compact in \(N\), and therefore lies in one member \(K\) of its increasing compact exhaustion. For \(m\in C_i\), the group \(mKm^{-1}\) contains \(K_i\); its probability average kills \(y_i\) by nesting of compact averages. Formula (6.750) now gives \(E_Kf=0\) on all these representatives and hence everywhere by covariance. Thus \(f\) is an algebraic sum of \(N\)-translation differences. Conversely (6.751) kills each such difference by right invariance of the quotient measure. This proves the exact kernel and (6.749). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.320 — the normalized geometric Jacquet filtration. For every smooth \(L\)-module \(\tau\), the \(M\)-module \(r_P^G i_Q^G\tau\) has a finite natural filtration with one quotient for each matrix in Lemma 6.317. With its representative and intersections as in (6.743), that quotient is \[ i_R^M\bigl(w^{-1}r_S^L\tau\bigr). \tag{6.753} \] Transport by \(w^{-1}\) means that \(t\in T\) acts by the normalized \(S\)-Jacquet action of \(wtw^{-1}\). This is a filtration, with no asserted splitting.

Proof: the actual map. Apply exact \(N\)-coinvariants to the finite support filtration (6.745). Exactness is the compact-exhaustion averaging proof of Lemma 6.251 and applies to these division radicals. On a cell, Lemmas 6.318–6.319 apply with \(H_0=H_N\) and \(\eta=\eta_w\). By (6.744) the fibre quotient is precisely the unnormalized \(N_S\)-quotient of \(\tau\). The map, including the normalization of \(r_P\), is \[ \Phi_f(m)=\delta_P(m)^{-1/2} \int_{H_N\backslash N}[f(nm)]\,d\bar n. \tag{6.754} \] It is defined on compact cell sections, is onto, and has exactly the cell Jacquet kernel by Lemma 6.319. It is not asserted as a convergent formula on arbitrary sections of the full induction.

Proof: every modulus factor. Write \(\delta_{H_N}(t)\) for the determinant of conjugation on its unipotent root spaces. The ordinary integral \(F_f\) before the factor \(\delta_P(m)^{-1/2}\) satisfies, on \(t\in T\), \[ F_f(tm)=\frac{\delta_P(t)}{\delta_{H_N}(t)} \delta_Q(wtw^{-1})^{1/2}\delta_S(wtw^{-1})^{1/2} (w^{-1}r_S\tau)(t)F_f(m). \tag{6.755} \] The last half-modulus converts the unnormalized \(S\)-quotient into its normalized action. The required identity is \[ \delta_P(t)\delta_Q(wtw^{-1})\delta_S(wtw^{-1}) =\delta_R(t)\delta_{H_N}(t)^2. \tag{6.756} \] Here is a direct division-block verification, for the full Levi \(T\). On a rectangular block between factors of sizes \(u,v\), conjugation is \(X\mapsto AXB^{-1}\), and \[ |\det_F(X\mapsto AXB^{-1})| =|\operatorname{Nrd}A|_F^{dv}|\operatorname{Nrd}B|_F^{-du}. \tag{6.757} \] To prove this, extend scalars to a splitting field in the definition of reduced norm. The rectangle becomes an \(ud\)-by-\(vd\) matrix space. Left multiplication repeats its determinant \(vd\) times, and right multiplication repeats its inverse determinant \(ud\) times. Determinants of an \(F\)-linear map commute with this scalar extension, proving the identity over \(F\) itself. This argument is algebraic in either characteristic.

For two distinct intersection blocks, compare their \(p\)- and \(q\)-labels. The root conditions for the five moduli in (6.756) are, respectively, \(p_i<p_j\), \(q_i<q_j\), \(q_i=q_j,\ p_i<p_j\), \(p_i=p_j,\ q_i<q_j\), and \(p_i<p_j,\ q_i\le q_j\). If both orders are strict and agree, \(P\) and \(Q\) contribute twice the \(H_N\) factor. If the \(q\)-labels agree, \(P\) and \(S\) do so. If the orders are opposite, the \(P\)- and \(Q\)-factors are inverse, by (6.757). If the \(p\)-labels agree, the \(Q\)-factor equals the \(R\)-factor. Equal labels in both contribute nothing. Multiplying these identities over unordered pairs of blocks proves (6.756), for arbitrary \(A,B\) and not merely diagonal scalar samples.

Substituting (6.756) into (6.755) proves \[ \Phi_f(tm)=\delta_R(t)^{1/2}(w^{-1}r_S\tau)(t)\Phi_f(m),\qquad \Phi_{\,r_P(m_0)f}(m)=\Phi_f(mm_0). \tag{6.758} \] The radical of \(R\) acts trivially in this covariance: it maps into \(U\), and every relevant modulus on it is one. The second identity follows because the action of \(r_P(m_0)\) includes \(\delta_P(m_0)^{-1/2}\), exactly cancelling the change from \(m\) to \(mm_0\) in (6.754). Thus the cell quotient is (6.753). Combining the cell maps through exact coinvariants proves the theorem. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.321 — cuspidal embeddings for division groups and separation in their products. Every irreducible admissible \(\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\)-module embeds into induction from an irreducible admissible cuspidal module on a standard Levi. For a finite product of division general-linear groups, an irreducible admissible cuspidal module is projective at its fixed scalar full central character and is not a subquotient of induction from a proper parabolic with scalar action of that centre.

Proof: embeddings. The maximal-block argument of Theorem 6.307 applies with the following division-group inputs, which also give a direct proof. A cyclic admissible \(V\) has finitely generated admissible \(r_PV\), by Lemmas 6.40 and 6.22. Choose \(P\) with the most Levi blocks among those with \(r_PV\ne0\). A finitely generated nonzero module has an irreducible quotient by the chain-union and Zorn argument in Theorem 6.307. Let that quotient be \(\sigma\); exact compact invariants make it admissible. Refining any proper parabolic of \(M\) increases the number of blocks, so \[ r_PV\twoheadrightarrow\sigma,\qquad r_A^M\sigma=0\ (A\ne M),\qquad V\hookrightarrow i_P^G\sigma. \tag{6.759} \] The last injection is the nonzero map furnished by normalized Frobenius, Theorem 6.296; its kernel is zero by irreducibility.

The normalized refinement identity used here is valid over \(D\). For a parabolic with division block sizes \(r_i\), (6.757) gives \[ \delta_P(m)=\prod_{i<j}|\operatorname{Nrd}m_i|_F^{d r_j} |\operatorname{Nrd}m_j|_F^{-d r_i}, \qquad r_A^M r_P^G=r_{P_A}^G. \tag{6.760} \] The old radical is normal in the refined one and the quotient is the new Levi radical; taking their algebraic relations in that order gives the same quotient. Partitioning the rectangular blocks multiplies the two moduli into the refined modulus, proving the second identity including normalization. Compact averaging proves the exactness used on \(r_PV\twoheadrightarrow\sigma\). These arguments impose neither characteristic zero nor a scalar centre on \(r_PV\).

The general local-unit tensor factorization of Lesson 12, Theorem 4.1, applies to the finite product Levi: the Hecke algebra is the tensor product by finite compact-open rectangle partitions, product averaging gives its local units, and admissibility makes their ranges finite-dimensional. It gives \(\sigma=\bigotimes_i\sigma_i\) with irreducible admissible factors. Jacquet relations for a product give the tensor product of its quotients: telescope each product-action difference one factor at a time. If any \(\sigma_i\) had a nonzero proper Jacquet quotient, this identity would contradict \(r_A\sigma=0\). Thus the factors are cuspidal, proving the embedding assertion in every division rank.

Proof: product projectors and separation. Write a cuspidal product module as \(\sigma=\bigotimes_i\sigma_i\), and use Theorem 6.312 in each factor. The scalar central character is a character of the entire product centre \(Z_M\). With the product Haar measure, \[ e_\sigma=\bigotimes_i e_{\sigma_i},\qquad \mathcal H_{\omega_M}(M)e_\sigma\simeq\sigma,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}_M(\sigma,X)\simeq e_\sigma X. \tag{6.761} \] Compact quotient support and multiplication factor on the rectangles, proving these identities directly from (6.726)–(6.727). The last functor is exact, so \(\sigma\) is projective in the prescribed scalar-central-character category. The natural Frobenius maps of Theorem 6.296 may be applied in each factor, with all other actions commuting. They give first Frobenius adjunction for a product parabolic and arbitrary smooth inducing module. A proper product Jacquet module of \(\sigma\) is zero by the tensor relation identity. Therefore, exactly as in (6.730), \[ \operatorname{Hom}_M(\sigma,i_A^M W) =\operatorname{Hom}_{M_A}(r_A\sigma,W)=0\quad(A\ne M). \tag{6.762} \] If a submodule of that induction surjected onto \(\sigma\), fixed-central-character projectivity would split it and contradict (6.762). This proves the product separation assertion. No finite-length theorem for arbitrary inner-form induction is needed. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.322 — uniqueness of cuspidal data of every irreducible subquotient. Let \(\tau\) be an irreducible admissible cuspidal module of \(L\), and let \(V\) be an irreducible subquotient of \(i_Q^G\tau\). If \(V\hookrightarrow i_P^G\sigma\) is a cuspidal embedding with irreducible admissible cuspidal \(\sigma\) on \(M\), then for one permutation representative, \[ w^{-1}Lw=M,\qquad \sigma\simeq w^{-1}\tau. \tag{6.763} \] In particular every irreducible admissible \(G\)-module has a uniquely determined cuspidal inducing datum up to conjugation by a permutation of its division blocks. This is the datum of an embedding, and also that of any cuspidal induction in which it occurs as a subquotient.

Proof. Induction of an admissible Levi module is admissible by the finite compact fixed-space coordinates (6.670). Submodules and quotients of admissible modules are admissible, since compact averaging is exact. Thus the given \(V\) is admissible and has a cuspidal embedding by Theorem 6.321. Frobenius applied to the specified embedding gives a nonzero, hence surjective, map \(r_PV\to\sigma\). Exactness and the subquotient hypothesis imply \[ \sigma\text{ is a subquotient of }r_PV, \qquad r_PV\text{ is a subquotient of }r_P i_Q^G\tau. \tag{6.764} \] Subquotients are transitive: take inverse images of the numerator and denominator under the preceding surjection. In a finite filtration, an irreducible subquotient is a subquotient of one layer. Indeed, intersect its numerator with the filtration and take the first index whose image under the quotient map is nonzero; that image is the whole irreducible module. This is the intersection argument in (6.732), without any length assumption on the layers.

Apply it to Theorem 6.320. If \(S\ne L\), cuspidality of \(\tau\) makes the layer zero. For \(S=L\), (6.744) or its two-label description shows \(w^{-1}Lw\subset M\): within each \(Q\)-block, both directions are allowed only if the \(P\)-labels agree. Thus the layer is \(i_R^M(w^{-1}\tau)\), whose inducing Levi is \(w^{-1}Lw=T\). Its centre \(Z_M\) lies in \(Z_T\), so \(w^{-1}\tau\), and therefore this induction, have scalar action of \(Z_M\). If \(R\ne M\), Theorem 6.321 excludes the cuspidal \(\sigma\) as a subquotient. Hence \(R=M=T\). The surviving layer is the irreducible \(w^{-1}\tau\) itself, proving (6.763). Applied to any two cuspidal embeddings of the same \(V\), this gives uniqueness; existence was already proved. It does not assert isomorphism of inductions in different orders, a converse common-subquotient statement, or an irreducibility criterion. \(\square\)

Example 6.323 — the two cells for division block sizes \((2,1)\) and \((1,2)\). Take the target \(P\) with Levi \(\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\times D^\times\) and the source \(Q\) with Levi \(D^\times\times\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\). There are exactly two transport matrices and representatives, in one-line permutation notation: \[ C_{\mathrm o}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\2&0\end{pmatrix},\quad w_{\mathrm o}=(2,3,1), \qquad C_{\mathrm c}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad w_{\mathrm c}=(1,2,3). \tag{6.765} \] The open cell has \(F_1\cap E_1=0\); the closed cell has \(F_1\subset E_1\). Here \(F_1\) is a line and \(E_1\) a plane over \(D\). For the open cell, \(H_N=1,R=M,S=L\). For the closed cell, \(H_N=N\), \(R=B_2(D)\times D^\times\) and \(S=D^\times\times B_2(D)\). These follow directly from the labels \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c|c} &p&q&\text{roots of }H_N\\ \hline \mathrm o&(1,1,2)&(2,2,1)&\varnothing\\ \mathrm c&(1,1,2)&(1,2,2)&\{(1,3),(2,3)\}. \end{array} \tag{6.766} \] For the closed cell on field scalars \(a,b,c\), put \(A=v_F(a),B=v_F(b),C=v_F(c)\), and \(|\varpi_F|=q_F^{-1}\). Record moduli as powers of \(q_F\). Then \[ \begin{aligned} \delta_P&=q_F^{-d^2(A+B-2C)},& \delta_Q&=q_F^{-d^2(2A-B-C)},\\ \delta_S&=q_F^{-d^2(B-C)},& \delta_R&=q_F^{-d^2(A-B)},&\delta_{H_N}&=\delta_P. \end{aligned} \tag{6.767} \] For example, \((A,B,C)=(2,-1,3)\), \(d=2\), gives exponents \(20,-8,16,-12,20\); hence \(20-8+16=-12+2\cdot20\). In the open cell the source modulus is the inverse of the target modulus and \(\kappa=\delta_P\), so (6.754) again gives no remaining character.

Let \(\tau=\chi\otimes\rho\), where \(\chi\) is irreducible admissible on \(D^\times\) and \(\rho\) is irreducible admissible cuspidal on \(\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\). There is no proper parabolic in \(D^\times\), so \(\chi\) is cuspidal. The closed layer vanishes because it takes the proper \(B_2(D)\)-Jacquet module of \(\rho\). The sole remaining layer gives an actual isomorphism \[ r_{(2,1)}^G i_{(1,2)}^G(\chi\otimes\rho) \simeq\rho\otimes\chi. \tag{6.768} \] This computation supplies no irreducibility assertion for the full induction.

The flag geometry can also be counted over a finite residue field \(k_D\) of size \(q_D\). Among the \(q_D^2+q_D+1\) lines in \(k_D^3\), \(q_D+1\) lie in a fixed plane and \(q_D^2\) do not. The numerator counts nonzero vectors and division by \(q_D-1\) identifies scalar multiples. Thus \[ \#O_{\mathrm c}(k_D)=q_D+1,\qquad \#O_{\mathrm o}(k_D)=q_D^2,\qquad (q_D=2):\ (3,4),\quad(q_D=3):\ (4,9). \tag{6.769} \] These finite counts describe the residue flags; they are not the local quotient Haar volumes.

Theorem 6.324 — finite length of cuspidal induction in every division rank. If \(\tau=\bigotimes_{i=1}^s\tau_i\) is irreducible admissible cuspidal on a Levi with \(s\) labelled division blocks, then \(I=i_Q^G\tau\) has finite composition length at most \(s!\). Repeated or isomorphic factors retain their labels in this bound.

Proof: the associated Jacquet modules. Let \(\mathcal A(L)\) be the finite set of standard parabolics whose ordered division block sizes are permutations of those of \(L\). For \(A=M_A N_A\) in this set, Theorem 6.320 gives a filtration of \(r_A I\). Proper source Jacquet modules vanish. In a remaining layer, every source block is whole inside a target block. There are \(s\) source and \(s\) target blocks, all nonempty, so each target contains exactly one source block. Consequently every nonzero layer is the irreducible transported \(\tau\), with no induction left inside \(M_A\). Thus \[ \ell(r_A I)=\#\{w\text{ in the cell representatives}:w^{-1}Lw=M_A\}, \qquad \sum_{A\in\mathcal A(L)}\ell(r_A I)=s!. \tag{6.770} \] The count follows directly from (6.742): choose an ordering of the \(s\) labelled source blocks; their sizes determine \(A\), and their assignment to those target blocks determines the transport matrix. Conversely every nonzero associated cell arises this way. Identical sizes or representations do not remove their separate cells. Length is additive along the finite filtration, so this counts multiplicity and requires no splitting or scalar action of \(Z_{M_A}\) on the whole Jacquet module.

For every subquotient \(X\) of \(I\), define \[ D_I(X)=\sum_{A\in\mathcal A(L)}\ell(r_A X),\qquad D_I(I)=s!,\qquad D_I(X)=D_I(X')+D_I(X'') \tag{6.771} \] whenever \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\) is exact with these terms subquotients of \(I\). Each summand is finite, because exact Jacquet functors make \(r_A X\) a subquotient of the already finite-length \(r_A I\). Their exactness proves additivity.

Proof: detection and composition length. If \(X\ne0\), take a nonzero vector and its cyclic submodule. A cyclic module has an irreducible quotient by the finite-generation Zorn argument. That quotient \(V\) is an irreducible subquotient of \(I\), hence admissible. By Theorems 6.321–6.322, its cuspidal embedding uses a parabolic \(A\in\mathcal A(L)\). Frobenius makes \(r_A V\ne0\), and exactness then makes \(r_A X\ne0\). Therefore \(D_I(X)\ge1\). A strict chain in \(I\) now satisfies \[ 0=X_0\subsetneq X_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq X_t=I \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t\le\sum_{j=1}^tD_I(X_j/X_{j-1})=s!, \qquad \ell(I)\le s!. \tag{6.772} \] Starting with \(0\subset I\), refine any reducible layer. The bound forces this process to stop with irreducible layers, proving finite length and its stated bound. This proof does not assume finite length in order to choose the irreducible subquotient: only a cyclic submodule and its maximal proper quotient were used. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.325 — finite-length induction and Jacquet modules for inner forms. Induction of every finite-length admissible Levi module has finite length. Jacquet modules of every finite-length admissible \(G\)-module also have finite length. These assertions hold for every \(D\) and both field characteristics.

Proof. For an irreducible admissible Levi module \(W\), factor it into its division general-linear factors by Lesson 12, Theorem 4.1, and embed each factor into a cuspidal induction using Theorem 6.321. Tensoring these injections and inducing gives an actual injection into a cuspidal induction on \(G\). Here are the required functor identifications over \(D\). Product sections identify product inductions on each product compact-open fixed space: the coordinates (6.670) are finite sums of tensor-product fixed spaces, with product compact averaging; their union gives the full algebraic identification. Induction is exact without a scalar-centre restriction by (6.731). Finally refinement is transitive with the explicit inverse \[ i_P^G i_B^M W_0\simeq i_{P_B}^G W_0,\qquad F(g)(m)=\delta_P(m)^{-1/2}f(mg),\qquad i_P^G W\hookrightarrow i_{P'}^G\rho_{\mathrm{cusp}}. \tag{6.773} \] Here \(P'\) is the standard parabolic refining the chosen factor parabolics. The covariance and inverse evaluation \(f(g)=F(g)(1)\) are proved by the modulus product in (6.760); radical relations and right smoothness are verified exactly by these substitutions. All the division flag spaces are compact, so there is no extra support condition. This proves the injection without invoking any inner-form mirabolic theory. Theorem 6.324 bounds its target length by \(s!\), with \(s\le r\) the number of chosen cuspidal factors. For a finite-length \(W\), induce its finite composition series using exactness, and apply this construction to each irreducible factor. Thus \[ \ell(i_P^G W)\le\sum_{a=1}^{\ell(W)}s_a! \le\ell(W)r!. \tag{6.774} \] No scalar central character on \(W\) is required.

For the Jacquet assertion first take irreducible admissible \(V\), embed it in a cuspidal induction, and apply an exact Jacquet functor. Its target has the finite geometric filtration of Theorem 6.320. Proper source Jacquet terms vanish. Each remaining term is an induction of a cuspidal module inside a product Levi. Product sections factor that induction into inductions in the individual division general-linear factors. Each has finite length by Theorem 6.324, so their external tensor product has finite length: tensor the finite series, use exactness over \(\mathbb C\), and use the irreducible product factorization on the resulting admissible simple factors. The geometric filtration is therefore finite length, as is its submodule \(r_A V\). For finite-length admissible \(V\), apply exact Jacquet functors to a composition series. This proves the general assertion. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.326 — conjugate cuspidal data, common constituents and intertwining. For two inductions \(I=i_Q^G\tau\) and \(J=i_P^G\sigma\) from irreducible admissible cuspidal data, the following are equivalent: their data are conjugate by a division-block permutation; \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(I,J)\ne0\); they have a common irreducible subquotient. Moreover the intertwining space is finite-dimensional, with the multiplicity bound stated below. No isomorphism of the full inductions or equality of all their composition multiplicities is asserted.

Proof: extensions between distinct cuspidals. In a product Levi, let \(\alpha\not\simeq\beta\) be irreducible admissible cuspidals. Every extension \(0\to\alpha\to E\to\beta\to0\) splits. If their central characters differ, choose a central \(z\) with values \(a\ne b\) and put \(T=\pi_E(z)\). Then \[ (T-a)(T-b)=0,\qquad p=\frac{T-b}{a-b},\qquad p^2=p,\quad pE=\alpha,\quad E=\alpha\oplus\ker p. \tag{6.775} \] Indeed \(T-b\) maps into \(\alpha\), where \(T-a=0\), and \(p\) restricts to the identity on \(\alpha\). All these operators commute with the group. If the characters agree, then for every central \(z\), \[ T_z-\omega(z)I\text{ factors through a group map }\beta\longrightarrow\alpha, \qquad T_z=\omega(z)I. \tag{6.776} \] The map is zero because the irreducibles are nonisomorphic. Thus \(E\) really belongs to the fixed-scalar-central-character category. Projectivity of \(\beta\), Theorem 6.321, splits the extension there. This use of projectivity permits no arbitrary central Jordan action.

It follows that a finite-length module all of whose constituents are admissible cuspidals is a direct sum of modules, each with just one irreducible isomorphism type among its constituents. Here are elementary induction details. An extension of a simple \(\beta\) by a finite-length module with no \(\beta\) constituent splits: quotient the kernel by its penultimate composition submodule, split the resulting extension between distinct simples, then lift that complementary \(\beta\) and use induction on the smaller kernel. For a general module \(X\), take a simple quotient \(\beta\) and apply induction to its kernel. Separate the kernel's \(\beta\)-part from the other parts. Modulo the \(\beta\)-part, the extension splits by the preceding argument; the inverse image of a complementary \(\beta\) then intersects the other parts trivially and together with them spans \(X\). This proves the decomposition. Every nonzero finite-length part has a simple quotient of its own type, so \[ X=\bigoplus_{\gamma}X_\gamma,\qquad [X:\gamma]>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \operatorname{Hom}(X,\gamma)\ne0, \qquad \dim\operatorname{Hom}(X,\gamma)\le[X:\gamma]. \tag{6.777} \] For the inequality, apply the left-exact contravariant Hom functor to a composition series. At each step its dimension increases by at most \(\dim\operatorname{Hom}(\gamma',\gamma)\), which is zero or one by irreducibility and admissible Schur's lemma. This argument does not say that \(X_\gamma\) is semisimple, or that its central action is scalar.

Proof: the induced modules. If the data are conjugate, \(M\) and \(L\) are associated. Every nonzero layer in the geometric filtration of \(X=r_P I\) is therefore an irreducible cuspidal transported \(\tau\), as in (6.770), and at least one is \(\sigma\). Formula (6.777) and first Frobenius give \[ \operatorname{Hom}_G(i_Q\tau,i_P\sigma) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_M(r_Pi_Q\tau,\sigma)\ne0,\qquad \dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(i_Q\tau,i_P\sigma) \le\#\{w:w^{-1}Lw=M,\ w^{-1}\tau\simeq\sigma\}. \tag{6.778} \] The set uses the cell representatives, so internal permutations in the source or target blocks are not counted again. The nonzero image of such an intertwiner has an irreducible subquotient, common to \(I\) and \(J\); both inductions have finite length by Theorem 6.324. Conversely a common irreducible subquotient forces their data to agree by Theorem 6.322, and a nonzero intertwiner supplies such a common subquotient. If the data are not conjugate, the Hom space is consequently zero. This proves the equivalence and the bound, without asserting injectivity or surjectivity of the intertwiner. \(\square\)

6.52 Reordered induction, generic constituents and ordinary parameter traces

All division-group statements in this section concern \(G=\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\) over a nonarchimedean field of either characteristic. A cuspidal factor is irreducible and admissible unless stated otherwise. The Whittaker assertions concern split general-linear groups. An ordering of cuspidal data retains the labels of repeated factors.

Lemma 6.327 — a common Jacquet-length detector. Fix a multiset \(\mathbf r\) of \(s\) positive division block dimensions, and let \(\mathcal A(\mathbf r)\) be the standard parabolics with those dimensions in any order. On finite-length admissible modules put \[ D_{\mathbf r}(X)=\sum_{A\in\mathcal A(\mathbf r)}\ell(r_A X),\qquad D_{\mathbf r}(X)=D_{\mathbf r}(X')+D_{\mathbf r}(X'') \tag{6.779} \] for every short exact sequence \(0\to X'\to X\to X''\to0\).
