If each constituent of \(X\) has cuspidal block dimensions \(\mathbf r\), then \[ D_{\mathbf r}(X)\ge\ell(X),\qquad D_{\mathbf r}(i_P\sigma)=s! \tag{6.780} \] for a cuspidal induction with these labelled blocks. In particular this is the same detector for every reordering of that induction.

For \(s=2\), every nonzero proper submodule \(S\) of \(I=i_P\sigma\) and its quotient are irreducible, and \[ D_{\mathbf r}(S)=D_{\mathbf r}(I/S)=1,\qquad r_P S\simeq\sigma,\qquad r_A S=0\quad(A\in\mathcal A(\mathbf r),\ A\ne P). \tag{6.781} \]

Proof. Corollary 6.325 makes each Jacquet module in (6.779) finite length. Exactness proves additivity. For an irreducible constituent with the specified block dimensions, its cuspidal embedding and first Frobenius give a nonzero Jacquet module for one \(A\) in the sum. Hence its detector is at least one. Adding along a composition series proves the first inequality. The second identity is the labelled-cell count (6.770). When \(s=2\), the two nonzero modules \(S,I/S\) therefore have detector one and length one. Inclusion \(S\hookrightarrow i_P\sigma\) gives a nonzero, hence surjective, map \(r_P S\to\sigma\). Its length is at most one by the detector. This proves the isomorphism and forces all the other summands to be zero. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.328 — two-block exchange and the opposite extensions. Let \(\rho\) and \(\tau\) be cuspidals of \(\mathrm{GL}_a(D)\) and \(\mathrm{GL}_b(D)\), and put \[ I=i_{(a,b)}^{\mathrm{GL}_{a+b}(D)}(\rho\otimes\tau),\qquad J=i_{(b,a)}^{\mathrm{GL}_{a+b}(D)}(\tau\otimes\rho). \tag{6.782} \] Their irreducible composition factors, including multiplicities, agree. If either module is irreducible, both are irreducible and isomorphic. If the ordered inducing data differ and both modules are reducible, there are nonisomorphic irreducibles \(S,T\) and nonsplit exact sequences \[ 0\longrightarrow S\longrightarrow I\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow0, \qquad 0\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow J\longrightarrow S\longrightarrow0. \tag{6.783} \] Each has a unique nonzero proper submodule. In this case every nonzero intertwiner factors through the indicated quotient and submodule; for \(A:I\to J\), \(B:J\to I\), \[ \dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(I,J)=\dim\operatorname{Hom}_G(J,I)=1, \qquad BA=0_I,\quad AB=0_J. \tag{6.784} \]

Proof. If \(a=b\) and \(\rho\simeq\tau\), the ordered Levi modules are isomorphic, so their inductions are isomorphic. In all other cases the ordered pairs \((P,\rho\otimes\tau)\) and \((Q,\tau\otimes\rho)\) differ. Their data are conjugate, so Theorem 6.326 supplies nonzero maps in both directions. Their common detector from Lemma 6.327 has value two on each module and is positive on each nonzero subquotient.

If \(I\) is irreducible, a nonzero \(I\to J\) is injective. Its cokernel has detector \(2-2=0\), so is zero. The same argument applies if \(J\) is irreducible. Suppose now both are reducible and choose a nonzero proper submodule \(S\subset I\). It and its quotient are irreducible by (6.781). For every nonzero proper \(S'\subset I\), that formula and first Frobenius give \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(S',J)=0\): if \(Q\ne P\), then \(r_Q S'=0\); if \(Q=P\), then \(r_P S'\simeq\rho\otimes\tau\) is not isomorphic to the ordered inducing module of \(J\). The latter assertion follows from the uniqueness of finite product factorization in Lesson 12, Theorem 4.1.

Consequently a nonzero \(A:I\to J\) kills every proper nonzero submodule of \(I\). There cannot be two different such submodules. They would be distinct simple submodules with zero intersection, and their sum would have detector two and hence be all of \(I\), forcing \(A=0\). Thus \(S\) is unique. The same argument gives a unique simple proper submodule \(T\subset J\). The image of \(A\), being the simple quotient \(I/S\), is \(T\). A nonzero reverse map gives \(J/T\simeq S\). Also \(S\not\simeq T\), since otherwise inclusion of \(T\) into \(J\) would contradict \(\operatorname{Hom}_G(S,J)=0\). A splitting would give another simple proper submodule, so both extensions are nonsplit. The matching-cell bound (6.778) is one for these distinct ordered data, proving the Hom dimensions. Each map kills the other's image, giving the zero compositions. This proves all assertions, including the composition comparison. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.329 — all reorderings have identical composition multiplicities. Let \(\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_s\) be labelled cuspidals of division block dimensions \(r_1,\ldots,r_s\). For any permutation \(\gamma\), define \[ I_\gamma=i_{(r_{\gamma(1)},\ldots,r_{\gamma(s)})}^{G} (\rho_{\gamma(1)}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_{\gamma(s)}). \tag{6.785} \] For every irreducible admissible \(V\), its composition multiplicity in \(I_\gamma\) is independent of \(\gamma\). In the group of finite-length classes, with the relations of short exact sequences, \[ [I_\gamma]=[I_{\mathrm{id}}],\qquad [I_\gamma:V]=[I_{\mathrm{id}}:V]. \tag{6.786} \]

Proof: composition multiplicities and exact functors. The independence of composition multiplicity from a chosen series follows by a direct common refinement. For two filtrations \(V_i\), \(W_j\) of one module, refine by intersections. The matched refinement factors are isomorphic to \[ \frac{V_i\cap W_j} {(V_{i-1}\cap W_j)+(V_i\cap W_{j-1})}. \tag{6.787} \] Indeed apply the quotient map to \(V_{i-1}+(V_i\cap W_j)\); the modular law for subspaces gives exactly this kernel. The symmetric refinement of the \(W\)-series gives the same quotient. If both original series are composition series, each has exactly one nonzero refinement factor per original simple layer. Their multisets therefore agree. This also proves multiplicity additivity in a short exact sequence by lifting a quotient series and adjoining a submodule series.

An exact functor carrying these modules to finite-length modules thus carries equality of their finite-length classes to equality of the resulting composition multiplicities. In particular tensoring with the other Levi factors and ordinary induction have this property: tensor products over \(\mathbb C\) are exact, admissible simple product factors are irreducible, and Corollary 6.325 gives finite length and exact induction.

Now exchange two adjacent factors. Merge their blocks into one larger block in a coarser parabolic. Inside that factor, Theorem 6.328 gives equality of the two composition classes. Tensor with the unchanged factors and induce from the coarser Levi. The explicit product and normalized transitivity maps (6.773) identify the outputs with the two adjacent orderings in (6.785). Every permutation is a product of adjacent exchanges: successively move its first desired label to the first position, its second to the second, and continue. This proves (6.786), with repeated labels still counted. All the modules are finite length by Theorem 6.324. In particular, \[ I_{\mathrm{id}}\text{ irreducible}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad I_\gamma\simeq I_{\mathrm{id}}\text{ for every }\gamma. \tag{6.788} \] If their common class has more than one constituent counted with multiplicity, every ordering is reducible. Equality of classes alone does not split or identify the modules, as Theorem 6.328 shows. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.330 — one generic irreducible for an exact cuspidal multiset. For split \(G_n\), any fixed multiset of cuspidals is the cuspidal datum of exactly one generic irreducible admissible representation. It occurs with multiplicity one in every ordering of the corresponding cuspidal induction. The datum includes the actual unramified twists, not only their equivalence after an unspecified twist.

Proof. Each cuspidal has one-dimensional Whittaker quotient by Corollary 6.302. Exactness of twisted coinvariants, heredity and Whittaker uniqueness, Lemma 6.288 and Theorems 6.294 and 6.291, give for any ordering \[ \dim(I_\gamma)_{U_n,\theta_n}=1, \qquad 1=\sum_V[I_\gamma:V],\dim V_{U_n,\theta_n}. \tag{6.789} \] The sum is finite by Theorem 6.324 and each nonzero dimension is one. There is therefore exactly one generic occurrence. Theorem 6.329 makes its isomorphism class independent of the order. Conversely any generic irreducible with the stated datum embeds in one such induction by Theorem 6.321 and so is this constituent. If \(\operatorname{cusp}(V)\) denotes the exact unordered cuspidal multiset, this proves \[ \{V\text{ irreducible admissible generic}:\operatorname{cusp}(V)=\{\rho_i\}\} =\{V_{\mathrm{gen}}\}. \tag{6.790} \] This concerns occurrence, not the position of that constituent as a submodule or quotient in each ordering. For a proper induction and a compatible compact discrete Euler test \(f\), Corollary 6.297 still gives only \[ \operatorname{Tr}V_{\mathrm{gen}}(f) =-\sum_{V\ne V_{\mathrm{gen}}}[I_\gamma:V]\operatorname{Tr}V(f). \tag{6.791} \] All factors on the right are nongeneric. They need not have zero trace, as Example 6.334 illustrates. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.331 — normalized unitary induction and smooth complements. If a smooth admissible Levi module \(W\) has an invariant positive definite inner product, normalized induction has one too. Its Hilbert completion has exactly the original smooth module. Every invariant submodule of that smooth module has an invariant smooth complement. Consequently a one-dimensional endomorphism algebra forces irreducibility, and in that case the invariant positive inner product is unique up to a positive factor.

Proof: quotient densities and the Haar sign. Put \(K=\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathcal O_D)\), \(P=MN\) and \(C=P\cap K\), and normalize their Haar measures to give \(K\) and \(C\) mass one. The group \(G\), and each factor of \(M\), is unimodular: on invertible division matrices the measure \(c|\operatorname{Nrd}g|_F^{-rd}\,dX\) is left and right invariant. Left and right matrix multiplication have the same additive determinant \(|\operatorname{Nrd}g|_F^{rd}\), by the splitting-matrix argument of (6.757).

In the coordinates \(p=mn\), left Haar on \(P\) is \(dp=dm\,dn\). Left translation preserves this product because its change in the \(N\)-variable is a left translate for each fixed \(m\). Right translation by \(m_0\) changes \(n\) to \(m_0^{-1}nm_0\); substituting gives, with our explicit integral convention, \[ \int_P\phi(pp_0)\,dp=\delta_P(p_0)\int_P\phi(p)\,dp. \tag{6.792} \] Here right translation in \(M\) preserves \(dm\), while conjugation on \(N\) has the already computed determinant \(\delta_P\). Right translation by its unipotent radical contributes one.

Division Iwasawa gives \(G=PK\). The right \(K\)-cosets of \(G\) have representatives in \(P\) and are parametrized by \(P/C\). Decompose \(P\) into the left translates \(p_iC\). Integrating \(\phi(p_i c k)\) over \(C\) and \(K\) removes the compact fibre, and every \(p_iK\) has Haar mass one. Thus, for \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(G)\), \[ \int_G\phi(g)\,dg=\int_K\int_P\phi(pk)\,dp\,dk, \qquad T\phi(g)=\int_P\phi(pg)\,dp, \quad T\phi(p_0g)=\delta_P(p_0)T\phi(g). \tag{6.793} \] Only finitely many cosets meet a compact support, so these computations are finite compact integrals. If a locally constant scalar \(u\) satisfies this \(\delta_P\)-covariance, set \(\phi=u\mathbf1_K\). On \(K\) its \(P\)-integral is over \(C\), where \(\delta_P=1\), so \(T\phi=u\) there and hence on \(G\). Since \(T\) commutes with right translation and \(dg\) is right invariant, \[ \mathcal I(u)=\int_Ku(k)\,dk,\qquad T(u\mathbf1_K)=u,\qquad \mathcal I(R_hu)=\mathcal I(u). \tag{6.794} \] This proves the required quotient-density invariance, including its sign.

Proof: the unitary completion and submodules. Use the inner-product convention linear in the first entry. The density \(\langle F(g),H(g)\rangle_W\) has exactly this covariance, so \[ \langle F,H\rangle_I=\int_K\langle F(k),H(k)\rangle_W\,dk, \qquad \widehat I^{,J}=I^J,\qquad \widehat I^{\mathrm{smooth}}=I. \tag{6.795} \] The norm is positive definite because a nonzero smooth section is nonzero on an open subset of \(K\). Its action is strongly continuous on smooth vectors, and unitarity extends that continuity to the completion. Admissibility of \(I\) is Theorem 6.296. Compact averaging of the dense original module has the finite-dimensional, already closed image \(I^J\); this proves the fixed-space and smooth-space identities, as in (6.723).

For any invariant submodule \(S\subset I\), let \(\overline S\) be its Hilbert closure. Bounded compact averaging similarly gives \((\overline S)^J=S^J\), since this is a subspace of the finite-dimensional \(I^J\). The orthogonal projection \(p\) onto \(\overline S\) commutes with \(G\), so maps each \(I^J\) into \(S^J\). Its restriction to \(I\) therefore has image exactly \(S\). Hence \[ I=S\oplus\bigl(I\cap(\overline S)^\perp\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{End}_G(I)=\mathbb C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad I\text{ irreducible}. \tag{6.796} \] A proper nonzero submodule would otherwise give a nontrivial idempotent endomorphism. Finally, each invariant positive inner product identifies \(I\) anti-linearly with its smooth dual by \(w\mapsto\langle\,\cdot\,,w\rangle\). This map is onto: a smooth functional fixed by \(J\) factors through compact averaging onto the finite space \(I^J\), where a vector represents it by finite-dimensional Riesz; self-adjointness of that average extends the equality to every vector. Composing the two identifications gives a group endomorphism. If that algebra is scalar, the inner products are proportional, and positivity makes the proportionality constant positive. Pulling back the target form by an algebraic group isomorphism therefore shows that it can be rescaled to extend to a unitary Hilbert isomorphism. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.332 — pairwise inequivalent unitary cuspidals induce irreducibly. For pairwise inequivalent unitary cuspidal factors, their normalized induction in every order is irreducible. This holds for all \(\mathrm{GL}_r(D)\) and both field characteristics.

Proof. Product inner products give an invariant positive inner product on the inducing module. The matching-cell estimate (6.778) gives \[ 1\le\dim\operatorname{End}_G(i_P\rho) \le\prod_{[\eta]}m_{[\eta]}!, \qquad m_{[\eta]}=\#\{i:\rho_i\simeq\eta\}. \tag{6.797} \] The product counts exactly the block permutations preserving the isomorphism types of the ordered factors. With no repeated type it is one, so Lemma 6.331 proves irreducibility; Theorem 6.329 then identifies the orders. By the norm uniqueness in Lemma 6.331, these identifications can be rescaled to unitary isomorphisms of their Hilbert completions.

More explicitly take unitary \(\rho_i\) on blocks of sizes \(r_i\), and put \(\rho_{i,z_i}(g)=z_i^{v_F(\operatorname{Nrd}g)}\rho_i(g)\). On the unitary parameter torus \(|z_i|=1\), pairwise inequivalence is guaranteed outside the finite collection of collision conditions \[ z_i^{r_i d}\omega_i(\varpi_F)=z_j^{r_i d}\omega_j(\varpi_F) \quad(r_i=r_j,\ i\ne j). \tag{6.798} \] These are necessary for isomorphism of the two factors, by their central uniformizer actions. Their complement is dense in the unitary torus: in any product of open arcs choose the parameters successively, avoiding the finitely many forbidden roots from earlier choices. On that complement every ordering is irreducible. At a collision condition the corollary makes no reducibility assertion. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.333 — ordinary compact tests have Laurent-polynomial matrices. Let \(W\) be any smooth admissible module of a standard Levi \(M=\prod_i\mathrm{GL}_{r_i}(D)\). For \(\mathbf z\in(\mathbb C^\times)^s\), put \[ W_{\mathbf z}(m)=\mathbf z^{\mathbf v(m)}W(m),\quad \mathbf v(m)=(v_F\operatorname{Nrd}m_i)_i,\quad I_{\mathbf z}=i_P^G W_{\mathbf z},\qquad I_{\mathbf z}^{J}\simeq\bigoplus_{i=1}^t W^{J_M}. \tag{6.799} \] For every ordinary compact test \(f\in\mathcal H(G)\), one may choose \(J\) so that its operator is represented on this same finite-dimensional space, for all parameters, by a matrix of Laurent polynomials. In particular its actual trace is a Laurent polynomial. No fixed scalar central character is imposed on \(W\).

Proof. Choose a deep principal \(J\), normal in \(K\), with \(f=e_J*f*e_J\). The ordinary coordinates before central pushforward in (6.670) give (6.799); they can also be read directly as the values of a section at the finitely many representatives \(k_i\in K\) of \(P\backslash G/J\). Since \(J\) is normal in \(K\), consistency of a value is exactly invariance under \(J_M\). Unramified characters and parabolic moduli are trivial on the compact groups involved, so the underlying fixed spaces are independent of \(\mathbf z\).

The compact union of the \(k_i\operatorname{supp}f\) meets only finitely many right \(J\)-cosets \(g_aJ\). Choose one factorization \(g_a=m_an_ak_{j_a}j_a'\) for each, independently of the parameters. Then \[ F_{\mathbf z}(g_a)=\delta_P(m_a)^{1/2}\mathbf z^{\mathbf v(m_a)} W(m_a)F_{\mathbf z}(k_{j_a}). \tag{6.800} \] Let \(c_{ia}=\int_{\{h:k_i h\in g_aJ\}}f(h)\,dh\), and let \(E_{J_M}\) be the compact averaging projector on \(W\). Evaluating the convolution at \(k_i\) and averaging the output, which is already \(J_M\)-fixed, gives the exact block matrix \[ \bigl(I_{\mathbf z}(f)\bigr)_{ij} =\sum_{a:j_a=j}c_{ia}\delta_P(m_a)^{1/2}\mathbf z^{\mathbf v(m_a)} E_{J_M}W(m_a)\big|_{W^{J_M}}. \tag{6.801} \] Every sum is finite and each coefficient operator acts between finite fixed spaces. Its exponents are integers and its coefficient matrices are independent of the parameters. Also \(f=e_J*f*e_J\) makes the whole operator zero on \(\ker e_J\), so this is its actual finite-rank trace matrix, not merely a compression with a different trace. Consequently \[ \operatorname{Tr}I_{\mathbf z}(f)\in \mathbb C[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_s^{\pm1}]. \tag{6.802} \] The proof uses ordinary compact tests. A varying central character is not inserted into one fixed \(\mathcal H_\omega(G)\). If all source factors are the same cuspidal on equal-sized blocks, Theorem 6.329 further makes this polynomial symmetric in the parameters. \(\square\)

Example 6.334 — explicit spherical traces and exceptional extensions. Take split \(\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\), \(q=q_F\), \(K=\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathcal O_F)\) of volume one, and the unramified characters \(\chi_z(x)=z^{v_F(x)}\). The induction \(I(z_1,z_2)=i_B(\chi_{z_1}\otimes\chi_{z_2})\) has one-dimensional \(K\)-fixed space, with section \(F(1)=1\). Put \(a=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F,1)\), \(T_1=\mathbf1_{KaK}\) and \(Z_1=\mathbf1_{\varpi_F K}\). Their actual operators have range in that line, and \[ \operatorname{Tr}I(z_1,z_2)(T_1)=q^{1/2}(z_1+z_2),\qquad \operatorname{Tr}I(z_1,z_2)(Z_1)=z_1z_2. \tag{6.803} \] Indeed the right \(K\)-coset representatives in \(KaK\) are \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\varpi_F&x\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(x\in\mathcal O_F/\varpi_F\), and \(\operatorname{diag}(1,\varpi_F)\). Their lattices reduce to the \(q\) lines generated by \((x,1)\) and the line generated by \((1,0)\). Their section values are \(q^{-1/2}z_1\), respectively \(q^{1/2}z_2\); each coset has Haar mass one. Summing proves the first formula, and a scalar uniformizer gives the second.

For \(T_2=\mathbf1_{Ka^2K}\), the upper triangular representatives have diagonal \((\varpi_F^2,1)\) with \(q^2\) choices of the upper entry modulo \(\varpi_F^2\), diagonal \((\varpi_F,\varpi_F)\) with \(q-1\) nonzero upper entries modulo \(\varpi_F\), and diagonal \((1,\varpi_F^2)\) once. To see completeness, the second-coordinate projection of a lattice is \(\varpi_F^v\mathcal O_F\), and its intersection with the first axis is \(\varpi_F^u\mathcal O_F e_1\). A lift of the projection generator gives the displayed upper triangular basis, with upper entry unique modulo \(\varpi_F^u\); its index gives \(u+v=2\). The quotient is cyclic in the first and last cases. In the middle case a unit upper entry expresses \(e_1\) as a multiple of \(\varpi_F e_2\), leaving a cyclic quotient of length two; the zero residue gives the scalar lattice with quotient \(\mathbb F_q^2\). A primitive quotient row extends to an invertible integral matrix, so these are exactly the right cosets of \(Ka^2K\). Their section values yield \[ \operatorname{Tr}I(z_1,z_2)(T_2) =q(z_1^2+z_2^2)+(q-1)z_1z_2, \qquad \operatorname{vol}(Ka^2K)=q^2+q. \tag{6.804} \] These are explicit symmetric Laurent traces for every pair of nonzero parameters, including reducible inductions.

Write \(\nu=|\cdot|_F\), \(I_-=i_B(\nu^{-1/2}\otimes\nu^{1/2})\), \(I_+=i_B(\nu^{1/2}\otimes\nu^{-1/2})\). The definitions and principal-series proof are Lesson 7, Theorem 4.2. Its exact sequences are \[ 0\to\mathbf1\to I_-\to\mathrm{St}\to0,\qquad 0\to\mathrm{St}\to I_+\to\mathbf1\to0. \tag{6.805} \] They are nonsplit. The unique generic constituent is \(\mathrm{St}\), but a nonzero \(I_+\to I_-\) has image \(\mathbf1\), whereas a nonzero reverse map has image \(\mathrm{St}\), by Theorem 6.328. The spherical trace at \((z_1,z_2)=(q^{1/2},q^{-1/2})\), or its reverse, is \(q+1\); the constant submodule already exhausts the one-dimensional \(K\)-fixed space of \(I_-\), so \(\mathrm{St}^K=0\). For its compact discrete Euler test, (6.674) gives \[ \operatorname{Tr}I_\pm(f_{\mathrm{St},m})=0,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\mathrm{St}(f_{\mathrm{St},m})=1,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}\mathbf1(f_{\mathrm{St},m})=-1. \tag{6.806} \] Thus equality of complete composition multiplicities and uniqueness of the generic factor still allow a nonzero generic trace cancelled by a nongeneric one.

Example 6.335 — the characteristic-two division self-twist and its parameters. Use \(D/F\), \(F=\mathbb F_2((\varpi))\), and the two-dimensional \(\rho\) of Example 6.315. Its finite quotient has generators \(\alpha\mapsto(123)\), \(\Pi\mapsto(12)\). In the basis \(e_1-e_3,e_2-e_3\), put \[ C=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2\\2&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad A^2=-3I,\quad AC=CA,\quad AT=-TA. \tag{6.807} \] The matrices \(C,T\) are the coordinate permutations on the sum-zero plane. Direct multiplication proves the remaining identities. Since \(v_F\operatorname{Nrd}(g)=v_D(g)\), define \(\rho_z(g)=z^{v_D(g)}\rho(g)\). Valuation parity is the sign of the finite quotient permutation: \(\Pi\) is odd, \(\alpha\) is even, and the scalar \(\varpi=\Pi^2\) has valuation two. The identities for \(A\) therefore intertwine \(\rho_z\) and \(\rho_{-z}\). Conversely their central uniformizer scalars are \(z^2\) and \(w^2\). Hence \[ A\rho_z(g)=\rho_{-z}(g)A,\qquad \rho_z\simeq\rho_w\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z^2=w^2. \tag{6.808} \] All these matrices and parameters are over \(\mathbb C\), so \(-3\ne0\) even though the base local field has characteristic two.

Let \(I_{z_1,z_2}=i_{(1,1)}^{\mathrm{GL}_2(D)}(\rho_{z_1}\otimes\rho_{z_2})\). For unit-modulus parameters the source factors are unitary, and Corollary 6.332 proves irreducibility if \(z_1^2\ne z_2^2\). For every ordinary compact test, the source isomorphisms (6.808), the polynomial lemma and reordering give \[ \operatorname{Tr}I_{z_1,z_2}(f) \in\mathbb C[z_1^{\pm2},z_2^{\pm2}]^{\mathfrak S_2},\qquad |z_1|=|z_2|=1,\ z_1^2\ne z_2^2 \ \Longrightarrow\ I_{z_1,z_2}\text{ irreducible}. \tag{6.809} \] Indeed independent sign changes preserve the source modules and hence the traces; coefficient comparison in a Laurent polynomial removes every odd exponent. Reordering makes the result symmetric. On \(z_1^2=z_2^2\) the factors are isomorphic; no reducibility assertion there follows from the distinct-factor corollary.

6.53 Normalized mirabolic derivatives and a sufficient irreducibility criterion

Throughout this subsection, \(G_n=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\) is split and \(F\) is nonarchimedean of either characteristic. Put \(G_0=P_1=1\), \(\nu(g)=|\det g|\), and use \(P_n=G_{n-1}\ltimes N_n\) and the Haar densities of (6.616)–(6.620). In particular \(\Delta_{P_n}=\nu^{-1}\). Fix the last-row character \(\psi_e\) of \(N_n\), with \(e=e_{n-1}\). Coinvariants without a normalization are the algebraic quotients of (6.657). Define \[ \begin{split} \Psi_n^-V&=\nu^{-1/2}V_{N_n,1},& \Psi_n^+\rho&=\nu^{1/2}\operatorname{infl}_{G_{n-1}}^{P_n}\rho,\\ \Phi_n^-V&=\nu^{-1/2}V_{N_n,\psi_e},& \Phi_n^+\tau&=\operatorname{cInd}_{P_{n-1}N_n}^{P_n} (\nu^{1/2}\tau\otimes\psi_e). \end{split} \tag{6.810} \] The target of \(\Phi_n^-\) is the category of smooth \(P_{n-1}\)-modules. Compact induction means locally constant sections with compact support modulo the indicated closed subgroup, with one open right stabilizer. Write \(\widehat\Phi_n^+\) for the same smooth section space with no compact-support condition. At \(n=1\), let \(\Psi_1^-\) and \(\Psi_1^+\) be the identity on vector spaces and let \(\Phi_1^-\) be zero. Every subsequent formula uses these boundary conventions. Identities involving \(\Phi_n^+\) or \(\widehat\Phi_n^+\) are understood for \(n\ge2\).

Lemma 6.336 — the open row orbit and its section module. For every smooth \(P_n\)-module \(V\), there is a natural exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow\Phi_n^+\Phi_n^-V \longrightarrow V\longrightarrow\Psi_n^+\Psi_n^-V \longrightarrow0. \tag{6.811} \] The functor \(\Phi_n^+\) identifies smooth \(P_{n-1}\)-modules with those \(P_n\)-modules whose trivial \(N_n\)-quotient is zero. It identifies their full lattices of submodules. Inflation \(\Psi_n^+\) identifies smooth \(G_{n-1}\)-modules with those on which \(N_n\) acts trivially. In addition, \[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_n^-\Phi_n^+\simeq1,\qquad \Phi_n^-\widehat\Phi_n^+\simeq1,\qquad \Psi_n^-\Psi_n^+\simeq1,\\ \Psi_n^-\Phi_n^+=0,\qquad\Phi_n^-\Psi_n^+=0,\\ \operatorname{Hom}_{P_n}(\Phi_n^+\tau,V) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{P_{n-1}}(\tau,\Phi_n^-V),\\ \operatorname{Hom}_{P_n}(V,\widehat\Phi_n^+\tau) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{P_{n-1}}(\Phi_n^-V,\tau). \end{gathered} \tag{6.812} \] All four functors in (6.810) are exact.

Proof: the Fourier algebra. Equations (6.677)–(6.679) give an action of \(\mathcal A=C_c^\infty(F^{n-1})\) on \(V\): the indicator of a dual ball acts as its compact character projector. Any finite collection of compact locally constant functions admits a common finite ball partition of its supports, so (6.678) proves multiplicativity and independence of the partition. Each vector has a local unit: a last-column lattice fixing it gives a compact dual ball whose projector fixes it. Fourier inversion here is precisely the finite character-sum identity (6.679).

For a row \(\xi\), the fibre of this algebra module is \(V_{N_n,\psi_\xi}\). Indeed a compact locally constant function vanishing at \(\xi\) is a finite sum of functions of the form \((\psi(\eta x)-\psi(\xi x))a(\eta)\). To see this, cover its compact support away from \(\xi\) by finitely many small balls on each of which one such nonzero character difference is constant, using (6.676). Multiplication by that nonzero constant can be inverted. Conversely each such difference vanishes at \(\xi\). Local units then identify the algebra-module fibre relations with the last-column relations on each vector.

Let \(Y=F^{n-1}\setminus\{0\}\). The module \(V^\circ=\mathcal A(Y)V\), where functions on \(Y\) have compact support there, is exactly the kernel of \(V\to V_{N_n,1}\). This follows from the preceding ideal description at zero. It is \(P_n\)-invariant: conjugation by \(a\in G_{n-1}\) sends a Fourier projector supported on \(B\) to that supported on \(Ba^{-1}\). Its fibre at zero is zero, whereas its fibre at every \(\xi\ne0\) is the full fibre of \(V\), by a cutoff equal to one near \(\xi\).

Proof: identification on the open orbit. Let \(q:V\to V_{N_n,\psi_e}\), and give its target the normalized action in (6.810). For \(v\in V^\circ\), set \[ F_v(g)=q(\pi(g)v),\qquad g\in P_n. \tag{6.813} \] For \(h\in P_{n-1}\) and \(x\in N_n\), this has covariance \(\nu(h)^{1/2}\tau(h)\psi_e(x)\), because the action on the quotient was multiplied by \(\nu(h)^{-1/2}\). It has an open right stabilizer fixing \(v\). On \(G_{n-1}\), its support projects to the Fourier support of \(v\) under the row map \(a\mapsto ea\), so it is compact modulo \(P_{n-1}N_n\). Also \[ F_{\mathbf1_Bv}(a)=\mathbf1_B(ea)F_v(a). \tag{6.814} \] If \(F_v=0\), transitivity of \(G_{n-1}\) on nonzero rows makes all nonzero fibres of \(v\) zero; its zero fibre is already zero. Lemma 6.299 gives \(v=0\).

For surjectivity, it suffices to make a section on a small compact row ball. At the row \(e\), lift its prescribed value to \(v\in V\). Choose a principal subgroup \(L\subset G_{n-1}\) fixing both \(v\) and the prescribed section on the right. The row orbit \(eL\) is a compact ball away from zero. Formula (6.813) agrees with that section on \(P_{n-1}L\), and (6.814) cuts it to this ball. Translate this construction to every nonzero row. A compact section has a finite cover by such balls; refine to a disjoint compact-open partition and add the resulting sections. This proves surjectivity and (6.811).

Evaluation at the identity identifies the nonzero fibre of either compact or full induction with the inducing module. For full induction this is still an algebraic assertion: a twisted average over a sufficiently large last-column lattice cuts any section to a compact row ball about \(e\), without changing its fibre. A section whose value at \(e\) is zero vanishes on a smaller such ball, since it has an open right stabilizer; its class in the fibre is therefore zero by (6.680). This proves the first two identities in (6.812). The other composite identities follow from inflation and from the disjoint zero and nonzero supports.

Any map from a module supported on \(Y\) into \(V\) lands in \(V^\circ\). Formula (6.813), its inverse and fibre evaluation therefore give the first adjunction in (6.812). For the second, a map \(T:\Phi_n^-V\to\tau\) gives the full-induction section \(g\mapsto T(q(\pi(g)v))\); conversely evaluate a map at the identity. The covariance and normalization are exactly those checked for (6.813). These constructions are inverse. The equivalence and the inflation assertion now give the claimed submodule lattices. Coinvariants are exact by Lemma 6.288. Inflation is exact, and the equivalence, or the local lifts of compact sections just constructed, proves exactness of \(\Phi_n^+\). This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.337 — derivative filtration and exact mirabolic length. Put \[ V^{(k)}=\Psi_{n-k+1}^-\Phi_{n-k+2}^-\cdots\Phi_n^-V, \qquad1\le k\le n. \tag{6.815} \] Every smooth \(V\) has a finite filtration whose successive quotients are \(\Phi_n^+\cdots\Phi_{n-k+2}^+\Psi_{n-k+1}^+V^{(k)}\). Every irreducible smooth \(P_n\)-module has exactly one nonzero derivative, which is an irreducible smooth \(G_{n-k}\)-module; these data classify such \(P_n\)-modules. No admissibility assertion for arbitrary smooth irreducibles is part of this statement. Moreover \[ \operatorname{length}_{P_n}V =\sum_{k=1}^n\operatorname{length}_{G_{n-k}}V^{(k)} \tag{6.816} \] whenever either side is finite; finiteness of one side implies finiteness of the other.

Proof. Repeatedly apply (6.811) to \(V,\Phi_n^-V,\Phi_{n-1}^-\Phi_n^-V,\ldots\). Applying the exact \(\Phi^+\) functors to each sequence yields the descending filtration with \(k\)-th layer displayed above. The last remaining functor is \(\Psi_1^-=1\), so there is no unaccounted final layer. If \(V\) is simple, the submodule in (6.811) is either zero or all of \(V\). In the first case \(V=\Psi_n^+\rho\) for a simple \(\rho\); in the second \(V=\Phi_n^+\tau\) for a simple \(\tau\). Recurse in the second case. The zero composite identities in (6.812) show that the resulting integer and representation are unique and that precisely its one derivative is nonzero. The submodule-lattice assertions show that each functor \(\Phi^+\) or \(\Psi^+\) preserves composition length. If every derivative has finite length, add lengths along the finite filtration. Conversely, exact derivative functors carry a finite simple series to series with simple or zero factors, by the classification just proved. Adding their lengths proves (6.816). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.338 — normalized pairings on the open row orbit. For a smooth group module write \(V^\vee\) for its smooth dual. A \(\Delta_H\)-pairing means a bilinear form with \(\Delta_H(h)B(hv,hw)=B(v,w)\). For smooth modules of the indicated groups there are natural identifications \[ \begin{split} \operatorname{Bil}_{\Delta_{P_n}}(\Psi_n^+\rho,\Psi_n^+\rho') &\simeq\operatorname{Bil}_1(\rho,\rho'),\\ \operatorname{Bil}_{\Delta_{P_n}}(\Phi_n^+\tau,\Phi_n^+\tau') &\simeq\operatorname{Bil}_{\Delta_{P_{n-1}}}(\tau,\tau'),\\ \operatorname{Bil}_{\Delta_{P_n}}(\Psi_n^+\rho,\Phi_n^+\tau)&=0. \end{split} \tag{6.817} \] The first two identifications preserve nondegeneracy with respect to either argument.

Proof: the measure and the dual. The first identity follows from \(\nu^{1/2}\nu^{1/2}=\Delta_{P_n}^{-1}\). For the open orbit put \(m=n-1\), use \(t_\xi\) from Lemma 6.280, and let a minus subscript on \(\Phi^+\) indicate replacement of \(\psi_e\) by \(\psi_e^{-1}\). First, row-section integration identifies the ordinary smooth dual \( (\Phi_n^+\tau)^\vee\) with \(\widehat\Phi_{n,-}^+(\tau^\vee)\): the product of its two normalized fibre covariances is \(\nu(h)\), exactly the density covariance for \(P_m\backslash G_m\). Twisting the full induced module by \(\nu\) is identified with twisting its inducing module by \(\nu|_{P_m}\), by multiplication of sections by \(\nu(a)\). Consequently \[ (\Delta_{P_n}\Phi_n^+\tau)^\vee \simeq\widehat\Phi_{n,-}^+ ((\Delta_{P_{n-1}}\tau)^\vee). \tag{6.818} \] Here the modular twist is inside the dual on both sides. Explicitly, pair a compact section \(f\) with a full section \(g\) on the right by \[ \mathcal B(f,g)=\int_{Y_m} \nu(t_\xi)^{-1}\langle f(t_\xi),g(t_\xi)\rangle \frac{d\xi}{\|\xi\|_\infty}. \tag{6.819} \] The two fibre actions have evaluation factor \(\nu(h)\), so their normalized section covariances give factor \(\nu(h)^2\). Multiplication by \(\nu(a)^{-1}\) in the integrand leaves factor \(\nu(h)\) under \(a\mapsto ha\), \(h\in P_m\). Lemma 6.280 then makes the integral independent of the row section and invariant under right translation of this density. More explicitly, \(T\phi(a)=\int_{P_m}\phi(ha)\,dh\) has covariance \(T\phi(ha)=\nu(h)T\phi(a)\), and (6.619) gives \(\int_{Y_m}T\phi(t_\xi)d\xi/\|\xi\|=\int_{G_m}\phi\). Local sections and a compact partition show that every compact density with this covariance is such a \(T\phi\). Right invariance of Haar on \(G_m\) proves the asserted invariance. Under simultaneous right translation by \(a\in G_m\), the extra factor \(\nu(\cdot)^{-1}\) in (6.819) leaves \(\mathcal B(af,ag)=\nu(a)\mathcal B(f,g)\). Last-column characters cancel. Thus (6.819) has precisely the required \(\Delta_{P_n}\)-covariance.

Proof: reconstruction of every smooth functional. Here is the local averaging argument for the ordinary smooth dual used above. Set \(H=G_m\), \(S=P_m\), \(C=\Phi_n^+\tau\), and first regard \(C\) as the compact section module on \(S\backslash H\). Choose probability averages \(E_L\) for compact open subgroups \(L\subset H\), and retain the fixed Haar densities in Lemma 6.280. For a principal \(L\), put \[ \mu_L=\operatorname{vol}(eL) =\frac{\operatorname{vol}_H L}{\operatorname{vol}_S(S\cap L)},\qquad f_{L,v}(s l)=\nu(s)^{1/2}\tau(s)E_{S\cap L}v \quad(s\in S,\ l\in L), \] and put \(f_{L,v}=0\) off \(SL\). The value is well defined, since \(S\cap L\) fixes the averaged vector and has modulus one. It is a smooth compact section. The volume identity follows from (6.619): on \(eL\) the row section belongs to \(L\), and the fibre in \(L\) is exactly \(S\cap L\).

Let \(\lambda\) be a smooth \(H\)-functional, fixed by a principal \(L_0\). For \(L\subset L_0\), define \[ \ell_\lambda(v)=\mu_L^{-1}\lambda(f_{L,v}). \] This does not depend on sufficiently small \(L\). Indeed, if \(L'\subset L\) is a smaller principal subgroup, normal in \(L\), averaging its section over \(L\) gives \[ E_L f_{L',v}=\frac{\mu_{L'}}{\mu_L}f_{L,v}. \] Both sides are right \(L\)-invariant and supported in \(SL\). At the identity, integrate over \((S\cap L)L'\subset L\); its probability mass is \([L:(S\cap L)L']^{-1}=\mu_{L'}/\mu_L\), and the remaining fibre average is \(E_{S\cap L}v\). This proves the displayed identity. Applying \(\lambda E_L=\lambda\) proves independence; a common smaller principal subgroup compares any two choices. Also \(\ell_\lambda\) is fixed by \(S\cap L\), because the defining section depends only on that average of \(v\). Thus \(\ell_\lambda\in\tau^\vee\).

With the contragredient action on functionals, define \[ g_\lambda(a)=\ell_{a\lambda},\qquad a\in H. \] If \(h\in S\), then \(\ell_{h\lambda}=\nu(h)^{1/2}\tau^\vee(h)\ell_\lambda\). For an explicit check, choose \(L\) small enough for both functionals, and write \(L'=h^{-1}Lh\). Right translation by \(h^{-1}\) sends \(f_{L,v}\) to the section on \(SL'\) with value \(\nu(h)^{-1/2}\tau(h^{-1})E_{S\cap L}v\) at the identity. This value is \(S\cap L'\)-fixed. Conjugation preserves Haar on \(H\), while conjugation by \(h^{-1}\) multiplies Haar on \(S\) by \(\nu(h)^{-1}\), by (6.617). Hence \(\mu_{L'}=\nu(h)\mu_L\). The ratio and the value just computed give exactly the claimed half-modulus. Sections for this conjugate subgroup use the conjugated row section; their comparison with a smaller principal subgroup is the same averaging identity. It follows that \[ g_\lambda(h a)=\nu(h)^{1/2}\tau^\vee(h)g_\lambda(a). \] If \(j\) fixes \(\lambda\), then \(g_\lambda(a j)=g_\lambda(a)\), so this is a full smooth induced \(H\)-section, with the original open right stabilizer.

The ordinary pairing is the row integral of \(\langle f(t_\xi),g(t_\xi)\rangle\) against \(d\xi/\|\xi\|\), without the additional factor in (6.819). On \(f_{L,v}\), when \(L\) fixes \(\lambda\), this integral against \(g_\lambda\) is \(\mu_L\ell_\lambda(v)=\lambda(f_{L,v})\). Such elementary sections and their right translates span all compact sections: use their open right stabilizers and a finite compact row-ball partition, as in the surjectivity proof of Lemma 6.336. The construction is \(H\)-equivariant, since \(g_{a\lambda}(b)=g_\lambda(ba)\). Equality therefore holds on every compact section. A nonzero full section is detected by a compact section on a sufficiently small row ball and a fibre vector with nonzero evaluation. Thus reconstruction and the ordinary integral pairing are inverse.

Finally reinstate the last column. Its action on a compact section at row \(\xi\) is \(\psi(\xi x)\); on the reconstructed dual section it is \(\psi(-\xi x)\). This follows either by inserting the character in the ordinary integral or by its injectivity just proved. A functional smooth for \(P_n\) is fixed by a compact last-column lattice and an open subgroup of \(H\). The reconstructed section is fixed by both. Shrink the latter subgroup to normalize that lattice; their product is an open subgroup of \(P_n\). Conversely a full smooth \(P_n\)-section gives a smooth functional by the invariant integral. This proves the asserted ordinary smooth-dual identity for \(P_n\), not merely for \(H\). Multiplication of sections by \(\nu(a)\), already computed above, gives exactly (6.818) and its pairing (6.819). No finite-dimensionality of the fibre or boundedness of a functional has been assumed.

The element \(s=\operatorname{diag}(-I_m,1)\) commutes with the embedded \(P_m\) and reverses the last-column character. Left translation by \(s\) identifies the minus full induction with the plus one and commutes with its right action. This remains true in characteristic two, when the additive inverse character is the same character. Apply the second adjunction of (6.812) and \(\Phi_n^-\Phi_n^+=1\) to (6.818); the result is the second line of (6.817).

To check nondegeneracy, regard a pairing as a map from one argument to the smooth dual of the other. On the open orbit the kernel is an open-orbit submodule. Exactness and faithfulness of \(\Phi^-\) on this subcategory make that kernel zero exactly when the kernel of the corresponding fibre map is zero. The fibre map under the adjunction is the pairing downstairs, by evaluation. This proves preservation in either argument. Finally an \(N_n\)-invariant pairing with a trivial \(N_n\)-module factors through the ordinary \(N_n\)-quotient of its other argument; that quotient of \(\Phi_n^+\tau\) is zero. This proves the last line. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.339 — a highest-derivative pairing. Suppose a \(\Delta_{P_n}\)-pairing of smooth modules \(V,W\) is nondegenerate with respect to \(V\). If \(V^{(k)}\) is its highest nonzero derivative, there is an ordinary \(G_{n-k}\)-invariant pairing of \(V^{(k)},W^{(k)}\) nondegenerate with respect to \(V^{(k)}\).

Proof. If \(k=1\), all derivatives of \(\Phi_n^-V\) vanish, so its derivative filtration makes it zero. Hence \(V=\Psi_n^+V^{(1)}\). The cross pairing in (6.817) kills \(\Phi_n^+\Phi_n^-W\), and the first line of that formula gives the required ordinary pairing, preserving nondegeneracy.

For \(k>1\), put \(V_1=\Phi_n^+\Phi_n^-V\), \(W_1=\Phi_n^+\Phi_n^-W\). The left radical of the restricted pairing on \(V_1\times W_1\) is a \(P_n\)-submodule \(R\) of \(V_1\), hence is itself an open-orbit module by Lemma 6.336. Its pairing with \(W\) factors through \(W/W_1\), an inflated module. The cross pairing in (6.817), with its arguments interchanged, makes this zero. Nondegeneracy on \(V\) forces \(R=0\). The second line of (6.817) now gives a \(\Delta_{P_{n-1}}\)-pairing on \(\Phi_n^-V,\Phi_n^-W\) nondegenerate in the first argument. Its highest derivative is of index \(k-1\), by (6.815). Induction gives the asserted ordinary pairing. This also handles \(k=n\), whose target group is \(G_0=1\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.340 — derivative modules of cuspidal induction. Let \(I=\rho_1\times\cdots\times\rho_s\), with labelled irreducible admissible cuspidals of degrees \(n_i\). For \(1\le k\le n\), the actual module \(I^{(k)}\) has a finite filtration with one quotient \[ I_{T^c}=\mathop{\times}_{i\notin T}\rho_i \quad\text{for every }T\subset\{1,\ldots,s\}, \quad\sum_{i\in T}n_i=k, \tag{6.820} \] where the remaining factors retain their original relative order and the empty product is the trivial \(G_0\)-module. A one-dimensional Whittaker space is suppressed in the notation for each quotient; no canonical basis of that space or splitting of the filtration is asserted. In particular \(I^{(k)}\) is admissible of finite length. Every irreducible subquotient has cuspidal datum drawn, with multiplicities, from the remaining labels for one such \(T\).

Proof: exact identification of the functor. For \(k<n\), let \(Q\) have blocks \((n-k,k)\). Taking the last-column relations in (6.815) generates the subgroup \(N_Q\rtimes U_k\). Its character is trivial on \(N_Q\) and is \(\psi(\sum_{j=n-k+1}^{n-1}u_{j,j+1})\) on the lower-right \(U_k\). To check this, take columns in order \(n,n-1,\ldots,n-k+1\): the first \(k-1\) quotients retain the last adjacent entry and kill the earlier entries of each column, and the last quotient kills its whole column. This is precisely the indicated rectangle and upper-unitriangular subgroup. Their ordered column multiplication is bijective, so the generated relations give equality of quotients, not merely a map. On \(a\in G_{n-k}\), the \(k\) normalizing factors in (6.815) multiply to \(\nu(a)^{-k/2}\). This is exactly \(\delta_Q(\operatorname{diag}(a,I_k))^{-1/2}\). Therefore, as actual \(G_{n-k}\)-modules, \[ I^{(k)}\simeq(r_QI)_{U_k,\psi_{U_k}}. \tag{6.821} \] For \(k=n\), (6.815) is directly the full Whittaker quotient, with no remaining determinant factor.

Apply the normalized geometric filtration of Theorem 6.320 to \(r_QI\). A cell that cuts an original cuspidal block has a zero proper Jacquet factor. A surviving cell assigns each original labelled block wholly to the left or wholly to the right target block. Such assignments are exactly the subsets \(T\) in (6.820), each with one cell. Its actual normalized quotient is \(I_{T^c}\otimes I_T\), by the row and column refinements in that theorem. Take the lower-right Whittaker quotient. This functor is exact, and Theorem 6.294 with Corollary 6.302 makes the Whittaker space of \(I_T\) one-dimensional. The resulting finite filtration is (6.820). Theorems 6.324–6.325 give admissibility and finite length of its factors and hence of the extension. The cuspidal datum assertion is Theorem 6.322 applied to these factors. For \(k=n\), Whittaker heredity gives the one stated trivial quotient. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.341 — length bounds and a unitary exact formula. With these labels, \[ \operatorname{length}_{G_{n-k}}I^{(k)} \le\sum_{\substack{T\subset\{1,\ldots,s\}\\\sum_{i\in T}n_i=k}} (s-|T|)!,\qquad \operatorname{length}_{P_n}I \le\sum_{t=1}^s\binom st(s-t)!. \tag{6.822} \] If the cuspidals are unitary and pairwise inequivalent, then \[ \operatorname{length}_{G_{n-k}}I^{(k)} =\#\{T:\sum_{i\in T}n_i=k\},\qquad \operatorname{length}_{P_n}I=2^s-1. \tag{6.823} \]

Proof. Apply the factorial bound of Theorem 6.324 to every quotient in (6.820), using \(0!=1\). Sum over \(k\) and use (6.816). Each nonempty subset occurs once. In the unitary case every nonempty remaining product is irreducible by Corollary 6.332, and the empty product has length one. Add the lengths along the filtration. The number of all nonempty labelled subsets is \(2^s-1\), by independently choosing whether each label is present. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.342 — the shifted support of a mirabolic submodule. If \(0\ne V\subset I|_{P_n}\) and \(V^{(k)}\) is its highest derivative, then every irreducible \(G_{n-k}\)-submodule \(\sigma\subset V^{(k)}\) is admissible and satisfies \[ \operatorname{cusp}(\sigma)\subset\{\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_s\},\qquad \nu\operatorname{cusp}(\sigma) \subset\{\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_s\}. \tag{6.824} \] Inclusions mean submultisets of exact cuspidal representations. If \(k=n\), both assertions concern the empty multiset.

Proof: duality of the inducing data. For an admissible Levi module, the compact-flag pairing \(\int_K\langle f(k),\widetilde f(k)\rangle\,dk\) identifies the smooth dual of its normalized induction with induction of its smooth dual in the same block order. Invariance follows from the positive-\(\delta_P\)-covariant integration in Lemma 6.331, applied to the fibre evaluation pairing. It is perfect on every sufficiently small principal fixed space: the finite flag coordinates (6.670) are a finite direct sum of Levi fixed spaces, their weights are nonzero Haar masses, and the dual of a Levi fixed space is its smooth-dual fixed space by averaging. Every smooth functional is fixed by one such principal group, so these finite pairings give surjectivity onto the whole smooth dual.

An irreducible admissible cuspidal has irreducible admissible cuspidal dual. Irreducibility and the fixed-space assertion follow from the nondegenerate averaging argument in the proof of Theorem 6.71 after (6.162). For cuspidality one may use Theorem 6.311: after its positive twist the original smooth module is unitary, and finite fixed-space Riesz representation identifies its smooth dual with its conjugate module. Complex conjugation commutes with the finite sums of radical relations, so all its proper radical quotients are still zero. Untwist to conclude. Thus \[ I^\vee\simeq\rho_1^\vee\times\cdots\times\rho_s^\vee. \tag{6.825} \] The same reasoning and an irreducible cuspidal embedding show that the cuspidal datum of any irreducible admissible \(X^\vee\) is the dual of that of \(X\): dualize its embedding, use exact smooth duality on admissible modules, and apply the subquotient uniqueness of Theorem 6.322. Exactness of this duality follows on each compact fixed space from finite-dimensional duality and averaging.

Proof: the highest derivative. Exactness makes \(V^{(k)}\) a submodule of the admissible finite-length module \(I^{(k)}\). This proves admissibility of \(\sigma\); the first inclusion follows from Theorem 6.340. The ordinary evaluation pairing of \(I\) and \(I^\vee\), restricted in the first argument to \(V\), is nondegenerate there. Twist its second argument by \(\nu\). The resulting pairing of \(V\) with \((\nu I^\vee)|_{P_n}\) has simultaneous factor \(\nu(p)\), and hence is a \(\Delta_{P_n}\)-pairing. Theorem 6.339 gives an ordinary pairing of \(V^{(k)}\) and \((\nu I^\vee)^{(k)}\), nondegenerate in the first argument. Restrict to \(\sigma\). Its map into the smooth dual is injective. Dualizing and using admissible biduality shows that \(\sigma^\vee\) is a quotient, hence a subquotient, of \((\nu I^\vee)^{(k)}\). Theorem 6.340 puts its cuspidal datum inside \(\{\nu\rho_i^\vee\}\). Dualizing that datum puts \(\operatorname{cusp}(\sigma)\) inside \(\{\nu^{-1}\rho_i\}\), which is exactly the second inclusion of (6.824). No general assertion that arbitrary smooth irreducibles are admissible was needed. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.343 — a sufficient irreducibility criterion. Suppose that among the cuspidals defining \(I\) there are no two occurrences with \(\rho_j\simeq\nu\rho_i\). Then \(I\) is irreducible, has no nonzero degenerate \(P_n\)-submodule, and has mirabolic length \(2^s-1\). Its derivative lengths are the subset counts in (6.823). This allows repeated isomorphic factors. It is a statement for split groups in both field characteristics.

Proof. A nonzero degenerate \(P_n\)-submodule \(V\subset I\) would have a highest nonzero derivative of some index \(k<n\), by Theorem 6.337. It has finite length by exactness and Theorem 6.340, so choose an irreducible submodule \(\sigma\subset V^{(k)}\). Its positive rank \(n-k\) makes its cuspidal datum nonempty. Choose a cuspidal \(\rho\) from that datum. The two inclusions (6.824) put both \(\rho\) and \(\nu\rho\) among the original cuspidals, a contradiction. Thus there is no such \(V\).

Theorem 6.329 and Corollary 6.330 give one generic occurrence in the finite composition multiset of \(I\), independent of order. If \(I\) were reducible, some irreducible constituent \(X\) would be nongeneric. It is admissible; Theorems 6.321–6.322 embed it into an induction with the same exact cuspidal multiset in some order. That order satisfies the same no-pair hypothesis. Its nonzero nongeneric submodule \(X|_{P_n}\) contradicts the preceding paragraph. Hence \(I\) is irreducible. Every submultiset satisfies the same no-pair hypothesis, so every remaining product in (6.820) is irreducible. Adding lengths gives (6.823), now under the stated hypothesis.

Finally \(\rho\not\simeq\nu\rho\): at \(\varpi_FI_a\), their central characters have absolute-value ratio \(|\varpi_F|^a\ne1\). Thus a multiset consisting of repeated copies of one cuspidal meets the hypothesis. The theorem supplies no converse reducibility assertion for a pair differing by \(\nu\), and no conclusion here identifies an inner-form reducibility exponent. \(\square\)

The ordered criterion in Theorem 6.348 determines a suitable inducing order for the generic constituent even when some cuspidals differ by \(\nu\). Theorem 6.349 gives the resulting full generic Kirillov construction. Theorem 6.374 isolates each split discrete series among all generic irreducibles with its central character.

The normalized functors and highest-derivative pairing may be compared with Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the free NUMDAM edition, Sections 3.2–3.8 and 4.7–4.8. The module filtration here follows directly from Theorem 6.320 and the explicit relation calculation (6.821).

6.54 Ordered cuspidal induction and the full generic Kirillov model

Let \(G_n=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\), where \(F\) is a nondiscrete nonarchimedean local field of either characteristic. All modules have complex scalars. Retain the normalized functors (6.810), \(\nu=|\det|\), \(G_0=P_1=1\), and the fixed nontrivial additive character \(\psi\). Besides ordinary normalized induction \(\rho\times\sigma\), use the following two products. For \(k,m\ge1\), with \(\rho\) on \(G_k\), \(\tau\) on \(P_m\), and \(n=k+m\), put \[ \begin{split} \rho\star\tau &=\operatorname{cInd}_{(G_k\times P_m)U_{k,m}}^{P_n} \bigl(\nu(A)^{m/2}\nu(B)^{-k/2}\rho\otimes\tau\bigr),\\ \tau\diamond\rho &=\operatorname{cInd}_{H_{m,k}}^{P_n} \bigl(\nu(A)^{k/2}\nu(B)^{-m/2}\tau\otimes\rho\bigr),\\ H_{m,k}&=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}A&X&b\\0&B&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}: A\in G_{m-1},\ B\in G_k,\ X\in M_{m-1,k}(F),\ b\in F^{m-1}\right\}. \end{split} \tag{6.826} \] In the first line, \(B\in P_m\) occupies the last \(m\) standard indices and \(U_{k,m}\) is the upper rectangle. In the second, \(\tau\) acts on \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A&b\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) at indices \((1,\ldots,m-1,n)\), and \(\rho\) acts on the middle \(k\) indices. Both displayed covariances include all normalizations; the rectangle acts trivially. In particular, \[ \delta_{M_{m-1,k}}(A,B)^{1/2}\nu(B)^{-1/2} =\nu(A)^{k/2}\nu(B)^{-m/2}. \tag{6.827} \] The extra negative half-power on \(B\) is part of \(\diamond\). It cannot be omitted. Products with a \(G_0\)-module mean tensoring by its vector space. A term involving the zero functor \(\Phi_1^-\) is zero; no group \(P_0\) is used.

Lemma 6.344 — a twisted relative affine section integral. Let \(N=F^l\) be a column space, let \(M\subset G_l\) be closed, and suppose \(M\) fixes a character \(\theta\) of \(N\). Let \(R\subset M\) be closed, let \(W\subset N\) be an \(R\)-stable linear subspace, and let \(\eta\) be a smooth \(R\ltimes W\)-module. For \(P=M\ltimes N\), the integral \[ \begin{split} \mathcal Qf(m)&=\int_{W\backslash N}\theta(x)^{-1}[f(xm)]\,d\bar x,\\ \left(\operatorname{cInd}_{R\ltimes W}^{P}\eta\right)_{N,\theta} &\simeq\operatorname{cInd}_{R}^{M} \bigl(\kappa\otimes\eta_{W,\theta|_W}\bigr),\qquad \kappa(r)=\frac{|\det(r|_N)|}{|\det(r|_W)|} \end{split} \tag{6.828} \] is onto and has exactly the algebraic twisted relation kernel. The quotient \(R\backslash M\) need not be compact.

Proof: the fibre integral. Put \(Y=\operatorname{cInd}_W^N\eta\). Choose increasing compact lattices exhausting \(N\). For any \(y\in Y\), one such \(K\) has support in \(WK\). Twisted averaging gives \(y_K=E_{K,\theta}y\), determined by \(v=y_K(0)\), with \(\eta(w)v=\theta(w)v\) for \(w\in W\cap K\). Its integral is \[ q(y)=\frac{\operatorname{vol}K}{\operatorname{vol}(W\cap K)}[v],\qquad (E_{L,\theta}y_K)(0)= \frac{\operatorname{vol}K\operatorname{vol}(W\cap L)} {\operatorname{vol}L\operatorname{vol}(W\cap K)} E_{W\cap L,\theta}v\quad(L\supset K). \tag{6.829} \] These are direct compact quotient integrals, as in (6.659)–(6.660). If \(q(y)=0\), express \(v\) by finitely many twisted \(W\)-relations and choose \(L\) containing their translating elements. The last average is zero, and \(E_{L,\theta}y_K\) is consequently zero on its entire support \(WL\). Thus the kernel is the algebraic relation space. Conversely any fibre quotient vector is attained by a section supported on \(WK\), whose value is a small \(W\cap K\)-average of a lift; the first positive scalar in (6.829) can be inverted. This proves the fibre assertion. All vector integrals are finite sums after a compact-open partition.

Proof: sections in stages and the uniform kernel. The exact stage maps are \(f\mapsto[m\mapsto(x\mapsto f(xm))]\) and their inverse by evaluation. Their \(R\)-action on \(Y\) is \((r y)(x)=\eta(r)y(r^{-1}x)\). It is smooth: a compact section is determined by finitely many cosets \(W x_i K\) and fibre values; a small subgroup of \(R\) preserves \(K\), fixes those values and has \(r^{-1}x_i\in x_i+K\). Compact support in stages gives finitely many values \(y_i\) on compact representative sets \(C_i\subset M\). Their fibre supports and the \(C_i\) give compact support of the inverse section modulo \(R\ltimes W\). A single small last-column lattice fixes the inverse section, since all conjugates needed over the finitely many compact \(C_i\) lie in prescribed stabilizing neighborhoods. Together with its open right \(M\)-stabilizer this proves actual smoothness. Restriction proves the converse.

Compact induction from a closed \(R\) is exact here without compactness of the whole quotient. At a compact open right level \(J\subset M\), a compact section has only finitely many nonzero double-coset values at \(Rm_iJ\). These values lie in invariants under the compact group \(R\cap m_iJm_i^{-1}\). Lift each by that compact average in a surjective fibre map, keeping all other coset values zero. The resulting section is still compactly supported modulo \(R\) and right \(J\)-invariant. Injections and kernels are pointwise. This proves exactness.

Changing variables in the fibre integral gives \(q(r y)=\kappa(r)\eta(r)q(y)\), since \(R\) preserves \(\theta\). Exact compact induction therefore makes (6.828) onto. If it kills \(f\), its finite values \(y_i\) on \(C_i\) lie in \(\ker q\). By (6.829), take lattices \(K_i\) whose twisted averages annihilate them. The union of \(\{m^{-1}x:m\in C_i,\ x\in K_i\}\) is compact, so it lies in one lattice \(K\). For \(m\in C_i\), \(mK\supset K_i\), and the twisted \(mK\)-average kills \(y_i\). The fixed character is unchanged under these conjugations. Hence \(E_{K,\theta}f=0\) everywhere, using covariance on the other representatives. Averaging differences are finite sums of twisted translation differences of smooth vectors. Conversely the integral kills every such difference. This proves the exact kernel. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.345 — the two-orbit mirabolic restriction. For all smooth \(\rho\) on \(G_a\) and \(\sigma\) on \(G_b\), with \(a,b>0\), there is an exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow(\rho|_{P_a})\diamond\sigma \longrightarrow(\rho\times\sigma)|_{P_{a+b}} \longrightarrow\rho\star(\sigma|_{P_b})\longrightarrow0. \tag{6.830} \] No splitting is asserted.

Proof: both orbits and their charts. Set \(N=a+b\), let \(Q\) be the ordinary \((a,b)\)-parabolic, and let \(E_a\) be the first standard column subspace. The quotient \(Q\backslash G_N\) identifies with the Grassmannian by \(Qg\mapsto g^{-1}E_a\). The mirabolic group preserves the last row \(e_N\). It has a closed orbit of planes inside \(\ker e_N\) and an open orbit of planes not contained there. It is transitive on each: in the closed case complete a basis of the plane inside \(F^{N-1}\); in the open case choose a basis of its intersection with that hyperplane and one vector \(y+e_N\), and use the upper-right translation to remove \(y\).

These operations give local sections, not just a set-theoretic orbit description. On a Grassmann pivot chart, choose the unique column basis with its specified pivot rows equal to the identity. Complete it by the nonpivot standard columns. On the closed orbit this gives \(C\in G_{N-1}\); \(\operatorname{diag}(C^{-1},1)\) sends the plane to \(E_a\). On an open chart choose pivots \(J\cup\{N\}\), with \(|J|=a-1\). The first \(a-1\) basis columns have last coordinate zero and the last is \(y+e_N\). Complete the first columns to \(C\in G_{N-1}\). The matrix \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}C^{-1}&-C^{-1}y\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) sends the plane to \(\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_{a-1},e_N)\). Every matrix entry and its inverse in these charts is rational with a nonzero pivot denominator, hence continuous. Their restrictions to compact open subcharts give local trivializations for smooth section values.

Take the identity as the closed representative. For the open representative use the permutation matrix \(w\) with \[ w e_i=e_i\ (i<a),\qquad w e_i=e_{i+1}\ (a\le i<N),\qquad w e_N=e_a. \tag{6.831} \] Thus \(w^{-1}E_a=\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_{a-1},e_N)\). The closed stabilizer \(Q\cap P_N\) is \((G_a\times P_b)U_{a,b}\). In the open stabilizer \(P_N\cap w^{-1}Qw\), the first source block acts on \((1,\ldots,a-1,N)\), the second on \((a,\ldots,N-1)\). The last-row condition forces the bottom-left-to-middle entries to zero. The remaining matrices are exactly \(H_{a,b}\) of (6.826). The source modulus on them is \(\nu(A)^{b/2}\nu(B)^{-a/2}\), exactly the \(\diamond\) covariance, including its extra half-power.

Restriction of a section to an orbit is identified with \(f_w(p)=f(wp)\); its inverse is determined by source covariance. The charts just constructed make these continuous inverses on the associated section bundles. On the closed orbit the full section space has compact quotient support automatically. On the open orbit the kernel of closed restriction has compact quotient support there. Restriction onto the closed orbit is onto: take a finite compact-open chart partition of the support, extend its finitely many fibre values to the chart neighborhoods, and put zero elsewhere. Smoothness follows from the open stabilizers of those values and the continuous matrix transition functions. A section vanishing on the closed subset has compact support in its open complement. Extension by zero and restriction therefore give the exact open/closed sequence, with the two covariances already computed. This proves (6.830). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.346 — the negative derivative product identities. For all smooth modules in the indicated ranks, \[ \Psi_n^-(\rho\star\tau)=\rho\times\Psi_m^-\tau,\qquad \Psi_n^-(\tau\diamond\rho)=\Psi_m^-\tau\times\rho, \tag{6.832} \] and \[ \begin{gathered} \Phi_n^-(\rho\star\tau)=\rho\star\Phi_m^-\tau,\\ 0\longrightarrow(\Phi_m^-\tau)\diamond\rho \longrightarrow\Phi_n^-(\tau\diamond\rho) \longrightarrow(\Psi_m^-\tau)\star(\rho|_{P_k})\longrightarrow0. \end{gathered} \tag{6.833} \] All maps are natural. The boundary conventions after (6.827) apply.

Proof: the common actual quotient map. Write \(l=n-1\) and \(V=N_n=F^l\). For \(\Psi^-\), the remaining group is \(G_l\), the character is one, and Lemma 6.344 applies directly to the source subgroup. For \(\Phi^-\), the remaining group is \(P_l\), the stabilizer of \(e_l\); write \(Q=P_l\ltimes V\). For either product the projection of its source subgroup to \(G_l\) is a parabolic \(R\). Its \(V\)-intersection is either all \(V\) for \(\star\), or its first \(m-1\) coordinate space for \(\diamond\). The quotient by the source subgroup is a vector bundle over \(R\backslash G_l\): choose a Gaussian representative in the latter quotient and a complement to that \(V\)-intersection. Changes of representative act linearly on the complement quotient. Thus the two Grassmann orbits of Theorem 6.345 pull back to exactly two \(Q\)-orbits, with continuous product charts. The compact section extension and restriction argument in that theorem applies also to this vector bundle; it uses only the compact support of each section, not compactness of the entire bundle.

On the orbit of \(w\), put \(R_w=P_l\cap w^{-1}Rw\), \(W_w=w^{-1}W\), and let \(\eta^w\) be its transported fibre action. Its section module is \(\operatorname{cInd}_{R_w\ltimes W_w}^{Q}\eta^w\). The map to the normalized derivative is explicitly \[ f_w\longmapsto\left[h\longmapsto \nu(h)^{-1/2}\int_{W_w\backslash V} \psi(-e_lx)[f_w(xh)]\,d\bar x\right],\qquad h\in P_l. \tag{6.834} \] For the ordinary quotient, replace the character by one, take \(h\in G_l\) and the single identity orbit. The integrals are on compactly supported orbit sections. Lemma 6.344 proves surjectivity and the full algebraic kernel on each orbit, uniformly on the compact representative sets of each section. The exterior \(\nu(h)^{-1/2}\) converts its ordinary right action into the normalized derivative action: right translation by \(h_0\) before this exterior factor contributes \(\nu(h_0)^{1/2}\), which is cancelled by the functor normalization. Exact twisted coinvariants pass the orbit support sequence to an exact sequence.

Proof: all characters and moduli. For \(\star\), put \(a=k\), \(b=m-1\); its projected parabolic has blocks \((a,b)\) and \(W=V\). The identity closed orbit has \(R_w=(G_a\times P_b)U_{a,b}\). Its fibre character on \(\tau\)'s last column is exactly the standard last-coordinate character. Thus its fibre quotient is \(\rho\otimes\tau_{N_m,\psi_e}\), and its quotient-measure factor \(\kappa\) is one. On the open orbit use (6.831) in dimension \(l\). Transporting \(\psi(e_lx)\) back gives \(\psi(x_a)\). The top \(a\) entries of the source last column act trivially, being in its upper rectangle. A nontrivial value of \(\psi(x_a)\) therefore annihilates every fibre vector. This orbit contributes zero. If \(m=1\), there is only the single orbit, the source is \(\Psi_n^+\rho\), and its nontrivial derivative is zero, as (6.833) requires.

For \(\diamond\), put \(a=m-1\), \(b=k\). At the closed identity orbit, \(R_w=(G_a\times P_b)U_{a,b}\) and \(W_w=F^a\). The character is trivial on \(W_w\), so its fibre is \(\tau_{N_m,1}\otimes\rho|_{P_b}\). At the open orbit use (6.831) with this \(a\). Here \(W_w=\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_{a-1},e_l)\), and the transported character is the standard nontrivial character on \(\tau\)'s last column. Its stabilizer in that block is \(P_a\), placed at indices \((1,\ldots,a-1,l)\). The middle block remains \(G_b\), so \(R_w=H_{a,b}\subset P_l\), with its indicated upper rectangle. Both quotient spaces \(V/W_w\) have determinant \(\nu(B)\), giving \(\kappa=\nu(B)\). The source covariance, fibre conversion and target normalization multiply as follows: \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} &\kappa&\text{resulting fibre covariance}\\\hline \star,\ \Psi^-\text{ or closed }\Phi^-&1& \nu(A)^{(m-1)/2}\nu(B)^{-k/2}\rho\otimes(\Psi_m^-\tau\text{ or }\Phi_m^-\tau)\\ \diamond,\ \Psi^-\text{ or either }\Phi^-&\nu(B)& \nu(A)^{k/2}\nu(B)^{-(m-1)/2} (\Psi_m^-\tau\text{ or }\Phi_m^-\tau)\otimes\rho . \end{array} \tag{6.835} \] Indeed the source \(\star\) exponents are \((m/2,-k/2)\), conversion of the last-column quotient into its normalized functor adds \(+1/2\) on \(B\), and target normalization subtracts \(1/2\) on both blocks. For \(\diamond\), the source exponents are \((k/2,-m/2)\), the fibre conversion adds \(+1/2\) on \(A\), the quotient integral adds \(+1\) on \(B\), and target normalization subtracts \(1/2\) on each. These give exactly (6.835), for arbitrary block matrices, since each character is a determinant. In the table all fibre actions are restricted to the stabilizers just specified. The closed term is \(\star\) and the open term is \(\diamond\) in their new ranks. With a trivial character and remaining group \(G_l\), the same calculation gives the two ordinary products in (6.832).

If \(m=1\) in \(\diamond\), then \(a=0\) and there is only the closed orbit. Its fibre quotient is \(\tau\), the \(G_0\)-module, and the resulting \(\Phi^-\)-module is \(\tau\otimes\rho|_{P_k}\). The left term in (6.833) is zero. This proves every boundary case and the theorem. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.347 — positive functors and a noncompact support test. Where the functors are defined, \[ \rho\star\Phi_m^+\tau=\Phi_n^+(\rho\star\tau),\qquad \rho\star\Psi_m^+\sigma=\Psi_n^+(\rho\times\sigma). \tag{6.836} \] If \(k>0\), every nonzero \(P_n\)-submodule \(Z\subset\tau\diamond\rho\) has \(\Phi_n^-Z\ne0\).

Proof: compact induction in stages. For closed matrix subgroups \(K\subset L\subset G\), the stage maps for bare compact induction are \[ f\longmapsto[g\longmapsto(h\longmapsto f(hg))],\qquad F\longmapsto[g\longmapsto F(g)(1)]. \tag{6.837} \] They are inverse and respect covariance and right translation. To check the spaces, a compact quotient support intersects each closed fibre \(K\backslash Lg\) in a compact set. Its image in \(L\backslash G\) is compact. Conversely a smooth compact outer section has finitely many values on compact representative sets at one right level. The finite union of the compact supports of those inner values times the representative sets has compact image in \(K\backslash G\). An open right stabilizer of the outer section fixes the evaluated section; a right stabilizer of \(f\) fixes the stage section. This proves the actual compact-section identity, not merely a formal evaluation identity.

Apply it to the first equality in (6.836). Both sides become compact induction from \(((G_k\times P_{m-1})U_{k,m-1})N_n\). The last-column character is \(\psi(x_{n-1})\). On the two remaining blocks, the left covariance is \(\nu(A)^{m/2}\nu(B)^{-k/2}\nu(B)^{1/2}\); the right covariance is \(\nu(A)^{(m-1)/2}\nu(B)^{-k/2}\nu(A)^{1/2}\nu(B)^{1/2}\). They agree exactly, as do the fibre actions. For \(\Psi^+\), the whole last column acts trivially on both sides. Restriction of a section to \(G_{n-1}\) and inflation are inverse; both have covariance \(\nu(A)^{m/2}\nu(B)^{(1-k)/2}\). The \(G_0\) boundary is plain tensoring. This proves (6.836).

Proof: the support test. If \(\Phi_n^-Z=0\), (6.811) says that \(N_n\) acts trivially on \(Z\). Translate a nonzero section so that \(f(1)\ne0\). It then satisfies \(f(x)=f(1)\ne0\) for every \(x\in N_n\). But \[ H_{m,k}N_n\text{ is closed in }P_n,\qquad H_{m,k}\backslash H_{m,k}N_n \simeq (H_{m,k}\cap N_n)\backslash N_n\simeq F^k. \tag{6.838} \] The first assertion follows by projecting onto the closed \((m-1,k)\)-parabolic in \(G_{n-1}\). The homeomorphism follows by cancelling its Levi and rectangle on the left; the remaining column quotient is its middle \(k\) entries. Thus the compact quotient support of \(f\) would contain this entire closed noncompact fibre. This is impossible for \(k>0\) over a local field. The case \(m=1\) has the same fibre and needs no first block. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.348 — the ordered nondegeneracy criterion. Let \(I=\rho_1\times\cdots\times\rho_s\) with irreducible admissible cuspidals, in the given order. Suppose \[ \rho_j\not\simeq\nu\rho_i\qquad(i<j). \tag{6.839} \] Then \(I|_{P_n}\) has no nonzero degenerate submodule, where degenerate means that its top derivative, or full Whittaker quotient, is zero.

Proof. Induct on \(s\). For \(s=1\), Corollary 6.302 makes the restriction simple with nonzero top derivative. Suppose \(s>1\), put \(a=\deg\rho_1\), and write \(I=\rho_1\times I_0\), with \(n_0=\deg I_0>0\). If a nonzero degenerate mirabolic submodule existed, choose a simple submodule \(Z\) of it, using finite mirabolic length from Theorem 6.308. It is still degenerate by exactness. Sequence (6.830) gives two possibilities: \(Z\) lies in \((\rho_1|_{P_a})\diamond I_0\), or it injects into \(\rho_1\star(I_0|_{P_{n_0}})\).

In the first case put \(T=\rho_1|_{P_a}\), \(S=T\diamond I_0\). Corollary 6.302 and (6.815) give \(T^{(i)}=0\) for \(i<a\) and a one-dimensional \(T^{(a)}\); choose an identification of this last space with \(\mathbb C\). Iterating (6.832)–(6.833) gives \[ S^{(i)}=0\ (i<a),\qquad (\Phi^-)^i S=((\Phi^-)^iT)\diamond I_0\ (i<a),\qquad (\Phi^-)^a S=I_0|_{P_{n_0}}. \tag{6.840} \] The last step uses \(\Psi_1^-\mathbb C=\mathbb C\), \(\Phi_1^-\mathbb C=0\) and the boundary term of (6.833). Since all derivatives of \(Z\) below \(a\) vanish, its nonzero derivative filtration implies \((\Phi^-)^{a-1}Z\ne0\). Apply the support test of Lemma 6.347 to its inclusion in \(((\Phi^-)^{a-1}T)\diamond I_0\). It gives \((\Phi^-)^aZ\ne0\). This is a degenerate submodule of \(I_0|_{P_{n_0}}\), since its top derivative is \(Z^{(n)}=0\). The later factors satisfy (6.839), contradicting induction. For \(a=1\) there are zero initial iterations and the same support test applies directly.

In the second case let \(k<n\) be the highest nonzero derivative of \(Z\). The \(\star\) identities give an actual injection \[ Z^{(k)}\ \longrightarrow\rho_1\times I_0^{(k)}. \tag{6.841} \] If \(k>n_0\) the right side is zero, so \(k\le n_0\). The right side has an actual finite filtration by \(\rho_1\) times the remaining cuspidal products of \(I_0\), by Theorem 6.340 and exact induction. Hence it is admissible and finite length. Choose an irreducible submodule \(\sigma\subset Z^{(k)}\). Its exact cuspidal datum contains \(\rho_1\): every filtration quotient on the right is a cuspidal induction containing that labelled factor, and Theorem 6.322 gives its entire datum, with multiplicities. Lemma 6.342, applied to \(Z\subset I\), therefore forces \(\nu\rho_1\) among the original factors. It cannot equal \(\rho_1\), by its central absolute value, so it equals some later \(\rho_j\), contrary to (6.839). Both cases are impossible. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.349 — a faithful generic Kirillov realization. Let \(V\) be irreducible admissible and generic on \(G_n\). For every nonzero Whittaker functional \(\ell\), the restriction map \[ V\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ind}_{U_n}^{P_n}\theta_n, \qquad v\longmapsto\bigl[p\longmapsto\ell(\pi(p)v)\bigr] \tag{6.842} \] is injective. Its image contains the compact Whittaker module \(\operatorname{cInd}_{U_n}^{P_n}\theta_n\). The image is the Kirillov model on \(P_n\); it need not consist only of compactly supported sections.

Proof: an order and the embedding. For a cuspidal \(\rho\) of rank \(r\), define the real number \[ t(\rho)=-\frac{\log_q|\omega_\rho(\varpi_F)|}{r},\qquad t(\nu\rho)=t(\rho)+1. \tag{6.843} \] The central character and its absolute value were proved in Theorem 6.311. Order the exact cuspidal multiset of \(V\) by nonincreasing \(t\). A later factor cannot be \(\nu\) times an earlier one, by the displayed strict increase. Let \(I\) be induction in this order. It has finite length, so choose an irreducible \(G_n\)-submodule \(X\). Theorem 6.348 makes \(X\) generic: otherwise its nonzero restriction would be a degenerate mirabolic submodule. Corollary 6.330 identifies \(X\) with \(V\). Thus \(V\) embeds in this \(I\) and inherits the absence of nonzero degenerate mirabolic submodules.

The map (6.842) is smooth, has the stated left Whittaker covariance and commutes with right \(P_n\)-translation. If its kernel is \(K\), exactness gives \[ K^{(n)}\hookrightarrow V^{(n)}\simeq\mathbb C, \qquad\ell|_K=0,\qquad K^{(n)}=0. \tag{6.844} \] Indeed \(\ell\) factors through the one-dimensional top quotient and is nonzero there, so is injective on it. The absence of a nonzero degenerate submodule forces \(K=0\). The compact image assertion follows from the canonical layer in Corollary 6.350 below. No irreducibility of the whole mirabolic restriction is asserted. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.350 — the essential compact socle and mirabolic endomorphisms. In Theorem 6.349, the restriction of \(V\) has a unique simple submodule, contained in every nonzero mirabolic submodule. It is \[ S=(\Phi^+)^{n-1}V^{(n)}\simeq \operatorname{cInd}_{U_n}^{P_n}\theta_n, \qquad\operatorname{End}_{P_n}V=\mathbb C. \tag{6.845} \] The same assertions hold for an ordered cuspidal induction satisfying (6.839). More generally, between any two smooth mirabolic modules with one-dimensional top derivative and no nonzero degenerate submodule, the Hom space has dimension at most one and every nonzero map is injective. If \(V\) is cuspidal, its whole Kirillov image is the compact module.

Proof. Iterating (6.811) identifies the deepest layer of the derivative filtration with \((\Phi^+)^{n-1}V^{(n)}\), as an actual submodule, and its top quotient maps isomorphically onto \(V^{(n)}\). This space is one-dimensional. Each \(\Phi^+\) preserves simple modules, so the layer is simple. Compact induction in stages, (6.837), identifies it with the displayed compact Whittaker module: the nested last columns multiply to \(U_n\), their characters multiply to \(\theta_n\), and every normalizing character is one on this unipotent source. At each intermediate induction, multiplying sections by the corresponding determinant character moves that character to the inducing subgroup, as in the proof of (6.818); its restriction to the ultimate unipotent source is one. The character multiplication follows entry by entry from the adjacent entries of successive last columns.

A nonzero submodule \(Z\subset V|_{P_n}\) has \(Z^{(n)}\ne0\). Its inclusion in \(V^{(n)}\) is therefore an isomorphism of one-dimensional spaces. Naturality of the deepest layer embeds its compact simple layer onto \(S\); hence \(S\subset Z\). This proves essentiality and uniqueness. For a mirabolic endomorphism \(T\), its top derivative is a scalar \(c\). Exactness gives \[ \bigl(\operatorname{im}(T-c)\bigr)^{(n)}=0. \tag{6.846} \] The image is a mirabolic submodule and therefore must be zero. Thus every endomorphism is scalar, even though the restriction need not be simple. More generally, a map between two smooth mirabolic modules with these top-derivative and nondegeneracy properties that kills the source compact socle has zero top derivative, because that socle maps isomorphically on top derivatives. Its image is then a degenerate submodule of the target and must be zero. Restriction to the source socle therefore injects the Hom space into maps between the two simple compact socles, a one-dimensional space by the equivalence of Lemma 6.336. A nonzero map cannot have a nonzero kernel, since that kernel would contain the source socle. This proves both assertions about maps.

For completeness, (6.842) maps \(S\) onto the entire compact Whittaker submodule. Evaluation at one gives an explicit adjunction between maps into full smooth Whittaker induction and functionals on the top quotient: a functional \(a\) gives \(s\mapsto[p\mapsto a(ps)]\), and evaluation is its inverse. Consequently this Hom space for \(S\) is one-dimensional. The natural inclusion of compact sections and the restriction of (6.842) are both nonzero maps in it. The latter is nonzero because \(S^{(n)}\to V^{(n)}\) is an isomorphism. They differ by a nonzero scalar, so have the same image. This proves the image assertion in Theorem 6.349 without assuming it there. For an ordered induction, top dimension one follows from Whittaker heredity, and Theorem 6.348 supplies the same absence of degenerate submodules; the identical proof applies. If \(V\) is cuspidal, Corollary 6.302 makes the restriction simple, so it equals \(S\). \(\square\)

Example 6.351 — a faithful model does not imply an irreducible induction. In degree two let \[ I_-=\nu^{-1/2}\times\nu^{1/2},\qquad I_+=\nu^{1/2}\times\nu^{-1/2},\qquad 0\to1\to I_-\to\mathrm{St}\to0,\qquad 0\to\mathrm{St}\to I_+\to1\to0. \tag{6.847} \] These are the proved nonsplit sequences of Example 6.334. The first order violates (6.839) and has the displayed degenerate mirabolic submodule. The second order satisfies (6.839), has no such submodule, and embeds faithfully in full Whittaker induction on \(P_2\), by the kernel argument (6.844). Nevertheless it is reducible as a \(G_2\)-module. The essential compact socle lies properly inside its Steinberg restriction. Indeed (6.340) gives mirabolic length three for \(I_+\), while its trivial quotient has length one; thus the Steinberg restriction has length two, whereas the compact socle is simple. Its mirabolic endomorphism algebra, and that of \(I_+\), is scalar by Corollary 6.350.

A higher example is \(J=\nu\times1\times\nu^{-1}\) on \(G_3\). It satisfies (6.839) in the displayed order. Its derivative filtrations from Theorem 6.340 give \[ \operatorname{length}_{G_2}J^{(1)}=2+1+2=5,\qquad \operatorname{length}_{G_1}J^{(2)}=3,\qquad \dim J^{(3)}=1,\qquad\operatorname{length}_{P_3}J=9. \tag{6.848} \] Indeed the three first-derivative quotients are \(\nu\times1\), \(\nu\times\nu^{-1}\), and \(1\times\nu^{-1}\). The first and last have length two by (6.847), after twisting, whereas the middle has length one by Theorem 6.343. The second derivative has the three one-dimensional remaining characters, and the top quotient is one-dimensional. Add lengths using (6.816). The induction \(J\) is reducible: induce the nontrivial exact sequence for \(\nu\times1\) with \(\nu^{-1}\); both end modules are nonzero, since a nonzero inducing vector gives a nonzero compact-flag section. Exactness is Theorem 6.306. Thus \(J\) has mirabolic length nine, an essential compact simple socle, scalar mirabolic endomorphisms and a faithful Whittaker realization, while remaining reducible on \(G_3\).
