The local-field support hypothesis is substantive. Over a finite field, the analogous \(\operatorname{Ind}_{G_1(\mathbb F_q)}^{P_2(\mathbb F_q)}1\) is the permutation module on \(\mathbb F_q\). Its nonzero constant functions form a trivial last-column submodule, whose nontrivial character quotient is zero. The fibre in (6.838) is then finite and compact, so that support contradiction is unavailable. Finite orbit and matrix calculations do not prove the local noncompact support test.

For comparison, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, Sections 4.9–4.15 and 7.1–7.3 of the free NUMDAM edition, treat these products and the generic Kirillov construction. The orbit-section maps, compact kernels and modulus factors needed here are proved above. The segment construction and complete split discrete-series classification are Theorems 6.367 and 6.373. Theorem 6.374 proves generic trace isolation, and Corollary 6.375 gives the full generic-segment product criterion. Individual representation transfers require further arguments.

6.55 Adjacent cuspidal twists and disconnected generic products

Let \(F\) be a nonarchimedean local field, of either characteristic, let \(q\) be its residue cardinality, and put \(G_n=\mathrm{GL}_n(F)\), \(K_n=\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal O_F)\) and \(\nu(g)=|\det g|_F\). Representations are smooth complex representations. Cuspidals and irreducibles in this section are admissible. Products mean normalized parabolic induction. The adjoint of a compact test is \(f^*(g)=\overline{f(g^{-1})}\); these groups are unimodular. A Hermitian form is conjugate-linear in its first variable. The reducibility assertion is related to Zelevinsky, §1.11; the form-continuity argument and the trace obstruction are given below in finite-dimensional terms.

Lemma 6.352 — invariant forms and finite Hecke spaces. Fix a unitary cuspidal \(\rho_0\) of \(G_r\), with its original smooth module, and set \[ I_s=\nu^s\rho_0\times\nu^{-s}\rho_0\qquad(s\in\mathbb R). \tag{6.849} \] Suppose that every \(I_s\) is irreducible. Each \(I_s\) then has a nondegenerate invariant Hermitian form, unique up to a nonzero real factor. For every principal congruence subgroup \(J\subset K_{2r}\), its nonzero fixed space \(E=I_s^J\) is one fixed finite-dimensional vector space, independent of \(s\). The restriction of an invariant nondegenerate form to \(E\) is nondegenerate. With a fixed basis of \(E\), the entire space of matrices satisfying \[ \mathcal L_s=\{H:H M_s(f)=M_s(f^*)^*H\quad (f\in e_J\mathcal H(G_{2r})e_J)\} \tag{6.850} \] is a complex line; its nonzero matrices are invertible. Here \(M_s(f)\) is the actual action on \(E\), and the last star denotes conjugate transpose. The matrices \(M_s(f)\) are Laurent-polynomial in \(X=q^s\).

Proof. The Hermitian dual of a unitary admissible smooth module is that module: on each finite compact fixed space the invariant positive form identifies its conjugate dual by ordinary finite-dimensional linear algebra, and compact averaging makes these identifications compatible. The original smooth vectors are retained by Theorem 6.311. The compact-flag duality used in Lemma 6.342 therefore identifies the smooth Hermitian dual of \(I_s\) with \(I_{-s}\). Theorem 6.329 identifies these two irreducible inductions. An isomorphism to the Hermitian dual gives a nonzero invariant sesquilinear form \(B\). Its adjoint \(B^*(v,w)=\overline{B(w,v)}\) is invariant as well. For a vector fixed by a compact open group, invariance shows that the corresponding functional is fixed by that group, so the adjoint again belongs to the smooth dual. At least one of \(B+B^*\) and \(i(B-B^*)\) is a nonzero Hermitian form. Its radical is an invariant submodule and is zero by irreducibility. Admissible Schur's lemma, proved using finite Hecke spaces in Lemma 6.287, makes any two such forms proportional; Hermitian symmetry makes their proportionality real.

The compact model consists of the same locally constant \(K_{2r}\)-functions for every \(s\): unramified twists are trivial on the compact Levi intersection. Admissibility and the actual matrices are Lemmas 6.296 and 6.333. Write \(e_J\) for normalized compact averaging. It is self-adjoint for every invariant Hermitian form, including an indefinite one. If \(v\in E\) is orthogonal to \(E\), then \[ B(v,w)=B(e_Jv,w)=B(v,e_Jw)=0\quad(w\in I_s), \tag{6.851} \] so \(v=0\). Thus its Gram matrix \(H_0\) is invertible and satisfies (6.850).

The \(e_J\mathcal H(G)e_J\)-module \(E\) is simple. Indeed a nonzero corner-submodule \(L\subset E\) generates \(I_s\), by irreducibility, and \(e_J\mathcal H(G)L=e_J\mathcal H(G)e_JL=L\), so \(L=E\). If \(H\) is any solution of (6.850), then \(H_0^{-1}H\) commutes with this corner action. A commuting matrix has a complex eigenvalue; its eigenspace is a nonzero invariant subspace, hence all of \(E\). It is scalar. This proves the assertions about \(\mathcal L_s\). Taking adjoints in its defining equations, and replacing \(f\) by \(f^*\), also shows that \(\mathcal L_s\) is stable under conjugate transpose. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.353 — continuity of the signature. Under the hypothesis of Lemma 6.352, every \(I_s\) is unitarizable, with its given smooth module.

Proof: a local analytic matrix, without a finite presentation. Fix one nonzero fixed space \(E\) of dimension \(d\), and fix \(s_0\). The equations (6.850) are complex-linear in the \(d^2\) entries of \(H\). A finite selection of tests already cuts out the one-dimensional solution space at \(s_0\): starting with all matrices, if the current intersection is larger than \(\mathcal L_{s_0}\), choose an equation that excludes a matrix in that difference. Dimension decreases, so this stops after finitely many choices. The resulting finite constraint matrix \(C(s)\) has real-analytic coefficients and rank \(d^2-1\) at \(s_0\). A nonzero minor of that size stays nonzero on a neighbourhood. For every nearby \(s\), the nonzero full solution line lies in \(\ker C(s)\), so its rank is at most \(d^2-1\). Consequently \[ \ker C(s)=\mathcal L_s,\qquad \dim\ker C(s)=1 \quad(s\text{ near }s_0). \tag{6.852} \] For \(d=1\) the same statement uses the empty rank-zero minor. No assertion that the Hecke algebra is finitely generated or finitely presented is involved.

Choose a Hermitian \(H_0\in\mathcal L_{s_0}\) and a vector \(v\) with \(v^*H_0v\ne0\). Such a vector exists: if every diagonal value were zero, expanding the values on \(v+w\) and \(v+iw\) would make every matrix coefficient zero. Scale \(H_0\) so that this value is one. Add the equation \(v^*Hv=1\) to the finite system and select a nonsingular square subsystem. Matrix inversion gives a unique real-analytic solution \(H(s)\) near \(s_0\). It solves the full system by (6.852). Its conjugate transpose is another solution with the same normalization, hence is equal to it. Thus \[ H(s)^*=H(s),\qquad\det H(s)\ne0,\qquad v^*H(s)v=1. \tag{6.853} \]

Definiteness up to sign and indefiniteness are disjoint open alternatives for this local family. For a positive matrix, the minimum of \(w^*Hw\) on the unit sphere is positive; entrywise continuity preserves a positive lower bound. Negative definiteness is identical after multiplication by \(-1\). For an indefinite matrix choose one positive and one negative vector; their strict signs persist. These alternatives cover every nonsingular Hermitian matrix. Indeed a semidefinite form with an isotropic nonzero vector has a radical: the values on \(v+zw\), for small complex \(z\) of both signs and phases, force \(B(v,w)=0\) for every \(w\). A nonsingular semidefinite form is therefore definite. Multiplication of \(H\) by a nonzero real scalar does not change which alternative holds. The alternatives consequently define disjoint open subsets of the real parameter line, independently of all local choices of normalization. At \(s=0\) normalized induction of the unitary \(\rho_0\otimes\rho_0\) has an invariant positive form by Lemma 6.331. The real line is connected, so every restriction to this fixed \(E\) is definite up to sign.

Repeat this conclusion for every principal congruence subgroup with nonzero fixed vectors. At a fixed \(s\), take a global invariant Hermitian form and scale it to be positive on one nonzero \(J_0\)-fixed vector. Every finer principal fixed space contains that vector. Its definite restriction must have the positive sign. Every smooth vector lies in one of those finer spaces, so the global form is positive definite. Its invariant completion is a strongly continuous unitary representation: orbit continuity holds first on the dense smooth subspace and then on the completion by the isometric action. Compact averaging has the same finite-dimensional image as before, since that image was already complete. Thus the completion has exactly the original smooth module, as in Lemma 6.331. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.354 — a uniform unitary trace bound. Let \(V_s\) be admissible smooth modules realized on a common compact model with \(D=\dim V_s^J\) independent of \(s\). If \(V_s\) is unitarizable, then for every ordinary bi-\(J\)-invariant compact test, \[ |\operatorname{Tr}V_s(f)|\le D\|f\|_1, \qquad \|f\|_1=\int_G|f(g)|\,dg. \tag{6.854} \] If one such trace is a nonconstant Laurent polynomial in \(q^s\), the modules cannot all be unitarizable for \(s\in\mathbb R\).

Proof. In the unitary completion, \(e_J\) is the orthogonal projection onto its original \(D\)-dimensional fixed space. The relation \(f=e_Jfe_J\) makes the integrated operator zero on its orthogonal complement and preserves that fixed space. For a smooth vector the integral is a finite sum over compact cosets; the triangle inequality and the isometric action give operator norm at most \(\|f\|_1\). Density extends this bound to the completion. In an orthonormal basis of the fixed space, each diagonal coefficient has absolute value at most this norm, proving (6.854). The bound does not depend on which invariant positive form realizes the unitary completion. Write a Laurent polynomial as \(p(X)=\sum_{a\le j\le b}c_jX^j\), with extreme nonzero coefficients. If \(b>0\), divide by \(X^b\) and let \(X\to\infty\); if \(a<0\), divide by \(X^a\) and let \(X\to0^+\). Unless it is constant, one of these gives unbounded absolute value. This contradicts (6.854). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.355 — adjacent cuspidal twists are reducible. For every cuspidal \(\rho\) of \(G_r\), \[ \rho\times\nu\rho \quad\text{is reducible}. \tag{6.855} \]

Proof. Theorem 6.311 writes \(\rho=\nu^t\rho_0\), with \(t\in\mathbb R\) and unitary \(\rho_0\). Multiplication of a section by the scalar character of its argument identifies twisting an induction with induction of the twisted data; explicitly, send a section \(f(g)\) to \(\nu(g)^{t+1/2}f(g)\), with inverse multiplication by \(\nu(g)^{-t-1/2}\). The covariance and right-translation formulas identify the twisted representations. Hence \(\rho\times\nu\rho\) is the twist by \(\nu^{t+1/2}\) of \(I_{-1/2}\) in (6.849). Twisting has an inverse and preserves irreducibility.

Suppose the module in (6.855) were irreducible. Theorem 6.329 makes \(I_{1/2}\) irreducible as well. For any other real \(s\), the two factors of \(I_s\) cannot be positive \(\nu\)-twists of one another. On the scalar \(\varpi_F1_r\), unitarity of \(\rho_0\) gives \[ \left|\omega_{\nu^s\rho_0}(\varpi_F1_r)\right|=q^{-rs}; \qquad \nu^s\rho_0\simeq\nu^{t'}\rho_0 \Longrightarrow s=t'. \tag{6.856} \] Thus the exceptional equalities would force \(2s=1\) or \(2s=-1\). The sufficient criterion in Theorem 6.343 proves irreducibility at every remaining \(s\). All modules \(I_s\) are therefore irreducible under the supposition, and Lemma 6.353 makes them all unitarizable.

But \(I_0\) and \(I_1\) have distinct exact cuspidal multisets, respectively \(\{\rho_0,\rho_0\}\) and \(\{\nu\rho_0,\nu^{-1}\rho_0\}\), by (6.856). Uniqueness in Theorem 6.322 makes these irreducibles nonisomorphic. Ordinary trace separation, Lemma 6.287, gives a compact test \(f\) with different traces at these two parameters. Take a sufficiently small principal \(J\) so that \(f=e_Jfe_J\). Lemma 6.333 identifies its actual trace with a Laurent polynomial: \[ \operatorname{Tr}I_s(f)=p(q^s),\qquad p(1)\ne p(q), \qquad D=\dim I_s^J\text{ is independent of }s. \tag{6.857} \] If \(D=0\) both displayed traces would vanish, so \(D>0\). Lemma 6.354 contradicts their simultaneous unitarizability. This proves reducibility. All integrations used compact support and all analytic matrices were finite; the argument applies in either field characteristic. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.356 — the complete two-cuspidal criterion and its extensions. For cuspidals \(\rho\) of \(G_a\) and \(\tau\) of \(G_b\), the product is reducible exactly when \[ a=b,\qquad \tau\simeq\nu\rho\quad\text{or}\quad\rho\simeq\nu\tau. \tag{6.858} \] For the adjacent pair put \(I_+=\nu\rho\times\rho\) and \(I_-=\rho\times\nu\rho\). There are nonisomorphic irreducibles \(S,T\) and nonsplit sequences \[ \begin{aligned} 0&\longrightarrow S\longrightarrow I_+\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow0,\\ 0&\longrightarrow T\longrightarrow I_-\longrightarrow S\longrightarrow0. \end{aligned} \tag{6.859} \] Here \(S\) is generic and \(T\) is nongeneric. Each displayed submodule is the unique nonzero proper submodule. For the standard parabolic with block sizes \((r,r)\), \[ r_{(r,r)}S\simeq\nu\rho\otimes\rho,\qquad r_{(r,r)}T\simeq\rho\otimes\nu\rho. \tag{6.860} \] Both intertwining spaces between \(I_+\) and \(I_-\) have dimension one, and both composites of nonzero opposite maps are zero.

Proof. The nonadjacent cases, including repeated isomorphic factors, are Theorem 6.343; adjacency is Theorem 6.355 and order comparison. Scalar absolute values make \(\rho\) and \(\nu\rho\) nonisomorphic, so Theorem 6.328 gives exactly (6.859), its nonsplitting and the intertwining assertions. Its detector calculation (6.781) gives (6.860). The order \((\nu\rho,\rho)\) satisfies Theorem 6.348, since \(\rho\not\simeq\nu^2\rho\); thus its simple submodule is generic. Whittaker heredity and exactness make its quotient nongeneric. The opposite sequences identify the other constituents as stated. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.357 — generic factors with no cross adjacency. Let \(V_1,V_2\) be generic irreducibles, of positive ranks, and let \(\mathcal S_1,\mathcal S_2\) be their exact cuspidal multisets. Suppose \[ \rho\in\mathcal S_1,\ \tau\in\mathcal S_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \tau\not\simeq\nu\rho\ \text{ and }\ \rho\not\simeq\nu\tau. \tag{6.861} \] Then \(V_1\times V_2\) is irreducible and generic, and is the unique generic irreducible with exact data \(\mathcal S_1\sqcup\mathcal S_2\). Every compact discrete pseudo-coefficient has zero trace on this product when central characters agree.

Proof. The proof of Theorem 6.349 embeds each \(V_i\) into a cuspidal induction ordered by descending central absolute exponent. Concatenate these two orders. Each internal order satisfies (6.839), and (6.861) supplies that condition across the two lists. Exactness of induction gives an embedding of \(A=V_1\times V_2\) into this ordered induction. Theorem 6.348 makes every nonzero mirabolic submodule of \(A\) nondegenerate.

The smooth contragredient of a generic irreducible is generic. In detail, Lemma 6.287 identifies it with the twist by the transpose-inverse involution of (6.639); that involution sends \(U_n\) to itself and its chosen character to its inverse. Conjugation by the diagonal with successive alternating signs restores the character. In characteristic two the inverse is already the same character. Thus transport of a nonzero functional proves genericity. The compact-flag dual pairing identifies \(A^\vee\) with \(V_1^\vee\times V_2^\vee\). Its cuspidal data are the dual data, and duality takes \(\nu\rho\) to \(\nu^{-1}\rho^\vee\), so (6.861) is preserved. The preceding ordered-embedding argument applies to \(A^\vee\) too.

Corollary 6.325 makes \(A\) finite length and admissible. It has a simple submodule \(X\) and a simple quotient \(Y\). The absence of degenerate mirabolic submodules makes \(X\) generic; applying that property to \(Y^\vee\subset A^\vee\) makes \(Y\) generic. Heredity gives \(\dim A_{U,\theta}=1\). Exactness of this quotient makes both maps \[ X_{U,\theta}\longrightarrow A_{U,\theta} \longrightarrow Y_{U,\theta} \tag{6.862} \] isomorphisms of lines. Their composite is nonzero, hence \(X\to Y\) is an isomorphism of irreducibles. It splits the quotient \(A\to Y\), giving \(A=X\oplus\ker(A\to Y)\). The kernel has zero Whittaker quotient, so its restriction is a degenerate mirabolic submodule and must be zero. Thus \(A\) is irreducible. Its exact data are the union by Theorem 6.322, and generic uniqueness is Theorem 6.330. Corollary 6.297 gives the trace assertion because this is a proper induction, without requiring its inducing factors to be tempered. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.358 — connected cuspidal data of a discrete series. For any cuspidal multiset \(\mathcal S\), make a graph on its distinct isomorphism classes, joining two classes precisely when one is \(\nu\) times the other. Retain repetitions as multiplicities on vertices. If this graph is disconnected, the generic irreducible with data \(\mathcal S\) is a proper irreducible parabolic induction. It is not square-integrable modulo the centre. Consequently the data of every unitary discrete series of split \(G_n\) are, for some cuspidal \(\rho\), integers \(a\le b\) and positive integers \(m_j\), \[ \bigsqcup_{j=a}^b\{\nu^j\rho\}^{m_j}. \tag{6.863} \] This assertion does not require the multiplicities \(m_j\) to be one.

Proof. For each connected component \(\mathcal S_i\), take the unique generic irreducible \(V_i\) with those data, whose existence follows from cuspidal Whittaker heredity and finite length and whose uniqueness is Theorem 6.330. There is no cross adjacency between components. Repeated application of Theorem 6.357 makes \(V_1\times\cdots\times V_c\) irreducible and generic with the full data. If \(c>1\), it is a proper induction, so every compact discrete test of its central character has trace zero.

If this product were a discrete series \(\pi\), its own compact test would instead have trace one by Corollary 6.117 applied to \(\tau=\pi\). The central character of the inducing product is exactly that of \(\pi\), since it is the same representation, so Corollary 6.297 applies to that very test and gives a contradiction. This uses the actual compact test and its normalization, rather than a general assertion about spectra of induced representations. Every discrete series is generic by Theorem 6.284, so the argument applies to it.

Finally a connected graph of these vertices lies on one \(\nu\)-orbit: follow a path from any base vertex. Equation (6.856), with the central absolute exponent in place of a unitary normalization, makes distinct integral powers nonisomorphic. A finite connected subset of the integer line has no missing integer between its least and greatest elements. This is exactly (6.863), retaining its positive multiplicities. A single vertex, with any multiplicity, is allowed by this conclusion; square-integrability imposes further conditions beyond connectedness. \(\square\)

Example 6.359 — the Gram matrix for a rank-two principal series. Take \(r=1\), \(\rho_0=1\), \(J=1+\varpi_FM_2(\mathcal O_F)\), and \(E=I_s^J\). Its compact model has the projective-line basis indexed by \(\mathbb P^1(\mathbb F_q)\). Set \(x=q^{-s}\), \(y=q^s\), so \(xy=1\). Let \(\mathbf j\) be the all-ones column and write \[ H_s=(qx-y)\operatorname{Id}+(y-x)\mathbf j\mathbf j^*. \tag{6.864} \] This matrix satisfies the adjoint relations for the compact permutation action and the actual Hecke operator \(U\) of Exercise 7.39. Its eigenvalues on the standard and constant compact types, respectively, are \[ \lambda_{\mathrm{std}}=qx-y\quad(\text{multiplicity }q),\qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{const}}=qy-x\quad(\text{multiplicity }1). \tag{6.865} \] It is positive for \(|s|<1/2\), singular at either endpoint, and indefinite outside. At \(s=1/2\) its radical on this fixed space is the standard compact type in the Steinberg submodule of \(I_+\); at \(s=-1/2\) it is the constant line in the trivial submodule of \(I_-\), for the normalization \(\rho=\nu^{-1/2}\) of (6.859).

Calculation. The finite projective action is two-transitive: a projective change of basis takes any two distinct lines to any other two. Thus its invariant matrices have one common diagonal entry and one common off-diagonal entry, and are \(a\operatorname{Id}+b\mathbf j\mathbf j^*\). In the ordering \((\infty,0,\text{other finite points})\), the matrix \(C=U/\sqrt q\) of (7.96) has entry \(x\) in column \(\infty\) of every row other than \(0\), and entry \(y\) in every finite column of row \(0\); all other entries vanish. The central uniformizer acts by \(xy=1\). If \(w\) exchanges \(0,\infty\) and permutes the remaining points, the adjoint double coset is consequently \(U^*=wUw\). Multiplying the two matrices, the equation \(HC=(wCw)^*H\) reduces to \[ (a+qb)x=(a+b)y. \tag{6.866} \] For clarity the two row types of \(HC\) are \(x(a+qb)\) in column \(\infty\), with the correction \(-ax\) in row \(0\), and \(by\) in each finite column, with the correction \(+ay\) in row \(0\). The adjoint equation exchanges the corresponding distinguished row and column types; (6.866) is their equality. Choosing \(a=qx-y\), \(b=y-x\) solves it. The all-ones matrix is zero on the sum-zero subspace and is multiplication by \(q+1\) on constants, proving (6.865). The sign assertions follow from \(y/x=q^{2s}\). At the positive endpoint the only nonzero quotient compact type is constant; at the negative endpoint the constant type is the trivial submodule, as in Example 6.351. These give exactly the stated radicals.

There is also a spherical trace comparison. For the normalized first spherical test \(T_1\) of (6.803), the unit spherical line has trace \(\sqrt q(x+y)\), and \(\|T_1\|_1=q+1\). The exact margin is \[ (q+1)^2-q(x+y)^2=(qx-y)(qy-x). \tag{6.867} \] It is negative for \(|s|>1/2\), so the unitary trace bound fails there. This concrete calculation concerns rank one inducing characters; the higher cuspidal ranks are covered by Theorem 6.355, using ordinary trace separation rather than a spherical vector. \(\square\)

6.56 Generic segments, discrete series and generic trace isolation

Keep \(F,q,G_n,K_n,\nu\) as in Section 6.55, with \(F\) of either nonarchimedean characteristic. Fix an irreducible admissible cuspidal \(\rho\) of \(G_r\), integers \(a\le b\), and put \[ \rho_j=\nu^j\rho,\quad s=b-a+1,\quad n=rs,\quad I[a,b]=\rho_b\times\rho_{b-1}\times\cdots\times\rho_a. \tag{6.868} \] Write \(S[a,b]\) for the unique generic irreducible with that exact cuspidal multiset, as supplied by Corollary 6.330. This definition does not assume square integrability. For an empty interval use the one-dimensional module on \(G_0\). The Jacquet modules below are normalized. Their finite length does not mean that their underlying vector spaces are finite-dimensional. Zelevinsky, §§2.1–2.2 and 3.7 of the free NUMDAM edition, gives related cuspidal-order and derivative constructions; his ascending segment convention is different from the descending generic convention (6.868).

Lemma 6.360 — actual cuspidal components selected by a central operator. Let \(R\) be the standard parabolic with \(s\) blocks of size \(r\). The actual module \(r_R I[a,b]\) is a direct sum of the \(s!\) distinct ordered tensors \[ L_{\boldsymbol j}=\rho_{j_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_{j_s}, \qquad (j_1,\ldots,j_s)\text{ a permutation of }(a,\ldots,b). \tag{6.869} \] Every submodule is the sum of a subset of these particular components.

Proof. The normalized geometric filtration in Theorem 6.320 has exactly these composition factors, each once: a cuspidal source block cannot be divided among target blocks, and the remaining cells are the labelled block permutations. Their entries are the actual twists, with no residual modulus, by (6.753)–(6.756). Put \(c=\omega_\rho(\varpi_F1_r)\). For each target block let \(Z_h\) be the action of its scalar uniformizer. These are commuting central endomorphisms. Set \[ B=q^{r(b-a)}+1,\qquad T=c^{-1}q^{rb}\sum_{h=1}^s B^{h-1}Z_h,\qquad \lambda_{\boldsymbol j}=\sum_{h=1}^s B^{h-1}q^{r(b-j_h)}. \tag{6.870} \] The operator acts on \(L_{\boldsymbol j}\) by \(\lambda_{\boldsymbol j}\). Each base-\(B\) digit \(q^{r(b-j_h)}\) is an integer strictly between zero and \(B\). Repeated division by \(B\), taking the remainder at each step, recovers every digit. Distinct permutations therefore give distinct eigenvalues.

A central operator preserves every term of a composition series. Successively applying its scalar factors gives \[ P(T)=0,\qquad P(X)=\prod_{\boldsymbol j}(X-\lambda_{\boldsymbol j}),\qquad p_{\boldsymbol j}(T)=\prod_{\boldsymbol l\ne\boldsymbol j} \frac{T-\lambda_{\boldsymbol l}}{\lambda_{\boldsymbol j}-\lambda_{\boldsymbol l}}. \tag{6.871} \] Indeed each scalar factor kills its corresponding quotient, and all factors commute, so their product kills the whole filtration. The roots are distinct. Evaluation at every root shows that \(\sum p_{\boldsymbol j}=1\), \(p_{\boldsymbol j}^2=p_{\boldsymbol j}\) and \(p_{\boldsymbol j}p_{\boldsymbol l}=0\) for unequal indices modulo \(P\): a polynomial zero at every root is divisible by \(P\), by successive division by its linear factors. Thus these are actual orthogonal projections on the module, even when it is infinite-dimensional. Their images each have the single composition factor \(L_{\boldsymbol j}\), hence length one and are that irreducible tensor. A submodule is preserved by all these polynomials and therefore decomposes by the same projections. Each intersection with a simple component is either zero or the whole component. This proves both assertions. The case \(s=1\) uses the empty product \(p=1\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.361 — the segment as an intersection of submodules. The module \(S[a,b]\) is the unique simple submodule of \(I[a,b]\), and lies in every nonzero submodule. For \(a<i\le b\), the exact induced embedding defines \[ J_i=\rho_b\times\cdots\times\rho_{i+1} \times S[i-1,i]\times\rho_{i-2}\times\cdots\times\rho_a \ \subset I[a,b]. \tag{6.872} \] Then, as actual submodules, \[ S[a,b]=\bigcap_{i=a+1}^b J_i,\qquad r_R S[a,b]=\rho_b\otimes\rho_{b-1}\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_a. \tag{6.873} \] For \(a=b\) the intersection means \(I[a,a]=\rho_a\).

Proof: existence and the pair profiles. Descending order satisfies (6.839), since the central absolute exponent increases strictly under \(\nu\). Theorem 6.348 makes every simple submodule of \(I[a,b]\) generic. Finite length supplies one, and Corollary 6.330 gives just one generic occurrence. Two different simple submodules would have zero intersection and give two occurrences, which is impossible. This proves uniqueness and containment in every nonzero submodule. Corollary 6.356 identifies \(S[i-1,i]\) with the actual generic submodule of the adjacent descending pair; exact induction and transitivity give (6.872).

Apply Theorem 6.320 to \(r_RJ_i\), with source blocks \(r,\ldots,r,2r,r,\ldots,r\). Every singleton cuspidal must occupy a whole target block: splitting it would take a proper zero Jacquet quotient. These singletons occupy \(s-2\) different target blocks. The two remaining blocks receive the \(2r\)-factor. In their increasing target order its contribution is exactly \(r_{(r,r)}S[i-1,i]=\rho_i\otimes\rho_{i-1}\), by (6.860). There is one surviving cell for every ordering of all the labels in which \(i\) precedes \(i-1\), and no others. The within-target parabolic is the entire target Levi, since every row receives one whole \(r\)-block. Formula (6.753) therefore gives precisely that ordered tensor; all its normalization factors have already been included. Thus \[ r_RJ_i=\bigoplus_{\boldsymbol j:\,i\text{ precedes }i-1} L_{\boldsymbol j}\ \subset r_RI[a,b]. \tag{6.874} \] The filtration first gives its factors; Lemma 6.360 identifies the actual submodule with this sum of components. For \(s\ge2\) its length is \(s!/2\), by exchanging the positions of the two specified labels.

Proof: the intersection and its length. Put \(J=\bigcap J_i\). Each \(J_i\) is nonzero, hence contains the unique simple submodule just proved; consequently \(J\ne0\). The intersection is the kernel of the map \(I\to\bigoplus_i I/J_i\). Exactness of Jacquet coinvariants identifies its Jacquet module with the intersection of (6.874) inside \(r_RI\). The only permutation in which every \(i\) precedes \(i-1\) is \((b,b-1,\ldots,a)\). Hence \(r_RJ\) is the single tensor in (6.873).

Every irreducible subquotient of \(J\) has the full exact cuspidal data, by Theorem 6.322. Its cuspidal embedding therefore uses \(s\) blocks of size \(r\), whose standard parabolic is precisely \(R\). First Frobenius makes its \(R\)-Jacquet module nonzero. Exactness and finite length now give \(\ell(J)\le\ell(r_RJ)=1\), also the detector inequality of Lemma 6.327. Since \(J\ne0\), it is the simple submodule \(S[a,b]\). This proves both equalities as modules, rather than equalities of composition classes. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.362 — every normalized Jacquet module of a generic segment. Let \(P\) have block dimensions \(n_1,\ldots,n_t\). Then \(r_PS[a,b]=0\) unless every \(n_j\) is divisible by \(r\). Otherwise write \(n_j=r\ell_j\), \(m_0=0\), \(m_j=\ell_1+\cdots+\ell_j\), so \(m_t=s\). There is an isomorphism of actual Levi modules \[ r_PS[a,b]\simeq\bigotimes_{j=1}^t S[b-m_j+1,\ b-m_{j-1}]. \tag{6.875} \] The right side is irreducible. Its blocks are consecutive chunks of the descending list, with their exact determinant twists.

Proof. The geometric filtration of \(r_PI[a,b]\) assigns each cuspidal whole to a target block; any split source cuspidal gives zero. If a target dimension is not a multiple of \(r\), no assignment is possible, and exactness gives the vanishing for \(S\). If all dimensions are multiples, each nonzero layer is an external product of normalized cuspidal inductions on the assigned subsets. Every constituent of \(r_PS\) consequently has, in each Levi factor, precisely the data of one such subset, by Theorem 6.322.

Refine \(P\) by the full \(r\)-block parabolic \(R\). Each such constituent has nonzero Jacquet module for this refinement inside the Levi: its irreducible external factors admit cuspidal embeddings, all with blocks of size \(r\), and first Frobenius makes those quotients nonzero. Here external tensor products commute with Jacquet quotients. Algebraically, the relation space for a product of radicals is the sum of the tensor relation spaces in the separate factors. Successive tensor quotients over \(\mathbb C\) give the claimed identity; normalized moduli are the products of those in the factors.

Normalized transitivity follows by taking these radical quotients in stages: the larger radical is the semidirect product of the outer radical with the within-Levi radical, its relation quotient is the iterated quotient, and its half-modulus is their product, by (6.698). Thus \[ r_R^G S=r_{R\cap M}^M(r_P^G S) =\rho_b\otimes\cdots\otimes\rho_a. \tag{6.876} \] Finite-length admissibility is Corollary 6.325. Every constituent on the middle expression has nonzero refined quotient, so exactness and its length one force \(r_PS\) itself to be nonzero and irreducible. Factor it as \(X_1\otimes\cdots\otimes X_t\), using Lesson 12, Theorem 4.1. Each refined quotient is nonzero. Since their external product is the simple tensor in (6.876), each is simple: a proper nonzero submodule in one factor would tensor to a proper nonzero submodule of the product, by exactness of vector-space tensor products. Uniqueness of external irreducible factorization therefore identifies them with the corresponding consecutive tensors in (6.876).

Choose a cuspidal embedding of \(X_j\). Its ordered data must be that same consecutive descending tensor, because first Frobenius makes them a quotient of the full \(r\)-block Jacquet module just identified. Descending cuspidal induction has no degenerate mirabolic submodule by Theorem 6.348, so \(X_j\) is generic. Corollary 6.330 identifies it with the indicated \(S\) on that chunk. This proves (6.875), including the full-block case \(P=G\). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.363 — derivatives as a partial Whittaker quotient. For a smooth \(G_n\)-module \(V\), let \(V^{(m)}\) be the normalized derivative of (6.815), \(1\le m\le n\). For \(0<m<n\), \[ V^{(m)}\simeq\bigl(r_{(n-m,m)}V\bigr)_{\,1\times U_m,\,1\times\theta_m} \quad\text{as }G_{n-m}\text{-modules}. \tag{6.877} \] For \(m=n\) this is the full Whittaker quotient on \(G_0\).

Proof: the actual quotient map and its normalization. Let \(Q_m\) consist of matrices \[ Q_m=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}1_{n-m}&X\\0&u\end{pmatrix}: X\in M_{n-m,m}(F),\ u\in U_m\right\},\qquad \vartheta_m\!\begin{pmatrix}1&X\\0&u\end{pmatrix}=\theta_m(u). \tag{6.878} \] Successively taking the last-column quotients in \(\Psi^-\) and \(\Phi^-\) gives precisely \(V_{Q_m,\vartheta_m}\) as a vector space. To verify the relation space directly, expand a member into its last-column factors. The last \(m-1\) columns contribute the selected last simple-root characters, and the remaining column and rectangular entries contribute character one. The relation for a product follows from \(h_1h_2v-\vartheta(h_1h_2)v=h_1(h_2v-\vartheta(h_2)v)+\vartheta(h_2)(h_1v-\vartheta(h_1)v)\). This proves equality of the algebraic relation spaces in both directions. Thus the map is the class of a vector sent to its successive classes, with the same inverse induced by the identity on \(V\).

The rectangular radical is normal in \(Q_m\), and the quotient is \(U_m\). Taking its trivial quotient and then its \(\theta_m\)-quotient gives the same vector quotient. On the surviving \(G_{n-m}\), each of the \(m\) normalized last-column functors contributes \(\nu^{-1/2}\), for a total \(\nu^{-m/2}\). For the parabolic \((n-m,m)\), \[ \delta^{1/2}(A,B)=\nu(A)^{m/2}\nu(B)^{-(n-m)/2}. \tag{6.879} \] Normalized Jacquet action on the first block also multiplies its raw action by \(\nu(A)^{-m/2}\). The second-block modulus is trivial on \(U_m\), so taking its Whittaker quotient introduces no first-block factor. This proves equivariance of the actual quotient map in (6.877). For \(m=n\) all that remains is \(U_n,\theta_n\), with the trivial \(G_0\)-action. No extra determinant shift is suppressed. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.364 — all derivatives and the mirabolic length of a segment. For \(n=rs\), the nonzero positive derivatives are exactly \[ S[a,b]^{(ir)}\simeq S[a+i,b]\quad(1\le i<s),\qquad S[a,b]^{(n)}\simeq\mathbb C. \tag{6.880} \] All other positive indices give zero. Its restriction to \(P_n\) has length \(s\).

Proof. For \(m<n\) use (6.877) and Theorem 6.362. Unless \(r\mid m\), its Jacquet module is zero. If \(m=ir\), (6.875) is \(S[a+i,b]\otimes S[a,a+i-1]\). The second factor is generic with a one-dimensional Whittaker quotient by Theorems 6.291 and 6.330. Taking that quotient gives (6.880); its scalar identification with \(\mathbb C\) requires a choice of nonzero functional, so the displayed isomorphism is not claimed to be canonical. The full derivative is likewise a line. The finite mirabolic filtration of Theorem 6.337 has these derivative modules as its successive smaller-group factors; the positive functors preserve their simple composition length. There are exactly \(s\) nonzero irreducible factors, so the length is \(s\), also (6.816). This includes \(s=1\), when the cuspidal restriction is simple, and \(r=1,s=2\), when the Steinberg restriction has length two. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.365 — a coefficient criterion before unitarization. Let \(V\) be a smooth admissible representation of split \(G_n\), with a scalar unitary central character. For a smooth-dual functional \(\lambda\) call \(g\mapsto\lambda(gv)\) an algebraic smooth coefficient. Fix \(1\le p<\infty\). All these coefficients belong to \(L^p(G_n/Z)\) if and only if, for every principal level \(J=1+\varpi_F^m M_n(\mathcal O_F)\) and every \(1\le h<n\), each eigenvalue \(\alpha\) of the normalized Jacquet action of \(a_h=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F1_h,1_{n-h})\) on its Levi fixed space satisfies \[ |\alpha|\delta_h^{1/2-1/p}<1,\qquad \delta_h=q^{-h(n-h)}. \tag{6.881} \] A zero Jacquet fixed space imposes no condition. No positive inner product on \(V\) is assumed.

Proof: finite matrices and necessity. Set \(T_c=e_J\pi(c)e_J\) on the finite space \(E=V^J\). Lemma 6.22 applies without unitarity. It identifies the stable image of \(T_{a_h}\) with the unnormalized Jacquet fixed space; its stable kernel is nilpotent. Therefore the nonzero eigenvalues of \(T_{a_h}\) are \(\delta_h^{1/2}\) times the normalized eigenvalues. Choose any basis \(v_i\) of \(E\), with coordinate functionals extended to smooth-dual functionals by \(\lambda_i\circ e_J\). Their coefficients at \(a_h^k\) are the matrix entries of \(T_{a_h}^k\), by the positive product identity (6.54). Their absolute values are constant on the corresponding central \(J\)-double coset, since the centre acts by a unitary scalar. The disjoint cosets have volumes \(\operatorname{vol}(\overline J)\delta_h^{-k}\), by (6.55). Integrability of all these coefficients forces every entry of \((\delta_h^{-1/p}T_{a_h})^k\) to be \(p\)-summable in \(k\). An eigenvalue of absolute value at least one contradicts that assertion: its powers give an operator norm at least one, whereas in a fixed finite-dimensional coordinate norm that operator norm is bounded by a constant times the largest matrix entry. This gives (6.881), including its strict boundary.

Proof: sufficiency on every Cartan face. The operators \(T_{a_h}\) commute by the probability-average identity (6.54), whose proof uses only smooth finite compact averages. For each normalized operator \(A_h=\delta_h^{-1/p}T_{a_h}\), condition (6.881) and its nilpotent part put all eigenvalues strictly inside the unit circle. Finite Jordan expansion, including the finitely many zero-root powers, gives \(\|A_h^k\|\le C_h\gamma^k\), with a common \(\gamma<1\) for this finite collection. Thus, for \(t_{\boldsymbol l}=\prod_h a_h^{l_h}\), \[ \sum_{\boldsymbol l\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{n-1}} \left(\prod_h\delta_h^{-l_h}\right)\|T_{t_{\boldsymbol l}}\|^p \le C\sum_{\boldsymbol l}\gamma^{p\sum_h l_h}<\infty. \tag{6.882} \] The sum includes zero coordinates, hence every boundary face; nilpotent initial terms have not been discarded.

For a given \(v,\lambda\), compactness of \(K_n\) and smoothness make their rotated sets \(K_nv\) and \(\{\lambda\circ\pi(k):k\in K_n\}\) finite. Choose a principal \(J\) fixing all of them. Every coefficient on \(k_1Jt_{\boldsymbol l}Jk_2\) is consequently one of finitely many fixed vector-functional matrix coefficients of \(T_{t_{\boldsymbol l}}\), bounded by a common constant times its chosen coordinate norm. Lemma 6.23 covers all of \(G_n/Z\) by finitely many such translates at each \(\boldsymbol l\), with total volume at most a fixed multiple of \(\prod_h\delta_h^{-l_h}\). Formula (6.882) proves the full integral bound. This repeats the finite-matrix argument of Theorem 6.25 with arbitrary coordinate functionals, so it does not require an orthonormal basis or an invariant norm. For \(n=1\), the central quotient is a point, and the empty conditions and conclusion hold directly. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.366 — the exact central exponents of a centred segment. Let \(\rho_0\) be unitary cuspidal of \(G_r\), let \(s\ge1\), and let \(\operatorname{St}_s(\rho_0)\) denote the generic irreducible with data \[ \{\nu^{j-(s-1)/2}\rho_0:0\le j<s\}. \tag{6.883} \] This notation here specifies its data and genericity. Its central character is \(\omega_{\rho_0}^{s}\). For the Jacquet module of block dimensions \(r\ell_1,\ldots,r\ell_t\), put \(m_j=\ell_1+\cdots+\ell_j\), \(m_0=0\). The average determinant exponent in block \(j\), and the absolute central exponent at a cut \(h=rM\), are respectively \[ t_j=\frac{s-m_j-m_{j-1}}2,\qquad \left|r_{(rM,r(s-M))}\operatorname{St}_s(\rho_0)(a_{rM})\right| =q^{-rM(s-M)/2}\quad(0<M<s). \tag{6.884} \] The second expression means the absolute value of its scalar action on that irreducible Jacquet module. At cuts not divisible by \(r\) the Jacquet module is zero.

Proof. Apply (6.875) with base cuspidal \(\nu^{-(s-1)/2}\rho_0\). The descending chunk in block \(j\) has exponents from \(s-m_j-(s-1)/2\) through \(s-m_{j-1}-1-(s-1)/2\). Their mean is the first formula. Their sum over all blocks is zero, giving the stated central character. For the prefix containing \(M\) cuspidals, the sum of their exponents is \[ \sum_{u=s-M}^{s-1}\left(u-\frac{s-1}2\right) =\frac{M(s-M)}2. \tag{6.885} \] The scalar uniformizer on its rank-\(rM\) group acts by \(\omega_{\rho_0}(\varpi_F1_r)^M\) times \(q^{-rM(s-M)/2}\). Its first factor has absolute value one, proving (6.884). These are normalized Jacquet exponents; the unnormalized finite Hecke eigenvalue also includes \(\delta_{rM}^{1/2}=q^{-r^2M(s-M)/2}\). This distinction fixes the sign and the factor \(r\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.367 — square-integrable representations from every centred cuspidal segment. The smooth module \(\operatorname{St}_s(\rho_0)\) has an irreducible admissible unitary discrete-series realization with its original smooth vectors, for every unitary cuspidal \(\rho_0\), every \(s\ge1\), and both field characteristics. Every \(S[a,b]\) is essentially discrete series. If \(\rho=\nu^t\rho_0\), \(t\in\mathbb R\), then \[ S[a,b]\simeq\nu^{,t+(a+b)/2}\operatorname{St}_{b-a+1}(\rho_0), \tag{6.886} \] and it is unitary precisely when \(t+(a+b)/2=0\).

Proof: integrability and a positive form. The module in (6.883) is irreducible admissible and has a unitary scalar central character. Lemma 6.366 makes every nonzero normalized maximal Jacquet eigenvalue strictly smaller than one in absolute value. All other such Jacquet modules vanish. Theorem 6.365 at \(p=2\) therefore makes every algebraic smooth coefficient square-integrable modulo the centre.

Choose a nonzero smooth-dual functional \(\lambda\), and define the actual linear map \[ \mathcal C_\lambda:V\longrightarrow L^2_\omega(G_n/Z),\qquad (\mathcal C_\lambda v)(g)=\lambda(\pi(g)v),\qquad B(v,w)=\int_{G_n/Z}(\mathcal C_\lambda v)(g) \overline{(\mathcal C_\lambda w)(g)}\,d\bar g. \tag{6.887} \] Here \(L^2_\omega\) consists of functions \(f(zg)=\omega(z)f(g)\), and its right action is \((R_hf)(g)=f(gh)\). The integral is finite by the coefficient criterion and Cauchy–Schwarz. The map intertwines \(\pi(h)\) with \(R_h\), by direct substitution. It is nonzero, since at the identity some \(\lambda(v)\ne0\), and that locally constant coefficient is nonzero on an open set of positive quotient measure. Its kernel is invariant and is zero by irreducibility. Consequently \(B\) is positive definite. Right translation preserves quotient Haar measure and the unitary central covariance, so \(B\) is invariant. In this formula it is linear in its first variable, as in Section 6.9.

Complete in this norm. The isometric action is strongly continuous, since the dense original vectors have open stabilizers. Its compact projection has precisely the original finite-dimensional fixed space: applying the projection to the dense subspace gives that space, already complete, and continuity gives no extra fixed vectors. Thus the smooth module of the completion is exactly \(V\). A nonzero closed invariant subspace has a nonzero compact fixed vector, by strong convergence of principal averages to the identity; that vector lies in \(V\) and generates it by algebraic irreducibility. The subspace is therefore the whole completion. This proves unitary irreducibility and admissibility.

To exhibit a Hilbert coefficient with the asserted integrability, choose a compact group fixing \(\lambda\). It satisfies \(\lambda(v)=\lambda(e_Jv)\). The finite-dimensional fixed space and its inherited positive norm make this a bounded functional, represented by a vector of \(V^J\). Hence the nonzero coefficient already used in (6.887) is a smooth Hilbert coefficient and lies in \(L^2\). This proves the discrete-series assertion; Theorems 6.15 and 6.34 then give the corresponding Hilbert-coefficient and uniform decay conclusions.

Proof: the exact twists. Theorem 6.311 gives \(\rho=\nu^t\rho_0\). Twisting the actual induction sections and using generic uniqueness gives (6.886), since both sides have exactly the same cuspidal data. Thus every segment is an essentially discrete series with this specified unitary twist. Its scalar central absolute value is \(|z|^{rs(t+(a+b)/2)}\), because the centred factor is unitary. If it were unitary this value would be one for \(z=\varpi_F\), forcing the exponent to vanish. Conversely the vanishing exponent leaves the unitary representation already constructed. The classification of all discrete series is Theorem 6.373. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.368 — the sharp coefficient boundary. If \(s\ge2\) and \(1\le p<\infty\), every nonzero smooth coefficient of \(\operatorname{St}_s(\rho_0)\) belongs to \(L^p(G_{rs}/Z)\) exactly when \[ p>\frac{2r}{r+1}. \tag{6.888} \] For \(s=1\), all smooth coefficients are compact modulo the centre and belong to every such \(L^p\).

Proof. At a cut \(h=rM\), substitute (6.884) and \(\delta_h=q^{-r^2M(s-M)}\) into (6.881). The expression is strictly smaller than one exactly when \(1+r-2r/p>0\), which is (6.888). All remaining Jacquet modules vanish. For \(s\ge2\) at least one cut is present, and its nonzero Jacquet module has a nonzero fixed space at some principal Levi level, by smoothness. Thus failure of the strict inequality, including equality, violates the necessary condition. This initially concerns all coefficients together. Every coefficient is a finite linear combination of left and right translates of any fixed nonzero coefficient: algebraic irreducibility of \(V\) and its smooth dual, Lemma 6.287, expresses the chosen vector and functional in finite spans of the corresponding orbits. Translation preserves quotient \(L^p\) norms, and finite sums preserve membership for \(p\ge1\). Hence one nonzero coefficient belongs precisely when all do. The cuspidal case \(s=1\) is Lemma 6.310. \(\square\)

A rank-six example. Let \(\rho_0\) be unitary cuspidal of \(G_2\) and take \(s=3\). The discrete series \(\operatorname{St}_3(\rho_0)\) has exact data \(\nu\rho_0,\rho_0,\nu^{-1}\rho_0\). Its maximal normalized Jacquet modules vanish at cuts \(1,3,5\). At either cut \(2\) or \(4\), \[ |\alpha|=q^{-2},\qquad\delta_h=q^{-8},\qquad |T_{a_h}|_{\mathrm{stable}}=q^{-6},\qquad |\delta_h^{-1/2}T_{a_h}|_{\mathrm{stable}}=q^{-2}. \tag{6.889} \] The stable absolute values mean the eigenvalue moduli; there may also be a nilpotent kernel on a principal fixed space. At the other cuts the entire fixed-space operator is nilpotent by Lemma 6.22. Its positive derivatives are at indices \(2,4,6\), with modules respectively \(S[0,1]\), \(\nu\rho_0\), and a line, where \(S[0,1]\) uses base \(\rho_0\). Thus the \(P_6\)-length is three. Indeed removing the lowest exponent leaves the exact exponents \(0,1\); removing two leaves exponent \(1\). The derivative at index two is the positive \(\nu^{1/2}\)-twist of \(\operatorname{St}_2(\rho_0)\), rather than a centred discrete series. The one-step case \(r=1,s=2\) is the Steinberg sequence of Section 6.55. The exclusion of other discrete-series data and the generic trace identity are proved in Theorems 6.373–6.374.

Lemma 6.369 — derivative layers of products of generic segments. Let \(A=S_1[a_1,b_1]\times\cdots\times S_t[a_t,b_t]\), where the base cuspidal for factor \(i\) has rank \(r_i\). Put \(s_i=b_i-a_i+1\) and \(N=\sum_i r_i s_i\). For \(0<m<N\), \(A^{(m)}\) has a finite filtration with quotients \[ \prod_{i=1}^t S_i[a_i+u_i,b_i],\qquad 0\le u_i\le s_i,\quad \sum_i r_i u_i=m, \tag{6.890} \] where empty segments are omitted. Every listed tuple contributes once. In particular these derivatives are finite length and admissible.

Proof. Apply the normalized geometric filtration to the target parabolic \((N-m,m)\). A cell assigns \(r_i(s_i-u_i)\) dimensions of the \(i\)-th source block to the first row, and \(r_i u_i\) to the second; all other assignments vanish by Theorem 6.362. Its source Jacquet module is the actual tensor of the upper suffix \(S_i[a_i+u_i,b_i]\) and lower prefix \(S_i[a_i,a_i+u_i-1]\). The normalized layer (6.753) is therefore the external product of their respective ordered inductions in the two target rows. This uses the same source-factor order in each row and includes all half-moduli. Take the second-row Whittaker quotient. It is exact by compact averaging, and heredity gives a one-dimensional quotient of every product of its generic prefix factors. Lemma 6.363 then gives exactly (6.890). Identifying that line with \(\mathbb C\) requires a choice, so the quotient isomorphisms are not declared canonical. Finite-length admissible induction is Corollary 6.325. For an empty target row the corresponding product or Whittaker quotient is its \(G_0\) line; this also gives the full top derivative and the zero-index identity. \(\square\)

Call two segments linked if their union is a segment, neither contains the other, and both lie on the same exact \(\nu\)-orbit of cuspidals. Thus disjoint adjacent intervals are linked, equal or nested intervals are not linked, and different orbits are not linked.

Lemma 6.370 — incompatible suffix and prefix selections. Suppose \(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_t\) are pairwise unlinked segments. Choose a suffix \(E_i\) and a prefix \(F_i\) of each \(\Delta_i\), allowing either to be empty. Here a nonempty suffix contains the upper endpoint and a nonempty prefix contains the lower endpoint. If at least one \(E_i\) is nonempty, then \[ \nu\!\left(\bigcup_i E_i\right) \ne\bigcup_i F_i. \tag{6.891} \] This is already an assertion about underlying sets; equality of multisets is consequently impossible as well.

Proof. Work on an exact \(\nu\)-orbit where a suffix occurs and identify its cuspidal classes with integers. Distinct integral twists are distinct by the central absolute exponent. If equality held, take the greatest integer \(x\) in the selected suffix union. A suffix containing \(x\) belongs to an interval \(\Delta_i\) ending at \(x\), since its whole upper end is selected. Equality puts \(x+1\) in a selected prefix of another interval \(\Delta_j\). Those two intervals have connected union: \(\Delta_j\) contains \(x+1\) and starts no later than that integer. It extends strictly past \(\Delta_i\). Being unlinked, it must contain \(\Delta_i\). Write \(c\) for its lower endpoint; then \(c\le x\), and its selected prefix contains \(c\).

Equality now puts \(c-1\) in a selected suffix of some \(\Delta_k\). This interval and \(\Delta_j\) again have connected union, since they contain the consecutive integers \(c-1,c\). The former cannot be contained in the latter, which starts at \(c\). Being unlinked, it must contain \(\Delta_j\). Its suffix containing \(c-1\) therefore continues at least through the upper endpoint of \(\Delta_j\), which is at least \(x+1\). This contradicts the definition of \(x\). All selected sets on this orbit are finite, so that greatest integer exists. Other orbits are disjoint and cannot affect the contradiction. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.371 — unlinked generic segments induce irreducibly. If the segments defining \(A\) in Lemma 6.369 are pairwise unlinked, then \(A\) is irreducible and generic. Its restriction to the mirabolic subgroup has no nonzero degenerate submodule.

Proof: exclusion of a degenerate submodule. Each segment embeds into its descending cuspidal induction by Theorem 6.361. Exact induction embeds \(A\) into a full cuspidal induction. It therefore has finite mirabolic length, by Theorem 6.308. Suppose \(0\ne Z\subset A|_{P_N}\) is degenerate. Its highest nonzero derivative has some index \(k<N\). It is a submodule of the finite-length admissible \(A^{(k)}\), by Lemma 6.369, so choose an irreducible admissible submodule \(\sigma\subset Z^{(k)}\).

The ordinary evaluation pairing of \(A\) with \(A^\vee\) separates vectors: compact averaging and finite fixed-space duality give a separating functional on any nonzero vector. Restrict its first argument to \(Z\) and twist its second by \(\nu\). As in Lemma 6.342 this is a \(\Delta_{P_N}\)-pairing nondegenerate in its first argument. The highest-derivative pairing of Theorem 6.339 gives \[ \sigma\hookrightarrow\bigl((\nu A^\vee)^{(k)}\bigr)^\vee, \qquad (\nu A^\vee)^{(k)}\twoheadrightarrow\sigma^\vee. \tag{6.892} \] The second arrow uses exact admissible smooth duality and biduality. Its source is finite length and admissible by the derivative layers for the dual segments. This use of the highest-derivative pairing does not assume that the highest derivative of an arbitrary irreducible is irreducible.

Each layer in Lemma 6.369 embeds in the full induction of its cuspidal data, by Theorem 6.361 and exact induction. Theorem 6.322 therefore shows that the data of \(\sigma\) are the multiset union of some suffixes \(E_i\subset\Delta_i\). At least one is nonempty, since its remaining rank is \(N-k>0\). The smooth dual of a generic segment is the generic segment on the dual data, by dual genericity and Corollary 6.330; its endpoints are reversed. Derivatives of those segments retain suffixes of the dual intervals, whose duals are prefixes of the original intervals. The extra \(\nu\) in (6.892) becomes \(\nu^{-1}\) on those prefixes after dualizing. Thus for some prefixes \(F_i\subset\Delta_i\), \[ \operatorname{cusp}(\sigma)=\bigsqcup_i E_i =\nu^{-1}\!\left(\bigsqcup_i F_i\right). \tag{6.893} \] For explicit endpoints, a suffix \([1-b_i+v_i,1-a_i]\) of the \(\nu\)-twisted dual interval becomes \([a_i-1,b_i-v_i-1]\), exactly \(\nu^{-1}\) times an original prefix. Determinant twists commute with the normalized derivative quotients because they are trivial on the unipotent relation groups. The underlying sets in (6.893) contradict Lemma 6.370. Hence \(Z\) does not exist.

Proof: irreducibility. Duality preserves the unlinked condition and takes the product to the product of its generic dual segments, by compact-flag duality. The preceding argument also excludes degenerate mirabolic submodules in \(A^\vee\). The module \(A\) is finite length and has a one-dimensional Whittaker quotient by heredity. Choose a simple submodule \(X\) and a simple quotient \(Y\). The absence of degenerate submodules in \(A\) and \(A^\vee\) makes both generic. Exactness gives isomorphisms of lines \(X_{U,\theta}\to A_{U,\theta}\to Y_{U,\theta}\). Thus the composite \(X\to Y\) is nonzero and is an isomorphism of simples. It splits \(A\to Y\). The remaining kernel has zero top Whittaker quotient and is a degenerate mirabolic submodule of \(A\), so is zero. This proves irreducibility and genericity. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.372 — the unique unlinked segment decomposition of a multiset. Every finite multiset \(\mathcal S\) of cuspidal classes has a unique expression as the multiset union of pairwise unlinked segments. On each exact \(\nu\)-orbit, choose an integer coordinate and let \(d(j)\) be its multiplicity. Its segments are the connected components of the finite level sets \[ E_h=\{j\in\mathbb Z:d(j)\ge h\}, \qquad h=1,2,\ldots. \tag{6.894} \] Each component is retained once at each level where it occurs. Repeated equal segments are permitted.

Proof: construction. Every finite connected subset of the integer line is an interval. Counting the levels containing an integer gives \(d(j)\), so the intervals in (6.894) reproduce the multiset. Two components from the same level are disjoint with at least one missing integer between them. For different levels, the higher-level component is contained in a unique lower-level component. It is either contained in the other selected component or separated from it by a missing integer at the lower level. Thus any two constructed intervals are nested or separated, and cannot be linked. Translation of the integer coordinate changes none of the actual cuspidal segments.

Proof: uniqueness. In any pairwise unlinked family the maximal distinct intervals are disjoint and not adjacent; every other interval is contained in one of them. Their union is the full support, so these maximal intervals are exactly its connected components. Remove one copy of each. This subtracts one from every positive multiplicity, leaves the remaining intervals pairwise unlinked, and strictly decreases the finite total multiplicity. Induction recovers the connected components at the next level, and then all further levels. It also recovers repeated equal maximal intervals, one copy per step. The empty multiset starts the induction. Different exact \(\nu\)-orbits are disjoint, so the construction and uniqueness apply independently on them. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.373 — generic factorization and the full split discrete-series classification. Every generic irreducible admissible representation of \(G_N\) is, up to permutation of its factors, the irreducible product of the generic segments in the unique decomposition of its exact cuspidal multiset from Lemma 6.372. In particular every unitary discrete series of split \(G_N\) is \[ \operatorname{St}_s(\rho_0),\qquad rs=N,\quad \rho_0\text{ unitary cuspidal on }G_r. \tag{6.895} \] The integer \(s\) and the isomorphism class of \(\rho_0\) are unique. These statements hold in both field characteristics.

Proof. The product attached to Lemma 6.372 is irreducible and generic by Theorem 6.371 and embeds into the full induction of the prescribed cuspidals, by Theorem 6.361 and exact induction. Theorem 6.322 therefore gives exactly that prescribed multiset. Generic uniqueness, Corollary 6.330, identifies it with the given representation. Reordering has the same conclusion for each order, since the unlinked hypothesis is order-independent. Conversely any factorization into pairwise unlinked generic segments gives that same cuspidal multiset and is the unique decomposition of Lemma 6.372.

Let \(\pi\) be a unitary discrete series. It is generic by Theorem 6.284. If its segment factorization had at least two factors, it would be a proper irreducible parabolic induction. Its own compact discrete test has trace one by Corollary 6.117 and trace zero by Corollary 6.297, a contradiction. Thus there is a single segment. Theorem 6.367 unitarizes it exactly by centring its cuspidal exponents; the unitary central character forces its remaining real twist to vanish. This gives (6.895). Conversely all the modules in that display are discrete series by Theorem 6.367. Exact cuspidal-data uniqueness recovers the number of cuspidals, their common rank and their ordered real exponents; the central middle twist recovers precisely \(\rho_0\). This proves uniqueness. The argument does not assume a classification of all nongeneric irreducibles. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.374 — compact trace isolation among every generic irreducible. Let \(\pi\) be a unitary discrete series of split \(G_N(F)\), with central character \(\omega\). Its compact discrete test \(f_{\pi,m}\), at a generating level as in Corollary 6.117, satisfies \[ \operatorname{Tr}\tau(f_{\pi,m})=\begin{cases} 1,&\tau\simeq\pi,\\ 0,&\tau\not\simeq\pi, \end{cases} \quad\text{for every generic irreducible admissible }\tau \text{ of central character }\omega. \tag{6.896} \] No temperedness or unitarity hypothesis on \(\tau\) is needed.

Proof. Factor \(\tau\) by Theorem 6.373. If it has at least two segment factors, it is itself a proper induction, so Corollary 6.297 gives trace zero for this very compact test. Its inducing factors are admissible and have the required common scalar action on the ambient centre, since the induced representation has character \(\omega\); no temperedness is required in that trace theorem. Such an induction cannot be \(\pi\), by the own-test contradiction used in Theorem 6.373.

If there is one segment, Theorem 6.367 expresses it as a real determinant twist of a centred unitary discrete series. Its unitary central character \(\omega\) forces that real exponent to be zero. Thus \(\tau\) is a unitary discrete series. It is covered by the tempered pseudo-coefficient identity in Corollary 6.117: its unitary coefficients are bounded and square-integrable, hence belong to every \(L^{2+\epsilon}\) by \(|c|^{2+\epsilon}\le\|c\|_\infty^\epsilon|c|^2\), the criterion of Corollary 6.26. That identity gives exactly (6.896). The traces throughout are the finite-rank integrated operators already constructed, not formal coefficient sums. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.375 — the complete reducibility criterion for generic segment products. A finite product of generic segments is irreducible if and only if no two of its segments are linked.

Proof: a linked pair has different derivative data. The unlinked direction is Theorem 6.371. For a linked pair choose coordinates on its common exact cuspidal orbit so that \(\Delta=[a,b]\), \(\Gamma=[c,d]\), where \(a<c\le b+1\) and \(b<d\). The cuspidal multiplicity function of the pair has height intervals \(U=[a,d]\) and \(H=[c,b]\), the latter omitted if empty. Its unique generic irreducible is consequently \(C=S[U]\times S[H]\), by Theorem 6.373. Put \[ E=[c-1,b],\qquad k=r(d-a). \tag{6.897} \] The interval \(E\) is nonempty. Lemma 6.369 makes \(S[E]\) an actual derivative filtration quotient of index \(k\) of \(S[\Delta]\times S[\Gamma]\): retain \(E\) from the first factor and remove all of the second. It is therefore an irreducible composition factor of that derivative.

It cannot occur in \(C^{(k)}\). Each of its layers is a product of a suffix of \(U\) with a suffix of \(H\). A nonempty suffix of \(U\) contains \(d\), which is absent from \(E\); if that suffix is empty, every remaining cuspidal lies in \(H=[c,b]\), which omits \(c-1\). Exact cuspidal-data uniqueness thus excludes the datum of \(S[E]\) from every layer. If the linked product were irreducible, heredity would make it generic and identify it with \(C\), contradicting these actual derivative composition factors. This proves reducibility of either ordering of a linked pair.

Proof: any number of factors. If a linked pair occurs in a list, choose one with the smallest distance between its positions. Every factor between them is unlinked with the first factor, or there would be a closer linked pair. Two unlinked factors commute by an actual isomorphism: both ordered products are irreducible and generic by Theorem 6.371 and have the same exact data, so Corollary 6.330 identifies them. Exact induction transports this isomorphism within a longer list. Move the first chosen factor across the intervening ones and make the linked pair consecutive. Its reducibility supplies a nonzero proper submodule with nonzero quotient. Exact induction preserves both nonzero modules: a nonzero fibre vector gives a nonzero section on a sufficiently small compact open flag chart, as in Lemma 6.306. Thus the whole product is reducible. This argument requires no commutativity assertion for arbitrary reducible products. \(\square\)

6.57. Finite cuspidal spaces and spectral traces over the rational function field

Let \(K=\mathbb F_q(t)\), \(R=\mathbb F_q[t]\), \(u=t^{-1}\), and let \(\infty\) be the rational place with completion \(\mathbb F_q((u))\). Write \(\mathbb A=\mathbb A_K\), \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n\), \(Z=\mathbb G_m\), and \(\mathcal K=\prod_vG(\mathcal O_v)\). Fix a smooth unitary character \(\Omega:K^\times\backslash\mathbb A^\times\to\mathbb C^\times\). The character is part of the hypotheses. Put \[ \begin{gathered} J(D)=\prod_vJ_v(m_v),\qquad D=\sum_vm_v[v],\qquad e=\deg D=m_\infty+\sum_{v\ne\infty}m_v\deg v,\\ J_v(0)=G(\mathcal O_v),\qquad J_v(m)=1+\mathfrak p_v^mM_n(\mathcal O_v)\quad(m\ge1). \end{gathered} \tag{6.898} \] Only finitely many \(m_v\) are nonzero. In particular \(J(D)\) is normal in \(\mathcal K\). A smooth automorphic function with central character \(\Omega\) satisfies \(F(\gamma zg)=\Omega(z)F(g)\). It is cuspidal when its integral over \(N(K)\backslash N(\mathbb A)\) is zero at every \(g\), for every proper parabolic radical \(N\). We give these unipotent quotients probability measure below.

Lemma 6.376 — additive approximation with its exact threshold. Let \(P=\prod_{v\ne\infty}P_v^{m_v}\in R\) be monic, where \(P_v\) is the monic polynomial of the finite place \(v\), and put \(d=\deg P\). For an integer \(\delta\), let \[ L_\delta=\prod_{v\ne\infty}\mathfrak p_v^{m_v}\mathcal O_v \ \times\ u^{m_\infty-\delta}\mathcal O_\infty. \qquad \mathbb A=K+L_\delta\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \delta\ge e-1. \tag{6.899} \] Moreover \[ U=\prod_{v\ne\infty}\mathcal O_v\times u\mathcal O_\infty, \qquad \mathbb A=K\oplus U \tag{6.900} \] as additive groups. The compact open group \(U\) is closed under multiplication, although it does not contain the identity of \(\mathbb A\).

Proof. At a finite place every principal part is represented by \(A_v/P_v^k\), with \(\deg A_v<k\deg P_v\): reduce \(P_v^kz_v\) modulo \(P_v^k\), using \(R/P_v^k=\mathcal O_v/\mathfrak p_v^k\). Subtract the sum of these finitely many proper rational fractions. The finite components are now integral. The Chinese remainder construction supplies a polynomial \(p\), \(\deg p<d\), with their prescribed residues modulo the \(P_v^{m_v}\). Explicitly, coprimality gives inverses of \(P/P_v^{m_v}\) modulo \(P_v^{m_v}\) by the Euclidean algorithm; multiply each residue by this inverse and by \(P/P_v^{m_v}\), sum, and reduce modulo \(P\). Subtract \(p\). The remaining finite components lie in their required ideals.

Divide the polynomial part of the remaining infinity component by \(P\), and subtract the multiple of \(P\) so obtained. This preserves the finite conditions. The infinity remainder belongs to \(u^{1-d}\mathcal O_\infty\). If \(d=0\), division by \(P=1\) removes the whole polynomial part and leaves \(u\mathcal O_\infty\). Thus the construction works precisely when the allowed infinity lattice contains this remainder lattice, namely when \(m_\infty-\delta\le1-d\).

For failure at \(\delta=e-2\), take all finite components zero and the infinity component \(t^{d-1}\), interpreted as \(u\) if \(d=0\). Any rational function satisfying the finite conditions must be a polynomial divisible by \(P\). For \(d>0\), subtracting a nonzero such polynomial introduces a term of degree at least \(d\); subtracting zero leaves the term of degree \(d-1\). Neither remainder lies in \(u^{2-d}\mathcal O_\infty\). For \(d=0\), a polynomial cannot cancel the coefficient of \(u\) modulo \(u^2\mathcal O_\infty\). Smaller \(\delta\) allow still smaller lattices, so also fail. Finally the construction with all \(m_v=0\) gives (6.900). An element of \(K\) integral at every finite place is a polynomial; if it also belongs to \(u\mathcal O_\infty\), it is zero. Closure of \(U\) under products is coordinatewise. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.377 — adelic diagonal representatives by polynomial row reduction. Every \(g\in G(\mathbb A)\) has a decomposition \(g=\gamma a(\boldsymbol d)k\), where \(\gamma\in G(K)\), \(k\in\mathcal K\), and \(a(\boldsymbol d)\) is the identity at the finite places and \(\operatorname{diag}(t^{d_1},\ldots,t^{d_n})\) at infinity. The sorted integers \(d_1\ge\cdots\ge d_n\) are unique. Modulo the additional action of \(Z(\mathbb A)\), they are unique up to a common integer shift, and we normalize \(d_n=0\).

Proof: the finite lattices. The module \[ L=K^n\cap\prod_{v\ne\infty}g_v\mathcal O_v^n \tag{6.901} \] is a full \(R\)-lattice. Indeed some nonzero polynomial \(Q\) clears all the finitely many nonintegral lattices and their inverses, giving \(QR^n\subset L\subset Q^{-1}R^n\). Every submodule of \(R^n\) is free of rank at most \(n\): project onto the first coordinate, whose image is a principal ideal; lift its generator, split off that generator, and apply induction to the kernel in \(R^{n-1}\). This proves finite generation as well. The two inclusions show that the rank here is \(n\).

Its completion at each finite \(v\) is exactly \(g_v\mathcal O_v^n\). To check the nontrivial inclusion, multiply a desired local vector by \(Q\). Prescribe a sufficiently accurate polynomial congruence for that vector at \(v\), and prescribe sufficiently deep zero congruences at the other primes dividing \(Q\). The Chinese remainder construction in Lemma 6.376 gives a polynomial vector with these congruences. Dividing by \(Q\) gives an element of \(L\) arbitrarily close to the local vector. The completion of the lattice spanned by any \(R\)-basis of \(L\) is closed, so density gives equality. If \(h\) has this basis as its columns, then \(h^{-1}g_v\in G(\mathcal O_v)\) at every finite place. Absorb those matrices on the right. It remains to reduce the infinity matrix.

Proof: termination of row reduction. For a nonzero Laurent row \(z\), write \(\ell(z)\) for its largest \(t\)-degree. Begin with the rows \(z_i\) of the infinity matrix and allow unimodular polynomial row operations. At every stage \[ \sum_i\ell(z_i)\ \ge\ \deg_t\det(g_\infty). \tag{6.902} \] The determinant is unchanged up to a nonzero constant. Let \(\ell_i=\ell(z_i)\). If the leading residues of \(t^{-\ell_i}z_i\) in \(\mathbb F_q^n\) are dependent, choose a nonzero dependence \(\sum c_i\overline{t^{-\ell_i}z_i}=0\). Select an index \(i\) of largest \(\ell_i\) among its nonzero coefficients and normalize \(c_i=1\). Replace \[ z_i\ \longmapsto\ z_i+\sum_{j\ne i,\ c_j\ne0} c_jt^{\ell_i-\ell_j}z_j. \tag{6.903} \] All powers are nonnegative. This is a unimodular polynomial operation, it strictly lowers \(\ell_i\), and it changes no other row. The integer sum in (6.902) therefore forces termination. At termination the normalized leading rows are independent. Thus \(\operatorname{diag}(t^{-\ell_i})Ag_\infty\in G(\mathcal O_\infty)\) for the accumulated \(A\in G(R)\). This gives the asserted diagonal form. These polynomial operations preserve all finite integral components; a permutation sorts the degrees.

Proof: uniqueness and the centre. For an infinity matrix define the finite integer \[ h_g(m)=\dim_{\mathbb F_q}\{p\in R^n:\deg_t(pg)\le m\}. \quad h_{a(\boldsymbol d)}(m)=\sum_i\max(0,m-d_i+1). \tag{6.904} \] Finiteness follows by bounding the degrees of \(p=(pg)g^{-1}\). The function is invariant under left \(G(R)\) and right \(G(\mathcal O_\infty)\). Its first difference is \(\#\{i:d_i\le m\}\), so recovers every degree. An equivalence between two finite-identity adelic representatives must have its rational left matrix and its inverse integral at every finite place, hence in \(G(R)\). This proves the global uniqueness too. For a central idele, multiply by the inverse of the rational function \(\prod_{v\ne\infty}P_v^{\operatorname{ord}_v(z_v)}\). All its finite coordinates are now units; its infinity coordinate is a power of \(t\) times a unit. It therefore shifts every \(d_i\) by the same integer, and every such shift occurs. \(\square\)

For example, over every \(\mathbb F_q\), the matrix \[ \begin{pmatrix}t^2&t\\t&1+u\end{pmatrix},\qquad z_1-tz_2=(0,-1),\qquad \det=t, \tag{6.905} \] has sorted profile \((1,0)\). The original sum of row degrees is \(3\); after this one operation it is \(1\), and the normalized leading rows are independent. This calculation also holds in characteristic two.

Theorem 6.378 — a uniform support bound for cusp forms of fixed level. Suppose \(n\ge2\). A \(J(D)\)-fixed cusp form can be nonzero at \(\gamma z a(\boldsymbol d)k\), with \(d_n=0\), only if \[ 0\le d_h-d_{h+1}\le e-2\quad(1\le h<n). \tag{6.906} \] Consequently the space is zero if \(e\le1\). If \(e\ge2\), it is supported on at most \((e-1)^{n-1}[\mathcal K:J(D)]\) right level cosets modulo \(G(K)Z(\mathbb A)\), and \[ \dim C_{\mathrm{cusp}}(J(D),\Omega) \le(e-1)^{n-1}[\mathcal K:J(D)]. \tag{6.907} \] Every such form is square-integrable modulo the centre.

Proof. Fix an adjacent gap \(\delta=d_h-d_{h+1}\ge e-1\), and let \(N_h\) be the upper rectangular radical of type \((h,n-h)\). It is an additive group of \(h(n-h)\) entries. For a cross-block entry \((i,j)\), its allowed lattice in \(N_h(\mathbb A)\cap aJ(D)a^{-1}\) is \(\mathfrak p_v^{m_v}\mathcal O_v\) at finite \(v\), and \(u^{m_\infty-(d_i-d_j)}\mathcal O_\infty\) at infinity. Since \(d_i-d_j\ge\delta\), this contains the entry lattice \(L_\delta\). Lemma 6.376, entry by entry, gives \[ N_h(\mathbb A)=N_h(K)\bigl(N_h(\mathbb A)\cap aJ(D)a^{-1}\bigr). \tag{6.908} \] Write \(n=\eta a j a^{-1}\) accordingly. Normality of \(J(D)\) in \(\mathcal K\) gives \(F(nak)=F(\eta ajk)=F(ak)\). The constant term, whose quotient measure is one, is therefore \(F(ak)\). Cuspidality forces this value to be zero. This proves (6.906), including the zero assertion when \(e\le1\).

For \(e\ge2\), the \(n-1\) successive gaps each have \(e-1\) choices and determine the normalized profile. Proposition 6.377 and a set of representatives for \(\mathcal K/J(D)\) give the stated finite set of possible cosets. Values at its representatives determine the form; stabilizers and \(\Omega\) can impose additional zero conditions. This proves an upper bound, without asserting that these values can be chosen freely. Each coset is the image of a compact open set and has finite quotient Haar measure, as established explicitly below. Thus finite support gives square-integrability. \(\square\)

For \(m\ge1\), the index in (6.907) is explicitly determined by \[ [G(\mathcal O_v):J_v(m)] =\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}(Q_v^n-Q_v^i)\,Q_v^{n^2(m-1)}, \qquad Q_v=q^{\deg v}. \tag{6.909} \] Reduction modulo \(\mathfrak p_v\) counts independent columns, giving the product. Each invertible residue matrix has \(Q_v^{n^2(m-1)}\) lifts modulo \(\mathfrak p_v^m\), all invertible. This proves the formula. At depth zero the index is one. Every compact open subgroup of \(G(\mathbb A)\) contains a \(J(D)\), so finiteness follows at any compact open level. When \(n=1\), the whole space with the specified central character is the single line \(F(g)=c\Omega(g)\); its level-fixed dimension is one or zero according as \(\Omega\) is trivial on that level or not.

Theorem 6.379 — a closed admissible cuspidal Hilbert space. The right regular representation on \(H_\Omega=L^2(G(K)Z(\mathbb A)\backslash G(\mathbb A),\Omega)\) has a closed invariant cuspidal subspace \(H_{\mathrm{cusp},\Omega}\). Its smooth vectors are precisely the smooth square-integrable functions satisfying the constant-term definition above. Its fixed space at every compact open level is finite-dimensional; at \(J(D)\) it satisfies Theorem 6.378.

Proof: the quotient and its measure. Write \(\overline G=G(\mathbb A)/Z(\mathbb A)\) and \(\overline\Gamma=G(K)/Z(K)\), embedded in \(\overline G\). The latter is discrete. Indeed its adjoint action on the full matrix algebra \(M_n\) has rational entries; a neighbourhood of the identity in which every entry of \(\operatorname{Ad}(\gamma)-1\) belongs to \(U\) forces all those entries to be zero by (6.900). A matrix commuting with every matrix unit is scalar, in every characteristic. Thus this neighbourhood contains only the identity of \(\overline\Gamma\). A subgroup with isolated identity is closed: choose a neighbourhood \(V\) with \(V^{-1}V\) containing no other subgroup element; each translate of \(V\) contains at most one such element, so any point of the closure is that element. In particular its intersection with a compact set is finite.

Haar measure on \(\overline G\), with counting measure on \(\overline\Gamma\), gives a locally finite measure on \(X=\overline\Gamma\backslash\overline G\): cover compact sets by finitely many small charts whose distinct rational translates are disjoint, and use Haar measure on each chart. The factors \(\Omega(z)\) define unitary transition functions for sections over this quotient. They are consistent because \(\Omega\) is trivial on \(K^\times\); their absolute values are one. This constructs the indicated Hilbert norm without requiring finite total volume of \(X\). For a compact set \(B\subset\overline G\), the unfolding of these charts gives \[ \int_B|\Phi(g)|^2\,dg \le M_B\|\Phi\|_{H_\Omega}^2, \qquad M_B=\max(1,\#(\overline\Gamma\cap BB^{-1})). \tag{6.910} \] To see the bound on multiplicity, if \(\gamma_0g,\gamma g\in B\), then \(\gamma\gamma_0^{-1}\in BB^{-1}\). The norm of the section is independent of the chosen lift.

Proof: bounded constant terms on compact sets. Give the additive group at each finite place measure \(\mathcal O_v=1\), and at infinity measure \(u\mathcal O_\infty=1\). Then \(U\) has measure one. For a standard parabolic radical \(N\), let \(N_U\) consist of the upper unitriangular block matrices with each allowed entry in \(U\). It is a compact open subgroup: multiplication and the finite inverse formula use only sums and products in \(U\). Successively reduce the entries by (6.900), in order of increasing root height, by left rational elementary matrices. This proves \[ N(\mathbb A)=N(K)N_U,\qquad N(K)\cap N_U=\{1\}. \tag{6.911} \] The root-coordinate changes are triangular with diagonal one. Product additive measure is consequently both left and right Haar measure on \(N(\mathbb A)\), and \(N_U\) has measure one. Thus (6.911) identifies the left quotient with a compact fundamental domain of probability measure. Quotient integration is right invariant: translation preserves Haar measure, and a compact translated domain can be partitioned among finitely many rational translates of \(N_U\). This also proves left \(N(\mathbb A)\)-invariance of the constant term as a function of \(g\).

For \(\Phi\in H_\Omega\) define \(C_P\Phi(g)=\int_{N_U}\Phi(ng)\,dn\), as a locally square-integrable section. Cauchy–Schwarz, change of variable by left translation, and (6.910) give, for compact \(C\subset\overline G\), \[ \int_C|C_P\Phi(g)|^2\,dg \le\int_{N_UC}|\Phi(h)|^2\,dh \le M_{N_UC}\|\Phi\|_{H_\Omega}^2. \tag{6.912} \] In the first inequality, each integral over \(nC\) is bounded by the integral over \(N_UC\), and the averaging measure has mass one. In particular these maps are well-defined on Hilbert equivalence classes and continuous into \(L^2\) on every compact set. Take the intersection of their kernels over a compact exhaustion and over the standard proper parabolics. Rational conjugacy covers the other parabolics, because \(\Phi\) is rationally invariant. This intersection is closed. Constant terms commute with right translations, so it is invariant.

Proof: smooth vectors and fixed spaces. Compactly supported locally constant sections on the small quotient charts are dense in \(H_\Omega\). Smoothness of \(\Omega\) allows the charts to be chosen with locally constant unitary frames. Translation is strongly continuous there, by continuity of Haar measure and compact approximation, and hence on all of \(H_\Omega\) by density and isometry. Averages over shrinking compact open groups converge strongly to the identity and preserve the closed cusp space. Its smooth vectors are therefore dense. A level-fixed Hilbert vector has a representative given by a constant value in a compatible frame on each open level coset. Its constant terms are right level invariant too. Their almost-everywhere vanishing, established by (6.912), is pointwise vanishing for these locally constant representatives. Theorem 6.378 applies to them and makes their fixed spaces finite-dimensional. Conversely each smooth cuspidal function is at some level, so that theorem gives its square-integrability. This proves all assertions, as well as the finite coset masses used in Theorem 6.378. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.380 — atomicity from finite compact fixed spaces.
