After scalar adjustment, \(g g_r^{-1}\) has norm one, so (6.976) makes the corresponding classes lie in finitely many compact right translates. This proves compactness. For Hausdorffness use the adjoint action on the full algebra \(D\). Its kernel on \(D^\times\) is exactly \(K^\times\), by the definition of the centre, and its rational matrix entries are additively discrete. Thus \(D^\times/K^\times\) is closed discrete in \(G/\mathbb A_K^\times\), as in Theorem 6.409. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.411 — finite-level inner spectrum over a function field. Suppose \(K\) is a global function field, \(D\) is as in Theorem 6.410, and \(\Omega\) is a smooth unitary idèle-class character. The right regular representation on \[ H_{D,\Omega}=L^2(D^\times\mathbb A_K^\times\backslash G,\Omega) \tag{6.977} \] is admissible and is a countable orthogonal Hilbert sum of irreducible admissible unitary representations, with finite multiplicities.

Proof. Local multiplicative measure is \(|\operatorname{nrd}x|_v^{-n}dx\). The left and right additive Jacobians are both \(|\operatorname{nrd}g|_v^n\), so this measure is bi-invariant. Product measures make \(G\) unimodular. Its central quotient is unimodular too. The closed discrete rational subgroup in Theorem 6.410 therefore gives quotient Haar measure; compactness makes its total volume finite and positive. The character defines unitary transition functions, consistently because \(\Omega\) is trivial on \(K^\times\).

Let \(J\subset G\) be compact open, with central intersection in \(\ker\Omega\); if this condition fails, its fixed space is zero. The level cosets are open in the compact quotient (6.975), so there are finitely many. A fixed section has one complex value on each compatible coset; incompatible arithmetic stabilizers force its value to be zero. Thus \(H_{D,\Omega}^J\) is finite-dimensional. Compactly supported locally constant sections on small quotient charts are dense, their translations are strongly continuous, and compact averages converge strongly to the identity, by the chart and Haar arguments in Theorem 6.379. The Hilbert space is separable because these groups have countable bases. Lemma 6.380 now proves exactly the stated decomposition and multiplicities. This assertion concerns the actual global representation; it does not assume a local tensor decomposition or a multiplicity-one theorem. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.412 — the finite inner kernel trace. Under Theorem 6.411, let \(f\) be smooth, compact modulo the centre, inverse-\(\Omega\)-covariant and bi-\(J\)-invariant. Put \(\overline G=G/\mathbb A_K^\times\), \(\Gamma=D^\times/K^\times\), and \[ K_f(x,y)=\sum_{\gamma\in\Gamma}f(x^{-1}\gamma y),\qquad w_x=\frac{\operatorname{vol}(\overline J)} {\#(\Gamma\cap x\overline Jx^{-1})}. \tag{6.978} \] For a set \(T_J\) of compatible level-coset representatives, \[ \operatorname{Tr}R(f) =\sum_{x\in T_J}w_xK_f(x,x) =\sum_{\Pi^J\ne0}m(\Pi)\operatorname{Tr}\Pi(f). \tag{6.979} \] Both sums are finite.

Proof. Every compact subset of the quotient has compact lifts: around each point choose a relatively compact group neighbourhood and cover the compact quotient by finitely many of their images. Let \(C_0\subset\overline G\) be their compact union. On \(C_0\times C_0\), a nonzero kernel summand requires \(\gamma\in\Gamma\cap C_0\operatorname{supp}(f)C_0^{-1}\), a finite set by rational discreteness. Thus the kernel is uniformly a finite sum there. Unfolding quotient charts identifies its operator with right convolution. Both the range and adjoint range are in the finite-dimensional fixed space from Theorem 6.411. The compatible level-coset basis has normalized values \(w_x^{-1/2}\), so its matrix entry is \(\sqrt{w_xw_y}K_f(x,y)\). This proves the first equality by its finite matrix trace. Incompatible rows and columns vanish by their nontrivial stabilizer phase. The Hilbert decomposition in Theorem 6.411 proves the last equality; only finitely many constituents have a nonzero fixed vector. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.413 — absolute elliptic unfolding and the scalar stabilizer. Let \(K\) be either kind of global field and \(D\) a global central division algebra. Let \(f\) be continuous, compact modulo the centre and inverse-\(\Omega\)-covariant. Assume its support at one place consists of separable regular elements. Then the absolute diagonal kernel is integrable, only finitely many projective rational conjugacy classes contribute, and \[ \int_{\Gamma\backslash\overline G}K_f(x,x)\,dx =\sum_{[\gamma]}\frac{V_{E_\gamma}}{e_\gamma} \int_{\mathbb A_{E_\gamma}^\times\backslash G} f(x^{-1}\gamma x)\,d\dot x, \tag{6.980} \] where \(E_\gamma=K[\gamma]\) is a separable field of degree \(n\), \[ V_E=\operatorname{vol}(E^\times\mathbb A_K^\times \backslash\mathbb A_E^\times),\qquad e_\gamma=[\Gamma_{\bar\gamma}:E_\gamma^\times/K^\times]. \tag{6.981} \] All orbital integrals in (6.980) are absolute, and \(e_\gamma\) is a finite positive integer. The quotient measures use the same Haar measure on each torus in both factors. Over a function field, for the tests of Theorem 6.412, the left side equals its finite spectral trace.

Proof: absolute integration. The compact lift \(C_0\) from Theorem 6.412 exists in both characteristics. The finite intersection argument there bounds uniformly, on \(C_0\), the sum of the absolute values of all diagonal summands. Their individual absolute values are unaffected by scalar frames. The quotient has finite volume, so this absolute kernel is integrable. Every contributing projective conjugacy class has a representative in that finite intersection: move a witnessing quotient point into \(C_0\) by a rational translate. Thus only finitely many classes contribute. Tonelli now permits their absolute regrouping.

Proof: centralizers and the finite factor. Local separable regularity implies that the global reduced characteristic polynomial has degree \(n\), is separable and equals the minimal polynomial. Indeed a nonzero polynomial relation over \(K\) remains one locally; the local minimal degree is \(n\). The algebra \(K[\gamma]\) is a field because it is a finite-dimensional commutative subalgebra of the division algebra. Its ordinary centralizer in \(D\) is exactly this field: after a separable splitting extension a regular matrix has diagonal centralizer of dimension \(n\), and the linear commuting equations descend; the contained field already has that dimension.

An element of the projective rational stabilizer satisfies \(h^{-1}\gamma h=z\gamma\) for \(z\in K^\times\). Reduced norms give \(z^n=1\). The map to such scalars has kernel \(E_\gamma^\times/K^\times\), and its image has at most \(n\) elements, including when the characteristic divides \(n\). Thus its index is exactly the finite integer \(e_\gamma\). Rational scalar phases are one, since \(\Omega(z)=1\). Unfolding a projective conjugacy class first gives integration over \(\Gamma_{\bar\gamma}\backslash\overline G\). Replacing its discrete subgroup by \(E_\gamma^\times/K^\times\) multiplies that integral by \(e_\gamma\); this accounts for the division in (6.980).

Finally disintegrate by the ordinary adelic torus \(\mathbb A_{E_\gamma}^\times/\mathbb A_K^\times\). The conjugation integrand is constant on its left cosets. Its rational quotient has positive finite volume \(V_{E_\gamma}\), by Theorem 6.409. Tonelli applied first to the absolute value proves the absolute orbital integral and then the stated equality. These are quotient integrations of the fixed Haar measures, so their product has the indicated normalization. Theorem 6.412 gives the final trace assertion in positive characteristic. \(\square\)

The compactness statements apply to a division algebra over the global field; they allow its local completions to be matrix algebras over division algebras. The finite spectral trace proved here is for global function fields. Theorem 6.421 gives the inner local tensor factors and Theorem 6.424 gives a finite split elliptic trace for genuine regular-support tests. Matching the split and inner traces, obtaining a finite outside-place spectral fibre without assuming a common level, and proving individual representation-transfer integrality require additional arguments. Formula (6.980) retains the finite projective stabilizer factor; it is one only when the rational scalar symmetry group is trivial.

6.62. Constant cyclic algebras with prescribed local inner forms

Put \(K=\mathbb F_q(t)\), \(n\ge2\), and \(L=\mathbb F_{q^n}(t)\). Let \(\sigma\) act on constants by \(x\mapsto x^q\) and fix \(t\). Frobenius always means arithmetic Frobenius. We first make explicit the algebra and its local calculations, including the places at which the constant tensor algebra is a product.

Lemma 6.414 — the cyclic algebra and its norm splitting. Let \(E/F\) be a cyclic Galois étale algebra of dimension \(n\), with generator \(\sigma\), and \(a\in F^\times\). The relations \[ C(E,\sigma,a)=\bigoplus_{j=0}^{n-1}Eu^j, \qquad ux=\sigma(x)u,\quad u^n=a \tag{6.982} \] define a central simple algebra of degree \(n\). It is split if and only if \(a=N_{E/F}(b)\) for some \(b\in E^\times\). Replacing \(u\) by \(b^{-1}u\) replaces its parameter by \(a/N_{E/F}(b)\).

Proof. Multiply basis terms by applying the indicated automorphism and introducing a factor \(a\) at a carry in the exponent. Associativity follows because the number of carries in a sum of three exponents is independent of the parentheses and \(\sigma(a)=a\). Over a separable closure the étale algebra has \(n\) primitive idempotents, permuted in one cycle by \(\sigma\). Represent them as diagonal matrix units, and represent \(u\) by the cyclic shift with wrap coefficient \(a\), oriented so that \(u e_i u^{-1}=\sigma(e_i)\). The diagonal units and this invertible shift generate every matrix unit. The resulting map is an isomorphism onto \(M_n\), since both dimensions are \(n^2\). A nonzero two-sided ideal would become a nonzero ideal in this matrix algebra and hence the whole algebra. Dimensions descend, proving simplicity. The commuting equations for the centre likewise descend its dimension one. Thus the centre is \(F\).

The étale norm equals \(\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}\sigma^j(b)\): after the same separable extension both expressions are the product of the \(n\) coordinates. If this norm is \(a\), multiplication by \(E\) and the operator \(T(y)=b\sigma(y)\) on the \(F\)-space \(E\) satisfy (6.982). The nonzero homomorphism from the simple algebra to \(\operatorname{End}_F(E)\) is injective and, by dimension, an isomorphism.

Conversely suppose the algebra acts as all endomorphisms of an \(n\)-dimensional \(F\)-space \(W\). Each field factor of \(E\) acts on a nonzero summand of \(W\), since the embedding is faithful. Each summand has dimension at least the degree of that field. The sum of these degrees is \(n\), so all summands have rank one over their field. Hence \(W\simeq E\) as an \(E\)-module. In this identification \(u\) is an invertible \(\sigma\)-semilinear map, necessarily \(b\sigma\) with \(b\in E^\times\). Its \(n\)-th power is multiplication by \(N(b)\), proving necessity. The parameter-change formula follows by multiplying \(b^{-1}u\) repeatedly. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.415 — constant local factors and matrix corners. At a place \(v\) of \(K\) of degree \(m\), put \(g=\gcd(n,m)\), \(N=n/g\). Then \[ L\otimes_KK_v\simeq\prod_{i=0}^{g-1}E_i, \qquad [E_i:K_v]=N, \tag{6.983} \] where each \(E_i\) is unramified. The automorphism \(\sigma\) cycles the factors, \(\tau=\sigma^g\) generates the automorphisms of one factor, and its local arithmetic Frobenius is \[ F_v=\sigma^m=\tau^{m/g}. \tag{6.984} \] For every local parameter \(a\in K_v^\times\), \[ C(L\otimes K_v,\sigma,a)\simeq M_g\bigl(C(E_0,\tau,a)\bigr). \tag{6.985} \]

Proof. The \(n\) embeddings of \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\) are labelled by \(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\). Frobenius of \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) advances the label by \(m\). Its \(g\) orbits each have length \(N\), proving the finite-field tensor decomposition and the indicated Frobenius. The coefficient-field construction and Laurent expansions in Lemma 6.384 extend it to the unramified local fields in (6.983).

Let \(e\) be the primitive idempotent of one factor, and write \(B\) for the left side of (6.985). The elements \[ E_{ij}=u^i e u^{-j}\qquad(0\le i,j<g) \tag{6.986} \] are matrix units. In fact \(e u^{k-j}e=0\) unless \(k=j\), for the distinct factors are orthogonal, and their diagonal sum is one. The corner \(eBe\) is spanned by \(eEu^{gj}\), \(0\le j<N\). In it \(u^g e\) acts by \(\tau\) and has \(N\)-th power \(ae\). Its dimension is \(N^2\), so it is exactly \(C(E_0,\tau,a)\). The maps \(b\mapsto(E_{0i}bE_{j0})_{ij}\) and \((b_{ij})\mapsto\sum E_{i0}b_{ij}E_{0j}\) give the matrix-algebra isomorphism. The idempotents come from an étale field tensor algebra; no division by \(g\) or semisimplicity of a cyclic group algebra is required. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.416 — unit norms in every residue characteristic. If \(E/F\) is an unramified extension of nonarchimedean local fields, its unit norm is onto \(\mathcal O_F^\times\). The same holds for the product algebra in (6.983). No restriction on the residue characteristic dividing the extension degree is needed.

Proof. Write \(Q\) for the residue cardinality of \(F\) and \(s=[E:F]\). The multiplicative group of a finite field is cyclic. To check the elementary fact used here, the exponent \(d\) of a finite subgroup of a field's multiplicative group has at most \(d\) roots, while every subgroup element is a root of \(X^d-1\). Combining elements of maximal prime-power orders gives an element of order \(d\); hence \(d\) equals the group order. The residue norm has exponent \((Q^s-1)/(Q-1)\), so its image has order \(Q-1\). Thus any target unit can first be matched modulo the maximal ideal.

Use the same uniformizer \(\pi\) in the unramified extension. For \(h\ge1\), multiplication of the conjugate factors gives \[ N_{E/F}(1+\pi^h b) \equiv1+\pi^h\operatorname{Tr}_{\kappa_E/\kappa_F}(\bar b) \pmod{\pi^{h+1}}. \tag{6.987} \] The residue trace is onto. Its polynomial \(X+X^Q+\cdots+X^{Q^{s-1}}\) is nonzero and has degree less than \(Q^s\); it cannot vanish at every element of \(\mathbb F_{Q^s}\). Its nonzero \(\mathbb F_Q\)-linear image is therefore all of \(\mathbb F_Q\). This remains true when the trace of one is zero. Choose a correction using (6.987) at each successive depth. The product of these corrections converges in \(\mathcal O_E^\times\), and continuity of the norm makes its norm exactly the target unit. For the product algebra choose a unit with the required field norm in one factor and one in the others. Its étale norm is the required unit. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.417 — the constant cyclic invariant with its sign. With (6.983), let \(b=v(a)\). In the arithmetic normalization of Lemma 6.1, \[ \operatorname{inv}_v C(L\otimes K_v,\sigma,a) =\frac{mb}{n}\pmod{\mathbb Z},\qquad \operatorname{ind}_v=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,mb)}. \tag{6.988} \] In particular a unit parameter gives a split algebra at every place, including those with \(g>1\).

Proof. Lemma 6.416 removes the unit part of the parameter. Use the degree-\(N\) corner in (6.985). Here is the normalization calculation in the cyclic cochains. The carry cocycle for \(w^N=\pi^b\), with generator \(\tau\), has valuation \(b\) at a carry. It is the boundary of the rational lift of the character \(\chi(\tau)=b/N\) of the cyclic group into \(\mathbb Q/\mathbb Z\). Evaluation at arithmetic Frobenius gives its invariant. This is precisely the valuation/carry proof in Proposition 24.1 of Brauer groups of local and global fields, used in Lemma 6.1. By (6.984) that evaluation is \[ \chi(F_v)=\frac{m}{g}\frac{b}{N}=\frac{mb}{n}. \tag{6.989} \] In particular the factor is \(m\), with this sign, rather than a choice of geometric Frobenius. Passing from a corner to its matrix algebra leaves its Brauer invariant unchanged.

For completeness, the denominator of this fraction is its division degree by Lemma 6.1. The ingredient there is an actual division representative: if \(c/d\) is reduced, the algebra of the unramified degree-\(d\) extension with parameter \(\pi^c\) has valuation \(\min_j(dv(x_j)+cj)\). The minimum is unique modulo \(d\), and the minimal product term cannot cancel, proving division. The injective unramified invariant and uniqueness of the division representative identify the corner with the corresponding matrix algebra. This proves the index in (6.988). A unit parameter also splits directly by Lemmas 6.414 and 6.416. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.418 — one prescribed inner form, a division place and split infinity. Let \(D_0\) be a central division algebra of degree \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q((t))\), and let \(n=rd\ge2\). There is an explicitly constructed central division algebra \(B\) of degree \(n\) over \(K\) with \[ B_0\simeq M_r(D_0),\qquad B_1\text{ division of degree }n, \qquad B_\infty\simeq M_n(K_\infty). \tag{6.990} \] At most one other finite place is nonsplit; it has degree coprime to \(n\).

Proof. Write the invariant of \(D_0\) as \(a/d\), with \(0<a<d\) coprime to \(d\), or \(a=0,d=1\). Choose a prime integer \(\ell>n\) and a monic irreducible \(P\in\mathbb F_q[t]\) of degree \(\ell\). The finite-field irreducible count proved in Theorem 6.390 gives such a polynomial. In particular it differs from \(t,t-1\). Choose \(0\le k<n\) with \[ \ell k\equiv-ar-1\pmod n, \quad A(t)=t^{ar}(t-1)P(t)^k, \quad B=C(L,\sigma,A(t)). \tag{6.991} \] The algebra is central simple of degree \(n\) by Lemma 6.414. At zero its invariant is \(ar/n=a/d\), so Lemma 6.1 and the equal degree give \(B_0\simeq M_r(D_0)\). At one its parameter has valuation one and the constant local extension is a field of degree \(n\). Remove the unit part by Lemma 6.416. The same minimum valuation \(\min_j(nv(x_j)+j)\) proves directly that \(B_1\) is division. Consequently the global algebra has no zero divisors: a nonzero rational zero divisor and its nonzero annihilator would remain nonzero after this scalar extension. Finite-dimensionality then makes \(B\) division.

At \(P\) the invariant is \(\ell k/n\). At every other finite place the parameter is a unit, so the algebra splits by Lemma 6.416, even when the constant tensor has several factors. At infinity its valuation is \(-ar-1-\ell k\), a multiple of \(n\). The constant local extension has degree \(n\), so a power of the base uniformizer has this norm; Lemma 6.416 supplies the remaining unit norm. Lemma 6.414 proves splitting there. These facts establish all the assertions without a global Brauer existence theorem. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.419 — finitely many prescribed coprime-degree inner forms. Let \(S\) be a finite set of finite places of \(K\), each of degree \(m_v\) coprime to \(n\). At each prescribe a degree-\(n\) central simple \(K_v\)-algebra \(A_v\). A global degree-\(n\) central division algebra realizes all these completions, is split at infinity, and is split outside \(S\) and at most two further finite places of degrees coprime to \(n\).

Proof. Write \(\alpha_v=\operatorname{inv}_v(A_v)\in\tfrac1n\mathbb Z/\mathbb Z\), and choose \(0\le b_v<n\) with \(m_vb_v\equiv n\alpha_v\pmod n\). Choose two fresh finite places \(w,z\) of distinct prime degrees \(\ell_w,\ell_z>n\), beyond the degrees occurring in \(S\); their existence is again the irreducible count. Choose residues \(b_w,b_z\) modulo \(n\) with \[ \ell_wb_w\equiv1\pmod n,\qquad \ell_zb_z\equiv-\sum_{v\in S}m_vb_v-\ell_wb_w\pmod n. \tag{6.992} \] Take representatives from \(0,\ldots,n-1\), and set \[ A(t)=\left(\prod_{v\in S}P_v(t)^{b_v}\right) P_w(t)^{b_w}P_z(t)^{b_z}. \tag{6.993} \] The invariant formula (6.988) gives the prescribed local classes and degrees, hence the prescribed algebras by Lemma 6.1. At \(w\), \(b_w\) is coprime to \(n\); the unique-minimum valuation proves that its local algebra, and therefore the global algebra, is division. The degree of \(A(t)\) is a multiple of \(n\), so infinity splits by the same norm construction as in Theorem 6.418. All other finite parameters are units. This proves the claim, including the possibility \(b_z=0\). \(\square\)

Corollary 6.420 — the product of the local elliptic signs. For either construction let \(B_v\simeq M_{r_v}(D_v)\), with \(\deg B=n\). Then \[ \prod_v(-1)^{n-r_v}=1. \tag{6.994} \]

Proof. Outside the indicated finite places the algebra is split, so the sign is one. If \(n\) is odd, every \(r_v\) divides \(n\), hence is odd and every exponent is even. If \(n\) is even, every exceptional degree \(m_v\) is odd. Formula (6.988) gives \(r_v=\gcd(n,m_vb_v)\), whose parity is that of \(b_v\). The total exponent modulo two is therefore \(\sum b_v\). It equals \(\sum m_vb_v=\deg A\) modulo two, which is zero because \(n\mid\deg A\). Infinity is split. This proves (6.994). It is a sign calculation for the constructed algebra, not a representation-transfer assertion. \(\square\)

6.63. Inner local factors and a finite elliptic split trace

The algebras of Section 6.62 are split outside an explicit finite set. This permits the local tensor argument and all unramified orbital tails to be made explicit. Write \(G=A^\times\) for the indicated ambient central simple algebra \(A\). An elliptic rational element below means one whose reduced characteristic polynomial is irreducible and separable of degree \(n\).

Theorem 6.421 — restricted local factors of the actual inner spectrum. Let \(B\) be a global central division algebra over a function field. In particular \(B\) may be either algebra constructed above. Every constituent of \(H_{B,\Omega}\) in Theorem 6.411 has a uniquely determined smooth restricted tensor product \[ \Pi=\bigotimes_v'\Pi_v, \tag{6.995} \] where each factor is irreducible, admissible and unitarizable, with central character \(\Omega_v\). Almost all have a one-dimensional maximal-compact fixed space. For a factorizable smooth compact-mod-centre bi-level test with normalized compact tail, \[ \operatorname{Tr}R(f)= \sum_{\Pi^J\ne0}m(\Pi)\prod_v\operatorname{Tr}\Pi_v(f_v), \tag{6.996} \] a finite sum with tail factors one.

Proof: finite splitting support. Every central simple algebra over either kind of global field is split outside finitely many places. Here is the factor-system argument, also proved at the start of Section 4 of Brauer groups of local and global fields. The algebraic crossed-product theorems cited and proved in that programme lesson's Noether prerequisites give a finite Galois splitting field and a finite list of nonzero factor-system values. Omit the finitely many places ramified in the field and those where any of these values is not a unit. Finiteness of the former set follows by clearing the coefficients and the nonzero discriminant of a separable defining polynomial, then lifting its coprime residual factors as in the order argument below. At a remaining place its decomposition group is cyclic unramified, and the localized cocycle takes values in its units. The cyclic resolution identifies its degree-two unit cohomology with the fixed units modulo unit norms. This group is zero by Lemma 6.416. Thus the local Brauer class is zero, and its degree identifies the algebra with the split matrix algebra. This argument uses no global sum or existence theorem.

Proof: local factors. Theorem 6.411 supplies an actual admissible discrete Hilbert representation. Its irreducible smooth constituents have finite-dimensional product Hecke corners. Apply the algebraic local-unit factorization in Lesson 12, Theorem 4.1 to one local Hecke algebra and its complement. This gives the unique local simple admissible factors; its hypotheses are precisely the finite corners already proved here.

Here is the infinite compatibility argument. A nonzero smooth vector is fixed by maximal compacts outside a finite set \(S_0\) containing all nonsplit places. At a split place transpose preserves every maximal-compact double coset by the Cartan decomposition of Lemma 6.23 and reverses convolution. Hence its spherical Hecke algebra is commutative. A nonzero simple finite-dimensional spherical module has an eigenline, which simplicity makes the whole module. Thus the local compact fixed line is one-dimensional.

For finite \(S\supset S_0\), write \(V_S=V^{\mathcal K^S}\). The tail Hecke algebras act on it by these scalar characters. It is a simple module for the \(S\)-algebra: if a submodule is nonzero, its global Hecke span is \(V\); averaging that span back to \(V_S\), the tail factors reduce to their scalars, so the original submodule is all of \(V_S\). Finite local-unit factorization identifies it with \(\bigotimes_{v\in S}\Pi_v\). For \(S\subset S'\), the embedding is tensoring with the one-dimensional \(\prod_{v\in S'-S}\mathcal K_v\)-fixed line. Choose coherent nonzero vectors in these lines, starting with one pure tensor at \(S_0\); uniqueness of the finite factorizations permits compatible normalizations on every finite enlargement. The union of the \(V_S\) is every smooth vector, proving (6.995) and its uniqueness. This is the finite-stage construction in Theorem 6.381 with its inner hypotheses supplied by Theorems 6.411 and 6.418–6.419.

Fix nonzero vectors in the other factors of a pure tensor. Restriction of its actual invariant Hilbert norm gives a positive invariant Hermitian form on \(\Pi_v\); a nonzero local vector gives a nonzero pure tensor. Thus the local factors are unitarizable. Their admissibility ensures that their Hilbert completions add no smooth vectors, by finite-dimensional compact averaging. Local scalar elements act by \(\Omega_v\), as they do in the original global representation. Finally, on a product fixed space the test operator is the tensor product of its local finite matrices and the identity on each tail line. Its trace is their product. The finite Hilbert sum at that level is Theorem 6.412, proving (6.996). \(\square\)

Lemma 6.422 — unramified étale orders and the tail orbital. Let \(\gamma\) be an elliptic rational element of a central simple algebra over a global field, and put \(E=K[\gamma]\). At almost every finite place, a split local identification can be chosen such that \[ \mathcal O_v[\gamma]=\prod_{w\mid v}\mathcal O_{E_w},\qquad \gamma\in\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathcal O_v). \tag{6.997} \] The \(\gamma\)-stable full lattices form one orbit of \(E_v^\times\). Give \(T_v/Z_v\) Haar measure with the image of \(\prod\mathcal O_{E_w}^\times\) of volume one. The normalized inverse-central-character compact indicator then has \[ O_\gamma(f_v)=1 \tag{6.998} \] at all these places, provided the character is unramified there.

Proof: the order. The finite-support argument in Theorem 6.421 applies in both global characteristics. First fix the integral reference compacts. A rational basis containing one spans an order \(\Lambda_v\) outside finitely many places, by clearing multiplication denominators. The reduced trace pairing is nondegenerate: after splitting, its matrix-unit dual bases prove this in every characteristic. Omit also the denominators and zeros of its basis Gram determinant. The resulting order is its own trace dual. At a split place it is a full matrix order. To see this directly, in a split representation take the stable lattice \(M=\Lambda_v\mathcal O_v^n\). It is full and bounded, since the order has finitely many lattice generators and contains one. Then \(\Lambda_v\subset\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal O_v}(M)\). Every element of the latter order pairs integrally with \(\Lambda_v\), since a product of two lattice endomorphisms has integral trace. Self-duality forces the reverse inclusion. A valuation-ring basis of \(M\) therefore identifies \(\Lambda_v\) with \(M_n(\mathcal O_v)\). Its units give the adelic reference maximal compacts outside this finite set.

The monic reduced polynomial \(P\) of \(\gamma\) has rational coefficients, nonzero constant coefficient and nonzero discriminant. Omit the finitely many places where \(\gamma\) or \(\gamma^{-1}\) is not in the reference order, any remaining coefficient denominators, the zeros of the constant and discriminant, and the nonsplit places. Thus \(\gamma\in\mathcal K_v\), and modulo the maximal ideal \(P\) is a product of distinct irreducible polynomials. Its local minimal polynomial is still \(P\), since it has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues after splitting. Hence \(\mathcal O_v[\gamma]\simeq\mathcal O_v[X]/(P)\).

These coprime factors lift to monic factors over \(\mathcal O_v\): at each step the error of a proposed factorization is corrected modulo the next uniformizer power by the Bezout identity for the relatively prime residual factors. The corrections converge, and their monicity fixes the degrees. Their quotient rings split as a product by the lifted Bezout identity. Each irreducible residual factor of degree \(s\) gives an unramified extension with that residue field. Its powers \(1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{s-1}\) are an integral basis: subtract the residue expansion of an integral element in this basis, divide the remainder by the uniformizer, and repeat. Completeness makes all resulting coefficients integral. Thus the quotient order is its full valuation ring, proving (6.997).

Proof: lattices and the measure. If a full lattice is stable under \(\gamma\), it is stable under \(\mathcal O_v[\gamma]\). Its idempotents split it into full rank-one modules in each \(E_w\). Each such module is a fractional ideal of its valuation ring, hence a uniformizer power times that ring: take an element of least valuation and divide all other elements by it. Therefore \(E_v^\times\) is transitive on these lattices.

The ordinary centralizer of \(\gamma\) is \(T_v=E_v^\times\). The support of the local orbital integral is the single double coset \(T_v\mathcal K_v\). Indeed a conjugate in \(Z_v\mathcal K_v\) has determinant of valuation zero, so its scalar has valuation zero and the conjugate is in \(\mathcal K_v\). Such conjugates correspond exactly to the stable lattices just classified. The intersection of the images of \(T_v\) and \(\mathcal K_v\) in the scalar quotient is the image of its integral units. Quotient measure gives the image of \(\mathcal K_v\) in \(T_v\backslash G_v\) volume \(\operatorname{vol}(\overline{\mathcal K}_v)\). The normalized test has the reciprocal value there; its unramified central phase is one on units. Their product is (6.998). This uses the unit-image torus measure, without replacing it by a full compact-torus normalization. \(\square\)

Proposition 6.423 — the absolute global orbital product. In Lemma 6.422, fix a smooth unitary idèle-class character \(\Omega\), and let \(f=\prod_v f_v\) be an inverse-\(\Omega\)-covariant compact-mod-centre factorizable test with normalized compact tail. Suppose all local factors are smooth at the nonarchimedean places and continuous compact-mod-centre at archimedean places. For a function field there are no latter places. For the following formula assume each exceptional local orbital integral is absolute; this is automatic for smooth compact-mod-centre tests over function fields by Lemma 6.144. With the restricted-product quotient Haar measures, \[ \int_{\mathbb A_E^\times\backslash G(\mathbb A_K)} f(x^{-1}\gamma x)\,d\dot x =\prod_v O_\gamma(f_v), \tag{6.999} \] and both the integral and the product of absolute orbitals are finite. All but finitely many factors are one.

Proof. Enlarge a finite set \(S\) until Lemma 6.422 applies to every place outside it, the character is unramified there, and every test is its normalized compact indicator there. The proof of that lemma gives more than an orbital value: its support in the local homogeneous space is exactly the compact image of \(\mathcal K_v\). With the test and quotient Haar normalizations, the integral on that image is one, also for the absolute value.

We spell out the restricted-product step. Both the group and the torus modulo scalar idèles are the restricted products of their local scalar quotients with the integral-unit images as compact subgroups. A tuple of local scalar cosets in these subgroups almost everywhere has integral-unit lifts there, giving an adelic lift. If an adelic tuple is scalar in every component, its scalar is a unit almost everywhere, since its image and inverse are integral there; it is consequently a scalar idèle. These two assertions prove the quotient identification, including its topology, on the usual product neighbourhoods.

In the homogeneous quotient, all outside-\(S\) components that contribute therefore have representatives in \(\mathcal K_v\). Their product is a compact fibre, with quotient probability measure after the test normalization. On cylinder functions quotient Haar disintegration is the product of the finitely many exceptional quotient measures and these compact measures: verify it by integrating first in the torus and then in the group. Such cylinders determine the measure; increasing finite product cylinders and Tonelli give the same assertion for nonnegative functions. Apply it first to \(\prod|f_v(x_v^{-1}\gamma x_v)|\). Its integral is the finite product of the exceptional absolute orbitals, so is finite. Absolute integration then gives (6.999).

For the asserted nonarchimedean automatic condition, \(\gamma\) is regular semisimple and hence has a closed ordinary orbit. On a compact projective support its reduced norm fixes the allowed central valuations in a bounded range. The quotient conjugator bound (6.329) of Lemma 6.144 makes the contributing centralizer quotient compact. A smooth test is bounded there and quotient Haar is finite on compact sets. This proves the required absolute local orbital, including when \(E_v\) is a product. No arbitrary archimedean convergence assertion is being inferred from it. \(\square\)

Theorem 6.424 — a finite regular-elliptic split trace. Let \(K=\mathbb F_q(t)\), \(G=\mathrm{GL}_n\), and \(\Omega\) a smooth unitary idèle-class character. Let \(f=\prod_vf_v\) be smooth, compact modulo the centre and inverse-\(\Omega\)-covariant, with normalized compact tail. Suppose one factor has support in the separable regular elliptic set and one factor satisfies the strong translated-unipotent vanishing (6.914). They may be at different places. Then \[ \sum_\Pi m(\Pi)\prod_v\operatorname{Tr}\Pi_v(f_v) =\sum_{[\gamma]}\frac{V_{E_\gamma}}{e_\gamma} \prod_vO_\gamma(f_v). \tag{6.1000} \] The left sum is over actual cuspidal constituents with fixed vectors at the test's level. The right sum is over the projective rational conjugacy classes meeting its support, with \(E_\gamma=K[\gamma]\), \(V_E\) and \(e_\gamma\) as in (6.981). Both sums are finite, and regrouping the diagonal rational kernel is absolute.

Proof: the geometric sum. A rational element meeting the supports is separable regular elliptic: a proper rational factor of its characteristic polynomial would remain a factor at the elliptic place. Lemma 6.388 gives only finitely many such projective rational classes. Its finiteness part uses the compact support bounds and rational prime-polynomial scalar normalization, not the special scalar-free affine spectrum in its separation part. Each centralizer is the degree-\(n\) field \(E_\gamma\). Theorem 6.409 gives \(0<V_{E_\gamma}<\infty\).

The rational projective stabilizer maps to \(\{z\in K^\times:z^n=1\}\), with kernel \(E_\gamma^\times/K^\times\), exactly as in Proposition 6.413. Its index is \(e_\gamma\). For each class apply Tonelli before assuming convergence. The ordinary field torus disintegration gives \[ \int_{\Gamma\backslash\overline G} \sum_{\delta\in\Gamma_{\bar\gamma}\backslash\Gamma} |f(x^{-1}\delta^{-1}\gamma\delta x)|\,dx =\frac{V_{E_\gamma}}{e_\gamma} \prod_vO_\gamma(|f_v|)<\infty, \tag{6.1001} \] where Proposition 6.423 proves the final absolute product. The rational scalar phase is one, because \(\Omega\) is trivial on \(K^\times\). Summing over the finite set of classes proves the absolute diagonal integral. Removing absolute values proves its geometric expression in (6.1000).

Proof: the spectral trace. Choose a principal level fixing the test on both sides. The strong factor and Theorem 6.382 make the operator zero on the noncuspidal orthogonal complement, with both its range and adjoint range in a finite cuspidal fixed space. Its kernel is zero outside the corresponding finite set of compatible level rows and columns. Consequently its integral over the whole quotient equals the finite weighted diagonal trace (6.916). The actual restricted cuspidal spectral expression is Theorem 6.381. Substituting the geometric expression just proved gives (6.1000). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.424 concerns tests with genuine regular elliptic support at a place. A compact discrete-series test that merely has zero traces on proper inductions need not have that support. Inserting a regular cut can change its traces and lose its isolation property. The formula therefore supplies this finite elliptic trace identity; the general split/inner comparison, the outside-place spectral fibre and individual representation-transfer integrality require their own arguments. The explicit global algebras and the inner local tensor decomposition above do not assert those remaining conclusions.

7. Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 7.1 — an unramified quadratic field. Let \(K/\mathbb Q_p\) be the unramified quadratic extension. Choose \(\xi\in\mathcal O_K^\times\) whose residue generates \(\mathbb F_{p^2}/\mathbb F_p\). Write explicitly the matching matrix and quaternion class, and their centralizers.

Exercise 7.14 — inseparable primary flags and compact germs. In Example 6.143 compute \(p(x_X)\) for \(X=E_{11}\) and \(X=I\). Determine the partitions, centralizer dimensions, orbit dimensions and the canonical kernel flags. For type \((2)\), check the dimension of the bundle in (6.320): its flag base, closed Levi orbit and radical. If a compact test has every proper translated constant term zero, which coefficient can remain in its germ expansion at \(P=p^2\)? Explain why this conclusion cannot be assigned to \(f_{\pi,m}\) merely from its known regular orbital values.

Exercise 7.15 — inseparable character values and a necessary quotient. Let \(F=\mathbb F_2((t))\), \(G=\mathrm{GL}_4(F)\), and let \(\gamma e_i=e_{i+1}\) for \(i<4\), \(\gamma e_4=te_1\). Prove that \(\gamma\) is \(F\)-irreducible and inseparable, find its stabilized chamber and the signs in (6.337), and compute its Steinberg character and the orbital integral of a unit Steinberg coefficient under both centralizer normalizations. For the repeated quadratic action \(s_0=s\oplus s\) of Example 6.143, show why \(\sigma(x)\) cannot replace \(\ell_{G_{s_0}}(x)\) in (6.329). Finally determine the type \((2)\) compact discrete-test coefficient in that example using the proved Schwartz argument.

Exercise 7.16 — quadratic lattice masses and the remaining character obstruction. For \(D=F\), \(q_F=2\), \(m=2\), and \(\boldsymbol n=(2,1)\), compute the additive stabilizer index, its invertible fraction, and the orbit cardinality in each quadratic ramification case. Calculate the two Cartan lists and the closed-primary Euler orbital. Explain how the exponential factors cancel in the Schwartz orbital sum. For the split degree-four character expansion (6.364), does its positive integral dimension sum alone imply that every coefficient is a nonnegative integer?

Exercise 7.17 — an inseparable fixed tree and a primary limit. In Example 6.168 compute the full fixed-vertex stabilizer volumes, the outward shell masses, the spherical factors and the exact convergence threshold. What is the closed germ on nearby elliptic regular classes? Next take \(p_j(T)=T^2+t^jT+t\), \(j\ge1\), over \(\mathbb F_2((t))\). With \(\alpha^2+t^j\alpha+t=0\) and \(\beta^2+\beta+1=0\), find the polynomial of \(\alpha+t^n\beta\) when \(n\ne j\), and prove that a sequence of such separable irreducible quartics tends to \((T^2-t)^2\). Finally compute \(h,\delta,m\) for a quadratic field in \(\mathrm{GL}_3(D)\), with \(D\) quaternion division. Distinguish the primary character-germ assertion from a closed-primary Schwartz bound in that rank.

Exercise 7.18 — paired lengths and a higher-rank singular orbital. In the characteristic-two model with \(Q=2\), determine the stabilizer residues and the orbit sizes for \(r=3,\boldsymbol n=(1)\) and \(r=4,\boldsymbol n=(1,1)\). Then compute \(B\), the Cartan list and the orbit size for \(r=4,\boldsymbol n=(2,1)\). Compute the closed Euler orbital, Steinberg degree and unit Iwahori Steinberg coefficient orbital in ranks three and four. Compare the rank-three normalization when \(d=4\) over \(\mathbb F_2((t))\). Explain why the unit \(u-\tau u\), rather than division by two, is the integral descent input.

Exercise 7.19 — valuation colors and exhaustive counting. In Example 6.184 compute every normalized orbit of index two and three in rank three, and the index-two orbits in rank four. Check each mass and compare their sums with the corresponding coefficients of (6.411). For a positive pair of length two, compute the four stabilizer depths in (6.402), its additive index, and its residual invertible fraction. Why do the linked residue blocks contribute one unit fraction rather than its square? Compute the rank-three and rank-four singular Steinberg orbitals, and explain which part of the proof turns the finite counts into an all-rank classification.

Exercise 7.20 — a quadratic action that is not an involution. Verify every relation in (6.428), prove that \(E/F\) is ramified and separable, and compute \(v_D(u-\tau u)\). In rank five, for \(\boldsymbol n=(2,1)\), calculate the exact mass, Cartan list, Euler orbital, Steinberg degree and unit Iwahori coefficient orbital. Check the criterion (6.427) in total degree ten. In mixed characteristic take \(E=\mathbb Q_2(\sqrt3)\) and \(\theta=1+\sqrt3\): find its Eisenstein polynomial and the recurrence coefficients \(a_\theta,b_\theta\). Explain why an involution identity is unnecessary for the stable intersection.

Exercise 7.21 — cubic submodules and weighted families. Over \(\mathbb F_8\), let \(z^3+z+1=0\). Exhibit a nonzero relation among the three vectors \((1,z),(1,z^2),(1,z^4)\), and explain why their lines do not give a direct sum. Count the normalized rank-three first-level lattices and their two centralizer orbits. For \(Q=2\), compute the masses of \(h_1,h_2,g_{1,0},g_{1,1},g_{2,0},g_{2,1}\). Calculate the Cartan list and both root heights in (6.438) at \(n=1\). Compare the index-two family mass with the total count, and state exactly what convergence (6.437) proves.

Exercise 7.22 — all cyclic quotients and cubic intermediate orbits. For \(r=3,Q=2,e=3\), count the normalized cyclic quotients of lengths one, two and three. Compute every mass \(w_{2,a}\) and \(w_{3,a}\), with the corresponding lengths of \(L_0/I\). Explain why the two equal masses at length two represent distinct orbits, and account for the entire index-two coefficient \(4248\). For the generator \(s=1+\theta\) in the cubic model, compute the exact Cartan list of every normalized length-\(n\) cyclic kernel. Determine the convergence threshold supplied by the primitive-row estimate, and explain its scope in ranks two and three.

Exercise 7.23 — dual masses and an intermediate intersection. At \(Q=2\), compute both cyclic orientations for \((u,v)=(3,1)\) and the dual family \((n,a)=(3,2)\): give quotient lengths, intersection lengths, Cartan lists and masses. For \(g_*\), use (6.458) to find \(L\cap E^3\), and use (6.459) to count additive and invertible stabilizer matrices. Check its Cartan list from the least valuations of \(A\) and \(A^{-1}\). Sum all index-four masses, including the cyclic quotients. Use (6.461) to count both noncyclic quotient types at index five. Explain why this proves a finite-index classification but does not establish the full cubic Schwartz integral, and why transposition requires the opposite algebra.

Exercise 7.24 — noncommutative cubic masses and a wild uniformizer. For \(d=6\), a totally ramified cubic field has quaternionic centralizer. At \(Q=4,r=3,n=2\), compute all cyclic-quotient orbit masses and their sum, and the equal-length quotient orbit \((2,2,0)\). Give the corresponding uniformizer Cartan lists. At \(Q=2,r=4,n=2\), compute every cyclic orbit and compare the sum with the primitive-row count. In Example 6.212 verify the trace, norm and Eisenstein identity, explain why the field is wild and \(\tau^3\ne1\), and compute its displayed mass. Finally, if a normalized rank-three cubic lattice has greatest quotient length \(u=5\), list the possible extreme Cartan deviations \((a,c)\) and the corresponding root heights.

Exercise 7.25 — the full height count and its trace consequence. Compute both columns of (6.489), their one-sided cumulative count at defect two, and their root-weighted sums. Derive the quadratic expression (6.484) by summing \(\min(v,u-v)\). Explain why the arbitrary-generator argument needs the compact stable-line/plane exclusion, rather than a bounded coordinate shift from a uniformizer. Compute all three quantities in (6.487) for \((Q,e,\delta)=(2,4,1)\) and \((4,3,2)\). State which primary partitions are covered and which general transfer assertions remain additional work.

Exercise 7.26 — coefficient colors and strict refinement bounds. In Example 6.228, prove that all three scalar colors are normalized, and compute the number of top cyclic over-lattices of types \((6,3,0)\) and \((3,1,1)\). Derive the counts \(576,64,56\) from the two rank-two primitive-row charts and the coefficient matrix. Compute the singular Euler, Steinberg-degree and unit-coefficient values for the unramified cubic and the mixed inseparable degree-six field. Explain why \(w\) is bounded, how the compact coefficient frame excludes an invariant plane, and why Corollary 6.226 covers all rank-three closed primary types without proving the general local representation correspondence.

Exercise 7.27 — rank four, real coefficients and trace excision. List the proper block sizes for all nonclosed primary partitions when \(hm=4\). Compute \(\eta_s\) and the closed compact germ for the inseparable quartic in Example 6.238. Verify the cycle and Cartan heights in (6.524). For \(P(x)=x^4\) over \(\mathbb F_2((t))\), compute the measure of \(\{x\in\mathcal O_F:v_F(P(x))\ge n\}\), and compare its exponent with Lemma 6.232. Derive the three-by-three table in Figure 20. Prove reality of the coefficients using inversion, compute the \(S_3\) example's identity value and norm, and state exactly which additional trace limit would prove elliptic orthogonality of a finite packet.

Exercise 7.28 — polynomial profiles and exact trace separation. Explain why the division average in (6.528) is unnormalized, why a locally constant profile on its compact polynomial image admits the central-covariant extension (6.530), and why changing the extension preserves the cocenter class when \(r\le4\). For a finite packet in Theorem 6.246, give an explicit sufficient inequality on \(n\) for invertibility of \(H_n\), and verify the exact trace values of (6.543). Compute \((B-A)A^{\mathsf t}\) for (6.546) and compare it with \(I-H\). Finally derive both constants in (6.545), retaining the centralizer degree and ramification index.

Exercise 7.29 — finite flag volumes and the central flat. For \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\), \(P\) upper triangular and \(J=1+\varpi_FM_2(\mathcal O_F)\), compute \(t,\operatorname{vol}(J),\operatorname{vol}(J_M),\operatorname{vol}(J_N)\) before central quotient and verify (6.548). Explain how the diagonal convolution calculation gives (6.555) modulo finite conjugation differences. For \(M=\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\times\mathrm{GL}_3(D)\), describe the flat, the product-cell stabilizer and the cancellation (6.560). Derive all factors in (6.570), including the separable and inseparable degrees. State precisely what (6.568) leaves to be proved for orthogonality.

Exercise 7.30 — finite flags, cyclic components and the trace normalization. Evaluate \(E_3\) on the three cycle types of \(S_3\), and compute the identity value and finite squared norm of its \(\mathrm{GL}_3(k)\) flag combination. For \(r=6,j=2\), describe the two vertex cycles, the signs of the two stable face types, and the dimensions of a compatible \(3+3\) flag in their graded pieces. For \(r=4,d=1,q_F=2,j=2\), compute \(u_2(\Omega^2)\). Verify the two halves in (6.600). Finally explain why (6.589) has no remaining formal-degree factor, and why (6.596)–(6.597) do not by themselves establish individual coefficient integrality or representation existence.

Exercise 7.31 — compact Fourier steps and rational support.

  1. In \(K=\mathbb F_2(t)\), with \(s=t^{-1}\), check the finite and infinite residues of \(t^{-1}dt\). In the representative group (6.602), detect an infinity component \(s^3+s^4\), and then a component \(t^2+t^3\) at the prime \(t\), by suitable rational parameters. Find trace-dual bases for \(\mathbb F_4(t)/\mathbb F_2(t)\), using \(\alpha^2+\alpha+1=0\).
  2. For \(n=4\), compute the dimensions of \(U^{(i)}\) and \(V_i\). At each stage identify the proper radical whose constant term makes \(C_{i,0}=0\). Explain why no assertion that \(F_i\) is itself a cusp form on \(\mathrm{GL}_i\) is needed.
  3. Put \(P=t^2+t+1\). Among matrices in \(\mathrm{GL}_2(K)\) with polynomial entries of degree less than three and determinant a unit at \(P\), prove that the inverse image of the scalar class modulo \(P^2\) contains only globally scalar matrices. Show that reduction modulo \(P\) alone does not suffice.
  4. Verify (6.615) and the traces of \((12)-(23)\) in all three irreducibles of \(S_3\). Explain precisely why a nonzero Poincaré function and local pseudo-coefficient trace zeros do not alone prove exact discrete-series globalization.

Exercise 7.32 — mirabolic densities and smooth evaluation.

  1. For \(m=2\), compute the \(\nu_2\)-measure of the shell \(\|\eta\|_\infty=q^{-b}\). Compute the Haar mass in (6.619) obtained by also requiring \(s\in P_2\cap\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathcal O)\). Give the values for \(q=2\), \(b=0,1,2\).
  2. Compute the three projective-chart masses for \(\mathbb P^2(F)\) when \(q=2\), and check the \(\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathcal O)\) volume in (6.638). Write the \(\sigma_2\) action explicitly. For \(n=3\), \(a=2\), compute the norm and evaluation of the vectors in (6.637), before and after normalization.
  3. In the finite group \(P_3(\mathbb F_2)\), compute the dimensions of the zero and nonzero last-column Fourier parts of the regular representation. Check the dimension of its nonzero part using the stabilizer \(P_2(\mathbb F_2)\). Explain why one must retain the zero part in this finite calculation.
  4. In Theorem 6.284, explain why a bounded nonzero component map \(T\) carries smooth vectors to the domain of \(\ell_n\), and why \(\ell_nT\) is nonzero. Identify exactly which multiplicity or uniqueness conclusions are not supplied by this argument.

Exercise 7.33 — transpose, relevant cells and Whittaker kernels. Use the notation of Section 6.46.

(a) Over \(F=\mathbb F_2((s))\), take the cyclic operator given by multiplication by \(T\) on \(F[T]/(T^4-s)\). Find its matrix and the Gram matrix for the coefficient-of-\(T^3\) pairing. Check the transpose intertwining identity directly. Explain why inseparability and characteristic two cause no difficulty.

(b) List all relevant permutations and their compatible diagonal parameters for \(n=3\). Count these parameter profiles over \(\mathbb F_3\). For each of the other two permutations, exhibit a simple-root stabilizer that prevents compatibility over a local field.

(c) Explain why an involution acting trivially on the successive quotients of a finite filtration acts trivially on the whole complex vector space. Give an example showing that the involution assumption matters.

(d) Derive the two character factors in (6.652), including the inverse on the right. Derive (6.655) directly from the bilinear form, and explain why fixing \(\ell'\) proves uniqueness of \(\ell\) without a bounded Hilbert-space evaluation functional.

(e) Combine Theorems 6.284 and 6.291. State precisely what follows for a split discrete series and which further local assertion is needed for prescribed-discrete-series globalization.

Exercise 7.34 — induction, Haar factors and the generic constituent.

  1. For block sizes \((2,3)\), compute \(w_*\), \(w_*^{-1}\), \(H_*\) and the character restricted to \(H_*\). Give the dimension of \(H_*\backslash U_5\) and its finite-field cardinality. For the shuffle \([1,3,4,5,2]\), exhibit the simple-root obstruction in (6.662).
  2. Let \(U=U_3(\mathbb F_3)\), \(H=\{1+xE_{12}\}\), \(\psi(x)=\exp(2\pi ix/3)\), and \(\rho_a(1+xE_{12})=\psi(ax)\). Compute the dimension of the \(\theta\)-quotient of \(\operatorname{Ind}_H^U\rho_a\) for \(a=0,1,2\). For \(a=1\), use counting Haar measures to compare \(\Phi(F)\) and \((E_{U,\theta}F)(1)\) on each standard coset-basis section.
  3. Assume a parabolic induction of generic irreducible admissible factors has a finite composition series. Prove that there is exactly one generic occurrence. What changes if one Levi factor has zero Whittaker quotient? Explain why this argument does not prove finite length or equality of generic constituents from different inductions.
  4. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), compute the numbers of complete and partial flags in dimensions three and four needed for induction from Levi block sizes \((2,1)\) and \((2,2)\). Use the constants-to-Steinberg exact sequence in each \(\mathrm{GL}_2\)-block to compute the dimensions and Whittaker dimensions of the induced Steinberg modules. Distinguish these finite groups from local-field representations.
  5. In the finite group \(G=\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb F_3)\), take \(P=B=MN\), use probability Haar measures on \(G,M,N\), and let \(f\) have value one at the identity and zero elsewhere. Compute both sides of the finite induced-trace identity for \(W=\mathbf1_M\) and for the regular \(M\)-module. State which normalization of the Hecke identity differs from this \(f\).
  6. Derive all three traces in (6.674). Explain why uniqueness of the generic factor and the zero trace of the entire induction cannot replace the remaining irreducibility or composition argument.

Exercise 7.35 — finite detection and ordered cuspidal blocks.

  1. Work over \(F=\mathbb F_2((\varpi))\), with \(\psi\) of conductor \(\mathcal O\). In \(F^2\), take \(L_0=\varpi^2\mathcal O^2\) and \(M=\varpi^{-1}\mathcal O^2\). Compute their annihilators, the number of dual cosets in (6.679), and the two Haar volumes when \(\operatorname{vol}\mathcal O^2=1\). Prove that a vector fixed by \(L_0\) is zero if each of those finitely many \(M\)-averages kills it.
  2. For \(P_3\), list \(\Omega_3\) and identify which quotients come from \(A(V)\) and from \(B(V)\). If \(\rho\) is irreducible admissible cuspidal, compute these four dimensions and its mirabolic length.
  3. For three labelled cuspidal blocks of degrees \((2,1,2)\), derive the entire table (6.694) from ordered partitions. Give the length bound and the multiplicity of the fully nondegenerate factor. Compare the bound with \(2^{n-1}n!/\prod n_j!\).
  4. For two cuspidal blocks of degrees \((2,2)\), compute all nonzero character profiles. Does the answer change if the two inducing representations are isomorphic? Explain which occurrences are being counted.
  5. Construct the finite module in Example 6.305 and prove its irreducibility directly. Compute its four quotients and show that \(D_3\) need not equal the composition length.
  6. Count ordered partitions of four and five labels, with the number of groups specified. Recover \(F_4\) and \(F_5\). Explain why finite length and uniqueness of a generic occurrence do not by themselves prove generic trace isolation.

Exercise 7.36 — normalized embeddings and induction.

  1. In Example 6.309 take \(a=\varpi^2\), \(b=\varpi^{-1}\), \(c=\varpi^3\), with \(|\varpi|=q^{-1}\). Compute \(\delta_P\), \(\delta_Q\), \(\delta_{B_3}\), the product of their positive half-factors, and the scalar in the inverse map (6.713).
  2. Use principal level \(J=1+\varpi M_3(\mathcal O)\) and torus characters trivial on \(1+\varpi\mathcal O\). Count the outer \((2,1)\)-flag pieces, the inner degree-two flag pieces and the full degree-three flag pieces. Verify the fixed-space dimension identity behind (6.700), for general residue cardinality and for two and three.
  3. Explain why the maximal-block Jacquet-module argument gives an irreducible admissible cuspidal quotient without first proving that the Jacquet module has finite length. List the possible degree patterns for \(G_4\), grouped by their resulting mirabolic length bounds. Explain why a central character on the whole Levi centre is unnecessary before taking the irreducible quotient.
  4. Suppose the chosen embeddings of generic irreducible admissible \(\tau_1\) on \(G_3\) and \(\tau_2\) on \(G_2\) have cuspidal degrees \((2,1)\) and \((1,1)\), respectively. Write the refined embedding for induction from \((3,2)\) to \(G_5\). Compute its mirabolic length bound and the multiplicity of its generic factor. Is this a claim that the induced module is irreducible?
  5. Let \(\rho\) be irreducible admissible cuspidal on \(G_2\) and let \(\chi\) be a smooth character of \(F^\times\). Define a two-dimensional \(F^\times\)-module by \(E(z)=\chi(z)\begin{pmatrix}1&v_F(z)\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). Prove that it is a smooth nonsplit extension of \(\chi\) by itself. For \(W=\rho\otimes E\) on the \((2,1)\)-Levi of \(G_3\), bound the length of \(i_P^{G_3}W\) and compute its trace on an ordinary compact Hecke test in terms of \(i_P^{G_3}(\rho\otimes\chi)\). Explain why ordinary induction exactness is the appropriate assertion here.
  6. Explain what (6.711) proves for a generic \(V\) and what it leaves open about arbitrary cuspidal inductions, ordering of data, irreducibility and trace isolation.

Exercise 7.37 — compact cuspidal projectors and their normalization.

  1. In Lemma 6.310, suppose a principal subgroup of division level \(m_0\) fixes \(v\) and the finite \(K\)-orbit of \(\ell\). Show that \(m=m_0+d-1\) fixes the functionals in (6.716). For \(r=3,d=2,m_0=2\), and annihilating gap bounds \((b_1,b_2)=(3,2)\), compute the two expanded radical levels and the number of allowed gap positions in each residue layer. Explain why these positions need not have nonzero coefficient values.
  2. For \(r=3,d=2\) and \(|\omega(z)|=|z|_F^3\), find the positive unramified twist giving unitary central character. Explain why the exponent uses \(rd\), rather than \(rd^2\).
  3. Let \(X\) be finite length with scalar central character \(\omega\), with exactly three composition factors isomorphic to \(\rho\). Compute \(\operatorname{Tr}X(e_\rho)\). Explain why Theorem 6.312 does not prove projectivity in the category allowing arbitrary central action, using Example 6.316.
  4. In the characteristic-two division example, identify the six quotient classes, calculate the coefficient table, and verify its convolution square and its operator on the sum-zero plane. Keep the quotient Haar mass explicit.
  5. Multiply the quotient Haar measure in that example by three. Find the new formal degree, idempotent function, squared coefficient norm and representation operator.
  6. On the same division group put \(\zeta_t(g)=t^{v_D(g)}\), \(t>0\), and \(\rho_t=\zeta_t\rho\). Use representatives \(s(a,\epsilon)=a\Pi^\epsilon\), \(a\in k^\times\), \(\epsilon\in\{0,1\}\). Derive the central factor in their multiplication, the twisted convolution rule and the idempotent for \(\rho_t\). For \(t=2\), compute its three odd-valuation coefficient values and the positive twist that returns \(\rho_t\) to the original unitary representation.

Exercise 7.38 — division flags and exact Jacquet quotients.

  1. For source and target division block sizes \((2,2)\), list all transport matrices and identify which geometric Jacquet layers can survive when both source factors are cuspidal. Describe the resulting filtration, including coincident source factors.
  2. Prove the modulus identity (6.756) by classifying pairs of distinct intersection blocks according to their two labels. Explain why the rectangle determinant (6.757) proves the identity on full division Levi blocks, rather than only on their scalar centres.
  3. Recalculate the closed-cell moduli of Example 6.323 for \(d=2\) and field valuations \((2,-1,3)\). Include the factor \(\delta_P^{-1/2}\), the quotient-measure factor and the conversion from the unnormalized source Jacquet module.
  4. Let an irreducible module occur in cuspidal induction from labelled division block factors \((\rho_a,\chi,\rho_b)\) of sizes \((2,1,2)\). Determine the necessary possibilities for its cuspidal embedding data when \(\rho_a\not\simeq\rho_b\), and when they are isomorphic. Give the composition-length and intertwining-dimension bounds between the corresponding ordered full inductions, and state what is not implied.
  5. Count the closed and open residue flag cells of Example 6.323 for residue fields of sizes two, three and four. Distinguish these counts from the local Haar measures in (6.754).
  6. In the finite group \(N=U_3(\mathbb F_2)\), let \(H_0=\{1+xE_{12}\}\). Compute the dimension of \(\operatorname{Ind}_{H_0}^N W\), its coinvariants and its full-group averaging projector for \(W=1\) and for the nontrivial character of \(H_0\). As a second model, take finite \(\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb F_2)\) with source \((1,2)\) and target \((2,1)\); use the sign and the sum-zero representations of \(\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb F_2)\simeq S_3\) as source factors. Determine the dimensions and characters of their target-radical invariants. Explain the limits of these finite computations.

Exercise 7.39 — exchange maps, unitary induction and parameter matrices.

  1. In the reducible, distinct-ordered-data case of Theorem 6.328, determine the kernels and images of the two nonzero intertwiners and both compositions. Explain why their existence does not identify the full modules, although their composition multisets agree.
  2. Take unitary cuspidals of division dimensions \((2,1,2)\), with the two dimension-two factors inequivalent. Determine the length and endomorphism dimension of every ordering of their induction. What can be concluded from the matching-cell bound if those two factors are instead isomorphic? Explain the split-group generic constituent assertion separately.
  3. For a division algebra of degree two and parabolic dimensions \((2,1)\), take \(p_0=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F I_2,1)\). Compute the right-shift Haar integral factor in (6.792), the normalized induction half-factor, and the value at a central uniformizer of a source-block unramified twist \(z^{v_F\operatorname{Nrd}}\) on \(\mathrm{GL}_2(D)\).
  4. For split \(\mathrm{GL}_2(F)\), let \(J=1+\varpi_F M_2(\mathcal O_F)\), \(a=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi_F,1)\) and \(U=\operatorname{vol}(J)^{-1}\mathbf1_{JaJ}\). On \(I(z_1,z_2)^J\), use the residue bottom-row lines \(\infty=(0,1)\) and \((1,x)\), \(x\in\mathbb F_q\), as the section-value coordinates. Compute the actual matrix for \(q=2\), its trace, and the characteristic polynomial for general \(q\). What happens at \(z_1=z_2=1\), and does that imply reducibility?
  5. Compute the two spherical traces (6.803)–(6.804) at \((z_1,z_2)=(q^{1/2},q^{-1/2})\). Account for them using the constant and Steinberg factors. Compare this with the discrete Euler trace in (6.806), retaining the nongeneric contribution.
  6. Verify the matrix \(A\) in (6.807) and its intertwining signs. Compare the source factors and the induced modules at the unitary parameter pairs \((1,-1)\) and \((1,i)\) in the characteristic-two division example. Explain why every ordinary compact-test trace is even in each parameter.

Exercise 7.40 — derivative modules, shifted support and repeated cuspidals.

  1. Let \(\rho_A,\rho_B,\rho_C\) be pairwise inequivalent unitary cuspidals of degrees \((2,1,2)\), respectively. List every quotient in the derivative filtrations of \(I=\rho_A\times\rho_B\times\rho_C\). Compute its exact mirabolic length and compare it with (6.691) and (6.822).
  2. For split \(G_3\), let \(I=1\times1\times1\) be normalized induction from the upper Borel. Decide irreducibility and compute all its derivative lengths and its mirabolic length. Specify whether the derivative filtrations are known to split.
  3. In degree two take the inducing \(P_1\)-module to be \(\mathbb C\). In (6.819), put \(F(\xi)=G(\xi)=\mathbf1_{\varpi^b\mathcal O^\times}(\xi)\). Compute the pairing and its simultaneous right-translation factor for \(a=\varpi^c\). Check both placements of \(\Delta_{P_2}\) relative to the smooth dual of \(\Psi_2^+1\).
  4. Compute the highest derivative of the trivial \(P_2\)-module. Apply (6.824) to its inclusion in \(i_B(\nu^{-1/2},\nu^{1/2})\). Explain why it gives no contradiction there, and why it is not a submodule of the opposite order.
  5. For general \(n,k\), identify the upper-right rectangle and the lower-right Whittaker roots in the derivative relation group. Compute the determinant exponent on \(G_{n-k}\). Partition the characters in \(\Omega_n\) by their rightmost zero and derive \(F_s=\sum_{t=1}^s\binom stF_{s-t}\), with \(F_0=1\), from (6.820).

Exercise 7.41 — orbit maps, normalized derivatives and the compact socle.

  1. For the restriction of \(\rho\times\sigma\) from \(G_4\), with both ranks two, write the open permutation in (6.831), its stabilizer in \(P_4\), and its source covariance. Isolate the extra factor in (6.827). Evaluate that covariance at the \(P_2\)-element \(\operatorname{diag}(\varpi,1)\) and the middle \(G_2\)-element \(\varpi I_2\).
  2. For \(\tau\diamond\rho\) with ranks \(m=3,k=2\), compute every factor of the normalized derivative map on the closed orbit when \(A=B=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi,1)\). On the open orbit take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(\varpi,1)\in P_2\) and \(B=\varpi I_2\). Check the two final covariances against (6.835).
  3. Over \(\mathbb F_q\), exhibit a nonzero submodule contradicting the support test of Lemma 6.347 outside its local-field hypotheses. Over \(\mathbb F_2\), explain why the two-dimensional sum-zero module of \(G_2(\mathbb F_2)\simeq S_3\) cannot have a faithful restriction Whittaker map on \(P_2(\mathbb F_2)\).
  4. Determine the mirabolic lengths of \(I_-,I_+\) and Steinberg in (6.847). Determine the kernel of their Whittaker restriction maps, and locate the compact simple socle inside the latter two modules.
  5. Verify every length in (6.848) and produce a nonzero degenerate submodule of \(\nu\times\nu^{-1}\times1\). Explain why this does not assert a general converse reducibility criterion.
  6. Put \(S=\operatorname{cInd}_{U_2}^{P_2}\theta_2\), \(T=\mathrm{St}|_{P_2}\), \(A=I_+|_{P_2}\). Determine all nine dimensions \(\dim\operatorname{Hom}_{P_2}(X,Y)\), for \(X,Y\in\{S,T,A\}\).

Exercise 7.42 — signatures, adjacent twists and support components.

  1. For the local matrix construction in Lemma 6.353, explain why finitely many equations suffice near one parameter even when no finite presentation of the corner algebra has been given. Include the case \(\dim E=1\), and explain why a global indefinite form cannot restrict degenerately to a compact fixed space.
  2. In Example 6.359 take \(q=4\). Compute \(H_s\), its two eigenvalues and rank at \(s=-1,-1/2,0,1/2,1\). Identify the two endpoint radicals and compute the spherical trace margin at these five parameters. Explain why a zero endpoint margin permits reducibility but does not prove it by itself.
  3. Suppose an actual compact trace on a common fixed space is \(p(q^s)=q^{2s}+3+q^{-s}\). Give an explicit inequality in \(s\) that contradicts the unitary bound with fixed-space dimension \(D\) and test norm \(L>0\). Explain why an arbitrary normalization of invariant positive forms cannot change that conclusion. Describe precisely how trace separation supplies a nonconstant polynomial in Theorem 6.355.
  4. For a cuspidal \(\rho\) of rank \(r\), identify the exact Jacquet modules, genericity, kernels and images in the two sequences (6.859). Describe which nonzero map between the two inductions has generic image. Explain why identical composition factors do not make those inductions isomorphic.
  5. Let \(\rho\) have rank \(r\) and let the exact data be \(\{\rho,\nu\rho,\nu\rho,\nu^3\rho,\nu^4\rho\}\). Determine the support components and the ranks of their generic factors. Prove that the generic representation with the full data is not a discrete series, retaining the repeated label. State the obstruction to drawing the same conclusion from connectedness alone.
  6. For \(m\ge2\), show that the generic representation with data \(\{\rho\}^m\) is irreducible induction and is not a discrete series, although its support graph is connected. More generally, explain why an argument using only zero trace on the whole adjacent induction cannot isolate its generic constituent. Use the rank-two Euler traces as an explicit example.

Exercise 7.43 — actual segment projections and coefficient exponents.

  1. In Lemma 6.360 take \(q=2,r=1,a=0,b=2\). List the central eigenvalue (6.870) for each permutation. Give the polynomial projection onto the component 210, and list the components of \(r_RJ_1\), \(r_RJ_2\), and their intersection. Explain why this remains a statement about actual modules when their vector spaces are infinite-dimensional.
  2. Let \(\rho\) have rank two. Compute \(r_{(4,2,2)}S[-1,2]\), every positive derivative, and its exact mirabolic length. Determine \(r_{(3,5)}S[-1,2]\). Retain all twists and indicate where an identification uses a chosen Whittaker line.
  3. For \(\operatorname{St}_3(\rho_0)\) with \(\rho_0\) unitary of rank two, calculate every maximal Jacquet cut, its normalized scalar modulus, the unnormalized stable Hecke eigenvalue modulus and its half-modulus. Give numerical values when \(q=2\).
  4. Derive the sharp \(L^p\) inequality for a general centred segment with \(s\ge2\). In the preceding rank-six example evaluate the expression in (6.881) at \(p=1,4/3,3/2,2\), including the equality case. Explain why a nilpotent part of a compact Hecke matrix does not alter the criterion.
  5. Let an irreducible admissible smooth module of unitary central character have all algebraic coefficients in \(L^2\). Prove directly that (6.887) gives a positive invariant norm, that its completion has exactly the original smooth module, and that one of its nonzero \(L^2\) coefficients becomes a Hilbert coefficient. Identify the separate roles of irreducibility and admissibility.
  6. If \(\rho=\nu^{3/4}\rho_0\) with \(\rho_0\) unitary of rank two, write \(S[-2,1]\) as an exact real determinant twist of a unitary discrete series. Determine whether \(S[-2,1]\) is unitary and compute its central absolute value at a scalar uniformizer.

Exercise 7.44 — unlinked intervals and generic trace isolation.

  1. On one exact cuspidal orbit the multiplicities at consecutive exponents \(-2,-1,0,1,2\) are \(1,3,2,3,1\). Find every height interval and its multiplicity. Check all pairs for linkage, recover the data and factor the corresponding generic representation. Explain why no different unlinked segment family gives the same data.

  2. Give a complete endpoint proof of Lemma 6.370 for intervals on \(\mathbb Z\), allowing empty selected tails and heads. Explain why the hypothesis of at least one nonempty suffix cannot be omitted. Describe exactly how the \(\nu\)-twist of the dual derivative yields original prefixes in (6.893).

  3. Let \(\rho_0\) be unitary cuspidal of rank \(r\). For exact multiplicities \(1,2,1\) at exponents \(-1,0,1\), identify the generic representation, prove it irreducible, and show that it is not a discrete series. State what its compact discrete-test trace is at every compatible central character.

  4. For \(G_2\), take \(\tau=\nu\times\nu^{-1}\), where the factors are characters of \(F^\times\). Prove that it is irreducible and generic with trivial central character, and prove directly from a spherical trace that it is not unitarizable. Compute its trace on \(f_{\mathrm{St},m}\). Contrast this with the generic constituent of the reducible induction \(\nu^{1/2}\times\nu^{-1/2}\).

  5. Explain the exact uses of local genericity, the discrete series' own compact test, and generic uniqueness in Theorems 6.373–6.374. Explain which additional assertions are still needed to derive an exact global prescribed-discrete-series globalization or an individual integral Jacquet–Langlands representation transfer.

  6. Apply Corollary 6.375 to the linked intervals \([0,2]\), \([1,3]\). Give the derivative index and its distinguishing irreducible quotient. Prove reducibility of the three-factor product with intervals \([0,1],[4,4],[1,2]\), using actual unlinked exchanges to make a linked pair adjacent.

Exercise 7.45 — rational-function support and the weighted trace. Over \(K=\mathbb F_q(t)\), put depth one at \(0\) and \(\infty\) and depth zero elsewhere. For \(n=2,q=2\), compute the normalized profiles permitted by cuspidality and the resulting dimension bound. For \(n=3,e=3\), list all permitted profiles. Check the reduction of (6.905) in characteristic two. For an abstract two-coset compatible kernel, take \(\operatorname{vol}(\overline J)=1\), arithmetic stabilizer orders \(2,3\), and kernel matrix \(\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}4&6\\6&9\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\). Compute its orthonormal matrix, rank, trace and nonzero eigenvalue. Explain exactly which additional hypotheses allow a nonzero trace to prescribe local discrete-series factors, and whether either dimension bound asserts existence of a cusp form.

Exercise 7.46 — a zero-trace class in characteristic three. Let \(K=\mathbb F_3(t)\), \(n=3\), \(\theta^3-\theta-1=0\), and \(h=(t/(t^2+1))^M\), \(M\ge1\). Compute the characteristic polynomial of \(\gamma=1+h\theta\) and its nonzero coefficient indices. Show that \(\gamma\) approaches the identity at \(0\) and \(\infty\) as \(M\) increases, and that \(t^2+1\) gives an available elliptic separating place. Recover a local proportionality scalar using its two nonzero coefficient ratios. What is the constant-extension factorization at a place of degree three? Finally take the prescribed representation at \(0\) to be \(\mathrm{St}_3\), and suppose the given strong auxiliary test at \(\infty\) has identity value \(2\). Compute their near-identity orbital product and express the resulting nonzero global trace using the torus volume and the other positive orbital factors. State which inputs this calculation assumes.

Exercise 7.47 — a characteristic-two auxiliary and its central character. Over \(F=\mathbb F_2((\varpi))\), take \(B=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\) and \(S=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\). Construct explicitly the depth-one two-dimensional type of Lemma 6.392 by making its constant \(B\)-action trivial. Prove its irreducibility. Compute the \(K_1\)- and \(K_2\)-fixed dimensions of its compact induction, its formal degree, and its ratio to the Steinberg degree. Find its central unit character. Over \(\mathbb F_2((u))\), use the group \((1+u\mathbb F_2[[u]])/(1+u^3\mathbb F_2[[u]])\) to give a determinant twist with trivial central unit character. Why is the corresponding torsion check different over \(\mathbb Q_2\)? Finally take trivial global central character over \(\mathbb F_2(t)\), prescribe \(\mathrm{St}_2\) at \(0\) and \(1\), and use a unit-vector coefficient of this trivial-centre auxiliary at infinity. Compute the orbital product near the common constant-field elliptic class and its nonzero trace, leaving the torus volume and other positive orbital factors explicit. Does this assert an automorphic representation unramified at every other place?

Exercise 7.48 — bounded norm-one sets and a projective stabilizer. (a) In \(\mathbb A_{\mathbb F_2(t)}\), let \(C_v=\mathcal O_v\) at finite places and \(C_\infty=u^{-2}\mathbb F_2[[u]]\), with \(u=t^{-1}\). List all valuation vectors of norm-one idèles in \(C\). (b) Do the same for \([-4,4]\times\prod_p\mathbb Z_p\subset\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q}\), including the real component. (c) Replace the one-dimensional function-field algebra in (a) by \(M_2\), take the analogous matrix box with \(u^{-M}\) at infinity, and let \(g_\infty=\operatorname{diag}(u^R,u^{-R})\), \(g_v=I\) at finite places. For \(R>M\ge0\), determine the rank of every nonzero rational matrix in \(gC\). Explain the division hypothesis in Theorem 6.410. (d) In the rational Hamilton quaternion algebra, compute \(e_i\) in (6.981). Compute also the additive Jacobian of left multiplication by \(\operatorname{diag}(2,3)\) on \(M_2(\mathbb A_{\mathbb Q})\) at the real place.

Exercise 7.49 — an explicit degree-six global algebra in characteristic two. (a) Prove that \(P=t^5+t^2+1\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb F_2\). Use Theorem 6.418 with \(n=6,r=3,d=2,a=1\) to write \(A(t)\) and compute every nonsplit local invariant, matrix size and the infinity completion. (b) At a place of degree two, describe the constant tensor algebra and the corner (6.985). (c) Let \(\theta\in\mathbb F_4\subset\mathbb F_{64}\) satisfy \(\theta^2+\theta+1=0\). Compute its absolute trace, the polynomial \(N_{\mathbb F_{64}/\mathbb F_2}(1+\theta X)\), and the first correction to the infinity unit in (a). Explain why a scalar sixth-root argument would be insufficient. (d) Compute the local elliptic sign product. At a good place where a regular polynomial factors into distinct residual degrees two and four, describe all stable lattices and their normalized orbital contribution.

Solution 7.1. Let \(\sigma\) be the nontrivial automorphism, \(t=\xi+\sigma\xi\), and \(n=\xi\sigma\xi\). The reduction of \(T^2-tT+n\) is irreducible and separable, so its lift is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q_p\). In the cyclic model \[ D_p=K\oplus K\Pi,\qquad \Pi^2=p,\qquad \Pi a=\sigma(a)\Pi, \] the element \(\xi\) has that reduced polynomial. The matching matrix is \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&-n\\1&t\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the matrix of multiplication by \(\xi\) on \(K\) in the basis \(1,\xi\). Its centralizer is the multiplication copy of \(K^\times\); the quaternion centralizer is also \(K^\times\), by Theorem 1.1. Conjugation by \(\Pi\) exchanges \(\xi\) and \(\sigma\xi\), so either root defines the same class. This remains valid at \(p=2\), because unramified residue extensions are separable.

Exercise 7.2 — check the Steinberg character. Verify (2.3) for the trivial representation of \(D^\times\) and the Steinberg representation of \(G\), including an unramified unitary character twist.

Solution 7.2. An elliptic matrix has no invariant \(F\)-line. Proposition 2.2 consequently gives zero character for \(C^\infty(\mathbb P^1(F))\) on the elliptic regular set. Subtracting the character one of its constant subrepresentation gives \(\Theta_{\mathrm{St}}=-1\). The trivial quaternion character is one, proving the required minus sign. Under a twist, the left side becomes \(-\chi(\det g)\), while the quaternion side becomes \(\chi(\operatorname{nrd}b)\). The determinants and norms match by Theorem 1.1, so the negative relation persists. The central characters are both \(\chi(z^2)\). The same computation in fact works for any quasicharacter; unitarity only ensures that the twist belongs to the discrete-series set in (2.2).

Exercise 7.3 — three dimensions. Evaluate both sides of (4.3) for \(p=11,13,37\), showing the mass and elliptic corrections.

Solution 7.3. The complete substitutions are:

\(p\) \((s_4,s_3)\) mass \((p-1)/12\) class-number corrections \(h\) genus \((p+1)/12-e_2/4-e_3/3\)
11 \((-1,-1)\) \(5/6\) \(1/2+2/3\) 2 \(1-0-0=1\)
